title: Vector Calculus
text:
(adapted from Fieller [1], Section 7.2)
This section covers derivatives of functions of vectors and matrices. Its linear algebra prerequisites, such as vectors, matrices, transposes, dot products, and quadratic forms, are covered in Linear Algebra.
Let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\) be column vectors of length \(p\) (see column vector and dot product).

title: Vector Calculus
section: 1 Checking a gradient by its shape
text:
1 Checking a gradient by its shape
The gradient always has the same shape as the input it is taken with respect to, because it holds exactly one partial derivative per component of that input:








Table 1: The shape of a gradient follows the shape of what it differentiates with respect to.








\(f\) is a function of
its gradient is



a single number
a single number — the ordinary derivative


a vector in \(\mathbb{R}^p\)

a vector in \(\mathbb{R}^p\)



a matrix in \(\mathbb{R}^{m \times n}\)

a matrix in \(\mathbb{R}^{m \times n}\)










The table is the cheapest check there is on a gradient just worked out by hand: if the shapes disagree, something went wrong. It is the shape rule of matrix multiplication again, applied to calculus.






DefDefinition 3 (Direction)






Definition 3 (Direction) A direction in \(\mathbb{R}^p\) is given by a nonzero vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}} \in \mathbb{R}^p\): moving from a point \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) in the direction \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}}\) means moving to the points \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}+ t \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}}\) with \(t > 0\). For any \(c > 0\), \(c \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}}\) reaches the same points (with \(t / c\) in place of \(t\)), so \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}}\) and \(c \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}}\) give the same direction.










ExmExample 3 (Moving from \({(2, -1)}^{\top}\) in the direction \({(1, 1)}^{\top}\))






Example 3 (Moving from \({(2, -1)}^{\top}\) in the direction \({(1, 1)}^{\top}\)) From \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= {(2, -1)}^{\top}\), moving in the direction \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}} = {(1, 1)}^{\top}\) reaches the points \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}+ t \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}} = {(2 + t,\ -1 + t)}^{\top}\) for \(t > 0\), such as \({(3, 0)}^{\top}\) at \(t = 1\). The vector \({(2, 2)}^{\top}\) gives the same direction: it reaches \({(3, 0)}^{\top}\) at \(t = \tfrac{1}{2}\). The vector \({(-1, -1)}^{\top}\) gives the opposite direction, reaching points such as \({(1, -2)}^{\top}\).










DefDefinition 4 (Level set)






Definition 4 (Level set) Let \(f : \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}\) and let \(c\) be a real number. The level set [6] of \(f\) at \(c\) is
\[
\mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\in \mathbb{R}^p : f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = c\right\}\mathclose{},
\]
the set of points where \(f\) takes the value \(c\). It is the preimage of \(\mathopen{}\left\{c\right\}\mathclose{}\) under \(f\), so we write it \({{{f}^{-1}\mathopen{}\left(\mathopen{}\left\{c\right\}\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}}}\). For \(p = 2\), a level set is often a curve in the plane.










ExmExample 4 (Level sets of \(x_1^2 + x_2^2\))






Example 4 (Level sets of \(x_1^2 + x_2^2\)) Let \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = x_1^2 + x_2^2\) for \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= {(x_1, x_2)}^{\top}\).

The level set at \(1\) is the circle of radius \(1\) around \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\). For example, \({(0.6, 0.8)}^{\top}\) is on it, since \(0.36 + 0.64 = 1\), and \({(1, 1)}^{\top}\) is not, since \(1 + 1 = 2\).
The level set at \(0\) is the single point \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\).
The level set at \(-1\) is empty, since \(x_1^2 + x_2^2 \ge 0\).











DefDefinition 5 (Level curve)






Definition 5 (Level curve) Let \(f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}\) and let \(c\) be a real number. The level curve of \(f\) at \(c\) is the level set of \(f\) at \(c\) when it is a curve in the plane. It is the special case \(p = 2\) of a level set. A contour line is a level curve drawn on a plot of \(f\).










ExmExample 5 (A level curve of \(x_1^2 + x_2^2\))






Example 5 (A level curve of \(x_1^2 + x_2^2\)) Let \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = x_1^2 + x_2^2\) for \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= {(x_1, x_2)}^{\top}\). The level curve at \(4\) is the circle of radius \(2\) around \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\).










LemTheorem 2 (Level sets of a linear function)






Theorem 2 (Level sets of a linear function) Let \({h\mathopen{}\left(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\right)\mathclose{}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} + \beta_{0}\) with \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\neq \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\). Every level set \({{{h}^{-1}\mathopen{}\left(\mathopen{}\left\{c\right\}\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}}}\) is a hyperplane with normal vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\), parallel to the level set \({{{h}^{-1}\mathopen{}\left(\mathopen{}\left\{0\right\}\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}}}\). Its dimension is \(p - 1\): a point for \(p = 1\), a line for \(p = 2\), and a two-dimensional plane for \(p = 3\).










ProofProof






Proof. For any \(c\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
{{{h}^{-1}\mathopen{}\left(\mathopen{}\left\{c\right\}\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}}}
&= {\mathopen{}\left\{ \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}: \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} + \beta_{0}= c \right\}\mathclose{}} \\
&= {\mathopen{}\left\{ \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}: \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} + (\beta_{0}- c) = 0 \right\}\mathclose{}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is the hyperplane with normal vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\) and offset \(\beta_{0}- c\). Changing \(c\) changes only the offset, so the level sets share the normal vector and are parallel. A hyperplane in \(\mathbb{R}^p\) has dimension \(p - 1\) by the hyperplane theorem, which gives the point, line and plane cases for \(p = 1, 2, 3\).










ExmExample 6 (Parallel level lines)






Example 6 (Parallel level lines) Let \({h\mathopen{}\left(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\right)\mathclose{}} = 2x_1 + x_2 + 1\), so \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}= {(2, 1)}^{\top}\) and \(\beta_{0}= 1\). The level set at \(c\) is the line \(x_2 = c - 1 - 2x_1\). For \(c = -1, 0, 1\) the lines are \(x_2 = -2 - 2x_1\), \(x_2 = -1 - 2x_1\) and \(x_2 = -2x_1\). They all have slope \(-2\) and differ only in the intercept, so they are parallel.










LemTheorem 3 (Stepping along the normal vector)






Theorem 3 (Stepping along the normal vector) Let \({h\mathopen{}\left(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\right)\mathclose{}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} + \beta_{0}\) with \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\neq \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\). For every \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\in \mathbb{R}^p\) and \(t \in \mathbb{R}\),
\[
{h\mathopen{}\left(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}+ t\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\right)\mathclose{}} = {h\mathopen{}\left(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\right)\mathclose{}} + t{\mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\right\rVert\mathclose{}}^2.
\]
So a step along \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\) with \(t > 0\) increases \(h\).










ProofProof






Proof. By linearity of the dot product,
\[
\begin{aligned}
{h\mathopen{}\left(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}+ t\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\right)\mathclose{}}
&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}+ t\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}} + \beta_{0}\\
&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} + t\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}} + \beta_{0}\\
&= {h\mathopen{}\left(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\right)\mathclose{}} + t{\mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\right\rVert\mathclose{}}^2.
\end{aligned}
\]










ExmExample 7 (A step along the normal vector)






Example 7 (A step along the normal vector) Let \({h\mathopen{}\left(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\right)\mathclose{}} = 2x_1 + x_2 + 1\), so \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}= {(2, 1)}^{\top}\) and \({\mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\right\rVert\mathclose{}}^2 = 5\). At \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\), \({h\mathopen{}\left(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\right)\mathclose{}} = 1\). A step of \(t = 1\) along \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\) lands at \({(2, 1)}^{\top}\), where \({h\mathopen{}\left({(2, 1)}^{\top}\right)\mathclose{}} = 4 + 1 + 1 = 6 = 1 + 5\).










LemTheorem 4 (The normal vector is the steepest direction)






Theorem 4 (The normal vector is the steepest direction) Let \({h\mathopen{}\left(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\right)\mathclose{}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} + \beta_{0}\) with \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\neq \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\). Among unit vectors \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}\) (\(\mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}\right\rVert\mathclose{} = 1\)), the change \({h\mathopen{}\left(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}+ t\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}\right)\mathclose{}} - {h\mathopen{}\left(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\right)\mathclose{}}\) with \(t > 0\) is largest for \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}/ \mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\right\rVert\mathclose{}\).










ProofProof






Proof. For a unit vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}\),
\[
{h\mathopen{}\left(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}+ t\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}\right)\mathclose{}} - {h\mathopen{}\left(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\right)\mathclose{}} = t\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}.
\]
Since \(t > 0\), maximizing this change is the same as maximizing \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}\). By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} \le \mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\right\rVert\mathclose{}\mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}\right\rVert\mathclose{} = \mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\right\rVert\mathclose{}\). Equality holds exactly when \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}= \alpha\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\) for some \(\alpha > 0\). The condition \(\mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}\right\rVert\mathclose{} = 1\) then forces \(\alpha\mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\right\rVert\mathclose{} = 1\), so
\[
\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}/ \mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\right\rVert\mathclose{}.
\]










ExmExample 8 (Two unit steps compared)






Example 8 (Two unit steps compared) Let \({h\mathopen{}\left(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\right)\mathclose{}} = 2x_1 + x_2 + 1\), so \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}= {(2, 1)}^{\top}\) and \(\mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\right\rVert\mathclose{} = \sqrt{5}\). A step of size \(1\) along the unit vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}/ \sqrt{5}\) raises \(h\) by \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}} / \sqrt{5} = \sqrt{5} \approx 2.24\). A step of size \(1\) along \({(1, 0)}^{\top}\) raises it by only \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}} \cdot {(1, 0)}^{\top} = 2\).





Show R codegradFns = ({
  "3 w1 w2 + w2^3 - 5 w1": {
    f: (a, b) => 3 * a * b + b ** 3 - 5 * a,
    grad: (a, b) => [3 * b - 5, 3 * a + 3 * b * b]
  },
  "w1^2 + 4 w2^2": {
    f: (a, b) => a * a + 4 * b * b,
    grad: (a, b) => [2 * a, 8 * b]
  }
})
gradDeg = (rad) => ((rad * 180 / Math.PI) % 360 + 360) % 360
// The chosen function, and its gradient at the chosen point.
gradF = gradFns[gradWhich].f
gradG = gradFns[gradWhich].grad(gradW1, gradW2)
gradLen = Math.hypot(...gradG)
gradPhi = gradDeg(Math.atan2(gradG[1], gradG[0]))
// The rate f changes at, per unit step in direction deg: the gradient dotted with that direction.
gradRate = (deg) => gradG[0] * Math.cos(deg * Math.PI / 180) + gradG[1] * Math.sin(deg * Math.PI / 180)


















































Turn the blue arrow in Figure 1 and watch the rate: it is largest along the red arrow, zero along the black level curve (Definition 4), and most negative pointing straight back. Then look for a point where the red arrow shrinks to nothing.

viewof gradW1 = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: 2, step: 0.05, label: "w1"})
viewof gradW2 = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: -1, step: 0.05, label: "w2"})

Show R code{
  const f2 = (v) => v.toFixed(2);
  const deg = "\u00b0";
  return md`f(w) = ${f2(gradF(gradW1, gradW2))};
gradient (${f2(gradG[0])}, ${f2(gradG[1])}), length ${f2(gradLen)}, at ${gradPhi.toFixed(0)}${deg}.
Along the blue arrow, f changes at rate ${f2(gradRate(gradTheta))} per unit step,
${(gradRate(gradTheta) / (gradLen || 1) * 100).toFixed(0)}% of the steepest rate.`;
}
Show R code{
  const u = [Math.cos(gradTheta * Math.PI / 180), Math.sin(gradTheta * Math.PI / 180)];
  const g = gradLen > 1e-9 ? gradG.map((v) => v / gradLen) : [0, 0];
  return Plot.plot({
    ariaLabel: 'Contour map of f over w1 and w2, ' +
      'with the chosen point, ' +

    width: 310, height: 310, marginLeft: 40,

      Plot.contour({x1: -3.5, y1: -3.5, x2: 3.5, y2: 3.5, value: gradF, clip: true,
                    thresholds: [gradF(gradW1, gradW2)], stroke: "#222", strokeWidth: 2}),
      Plot.arrow([0], {x1: gradW1, y1: gradW2, x2: gradW1 + u[0], y2: gradW2 + u[1],
                       stroke: "#1f77b4", strokeWidth: 2.5, clip: true}),
      Plot.arrow([0], {x1: gradW1, y1: gradW2, x2: gradW1 + g[0], y2: gradW2 + g[1],
                       stroke: "#d62728", strokeWidth: 3, clip: true}),
      Plot.dot([0], {x: gradW1, y: gradW2, r: 5, fill: "#222"})
    ]

}
Show R codePlot.plot({
  ariaLabel: 'The rate at which f changes when stepping from the chosen point, ' +
