})


Figure 1: A gradient explorer: the red arrow points along the gradient at the chosen point, and the blue arrow along the chosen step direction (Definition 3).







































































ExrExercise 5 (Take a gradient by hand)






Exercise 5 (Take a gradient by hand) Let \(f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}\) be
\[f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}) = 3 w_1 w_2 + w_2^3 - 5 w_1\]

Compute \(\partial f / \partial w_1\) (Definition 1), treating \(w_2\) as a constant.
Compute \(\partial f / \partial w_2\), treating \(w_1\) as a constant.
Assemble \(\nabla_{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}} f\) and evaluate it at \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}^{\top}\).
Check the shape of your answer against Table 1.











SolutionSolution 5






Solution 5. 1. Differentiate with respect to \(w_1\), holding \(w_2\) fixed. The first term is the constant \(3w_2\) times \(w_1\), so it contributes \(3w_2\). The second term has no \(w_1\) in it, so it contributes \(0\). The third term is \(-5\) times \(w_1\), so it contributes \(-5\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial f}{\partial w_1}
&= 3w_2 + 0 - 5 \\
&= 3w_2 - 5
\end{aligned}
\]
2. Now with respect to \(w_2\), holding \(w_1\) fixed. The first term is the constant \(3w_1\) times \(w_2\), contributing \(3w_1\). The second term contributes \(3w_2^2\). The third has no \(w_2\) in it, contributing \(0\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial f}{\partial w_2}
&= 3w_1 + 3w_2^2 + 0 \\
&= 3w_1 + 3w_2^2
\end{aligned}
\]
3. Stack the two, in the order the coordinates are numbered:
\[\nabla_{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}) = \begin{bmatrix} 3w_2 - 5 \\ 3w_1 + 3w_2^2 \end{bmatrix}\]
The gradient is a vector-valued function of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}\), not a single vector. At \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}^{\top}\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}} f
&= \begin{bmatrix} 3(-1) - 5 \\ 3(2) + 3(-1)^2 \end{bmatrix} \\
&= \begin{bmatrix} -3 - 5 \\ 6 + 3 \end{bmatrix} \\
&= \begin{bmatrix} -8 \\ 9 \end{bmatrix}
\end{aligned}
\]
4. The input was a vector in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) and so is the answer, as Table 1 requires. Note the signs: from this point, increasing \(w_1\) decreases \(f\) while increasing \(w_2\) increases it, so the uphill direction is neither axis.










DefDefinition 6 (Row-vector derivative)






Definition 6 (Row-vector derivative) If \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})\) is a scalar-valued function of a \(p \times 1\) vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\), such as \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}) = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\), then its row-vector derivative is the row vector of its partial derivatives (Definition 1):
\[
\frac{\partial f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})}{\partial {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}^{\top}} =
\begin{bmatrix}
\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{1}}f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}) &
\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{2}}f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}) &
\cdots &
\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{p}}f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})
\end{bmatrix}
\tag{1}\]
When the derivative of a scalar-valued function is written as a row vector, it is also called the total derivative [7] of \(f\).










RemarkRemark 1 (Other notation for the row-vector derivative)






Remark 1 (Other notation for the row-vector derivative). Some sources write the same row vector as \(\frac{\partial}{\partial {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}^{\top}} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})\), with the operator on the left, read as each operator \(\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{i}}\) applied to \(f\) rather than as a matrix product (see Remark 2).










RemarkRemark 2 (Which side the operator goes on)






Remark 2 (Which side the operator goes on). Read \(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}\) as a \(p \times 1\) column vector of operators with entries \(\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{1}}, \ldots, \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{p}}\), and \(\frac{\partial}{\partial {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}^{\top}}\) as the \(1 \times p\) row vector of operators with the same entries. Writing either one next to \(f\) can be read in two ways:


As a matrix product, with \(f\) a \(1 \times 1\) matrix, under the shape rule of matrix multiplication. The column-vector operator works on the left: \(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} f\) is \((p \times 1)(1 \times 1)\), a \(p \times 1\) column vector (Definition 2). The row-vector operator does not: \(\frac{\partial}{\partial {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}^{\top}} f\) is \((1 \times p)(1 \times 1)\), whose inner dimensions \(p\) and \(1\) do not match when \(p > 1\). For the shape rule to give the \(1 \times p\) row vector, the operator would have to go on the right of \(f\), as in \((1 \times 1)(1 \times p)\), which changes its meaning (see below).

As a scalar multiple, with \(f\) a scalar, the way \(c \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) is read in scalar multiplication, which has no shape rule: each entry of the operator vector is applied to \(f\). Then both \(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} f\) and \(\frac{\partial}{\partial {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}^{\top}} f\) work with the operator on the left.

The fraction \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}^{\top}}\) of Equation 1 means the same thing under both readings: the transpose in the denominator says the result is a row vector, without making the derivative a product.
Treating the operators as vectors is sound for checking shapes, but “multiplying” an operator by a function means applying the operator to it, so two rules of ordinary matrix algebra do not carry over: scalars commute with matrices, and products can be regrouped.


Scalars do not commute with operators. \(\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{i}} f\) is a function, but \(f \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{i}}\) is still an unapplied operator, waiting for something to act on. So, unlike \(c \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}c\), the operator cannot move to the other side of \(f\) without changing the meaning. Putting the row-vector operator on the right of \(f\) gives the row-vector derivative only under the convention that it acts on the factor to its left.

Products cannot be regrouped. An operator acts on the whole product to its right, so by the product rule, \(\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{i}} (f g) \ne \mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{i}} f\right)\mathclose{} g\) in general. For example, with \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}) = \beta_{1}\), \(\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{1}} (f f) = 2 \beta_{1}\) but \(\mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{1}} f\right)\mathclose{} f = \beta_{1}\).











LemTheorem 5 (Row and column derivatives are transposes)






Theorem 5 (Row and column derivatives are transposes) \[\frac{\partial f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})}{\partial {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}^{\top}} = {\mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}\right)\mathclose{}}^{\top} \tag{2}\]
\[\frac{\partial f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} = {\mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})}{\partial {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}^{\top}}\right)\mathclose{}}^{\top} \tag{3}\]










ProofProof






Proof. By Definition 2 and Definition 6, entry \(j\) of both \(\frac{\partial f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}\) and \(\frac{\partial f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})}{\partial {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}^{\top}}\) is \(\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{j}} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})\); the first is a \(p \times 1\) column vector and the second a \(1 \times p\) row vector with the same entries in the same order, so each is the transpose of the other.










ExmExample 9 (Row and column derivatives of a linear function)






Example 9 (Row and column derivatives of a linear function) For \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}) = 3\beta_{1} + 5\beta_{2}\):
\[
\frac{\partial f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} = \begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\frac{\partial f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})}{\partial {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}^{\top}} = \begin{bmatrix}3 & 5\end{bmatrix},
\]
and each is the transpose of the other.










DefDefinition 7 (Derivative of a vector-valued function)






Definition 7 (Derivative of a vector-valued function) If
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}) \\
&= {(y_1, \ldots, y_q)}^{\top}
\end{aligned}
\]
is a \(q \times 1\) vector-valued function of the \(p \times 1\) vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\), its derivative with respect to \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\) is the \(p \times q\) matrix whose \((i, j)\) entry is
\[
\mathopen{}\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}}^{\top}\right]\mathclose{}_{ij} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{i}} y_j,
\qquad i = 1, \ldots, p, \quad j = 1, \ldots, q.
\]
Both \(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\) and \(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}}^{\top}\) denote this \(p \times q\) matrix.










DefDefinition 8 (Denominator layout)






Definition 8 (Denominator layout) Writing derivatives as in Definition 7 is the denominator layout [8], which these notes use throughout: rows index the entries of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\) (the denominator) and columns index the entries of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\) (the numerator), so column \(j\) is the vector derivative \(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} y_j\) (Definition 2).










ExmExample 10 (Differentiating a \(3 \times 1\) function of a \(2 \times 1\) vector)






Example 10 (Differentiating a \(3 \times 1\) function of a \(2 \times 1\) vector) Let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}= {(\beta_{1}, \beta_{2})}^{\top}\) (\(p = 2\)) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}) = {(\beta_{1}^2,\ \beta_{1}\beta_{2},\ 3\beta_{2})}^{\top}\) (\(q = 3\)). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}}^{\top}}_{2 \times 3}
&= \begin{bmatrix}
\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{1}} \beta_{1}^2 & \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{1}} \beta_{1}\beta_{2} & \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{1}} 3\beta_{2} \\
\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{2}} \beta_{1}^2 & \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{2}} \beta_{1}\beta_{2} & \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{2}} 3\beta_{2}
\end{bmatrix} \\
&= \begin{bmatrix}
2\beta_{1} & \beta_{2} & 0 \\
0 & \beta_{1} & 3
\end{bmatrix}
\end{aligned}
\]










DefDefinition 9 (Jacobian matrix)






Definition 9 (Jacobian matrix) Let
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}) \\
&= {(y_1, \ldots, y_q)}^{\top}
\end{aligned}
\]
be a \(q \times 1\) vector-valued function of the \(p \times 1\) vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\). The Jacobian matrix [9] of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\) is the \(q \times p\) matrix whose \((j, i)\) entry is \(\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{i}} y_j\), for \(j = 1, \ldots, q\) and \(i = 1, \ldots, p\). It is the transpose of the derivative \(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}}^{\top}\) of Definition 7.










DefDefinition 10 (Numerator layout)






Definition 10 (Numerator layout) Writing derivatives as in Definition 9, with rows indexing the entries of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\) (the numerator) and columns indexing the entries of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\) (the denominator), is the numerator layout [8].










ExmExample 11 (The Jacobian matrix of a \(3 \times 1\) function of a \(2 \times 1\) vector)






Example 11 (The Jacobian matrix of a \(3 \times 1\) function of a \(2 \times 1\) vector) For \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}) = {(\beta_{1}^2,\ \beta_{1}\beta_{2},\ 3\beta_{2})}^{\top}\) of Example 10, the Jacobian matrix is the \(3 \times 2\) matrix
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{1}} \beta_{1}^2 & \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{2}} \beta_{1}^2 \\
\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{1}} \beta_{1}\beta_{2} & \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{2}} \beta_{1}\beta_{2} \\
\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{1}} 3\beta_{2} & \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{2}} 3\beta_{2}
\end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix}
2\beta_{1} & 0 \\
\beta_{2} & \beta_{1} \\
0 & 3
\end{bmatrix},
\]
the transpose of the \(2 \times 3\) matrix found there.










RemarkRemark 3 (Numerator layout)






Remark 3 (Numerator layout). Some sources use the numerator layout (Definition 10) throughout, so that their derivative of a vector-valued function is the Jacobian matrix, the transpose of the derivative used in these notes. In numerator layout, the derivative of a scalar-valued function is a row vector: the row-vector derivative (Definition 6). Check a source’s layout before combining its formulas with these.










DefDefinition 11 (Constant)






Definition 11 (Constant) A \(q \times 1\) vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) is constant with respect to the \(p \times 1\) vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\) if its derivative (Definition 7) is zero:
\[
\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top}}_{p \times q}
= \underbrace{\mathbf{0}}_{p \times q}
\]










ExmExample 12 (A constant vector)






Example 12 (A constant vector) Let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}= {(\beta_{1}, \beta_{2})}^{\top}\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= {(3, 5)}^{\top}\), so \(x_1 = 3\) and \(x_2 = 5\) do not depend on \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\). Expanding \(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top}\) into its matrix of scalar partial derivatives (Definition 7) and evaluating each entry:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top}}_{2 \times 2}
&= \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} \begin{bmatrix}x_1 & x_2\end{bmatrix} \\
&= \begin{bmatrix}
\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{1}} x_1 & \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{1}} x_2 \\
\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{2}} x_1 & \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{2}} x_2
\end{bmatrix} \\
&= \begin{bmatrix}
\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{1}} 3 & \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{1}} 5 \\
\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{2}} 3 & \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{2}} 5
\end{bmatrix} \\
&= \begin{bmatrix}
0 & 0 \\
0 & 0
\end{bmatrix} \\
&= \underbrace{\mathbf{0}}_{2 \times 2}
\end{aligned}
\]
Every entry is the derivative of a constant, so \(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top} = \underbrace{\mathbf{0}}_{2 \times 2}\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) is constant with respect to \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\) (Definition 11).










ExmExample 13 (A vector that is not constant)






Example 13 (A vector that is not constant) With the same \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\), let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= {(\beta_{1}, 3)}^{\top}\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top}}_{2 \times 2}
&= \begin{bmatrix}
\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{1}} \beta_{1} & \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{1}} 3 \\
\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{2}} \beta_{1} & \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{2}} 3
\end{bmatrix} \\
&= \begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 \\
0 & 0
\end{bmatrix},
\end{aligned}
\]
which is not \(\underbrace{\mathbf{0}}_{2 \times 2}\), so this \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) is not constant with respect to \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\): its first entry changes when \(\beta_{1}\) does.










ExrExercise 6 (Partial derivative with respect to an unreferenced variable)






Exercise 6 (Partial derivative with respect to an unreferenced variable) Adapted from Miller [3], Question 1.1.46.
Find \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\) and \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\) for
\[f(x, y, t) = 5t^4 - 4t^5 \cos(t\sin t)\]










SolutionSolution 6






Solution 6. Although the function is declared as a function of three variables \((x, y, t)\), its expression depends solely on \(t\).
Because neither \(x\) nor \(y\) appears in the formula, \(f\) is constant with respect to both \(x\) and \(y\):
\[\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 0, \qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = 0\]
Remark: Always verify which variables actually appear in a formula before performing lengthy algebraic differentiation.










LemTheorem 6 (Derivative of a dot product)






Theorem 6 (Derivative of a dot product) If \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) is constant with respect to \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\), then:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})}_{p \times 1}
&=
\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})}_{p \times 1} \\
&=
\underbrace{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}_{p \times 1}
\end{aligned}
\]










ProofProof






Proof. \[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})
&=
\begin{bmatrix}
\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{1}}(x_1\beta_{1}+x_2\beta_{2} +...+x_p \beta_{p} ) \\
\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{2}}(x_1\beta_{1}+x_2\beta_{2} +...+x_p \beta_{p} ) \\
\vdots \\
\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{p}}(x_1\beta_{1}+x_2\beta_{2} +...+x_p \beta_{p} )
\end{bmatrix}
\\ &=
\begin{bmatrix}
x_{1} \\
x_{2} \\
\vdots \\
x_{p}
\end{bmatrix}
\\ &= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExmExample 14 (Derivative of a dot product)






Example 14 (Derivative of a dot product) Let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= {(3, 5)}^{\top}\) (constant with respect to \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\); see Example 12) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}= {(\beta_{1}, \beta_{2})}^{\top}\). Then \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}= 3\beta_{1} + 5\beta_{2}\), and by Theorem 6:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})}_{2 \times 1}
&= \underbrace{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}_{2 \times 1} \\
&= \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\
5 \end{pmatrix}
\end{aligned}
\]
Verifying entry-wise:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}(3\beta_{1} + 5\beta_{2})
&= \begin{pmatrix} \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{1}}(3\beta_{1} + 5\beta_{2}) \\
\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{2}}(3\beta_{1} + 5\beta_{2}) \end{pmatrix} \\
&= \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\
5 \end{pmatrix}
\end{aligned}
\]
Both methods agree.










LemTheorem 7 (Product rule for dot-products)






Theorem 7 (Product rule for dot-products) If \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\) are differentiable \(p \times 1\) vector functions of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\), then:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial \underbrace{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}_{p \times 1}} \underbrace{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}}_{p \times 1} \cdot \underbrace{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}}_{p \times 1}
&=
\mathopen{}\left(
    \frac{\partial}{\partial \underbrace{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}_{p \times 1}} \underbrace{{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}}^{\top}}_{1 \times p}
  \right)\mathclose{}
\underbrace{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}}_{p \times 1}
+
\mathopen{}\left(
  \frac{\partial}{\partial \underbrace{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}_{p \times 1}} \underbrace{{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}}^{\top}}_{1 \times p}
\right)\mathclose{}
\underbrace{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}}_{p \times 1}
\end{aligned}
\]










ProofProof






Proof. Entry-wise, for \(i = 1, \ldots, p\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathopen{}\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}})\right]\mathclose{}_i
&= \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i} \sum_{k=1}^{p} a_k b_k \\
&= \sum_{k=1}^{p} \mathopen{}\left(b_k \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i} a_k + a_k \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i} b_k\right)\mathclose{} \\
&= \mathopen{}\left[\mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}}^{\top}\right)\mathclose{}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\right]\mathclose{}_i
  + \mathopen{}\left[\mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}}^{\top}\right)\mathclose{}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}\right]\mathclose{}_i
\end{aligned}
\]










ExmExample 15 (Example of the dot-product rule)






Example 15 (Example of the dot-product rule) Apply Theorem 7 with the vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}= {(\beta_{1}, \beta_{2})}^{\top}\) in the role of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\). Let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}) = {(\beta_{1}, \beta_{1}\beta_{2})}^{\top}\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}) = {(\beta_{2}, \beta_{1})}^{\top}\). Then:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}
&= \beta_{1} \cdot \beta_{2} + \beta_{1}\beta_{2} \cdot \beta_{1} \\
&= \beta_{1}\beta_{2} + \beta_{1}^2\beta_{2}
\end{aligned}
\]
By direct calculation:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}})}_{2 \times 1}
&= \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}(\beta_{1}\beta_{2} + \beta_{1}^2\beta_{2}) \\
&= \begin{pmatrix} \beta_{2} + 2\beta_{1}\beta_{2} \\ \beta_{1} + \beta_{1}^2 \end{pmatrix}
\end{aligned}
\]
By the product rule (Theorem 7), using \(\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}}^{\top}}_{2 \times 2}
= \begin{pmatrix}1 & \beta_{2} \\ 0 & \beta_{1}\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}}^{\top}}_{2 \times 2}
= \begin{pmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}})}_{2 \times 1}
&=
\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}1 & \beta_{2} \\ 0 & \beta_{1}\end{pmatrix}}_{2 \times 2}
\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}\beta_{2} \\ \beta_{1}\end{pmatrix}}_{2 \times 1}
+
\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}}_{2 \times 2}
\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}\beta_{1} \\ \beta_{1}\beta_{2}\end{pmatrix}}_{2 \times 1}
\\
&=
\begin{pmatrix}\beta_{2} + \beta_{1}\beta_{2} \\ \beta_{1}^2\end{pmatrix}
+
\begin{pmatrix}\beta_{1}\beta_{2} \\ \beta_{1}\end{pmatrix}
\\
&=
\begin{pmatrix}\beta_{2} + 2\beta_{1}\beta_{2} \\ \beta_{1}^2 + \beta_{1}\end{pmatrix}
\end{aligned}
\]
Both methods agree.










LemTheorem 8 (Derivative of a linear map)






Theorem 8 (Derivative of a linear map) If \(\mathbf{A}\) is an \(m \times p\) matrix that is constant with respect to \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\), then:
\[
\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} (\mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})}_{p \times m} =
\underbrace{{\mathbf{A}}^{\top}}_{p \times m}
\]










ProofProof






Proof. For entry \((i,j)\), where row \(i\) indexes the denominator \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\) (see Definition 7) and column \(j\) indexes the numerator \(\mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathopen{}\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} (\mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})\right]\mathclose{}_{ij}
&= \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{i}} (\mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})_j \\
&= \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{i}} \sum_{k=1}^{p} a_{jk} \beta_{k} \\
&= a_{ji} \\
&= \mathopen{}\left[{\mathbf{A}}^{\top}\right]\mathclose{}_{ij}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExmExample 16 (Derivative of a linear map)






Example 16 (Derivative of a linear map) Let \(\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\) (\(1 \times 2\)) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}= {(\beta_{1}, \beta_{2})}^{\top}\). Then \(\mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}= 2\beta_{1} + 3\beta_{2}\), and by Theorem 8:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}(\mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})}_{2 \times 1}
&= \underbrace{{\mathbf{A}}^{\top}}_{2 \times 1} \\
&= \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\
3 \end{pmatrix}
\end{aligned}
\]










LemTheorem 9 (Vector-derivative of a matrix-vector product)






Theorem 9 (Vector-derivative of a matrix-vector product) If \(\mathbf{A}\) is an \(m \times q\) matrix that is constant with respect to \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\), and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})\) is a \(q \times 1\) vector that depends on the \(p \times 1\) vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\), then:
\[
\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} (\mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}})}_{p \times m} =
\underbrace{\mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\right)\mathclose{}}_{p \times q}
\underbrace{{\mathbf{A}}^{\top}}_{q \times m}
\]










ProofProof






Proof. For entry \((i,j)\), where row \(i\) indexes the denominator \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\) and column \(j\) indexes the numerator \(\mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\) (see Definition 7):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathopen{}\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} (\mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}})\right]\mathclose{}_{ij}
&= \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{i}} (\mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}})_j \\
&= \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{i}} \sum_{k=1}^{q} a_{jk} v_k \\
&= \sum_{k=1}^{q} a_{jk} \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{i}} v_k \\
&= \sum_{k=1}^{q} \mathopen{}\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\right]\mathclose{}_{ik} \mathopen{}\left[{\mathbf{A}}^{\top}\right]\mathclose{}_{kj} \\
&= \mathopen{}\left[\mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\right)\mathclose{} {\mathbf{A}}^{\top}\right]\mathclose{}_{ij}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExmExample 17 (Vector-derivative of a matrix-vector product)






Example 17 (Vector-derivative of a matrix-vector product) Let \(\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\) (\(1 \times 2\), constant) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}) = {(\beta_{1}^2, \beta_{2}^2)}^{\top}\). Then \(\mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}} = 2\beta_{1}^2 + 3\beta_{2}^2\). By Theorem 9:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}(\mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}})}_{2 \times 1}
&= \begin{pmatrix} 2\beta_{1} & 0 \\
0 & 2\beta_{2} \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\
3 \end{pmatrix} \\
&= \begin{pmatrix} 4\beta_{1} \\
6\beta_{2} \end{pmatrix}
\end{aligned}
\]










RemarkRemark 4 (The derivative of a linear map as a special case)






Remark 4 (The derivative of a linear map as a special case). This result generalizes Theorem 8, which is the special case \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\) (so that \(q = p\), \(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}= \mathbf{I}_p\), and \(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} (\mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}) = \mathbf{I}_p {\mathbf{A}}^{\top}\), which is \({\mathbf{A}}^{\top}\)). For example, Example 16 is the case \(\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\) and
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}} &= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\\
&= {(\beta_{1}, \beta_{2})}^{\top},
\end{aligned}
\]
where this result gives \(\mathbf{I}_2 {\mathbf{A}}^{\top} = {(2, 3)}^{\top}\).










LemTheorem 10 (Vector-derivative of a product of matrices)






Theorem 10 (Vector-derivative of a product of matrices) If \(\mathbf{A}\) (\(k \times m\)) and \(\mathbf{B}\) (\(m \times q\)) are constant with respect to \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\), and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})\) is a \(q \times 1\) vector that depends on the \(p \times 1\) vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\), then:
\[
\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} (\mathbf{A} \mathbf{B} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}})}_{p \times k} =
\underbrace{\mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\right)\mathclose{}}_{p \times q}
\underbrace{{\mathbf{B}}^{\top}}_{q \times m}
\underbrace{{\mathbf{A}}^{\top}}_{m \times k}
\]










ProofProof






Proof. Apply Theorem 9 with the constant \(k \times q\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}\), then use the transpose of a product:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} (\mathbf{A} \mathbf{B} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}})
&= \mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\right)\mathclose{} {(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})}^{\top}
&& \text{(derivative of a matrix-vector product)}
\\
&= \mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\right)\mathclose{} {\mathbf{B}}^{\top}\,{\mathbf{A}}^{\top}
&& \text{(transpose of a product)}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExmExample 18






Example 18 Let \(\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\end{pmatrix}\) (\(1 \times 2\)), \(\mathbf{B} = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 0 \\
0 & 3\end{pmatrix}\) (\(2 \times 2\)), and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}) = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\) where \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}= {(\beta_{1}, \beta_{2})}^{\top}\). Then \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}} = 2\beta_{1}\), and:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}})}_{2 \times 1}
&= \underbrace{\mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\right)\mathclose{}}_{2 \times 2}
\underbrace{{\mathbf{B}}^{\top}}_{2 \times 2}
\underbrace{{\mathbf{A}}^{\top}}_{2 \times 1} \\
&= \mathbf{I}_2
\begin{pmatrix}2 & 0 \\
0 & 3\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}1 \\
0\end{pmatrix} \\
&= \begin{pmatrix}2 \\
0\end{pmatrix}
\end{aligned}
\]










CorCorollary 1 (Derivative of a dot product, transpose-product form)






Corollary 1 (Derivative of a dot product, transpose-product form) If \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) is constant with respect to \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\), then:
\[
\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} (\underbrace{{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top}}_{1 \times p} \underbrace{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}_{p \times 1})}_{p \times 1} =
\underbrace{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}_{p \times 1}
\]










ProofProof






Proof. Using Theorem 6:
Since \({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\) (see dot product), and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) is constant with respect to \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})
&= \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}) \\
&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}
\end{aligned}
\]
by Theorem 6.










ProofProof






Proof. Using Theorem 9:
Since \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) is constant with respect to \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\), \(\mathbf{A} = {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top}\) is a constant \(1 \times p\) matrix. Applying Theorem 9 with \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\) (so \(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}= \mathbf{I}\)):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})
&= \mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\right)\mathclose{} {({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top})}^{\top} \\
&= \mathbf{I} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\\
&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExmExample 19 (Derivative of a transpose product)






Example 19 (Derivative of a transpose product) Let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= {(3, 5)}^{\top}\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}= {(\beta_{1}, \beta_{2})}^{\top}\). Then \({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}= 3\beta_{1} + 5\beta_{2}\), and by Corollary 1:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}\mathopen{}\left(\underbrace{{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top}}_{1 \times 2}\underbrace{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}_{2 \times 1}\right)\mathclose{}}_{2 \times 1}
&= \underbrace{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}_{2 \times 1} \\
&= \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\
5 \end{pmatrix}
\end{aligned}
\]










RemarkRemark 5 (The coefficient gets transposed)






Remark 5 (The coefficient gets transposed). This vector derivative formula looks a lot like non-vector calculus, except that you have to transpose the coefficient: in scalar calculus \(\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(cx) = c\), but here the coefficient \({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top}\) (a row vector) becomes \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) (a column vector) in the result. For example, with \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= {(2, -1)}^{\top}\), \({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}= 2\beta_{1} - \beta_{2}\), whose vector derivative is the column vector \({(2, -1)}^{\top} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\), not the row vector \({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top} = (2, -1)\).










LemTheorem 11 (Derivative of a quadratic form)






Theorem 11 (Derivative of a quadratic form) For a quadratic form (see quadratic form), if \(\mathbf{S}\) is a \(p \times p\) matrix that is constant with respect to \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\), then:
\[
\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} ({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})}_{p \times 1} = \underbrace{(\mathbf{S} + {\mathbf{S}}^{\top}) \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}_{p \times 1}.
\]










ProofProof






Proof. Expanding entry-wise, \({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}} = \sum_{j=1}^p\sum_{k=1}^{p} s_{jk} \beta_{j} \beta_{k}\). Differentiating component-wise with respect to \(\beta_{i}\) for \(i = 1, \ldots, p\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathopen{}\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})\right]\mathclose{}_i
&= \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{i}} \sum_{j=1}^p\sum_{k=1}^{p} s_{jk} \beta_{j} \beta_{k}
&& \text{(expand quadratic form)} \\
&= \sum_{k=1}^{p} s_{ik} \beta_{k} + \sum_{j=1}^ps_{ji} \beta_{j}
&& \text{(product rule for } \beta_{i} \beta_{k} \text{)} \\
&= [\mathbf{S}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}]_i + [{\mathbf{S}}^{\top}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}]_i
&& \text{(matrix-vector multiplication definition)} \\
&= [(\mathbf{S} + {\mathbf{S}}^{\top})\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}]_i
&& \text{(linearity of matrix multiplication)}
\end{aligned}
\]










CorCorollary 2 (Derivative of a quadratic form with a symmetric matrix)






Corollary 2 (Derivative of a quadratic form with a symmetric matrix) If, in addition, \(\mathbf{S}\) is symmetric (and, as in Theorem 11, \(p \times p\) and constant with respect to \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\)), then
\[
\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} ({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})}_{p \times 1} = \underbrace{2 \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}_{p \times 1}.
\]










ProofProof






Proof. If \(\mathbf{S} = {\mathbf{S}}^{\top}\), then \(\mathbf{S} + {\mathbf{S}}^{\top} = 2\mathbf{S}\), so Theorem 11 gives \(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}) = 2\mathbf{S}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\).










RemarkRemark 6 (Like the derivative of \(cx^2\))






Remark 6 (Like the derivative of \(cx^2\)). This operation is like taking the derivative of \(cx^2\) with respect to \(x\) in non-vector calculus: \(\frac{\partial}{\partial x} (cx^2) = 2cx\), and Corollary 2 says \(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} ({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}) = 2 \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\). For example, with \(p = 1\), \(\mathbf{S} = (3)\), and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}= (\beta_{1})\), \({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}} = 3\beta_{1}^2\), and its derivative is \(6\beta_{1} = 2 \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\).










ExmExample 20 (Derivative of a quadratic form)






Example 20 (Derivative of a quadratic form) Let \(\mathbf{S} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) (\(2 \times 2\), symmetric and constant) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}= {(\beta_{1}, \beta_{2})}^{\top}\). Then \({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}} = 3\beta_{1}^2 + 2\beta_{1}\beta_{2} + 2\beta_{2}^2\). By Corollary 2:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})}_{2 \times 1}
&= 2 \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\\
&= 2 \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \beta_{1} \\ \beta_{2} \end{pmatrix} \\
&= \begin{pmatrix} 6\beta_{1} + 2\beta_{2} \\ 2\beta_{1} + 4\beta_{2} \end{pmatrix}
\end{aligned}
\]
Differentiating component-wise directly:
\[
\begin{pmatrix} \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{1}}(3\beta_{1}^2 + 2\beta_{1}\beta_{2} + 2\beta_{2}^2) \\ \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_{2}}(3\beta_{1}^2 + 2\beta_{1}\beta_{2} + 2\beta_{2}^2) \end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix} 6\beta_{1} + 2\beta_{2} \\ 2\beta_{1} + 4\beta_{2} \end{pmatrix}
\]
Both methods agree.
For a matrix that is not symmetric, such as \(\mathbf{S} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\), Theorem 11 gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
(\mathbf{S} + {\mathbf{S}}^{\top}) \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}
&= \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 6 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \beta_{1} \\ \beta_{2} \end{pmatrix} \\
&= \begin{pmatrix} 2\beta_{1} + 2\beta_{2} \\ 2\beta_{1} + 6\beta_{2} \end{pmatrix},
\end{aligned}
\]
which matches differentiating \({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}} = \beta_{1}^2 + 2\beta_{1}\beta_{2} + 3\beta_{2}^2\) directly.










CorCorollary 3 (Derivative of a simple quadratic form)






Corollary 3 (Derivative of a simple quadratic form) \[
\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})}_{p \times 1} = \underbrace{2\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}_{p \times 1}
\]










ProofProof






Proof. Applying Corollary 2 with \(\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{I}_{p \times p}\) (which is symmetric and constant with respect to \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\)):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})
&= \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}^{\top} \mathbf{I}_{p \times p} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})
&& \text{(rewrite with identity matrix)} \\
&= 2\mathbf{I}_{p \times p}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}
&& \text{(derivative of a quadratic form, with } \mathbf{S} = \mathbf{I}_{p \times p} \text{)} \\
&= 2\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}
&& \text{(identity matrix property)}
\end{aligned}
\]










RemarkRemark 7 (Like the derivative of \(x^2\))






Remark 7 (Like the derivative of \(x^2\)). This vector derivative is like taking the derivative of \(x^2\): in scalar calculus \(\frac{\partial}{\partial x} x^2 = 2x\), and Corollary 3 says \(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}} (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}) = 2\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\). For example, with \(p = 1\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}= (\beta_{1})\), \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}} = \beta_{1}^2\), and its derivative is \(2\beta_{1} = 2\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\).










ExmExample 21 (Derivative of a sum of squares)






Example 21 (Derivative of a sum of squares) Let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}= {(\beta_{1}, \beta_{2})}^{\top}\), so \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}} = \beta_{1}^2 + \beta_{2}^2\). By Corollary 3:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})}_{2 \times 1}
&= 2\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\\
&= \begin{pmatrix} 2\beta_{1} \\ 2\beta_{2} \end{pmatrix}
\end{aligned}
\]
Direct partial differentiation yields the same column vector.










DefDefinition 12 (Residual vector and residuals)






Definition 12 (Residual vector and residuals) Let \(\mathbf{X}\) be an \(n \times p\) matrix, \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\in \mathbb{R}^n\), and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\in \mathbb{R}^p\). The residual vector of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\) is \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\varepsilon}}\vphantom{\varepsilon}}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}- \mathbf{X}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\), and its entries \(\varepsilon_i = y_i - (\mathbf{X}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})_i\) are the residuals [10].










DefDefinition 13 (Squared error)






Definition 13 (Squared error) In the setting of Definition 12, the square \(\varepsilon_i^2\) is the \(i\)th squared error.










DefDefinition 14 (Residual sum of squares)






Definition 14 (Residual sum of squares) In the setting of Definition 12, the sum of the squared errors (Definition 13)
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\varepsilon}}\vphantom{\varepsilon}}\cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\varepsilon}}\vphantom{\varepsilon}}
&= \sum_{i=1}^n\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\varepsilon}}\vphantom{\varepsilon}}_i^2 \\
&= \mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}- \mathbf{X}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\right\rVert\mathclose{}^2
\end{aligned}
\]
is the residual sum of squares [11].










RemarkRemark 8 (Least squares solutions minimize the residual sum of squares)






Remark 8 (Least squares solutions minimize the residual sum of squares). A least squares solution of \(\mathbf{X}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\) makes \(\mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}- \mathbf{X}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\right\rVert\mathclose{}\) as small as possible, and so makes the residual sum of squares (Definition 14) as small as possible too.










ExmExample 22 (Residuals of a constant fit)






Example 22 (Residuals of a constant fit) Let \(\mathbf{X}= {(1, 1)}^{\top}\) (\(n = 2\), \(p = 1\)) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}= {(1, 3)}^{\top}\). For \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}= (2)\), \(\mathbf{X}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}= {(2, 2)}^{\top}\), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\varepsilon}}\vphantom{\varepsilon}}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})
&= {(1, 3)}^{\top} - {(2, 2)}^{\top}
&& \text{(definition of the residual vector)}
\\
&= {(-1, 1)}^{\top},
&& \text{(subtract entry by entry)}
\end{aligned}
\]
the squared errors are \((-1)^2 = 1\) and \(1^2 = 1\), and the residual sum of squares is \(1 + 1 = 2\). For \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}= (1)\) the residuals are \(0\) and \(2\), and the residual sum of squares is \(0 + 4 = 4\).
