LemTheorem 12 (Vector chain rule)






Theorem 12 (Vector chain rule) Let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) be a \(p \times 1\) vector, let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{g}}\vphantom{g}}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\) be a \(q \times 1\) vector-valued function of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\), and let \(z = f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}})\) be a scalar-valued function of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\), where \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{g}}\vphantom{g}}\) and \(f\) have continuous partial derivatives. Then \(z = f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{g}}\vphantom{g}}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}))\), as a function of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\), satisfies
\[
\underbrace{\frac{\partial z}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}}_{p \times 1}
= \underbrace{\frac{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}}_{p \times q}
\underbrace{\frac{\partial z}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}}}_{q \times 1}
\]
where \(\frac{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}\) is the derivative of Definition 7 and \(\frac{\partial z}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}\) and \(\frac{\partial z}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}}\) are vector derivatives (Definition 2).










RemarkRemark 9 (The order of the factors matters)






Remark 9 (The order of the factors matters). The vector chain rule (Theorem 12) is like the univariate chain rule, but the order matters now: \(\frac{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}\) is \(p \times q\) and \(\frac{\partial z}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}}\) is \(q \times 1\), so the product \(\frac{\partial z}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}} \frac{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}\) in the other order is not even defined unless \(p = 1\).
The version presented here is for the gradient (Definition 2), a column vector. The total derivative (Definition 6), a row vector, is the transpose of the gradient (Theorem 5), and transposing both sides gives \({\mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}\right)\mathclose{}}^{\top} = {\mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}}\right)\mathclose{}}^{\top} {\mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}\right)\mathclose{}}^{\top}\), with the factors in the reverse order; there \({\mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}\right)\mathclose{}}^{\top}\) is the Jacobian matrix of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\) as a function of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) (Definition 9).










ExmExample 23 (Applying the vector chain rule)






Example 23 (Applying the vector chain rule) Let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= {(x_1, x_2)}^{\top}\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{g}}\vphantom{g}}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) \\
&= {(x_1 + x_2,\ x_1 x_2)}^{\top},
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
z &= f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}) \\
&= y_1^2 + y_2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\underbrace{\frac{\partial z}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}}_{2 \times 1}
&= \underbrace{\frac{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}}_{2 \times 2}
\underbrace{\frac{\partial z}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}}}_{2 \times 1}
&& \text{(vector chain rule)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix}
1 & x_2 \\
1 & x_1
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
2y_1 \\
1
\end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(differentiate } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{g}}\vphantom{g}} \text{ and } f \text{)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix}
2(x_1 + x_2) + x_2 \\
2(x_1 + x_2) + x_1
\end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(multiply, and substitute } y_1 = x_1 + x_2 \text{)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix}
2x_1 + 3x_2 \\
3x_1 + 2x_2
\end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(collect terms)}
\end{aligned}
\]
This matches differentiating \(z\) directly:
\[
\begin{aligned}
z &= (x_1 + x_2)^2 + x_1 x_2 \\
&= x_1^2 + 3x_1 x_2 + x_2^2,
\end{aligned}
\]
so \(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_1} z = 2x_1 + 3x_2\) and \(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_2} z = 3x_1 + 2x_2\). The product in the other order, a \(2 \times 1\) matrix times a \(2 \times 2\) matrix, is not defined. The total derivative is the transpose, the row vector \((2x_1 + 3x_2,\ 3x_1 + 2x_2)\).





See Felippa [12], and Wikipedia contributors [4], section “Relationship with Frechet derivative”.







CorCorollary 4 (Vector chain rule for quadratic forms)






Corollary 4 (Vector chain rule for quadratic forms) If \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\varepsilon}}\vphantom{\varepsilon}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\varepsilon}}\vphantom{\varepsilon}}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})\) is an \(n \times 1\) vector-valued function of the \(p \times 1\) vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\), with continuous partial derivatives, then
\[
\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}{\mathopen{}\left(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\varepsilon}}\vphantom{\varepsilon}}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})\cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\varepsilon}}\vphantom{\varepsilon}}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})\right)\mathclose{}}}_{p \times 1}
= \underbrace{\mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\varepsilon}}\vphantom{\varepsilon}}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})\right)\mathclose{}}_{p \times n}
\underbrace{\mathopen{}\left(2 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\varepsilon}}\vphantom{\varepsilon}}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}})\right)\mathclose{}}_{n \times 1}
\]










ProofProof






Proof. Apply Theorem 12 with \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\), \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\varepsilon}}\vphantom{\varepsilon}}\), \(q = n\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
z &= f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\varepsilon}}\vphantom{\varepsilon}}) \\
&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\varepsilon}}\vphantom{\varepsilon}}\cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\varepsilon}}\vphantom{\varepsilon}}\\
&= {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\varepsilon}}\vphantom{\varepsilon}}}^{\top}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\varepsilon}}\vphantom{\varepsilon}}:
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}\mathopen{}\left(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\varepsilon}}\vphantom{\varepsilon}}\cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\varepsilon}}\vphantom{\varepsilon}}\right)\mathclose{}
&= \mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\varepsilon}}\vphantom{\varepsilon}}\right)\mathclose{} \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\varepsilon}}\vphantom{\varepsilon}}}\mathopen{}\left({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\varepsilon}}\vphantom{\varepsilon}}}^{\top}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\varepsilon}}\vphantom{\varepsilon}}\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(vector chain rule)}
\\
&= \mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\varepsilon}}\vphantom{\varepsilon}}\right)\mathclose{} \mathopen{}\left(2\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\varepsilon}}\vphantom{\varepsilon}}\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(derivative of a simple quadratic form, in } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\varepsilon}}\vphantom{\varepsilon}}\text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
The second step is Corollary 3, applied to the \(n \times 1\) vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\varepsilon}}\vphantom{\varepsilon}}\) in place of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\).










ExmExample 24 (Derivative of the residual sum of squares)






Example 24 (Derivative of the residual sum of squares) Let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\) (\(n \times 1\)) and \(\mathbf{X}\) (\(n \times p\)) be constant with respect to \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\), and let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\varepsilon}}\vphantom{\varepsilon}}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}) = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}- \mathbf{X}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\) be the residual vector (Definition 12). By Theorem 8, \(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}(\mathbf{X}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}) = {\mathbf{X}}^{\top}\), and \(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}= \mathbf{0}_{p \times n}\) because \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\) is constant, so \(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\varepsilon}}\vphantom{\varepsilon}}= -{\mathbf{X}}^{\top}\) (\(p \times n\)). By Corollary 4:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}\mathopen{}\left(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\varepsilon}}\vphantom{\varepsilon}}\cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\varepsilon}}\vphantom{\varepsilon}}\right)\mathclose{}
&= \mathopen{}\left(-{\mathbf{X}}^{\top}\right)\mathclose{} \mathopen{}\left(2\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\varepsilon}}\vphantom{\varepsilon}}\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(vector chain rule for quadratic forms)}
\\
&= -2\,{\mathbf{X}}^{\top}\mathopen{}\left(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}- \mathbf{X}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(substitute } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\varepsilon}}\vphantom{\varepsilon}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}- \mathbf{X}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Setting this \(p \times 1\) vector to \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\) gives the normal equations \({\mathbf{X}}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}= {\mathbf{X}}^{\top}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\) of least squares.










TipVideos



Jon Krohn’s “Calculus for Machine Learning” YouTube playlist has videos on the chain rule for partial derivatives:

The Chain Rule for Partial Derivatives
Exercises on the Multivariate Chain Rule









DefDefinition 15 (Matrix derivative (gradient))






Definition 15 (Matrix derivative (gradient)) For a scalar-valued function \(f(\mathbf{X})\) of an \(m \times n\) matrix \(\mathbf{X}\), the matrix derivative [8] is the \(m \times n\) matrix whose \((i,j)\) entry is the partial derivative of \(f\) with respect to the \((i,j)\) entry of \(\mathbf{X}\):
\[
\mathopen{}\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{X}} f\right]\mathclose{}_{ij} = \frac{\partial}{\partial X_{ij}} f
\]
Like the vector derivative (Definition 2), the matrix derivative is also called the gradient of \(f\) with respect to \(\mathbf{X}\), written \(\nabla_{\mathbf{X}} f\).










ExmExample 25 (The matrix derivative of a trace)






Example 25 (The matrix derivative of a trace) Let \(\mathbf{X}\) be a \(2 \times 2\) matrix and
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(\mathbf{X}) &= \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{X}) \\
&= X_{11} + X_{22}
\end{aligned}
\]
(see trace). Then \(\frac{\partial}{\partial X_{ij}} f = 1\) if \(i = j\) and \(0\) otherwise, so:
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{X}} f = \mathbf{I}_2
\]










LemTheorem 13 (Matrix derivative of the trace of a matrix product)






Theorem 13 (Matrix derivative of the trace of a matrix product) If \(\mathbf{A}\) (\(r \times m\)) and \(\mathbf{B}\) (\(n \times r\)) are constant with respect to the \(m \times n\) matrix \(\mathbf{X}\), then:
\[
\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{X}} \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{A} \mathbf{X} \mathbf{B})}_{m \times n} =
\underbrace{{\mathbf{A}}^{\top}}_{m \times r}
\underbrace{{\mathbf{B}}^{\top}}_{r \times n}
\]










ProofProof






Proof. Write \(A_{kl}\), \(X_{kl}\), and \(B_{kl}\) for the entries of \(\mathbf{A}\), \(\mathbf{X}\), and \(\mathbf{B}\). For entry \((i,j)\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathopen{}\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{X}} \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{A} \mathbf{X} \mathbf{B})\right]\mathclose{}_{ij}
&= \frac{\partial}{\partial X_{ij}} \sum_{a=1}^{r} \sum_{b=1}^{m} \sum_{c=1}^{n} A_{ab} X_{bc} B_{ca}
&& \text{(trace of the } r \times r \text{ product } \mathbf{A}\mathbf{X}\mathbf{B} \text{)}
\\
&= \sum_{a=1}^{r} A_{ai} B_{ja}
&& \text{(only the terms with } b = i,\ c = j \text{ depend on } X_{ij} \text{)}
\\
&= \sum_{a=1}^{r} \mathopen{}\left[{\mathbf{A}}^{\top}\right]\mathclose{}_{ia} \mathopen{}\left[{\mathbf{B}}^{\top}\right]\mathclose{}_{aj}
&& \text{(definition of the transpose)}
\\
&= \mathopen{}\left[{\mathbf{A}}^{\top}\,{\mathbf{B}}^{\top}\right]\mathclose{}_{ij}
&& \text{(definition of matrix multiplication)}
\end{aligned}
\]










RemarkRemark 10 (Why the theorem uses the trace)






Remark 10 (Why the theorem uses the trace). The trace makes \(\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{A} \mathbf{X} \mathbf{B})\) a scalar, so its matrix derivative (Definition 15) is again an \(m \times n\) matrix. The matrix product \(\mathbf{A} \mathbf{X} \mathbf{B}\) itself (without the trace) is an \(r \times r\) matrix, and each of its \(r^2\) entries has a partial derivative with respect to each of the \(m n\) entries of \(\mathbf{X}\). Those \(r^2 m n\) partial derivatives form a four-index array (a fourth-order tensor), not a matrix, which is why this result is stated for the scalar \(\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{A} \mathbf{X} \mathbf{B})\).
For example, with
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{A} &= \mathbf{B} \\
&= \mathbf{I}_2,
\end{aligned}
\]
the product \(\mathbf{A} \mathbf{X} \mathbf{B} = \mathbf{X}\) has \(4\) entries, each with \(4\) partial derivatives, \(16\) in all, while its trace \(X_{11} + X_{22}\) has the \(4\) partial derivatives that form the \(2 \times 2\) matrix \(\mathbf{I}_2\) of Example 25.










ExmExample 26 (Differentiating a weighted trace)






Example 26 (Differentiating a weighted trace) Let \(\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{I}_2\) (\(2 \times 2\)) and \(\mathbf{B} = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 0 \\
0 & 3\end{pmatrix}\) (\(2 \times 2\)). Then \(\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{A} \mathbf{X} \mathbf{B}) = 2X_{11} + 3X_{22}\), and:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{X}} \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{A} \mathbf{X} \mathbf{B})}_{2 \times 2}
&= \underbrace{{\mathbf{A}}^{\top}}_{2 \times 2} \underbrace{{\mathbf{B}}^{\top}}_{2 \times 2} \\
&= \mathbf{I}_2 \begin{pmatrix}2 & 0 \\
0 & 3\end{pmatrix} \\
&= \begin{pmatrix}2 & 0 \\
0 & 3\end{pmatrix}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExrExercise 7 (A gradient that does not mention its variable)






Exercise 7 (A gradient that does not mention its variable) Take
\[A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 4 & 3 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\]
let \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 3}\) vary, and define
\[g(W) = \sum_{i=1}^{2} \sum_{j=1}^{3} W_{ij} A_{ij}\]
which is the entry-by-entry version of the inner product for matrices. Compute \(\nabla_W\, g(W)\), and say what is unusual about the answer.










SolutionSolution 7






Solution 7. Written out over the six positions,
\[g(W) = 2W_{11} - W_{12} + 0\,W_{13} + 4W_{21} + 3W_{22} - 2W_{23}\]
Each \(W_{ij}\) appears in exactly one term, multiplied by \(A_{ij}\) and by nothing else, so differentiating with respect to it leaves \(A_{ij}\) behind:
\[\frac{\partial g}{\partial W_{ij}} = A_{ij}\]
Collecting those partial derivatives into a matrix of the same shape as \(W\), as Table 1 requires,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_W\, g(W)
&= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 4 & 3 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \\
&= A
\end{aligned}
\]
What is unusual is that the gradient came out constant: it does not mention \(W\) at all. The constant answer is not a quirk of this particular \(A\). \(g\) is a linear function of \(W\), and the gradient of a linear function is constant everywhere, for the same reason the derivative of \(f(w) = cw\) is \(c\) no matter where it is evaluated.
A constant gradient is the easy case, and it is not the case we usually face. Most functions we minimize are curved — the residual sum of squares of a linear model (Definition 14) is the standard example — so their gradient changes from point to point and the downhill direction has to be worked out afresh at every step.










LemTheorem 14 (Gradient of an entrywise inner product with a fixed matrix)






Theorem 14 (Gradient of an entrywise inner product with a fixed matrix) Let \(A\) be a fixed \(m \times n\) matrix, and for \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}\) define
\[g(W) = \sum_{i=1}^{m} \sum_{j=1}^{n} W_{ij} A_{ij}\]
Then for every \(W\), \(\nabla_W\, g(W) = A\). In particular, the gradient is constant: it does not depend on \(W\).










ProofProof






Proof. This is the solution to Exercise 7, worked in Solution 7, where \(m = 2\), \(n = 3\), and the entries of \(A\) are given. The same argument works for every \(A\): each \(W_{ij}\) appears in exactly one term, multiplied by \(A_{ij}\), so \(\frac{\partial g}{\partial W_{ij}} = A_{ij}\).

2 Second partial derivatives and the Hessian






DefDefinition 16 (Open ball)






Definition 16 (Open ball) Let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\in \mathbb{R}^p\) and \(r > 0\). The open ball [13] of radius \(r\) around \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) is the set \(\mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\in \mathbb{R}^p : \mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\right\rVert\mathclose{} < r\right\}\mathclose{}\), of points whose distance from \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) (the Euclidean norm of the difference) is less than \(r\).










DefDefinition 17 (Closed ball)






Definition 17 (Closed ball) For \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) and \(r\) as in Definition 16, the closed ball of radius \(r\) around \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) is \(\mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\in \mathbb{R}^p : \mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\right\rVert\mathclose{} \le r\right\}\mathclose{}\).










DefDefinition 18 (Unit ball)






Definition 18 (Unit ball) The open and closed balls (Definition 16, Definition 17) of radius \(1\) around \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\) are the open and closed unit balls.










ExmExample 27 (Points in the unit balls of \(\mathbb{R}^2\))






Example 27 (Points in the unit balls of \(\mathbb{R}^2\))  


\({(0.5, 0.5)}^{\top}\) has
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathopen{}\left\lVert{(0.5, 0.5)}^{\top}\right\rVert\mathclose{}^2 &= 0.25 + 0.25 \\
&= 0.5 \\
&< 1,
\end{aligned}
\]
so it is in both the open and the closed unit ball.


\({(0.6, 0.8)}^{\top}\) has
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathopen{}\left\lVert{(0.6, 0.8)}^{\top}\right\rVert\mathclose{}^2 &= 0.36 + 0.64 \\
&= 1,
\end{aligned}
\]
so it is in the closed unit ball but not the open one.

For \(p = 1\), the open ball of radius \(r\) around \(c\) is the open interval \((c - r, c + r)\).











DefDefinition 19 (Second partial derivative)






Definition 19 (Second partial derivative) Let \(f\) be a scalar-valued function of a \(p \times 1\) vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\), and let \(i, j \in \mathopen{}\left\{1, \ldots, p\right\}\mathclose{}\). Suppose the partial derivative \(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_j} f\) (Definition 1) exists at every point of an open ball around \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) (Definition 16). The second partial derivative of \(f\) at \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\), first with respect to \(x_j\) and then with respect to \(x_i\), is
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i} \mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_j} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right)\mathclose{},
\]
the partial derivative with respect to \(x_i\) of the function \(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_j} f\), when it exists.










ExmExample 28 (Second partial derivatives of \(x_1^2 x_2 + 3 x_2\))






Example 28 (Second partial derivatives of \(x_1^2 x_2 + 3 x_2\)) For \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = x_1^2 x_2 + 3 x_2\) of Example 1, \(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_1} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = 2 x_1 x_2\) and \(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_2} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = x_1^2 + 3\). Differentiating each of these again:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial x_1} \mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_1} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right)\mathclose{} &= \frac{\partial}{\partial x_1} (2 x_1 x_2) \\
&= 2 x_2;
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial x_2} \mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_1} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right)\mathclose{} &= \frac{\partial}{\partial x_2} (2 x_1 x_2) \\
&= 2 x_1;
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial x_1} \mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_2} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right)\mathclose{} &= \frac{\partial}{\partial x_1} (x_1^2 + 3) \\
&= 2 x_1;
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial x_2} \mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_2} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right)\mathclose{} &= \frac{\partial}{\partial x_2} (x_1^2 + 3) \\
&= 0.
\end{aligned}
\]

The two mixed partial derivatives are both \(2 x_1\).










DefDefinition 20 (Mixed partial derivative)






Definition 20 (Mixed partial derivative) When \(i \ne j\), the second partial derivative of Definition 19 is a mixed partial derivative.










DefDefinition 21 (Hessian matrix)






Definition 21 (Hessian matrix) Let \(f\) be a scalar-valued function of a \(p \times 1\) vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) whose first partial derivatives exist on an open ball around \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) (Definition 16) and whose second partial derivatives (Definition 19) exist at \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\). The Hessian matrix [14] of \(f\) at \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) is the derivative (Definition 7) of the transposed gradient \({\mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right)\mathclose{}}^{\top}\) (Definition 2):
\[
\underbrace{\mathbf{H}_f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})}_{p \times p} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} {\mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right)\mathclose{}}^{\top}.
\tag{4}\]










ExmExample 29 (A Hessian matrix)






Example 29 (A Hessian matrix) Let \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = e^{2x_1 + x_2} - x_1\) for \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= {(x_1, x_2)}^{\top}\), where \(e\) is Euler’s number, and write \(u = 2x_1 + x_2\). By the chain rule, \(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_1} e^{u} = 2 e^{u}\) and \(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_2} e^{u} = e^{u}\), so
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = \begin{bmatrix} 2 e^{u} - 1 \\ e^{u} \end{bmatrix}.
\]
Differentiating each entry again,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{H}_f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})
&= \begin{bmatrix}
\frac{\partial}{\partial x_1} (2 e^{u} - 1) & \frac{\partial}{\partial x_1} e^{u} \\
\frac{\partial}{\partial x_2} (2 e^{u} - 1) & \frac{\partial}{\partial x_2} e^{u}
\end{bmatrix} \\
&= \begin{bmatrix}
4 e^{u} & 2 e^{u} \\
2 e^{u} & e^{u}
\end{bmatrix},
\end{aligned}
\]
and at \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\), where \(u = 0\), \(\mathbf{H}_f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}) = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).










ExmExample 30 (A function with a gradient but no Hessian at a point)






Example 30 (A function with a gradient but no Hessian at a point) Let \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = x_1 \mathopen{}\left|x_1\right|\mathclose{}\) for \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= {(x_1, x_2)}^{\top}\), where \(\mathopen{}\left|\cdot\right|\mathclose{}\) is the absolute value. For \(x_1 > 0\), \(f = x_1^2\) and \(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_1} f = 2 x_1\); for \(x_1 < 0\), \(f = -x_1^2\) and \(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_1} f = -2 x_1\); and at \(x_1 = 0\) the difference quotient is \(h \mathopen{}\left|h\right|\mathclose{} / h = \mathopen{}\left|h\right|\mathclose{} \to 0\). So the gradient exists everywhere: it is \({(2 \mathopen{}\left|x_1\right|\mathclose{},\ 0)}^{\top}\). But \(2 \mathopen{}\left|x_1\right|\mathclose{}\) has no derivative in \(x_1\) at \(x_1 = 0\) (its difference quotient \(2 \mathopen{}\left|h\right|\mathclose{} / h\) is \(2\) for \(h > 0\) and \(-2\) for \(h < 0\)), so \(\mathopen{}\left[\mathbf{H}_f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right]\mathclose{}_{11}\), and with it the Hessian, does not exist at any \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) with \(x_1 = 0\).










LemTheorem 15 (Other ways to write the Hessian, and its entries)






Theorem 15 (Other ways to write the Hessian, and its entries) Let \(f\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) be as in Definition 21.


The Hessian can be written with the row-vector derivative (Definition 6) of \(f\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{H}_f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})
&= \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} \mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})}{\partial {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top}}\right)\mathclose{} \\
&= \frac{\partial^2 f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} \partial {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top}}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}\]


The \((i, j)\) entry of the Hessian is
\[
\mathopen{}\left[\mathbf{H}_f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right]\mathclose{}_{ij} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i} \mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_j} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right)\mathclose{}.
\tag{6}\]












ProofProof






Proof. Part 1. By Theorem 5, the transposed gradient \({\mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right)\mathclose{}}^{\top}\) equals the row-vector derivative \(\frac{\partial f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})}{\partial {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top}}\). Substituting it into Equation 4 gives the first line. The second line is the same expression written as a second derivative. It follows the shape rule of matrix multiplication (Remark 2): the \(p \times 1\) column-vector operator \(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}\) stands on the left of a \(1 \times p\) row vector, giving a \(p \times p\) matrix.
Part 2. Let \(y_j \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_j} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\) be entry \(j\) of the gradient. By Definition 7, the \((i, j)\) entry of the derivative of the vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}= (y_1, \ldots, y_p)\) with respect to \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathopen{}\left[\mathbf{H}_f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right]\mathclose{}_{ij}
&= \mathopen{}\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}}^{\top}\right]\mathclose{}_{ij}
&& \text{(}\href{#eq-hessian}{\text{Equation~4}}\text{, with } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\text{ the gradient)}
\\
&= \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i} y_j
&& \text{(}\href{#def-vector-valued-derivative}{\text{Definition~7}}\text{)}
\\
&= \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i} \mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_j} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right)\mathclose{}.
&& \text{(} y_j = \frac{\partial}{\partial x_j} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExmExample 31 (Computing the Hessian entry by entry, and checking it by finite differences)






Example 31 (Computing the Hessian entry by entry, and checking it by finite differences) Take \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = e^{2x_1 + x_2} - x_1\) from Example 29. By Equation 6, entry \((i, j)\) of the Hessian is the derivative with respect to \(x_i\) of the derivative with respect to \(x_j\). The code differentiates f symbolically in that order with D(), evaluates the four entries at \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= (0.5, -1)\), and compares them with central differences of the gradient.

f_expr <- quote(exp(2 * x1 + x2) - x1)
vars <- c("x1", "x2")
point <- c(x1 = 0.5, x2 = -1)

grad_expr <- lapply(vars, function(v) D(f_expr, v))
hess_expr <- lapply(vars, function(i) {
  lapply(grad_expr, function(g_j) D(g_j, i))
})
H <- sapply(1:2, function(j) {
  sapply(1:2, function(i) eval(hess_expr[[i]][[j]], as.list(point)))
})

grad_at <- function(x) {
  sapply(grad_expr, function(g) eval(g, as.list(setNames(x, vars))))
}
h <- 1e-5
H_fd <- sapply(1:2, function(j) {
  sapply(1:2, function(i) {
    step <- replace(c(0, 0), i, h)
    (grad_at(point + step)[j] - grad_at(point - step)[j]) / (2 * h)
  })
})

H
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]    4    2
#> [2,]    2    1
H_fd
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]    4    2
#> [2,]    2    1

At this point \(u = 2x_1 + x_2 = 0\), so the closed form in Example 29 gives \(4 e^u = 4\) for entry \((1, 1)\), and the code gives 4. The off-diagonal entries are 2 and 2, which are equal. The finite differences agree with the symbolic entries to within 0.00000000026.

DefDefinition 22 (Continuity at a point in several variables)






Definition 22 (Continuity at a point in several variables) A function \(f\) from \(\mathbb{R}^p\) to \(\mathbb{R}^q\) is continuous at \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) if for every \(\varepsilon> 0\) there is a \(\delta> 0\) such that \(\mathopen{}\left\lVert f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}) - f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right\rVert\mathclose{} < \varepsilon\) whenever \(\mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\right\rVert\mathclose{} < \delta\). For \(q = 1\), \(\mathopen{}\left\lVert f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}) - f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right\rVert\mathclose{} = \mathopen{}\left|f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}) - f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right|\mathclose{}\).










DefDefinition 23 (Continuity on a set in several variables)






Definition 23 (Continuity on a set in several variables) A function \(f\) from \(\mathbb{R}^p\) to \(\mathbb{R}^q\) is continuous on a set if it is continuous at every point of the set (Definition 22).










ExmExample 32 (A continuous function, and a discontinuous one)






Example 32 (A continuous function, and a discontinuous one)  


\(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = x_1 + x_2\) is continuous at every \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\). Each \(\mathopen{}\left|y_i - x_i\right|\mathclose{} \le \mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\right\rVert\mathclose{}\), since the squared length is a sum of nonnegative squares, so
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathopen{}\left|f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}) - f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right|\mathclose{}
&= \mathopen{}\left|(y_1 - x_1) + (y_2 - x_2)\right|\mathclose{}
&& \text{(subtract)}
\\
&\le \mathopen{}\left|y_1 - x_1\right|\mathclose{} + \mathopen{}\left|y_2 - x_2\right|\mathclose{}
&& \text{(triangle inequality for numbers)}
\\
&\le 2\,\mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\right\rVert\mathclose{},
&& \text{(each term is at most } \mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\right\rVert\mathclose{} \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
which is less than \(\varepsilon\) whenever \(\mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\right\rVert\mathclose{} < \delta= \varepsilon/ 2\).

\(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = 1\) if \(x_1 > 0\) and \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = 0\) otherwise is not continuous at \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\): for \(\varepsilon= \tfrac{1}{2}\) and any \(\delta> 0\), the point \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}= {(\delta/ 2, 0)}^{\top}\) has \(\mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\right\rVert\mathclose{} = \delta/ 2 < \delta\) but \(\mathopen{}\left|f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}) - f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}})\right|\mathclose{} = 1 > \tfrac{1}{2}\).











LemTheorem 16 (Continuity in one variable, and sums, multiples and compositions)






Theorem 16 (Continuity in one variable, and sums, multiples and compositions)  

For \(p = q = 1\), a function \(f\) is continuous at \(x\) in the sense of Definition 22 exactly when \(\lim_{y \to x} f(y) = f(x)\) (limit), which is the usual continuity at \(x\).
If \(f : \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}^q\) is continuous at \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) and \(g : \mathbb{R}^q \to \mathbb{R}^r\) is continuous at \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\), then the composition \(g \circ f\) is continuous at \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\).
If \(f, g : \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}\) are continuous at \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\), then \(f + g\) is continuous at \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\).
If \(f : \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}\) is continuous at \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) and \(c \in \mathbb{R}\), then \(c f\) is continuous at \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\).

If the hypotheses of part 2, 3 or 4 hold at every point of a set, the conclusion holds at every point of that set.










ProofProof






Proof. Let \(\varepsilon> 0\) be given.
Part 1. For \(p = q = 1\), \(\mathopen{}\left\lVert f(y) - f(x)\right\rVert\mathclose{} = \mathopen{}\left|f(y) - f(x)\right|\mathclose{}\) and \(\mathopen{}\left\lVert y - x\right\rVert\mathclose{} = \mathopen{}\left|y - x\right|\mathclose{}\). Definition 22 then asks for a \(\delta> 0\) such that \(\mathopen{}\left|f(y) - f(x)\right|\mathclose{} < \varepsilon\) whenever \(\mathopen{}\left|y - x\right|\mathclose{} < \delta\). The limit definition with \(L = f(x)\) asks for the same inequality, but only whenever \(0 < \mathopen{}\left|y - x\right|\mathclose{} < \delta\). The two agree, because at \(y = x\) the inequality \(\mathopen{}\left|f(x) - f(x)\right|\mathclose{} = 0 < \varepsilon\) holds for every \(\delta\).
Part 2. Because \(g\) is continuous at \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\), there is a \(\delta_g > 0\) such that \(\mathopen{}\left\lVert g(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}) - g(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}))\right\rVert\mathclose{} < \varepsilon\) whenever \(\mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}} - f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right\rVert\mathclose{} < \delta_g\). Because \(f\) is continuous at \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\), applied with \(\delta_g\) in the role of \(\varepsilon\), there is a \(\delta> 0\) such that \(\mathopen{}\left\lVert f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}) - f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right\rVert\mathclose{} < \delta_g\) whenever \(\mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\right\rVert\mathclose{} < \delta\). So if \(\mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\right\rVert\mathclose{} < \delta\), then \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}} = f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}})\) has \(\mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}} - f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right\rVert\mathclose{} < \delta_g\), and therefore \(\mathopen{}\left\lVert g(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}})) - g(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}))\right\rVert\mathclose{} < \varepsilon\).
Part 3. Because \(f\) and \(g\) are continuous at \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\), there are \(\delta_f > 0\) and \(\delta_g > 0\) such that \(\mathopen{}\left|f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}) - f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right|\mathclose{} < \varepsilon/ 2\) whenever \(\mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\right\rVert\mathclose{} < \delta_f\), and \(\mathopen{}\left|g(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}) - g(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right|\mathclose{} < \varepsilon/ 2\) whenever \(\mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\right\rVert\mathclose{} < \delta_g\). Let \(\delta\stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\min\mathopen{}\left\{\delta_f, \delta_g\right\}\mathclose{}\). If \(\mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\right\rVert\mathclose{} < \delta\), then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathopen{}\left|(f + g)(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}) - (f + g)(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right|\mathclose{}
&= \mathopen{}\left|\mathopen{}\left(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}) - f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right)\mathclose{} + \mathopen{}\left(g(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}) - g(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right)\mathclose{}\right|\mathclose{}
&& \text{(regroup)}
\\
&\le \mathopen{}\left|f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}) - f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right|\mathclose{} + \mathopen{}\left|g(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}) - g(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right|\mathclose{}
&& \text{(triangle inequality for numbers)}
\\
&< \frac{\varepsilon}{2} + \frac{\varepsilon}{2}
&& \text{(choice of } \delta\text{)}
\\
&= \varepsilon.
&& \text{(add)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Part 4. Because \(f\) is continuous at \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\), there is a \(\delta> 0\) such that \(\mathopen{}\left|f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}) - f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right|\mathclose{} < \varepsilon/ (\mathopen{}\left|c\right|\mathclose{} + 1)\) whenever \(\mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\right\rVert\mathclose{} < \delta\). For such \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathopen{}\left|c f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}) - c f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right|\mathclose{}
&= \mathopen{}\left|c\right|\mathclose{}\,\mathopen{}\left|f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}) - f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right|\mathclose{}
&& \text{(factor out } c \text{)}
\\
&\le \mathopen{}\left|c\right|\mathclose{}\,\frac{\varepsilon}{\mathopen{}\left|c\right|\mathclose{} + 1}
&& \text{(choice of } \delta\text{)}
\\
&< \varepsilon.
&& \text{(} \mathopen{}\left|c\right|\mathclose{} < \mathopen{}\left|c\right|\mathclose{} + 1 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExmExample 33 (Choosing \(\delta\) for a sum, a multiple and a composition)






Example 33 (Choosing \(\delta\) for a sum, a multiple and a composition) Let \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = x_1\) and \(g(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = x_2\) on \(\mathbb{R}^2\), and \(h(t) = 3t\) on \(\mathbb{R}\). Since \(\mathopen{}\left|y_i - x_i\right|\mathclose{} \le \mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\right\rVert\mathclose{}\), the functions \(f\) and \(g\) are continuous with \(\delta= \varepsilon\), and \(h\) is continuous with \(\delta= \varepsilon/ 3\), because \(\mathopen{}\left|h(s) - h(t)\right|\mathclose{} = 3\,\mathopen{}\left|s - t\right|\mathclose{}\). Take \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= (1, 2)\) and \(\varepsilon= 0.1\). The proof of Theorem 16 gives these values of \(\delta\):

for \(f + g\) (part 3), \(\delta= \min\mathopen{}\left\{\varepsilon/ 2, \varepsilon/ 2\right\}\mathclose{}\);
for \(3 f\) (part 4), \(\delta= \varepsilon/ (3 + 1)\);
for \(h \circ (f + g)\) (part 2), the outer value \(\delta_h = \varepsilon/ 3\) plays the role of \(\varepsilon\) for \(f + g\), so \(\delta= \delta_h / 2\).

The code draws many points \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\) at distance less than \(\delta\) from \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) and finds the largest change in each function.

set.seed(571)
eps <- 0.1
x <- c(1, 2)
f <- function(x) x[1]
g <- function(x) x[2]
h <- function(t) 3 * t

fun_sum <- function(x) f(x) + g(x)
fun_multiple <- function(x) 3 * f(x)
fun_composition <- function(x) h(fun_sum(x))

deltas <- c(
  sum = eps / 2,
  multiple = eps / (3 + 1),
  composition = (eps / 3) / 2
)
funs <- list(
  sum = fun_sum, multiple = fun_multiple, composition = fun_composition
)

n <- 10000L
largest_change <- sapply(names(funs), function(nm) {
  radius <- deltas[[nm]] * sqrt(runif(n))
  angle <- runif(n, 0, 2 * pi)
  y <- cbind(x[1] + radius * cos(angle), x[2] + radius * sin(angle))
  max(abs(apply(y, 1, funs[[nm]]) - funs[[nm]](x)))
})
data.frame(delta = deltas, largest_change = largest_change, eps = eps)


  



For 3 of the 3 functions, the largest change among the 10000 points is below \(\varepsilon= 0.1\), as Theorem 16 guarantees.










ExmExample 34 (Partial derivatives can exist where a function is not continuous)






Example 34 (Partial derivatives can exist where a function is not continuous) Let \(f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}\) be
\[
f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) =
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{x_1 x_2}{x_1^2 + x_2^2} & \text{if } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\ne \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}, \\
0 & \text{if } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}.
\end{cases}
\]
Both partial derivatives exist at \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\). For \(h \ne 0\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(h, 0) &= \frac{h \cdot 0}{h^2 + 0} \\
&= 0,
\end{aligned}
\]
so
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{f(0 + h, 0) - f(0, 0)}{h}
&= \frac{0 - 0}{h}
&& \text{(} f(h, 0) = 0 \text{ and } f(0, 0) = 0 \text{)}
\\
&= 0,
&& \text{(} 0 / h = 0 \text{ for } h \ne 0 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
and the limit as \(h \to 0\) is \(0\): \(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_1} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}) = 0\) (Definition 1). The same steps with \(f(0, h) = 0\) give \(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_2} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}) = 0\).
But \(f\) is not continuous at \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\) (Definition 22). Take \(\varepsilon= \tfrac{1}{4}\) and any \(\delta> 0\), and let \(t = \delta/ 2\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}= {(t, t)}^{\top}\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\right\rVert\mathclose{} &= \sqrt{t^2 + t^2} \\
&= t \sqrt{2} \\
&= \delta/ \sqrt{2} \\
&< \delta,
\end{aligned}
\]
but
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathopen{}\left|f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}) - f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}})\right|\mathclose{}
&= \mathopen{}\left|\frac{t \cdot t}{t^2 + t^2} - 0\right|\mathclose{}
&& \text{(} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\ne \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\text{, since } t > 0 \text{)}
\\
&= \frac{t^2}{2 t^2}
&& \text{(} t^2 + t^2 = 2 t^2 \text{)}
\\
&= \tfrac{1}{2},
&& \text{(cancel } t^2 > 0 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
which is more than \(\varepsilon= \tfrac{1}{4}\).
The partial derivatives only look along the two coordinate axes, where \(f\) is \(0\); along the line \(x_1 = x_2\), \(f\) is \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) everywhere except at \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\). So partial derivatives existing at a point says little about how \(f\) behaves near it.










LemTheorem 17 (Symmetry of the Hessian)






Theorem 17 (Symmetry of the Hessian) If the second partial derivatives of \(f\) exist and are continuous (Definition 22) on an open ball around \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) (Definition 16), then \(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i} \mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_j} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right)\mathclose{} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x_j} \mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right)\mathclose{}\) for all \(i, j\) [15], so \(\mathbf{H}_f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\) (Definition 21) is symmetric (symmetric matrix).




The proof applies the one-variable mean value theorem twice, which these notes do not develop; see [16], Theorem 9.41, which is stated for two variables: apply it to \(f\) as a function of \(x_i\) and \(x_j\), with the other coordinates held fixed.






ExmExample 35 (Mixed partial derivatives agree)






Example 35 (Mixed partial derivatives agree) In Example 29, the \((1, 2)\) and \((2, 1)\) entries of \(\mathbf{H}_f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\) are both \(2 e^{2x_1 + x_2}\).










ExmExample 36 (Without continuity, the mixed partials can differ)






Example 36 (Without continuity, the mixed partials can differ) Let \(f(x_1, x_2) = \dfrac{x_1 x_2 (x_1^2 - x_2^2)}{x_1^2 + x_2^2}\) for \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\ne \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\), and \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}) = 0\). For \(x_2 \ne 0\), the partial derivative (Definition 1) in \(x_1\) at \((0, x_2)\) is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial x_1} f(0, x_2)
&= \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(h, x_2) - f(0, x_2)}{h}
&& \text{(definition of the partial derivative, }\href{#def-partial-derivative}{\text{Definition~1}}\text{)}
\\
&= \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{x_2 (h^2 - x_2^2)}{h^2 + x_2^2}
&& \text{(} f(0, x_2) = 0 \text{; cancel } h \text{)}
\\
&= \frac{x_2 \cdot (-x_2^2)}{x_2^2} \\
&= -x_2,
&& \text{(the quotient is continuous at } h = 0 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial x_1} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}) &= \lim_{h \to 0} (0 - 0)/h \\
&= 0,
\end{aligned}
\]
so \(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_1} f(0, x_2) = -x_2\) holds at \(x_2 = 0\) too. In the same way, with the roles of \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) swapped, \(f(x_1, k) / k = x_1 (x_1^2 - k^2) / (x_1^2 + k^2) \to x_1\), so \(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_2} f(x_1, 0) = x_1\) for every \(x_1\). So at \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\) (Definition 21)
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathopen{}\left[\mathbf{H}_f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}})\right]\mathclose{}_{21}
&= \frac{\partial}{\partial x_2} \mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_1} f\right)\mathclose{} \\
&= \frac{d }{d x_2} (-x_2) \\
&= -1, \\
\mathopen{}\left[\mathbf{H}_f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}})\right]\mathclose{}_{12}
&= \frac{\partial}{\partial x_1} \mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_2} f\right)\mathclose{} \\
&= \frac{d }{d x_1} x_1 \\
&= 1:
\end{aligned}
\]
the Hessian at \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\) is not symmetric. By Theorem 17, then, the second partial derivatives of this \(f\) cannot all be continuous near \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\).










LemTheorem 18 (Hessian of a quadratic form)






Theorem 18 (Hessian of a quadratic form) If \(\mathbf{S}\) is a symmetric \(p \times p\) matrix that is constant with respect to \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\), then \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) has \(\mathbf{H}_f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = 2 \mathbf{S}\) for every \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\).










ProofProof






Proof. \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{H}_f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})
&= \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} {\mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} ({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right)\mathclose{}}^{\top}
&& \text{(}\href{#def-hessian}{\text{Definition~21}}\text{)}
\\
&= \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} {\mathopen{}\left(2 \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\right)\mathclose{}}^{\top}
&& \text{(}\href{#cor-quadratic-form-symmetric}{\text{Corollary~2}}\text{)}
\\
&= \mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\right)\mathclose{}\,{(2 \mathbf{S})}^{\top}
&& \text{(}\href{#thm-deriv-matrix-vector}{\text{Theorem~9}}\text{, with } \mathbf{A} = 2 \mathbf{S} \text{ and } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\text{; } \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} {(2 \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})}^{\top} = \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} (2 \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) \text{, }\href{#def-vector-valued-derivative}{\text{Definition~7}}\text{)}
\\
&= \mathbf{I}_p\,{(2 \mathbf{S})}^{\top}
&& \text{(} \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= \mathbf{I}_p \text{, }\href{#rem-deriv-matrix-vector-special-case}{\text{Remark~4}}\text{)}
\\
&= 2 \mathbf{S}.
&& \text{(} \mathbf{S} \text{ is symmetric)}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExmExample 37 (The Hessian of a \(2 \times 2\) quadratic form)






Example 37 (The Hessian of a \(2 \times 2\) quadratic form) For \(\mathbf{S} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\) as in Example 20, Theorem 18 gives \(\mathbf{H}_f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\). Directly, the gradient found there, with \(\beta_{i}\) renamed \(x_i\), is \({(6 x_1 + 2 x_2,\ 2 x_1 + 4 x_2)}^{\top}\), and differentiating its entries by \(x_1\) and by \(x_2\) (Definition 21) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{H}_f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})
&= \begin{bmatrix}
\frac{\partial}{\partial x_1} (6 x_1 + 2 x_2) & \frac{\partial}{\partial x_1} (2 x_1 + 4 x_2) \\
\frac{\partial}{\partial x_2} (6 x_1 + 2 x_2) & \frac{\partial}{\partial x_2} (2 x_1 + 4 x_2)
\end{bmatrix} \\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Proof Writing
text: This page collects general advice on how to write proofs and derivations. The goal of a proof is not just to convince yourself that a result is true; it is to convince a reader, and to show them why it is true. Each principle on this page serves that goal. The symbols for logical entailment are listed under Definitions for proofs below.

title: Proof Writing
text:
1 Definitions for proofs






DefDefinition 1 (Proposition, statement)






Definition 1 (Proposition, statement) A proposition [1], or statement, is a declarative sentence that is either true or false.










ExmExample 1 (Propositions, and a sentence that is not one)






Example 1 (Propositions, and a sentence that is not one)  

“\(2 + 3 = 5\)” is a proposition, and it is true.
“\(7\) is even” is a proposition, and it is false.
“\(x > 2\)” is not a proposition on its own: it is true when \(x = 3\) and false when \(x = 1\), so it has no truth value until \(x\) is given a value.











DefDefinition 2 (Predicate)






Definition 2 (Predicate) A predicate [2] \(P(x)\) is a declarative sentence about a variable \(x\) that becomes a proposition (Definition 1) whenever a value is substituted for \(x\).










ExmExample 2 (A predicate)






Example 2 (A predicate) Let \(P(x)\) be the predicate “\(x > 2\)”, for real numbers \(x\).


\(P(3)\) is the proposition “\(3 > 2\)”, which is true.

\(P(1)\) is the proposition “\(1 > 2\)”, which is false.











DefDefinition 3 (Logical connective)






Definition 3 (Logical connective) A logical connective [3] builds a new proposition (Definition 1) from one or two propositions \(P\) and \(Q\), with a truth value that depends only on the truth values of \(P\) and \(Q\). These notes use five, each defined next: not, and, or, implies, and if and only if. 










DefDefinition 4 (Not)






Definition 4 (Not) The logical connective (Definition 3) not [4] is written \(\neg P\) (“not \(P\)”); it is true when \(P\) is false, and false when \(P\) is true.










ExmExample 3 (Negating a true and a false proposition)






Example 3 (Negating a true and a false proposition) Let \(P\) be “\(5 > 3\)”, which is true, and let \(Q\) be “\(2 > 3\)”, which is false.


\(\neg P\), “it is not true that \(5 > 3\)”, is false, because \(P\) is true.

\(\neg Q\), “it is not true that \(2 > 3\)”, is true, because \(Q\) is false.











DefDefinition 5 (And)






Definition 5 (And) The logical connective (Definition 3) and is written [5] \(P \land Q\) (“\(P\) and \(Q\)”); it is true when \(P\) and \(Q\) are both true, and false otherwise.










ExmExample 4 (Two propositions joined by “and”)






Example 4 (Two propositions joined by “and”) Let \(P\) be “\(3 < 5\)”, which is true, let \(Q\) be “\(5 < 4\)”, which is false, and let \(R\) be “\(5 < 7\)”, which is true.


\(P \land R\) is true, because \(P\) and \(R\) are both true.

\(P \land Q\) is false, because \(Q\) is false.











DefDefinition 6 (Or)






Definition 6 (Or) The logical connective (Definition 3) or is written [6] \(P \lor Q\) (“\(P\) or \(Q\)”); it is true when at least one of \(P\) and \(Q\) is true, and false when both are false.










ExmExample 5 (Two propositions joined by “or”)






Example 5 (Two propositions joined by “or”) Let \(P\) be “\(3 < 2\)”, which is false, let \(Q\) be “\(5 < 7\)”, which is true, and let \(R\) be “\(5 < 4\)”, which is false.


\(P \lor Q\) is true, because \(Q\) is true.

\(P \lor R\) is false, because \(P\) and \(R\) are both false.











DefDefinition 7 (Implies)






Definition 7 (Implies) The logical connective (Definition 3) implies is written [7] \(P \Rightarrow Q\) (“if \(P\), then \(Q\)”, or “\(P\) implies \(Q\)”); it is false when \(P\) is true and \(Q\) is false, and true otherwise.










ExmExample 6 (Implications with a true and a false premise)






Example 6 (Implications with a true and a false premise) Take \(x = 3\).


\(x > 2 \Rightarrow x > 1\) is true: the premise \(3 > 2\) is true and the conclusion \(3 > 1\) is true.

\(x > 2 \Rightarrow x > 4\) is false: the premise \(3 > 2\) is true, but the conclusion \(3 > 4\) is false.

\(x > 5 \Rightarrow x > 4\) is true: the premise \(3 > 5\) is false, so the implication is true whatever the conclusion.











DefDefinition 8 (If and only if)






Definition 8 (If and only if) The logical connective (Definition 3) if and only if is written [8] \(P \Leftrightarrow Q\) (“\(P\) if and only if \(Q\)”); it is true when \(P\) and \(Q\) have the same truth value, and false otherwise.










ExmExample 7 (“If and only if” with equal and different truth values)






Example 7 (“If and only if” with equal and different truth values) Take \(x = 4\).

“\(x\) is even \(\Leftrightarrow x > 3\)” is true: \(4\) is even and \(4 > 3\), so both sides are true.
“\(x > 3 \Leftrightarrow x > 5\)” is false: \(4 > 3\) is true, but \(4 > 5\) is false.











ExmExample 8 (Truth values of connectives)






Example 8 (Truth values of connectives) Let \(P\) be “\(2 + 3 = 5\)”, which is true, and let \(Q\) be “\(7\) is even”, which is false.


\(\neg Q\), “\(7\) is not even”, is true, because \(Q\) is false.

\(P \land Q\) is false, because \(Q\) is false.

\(P \lor Q\) is true, because \(P\) is true.

\(P \Rightarrow Q\) is false, because \(P\) is true and \(Q\) is false.

\(Q \Rightarrow P\) is true, because \(Q\) is false.

\(P \Leftrightarrow Q\) is false, because \(P\) and \(Q\) have different truth values.











DefDefinition 9 (Truth table)






Definition 9 (Truth table) A truth table [9] for a proposition built from propositions \(P_1, \ldots, P_n\) with logical connectives has one row for each of the \(2^n\) combinations of truth values of \(P_1, \ldots, P_n\),  and gives the truth value of the proposition in each row. 










ExmExample 9 (A truth table for \(P \Rightarrow Q\))






Example 9 (A truth table for \(P \Rightarrow Q\)) The proposition \(P \Rightarrow Q\) is built from two propositions, so its truth table has \(2^2 = 4\) rows. By the definition of implies, \(P \Rightarrow Q\) is false only in the row where \(P\) is true and \(Q\) is false:

DefDefinition 10 (Logically equivalent)






Definition 10 (Logically equivalent) Two propositions \(A\) and \(B\), each built from some or all of the propositions \(P_1, \ldots, P_n\) with logical connectives, are logically equivalent [10], written \(A \equiv B\), when they have the same truth value  in every row of a truth table on \(P_1, \ldots, P_n\).










ExmExample 10 (\(P \Rightarrow Q\) is logically equivalent to \(\neg P \lor Q\))






Example 10 (\(P \Rightarrow Q\) is logically equivalent to \(\neg P \lor Q\)) Adding a column for \(\neg P \lor Q\) to the truth table of Example 9 gives:

The last two columns agree in every row, so \((P \Rightarrow Q) \equiv (\neg P \lor Q)\).










LemTheorem 1 (De Morgan’s laws for propositions)






Theorem 1 (De Morgan’s laws for propositions) For any propositions \(P\) and \(Q\) [11]:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\neg (P \land Q) &\equiv \neg P \lor \neg Q \\
\neg (P \lor Q) &\equiv \neg P \land \neg Q
\end{aligned}
\]










ProofProof






Proof. Each side of each law is built from \(P\) and \(Q\), so by Definition 10 it is enough to compare the two sides in each of the four rows of a truth table:










\(P\)
\(Q\)
\(\neg (P \land Q)\)
\(\neg P \lor \neg Q\)
\(\neg (P \lor Q)\)
