Together, Theorem 2 and Theorem 3 establish the chain:
\[\text{differentiable on } [a, b] \;\Rightarrow\; \text{continuous on } [a, b] \;\Rightarrow\; \text{integrable on } [a, b]\]
Example 16 and Example 18 show that neither implication reverses in general.






LemTheorem 4 (Equal-width Riemann sums converge to the integral)






Theorem 4 (Equal-width Riemann sums converge to the integral) If \(f\) is Riemann integrable on \([a, b]\) (Definition 13), then for every choice of the sample points \(x_i^*\), the equal-width Riemann sums (Definition 15) converge to the integral:
\[\lim_{n \to \infty} S_n = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx.\]










ProofProof






Proof. The \(n\) equal-width subintervals form a partition of \([a, b]\) whose mesh (Definition 9) is \((b - a)/n\), which goes to \(0\) as \(n \to \infty\). So \(S_n\) is one of the sums in the limit that defines the integral (Definition 12), along a sequence of partitions whose mesh goes to \(0\), and a limit that has the same value for every choice of partitions has that value along this sequence too.










ExmExample 19 (Equal-width sums for \(\int_0^1 x\,dx\))






Example 19 (Equal-width sums for \(\int_0^1 x\,dx\)) Let \(f(x) = x\) on \([0, 1]\), which is continuous and so Riemann integrable (Theorem 3), and take each sample point at the right end of its subinterval, \(x_i^* = i/n\). With \(\Delta x = 1/n\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_n
&= \sum_{i=1}^n\frac{i}{n} \cdot\frac{1}{n}
&& \text{(equal-width Riemann sum with } x_i^* = i/n \text{)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{n^2} \sum_{i=1}^ni
&& \text{(factor out } 1/n^2 \text{)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{n^2} \cdot\frac{n(n+1)}{2}
&& \text{(sum of the first } n \text{ integers)}
\\
&= \frac{n+1}{2n}
&& \text{(cancel one factor of } n \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
So \(S_{10} = 0.55\), \(S_{100} = 0.505\), \(S_{1000} = 0.5005\), and \(S_n \to \frac{1}{2}\) as \(n \to \infty\). By Theorem 4, \(\int_0^1 x\,dx = \frac{1}{2}\).











DefDefinition 16 (Accumulation function)






Definition 16 (Accumulation function) Let \(f\) be Riemann integrable on \([a, b]\) (Definition 13). The accumulation function of \(f\) from \(a\) is the function \(F\) on \([a, b]\) with \(F(a) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}0\) and
\[F(x) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\int_a^x f(t)\,dt \quad \text{for } a < x \le b.\]
So \(F(x)\) is the integral of \(f\) accumulated from \(a\) up to \(x\).










ExmExample 20 (The accumulation function of a constant)






Example 20 (The accumulation function of a constant) Let \(f(t) = 2\) on \([0, 3]\), which is Riemann integrable (Example 12). For \(0 < x \le 3\), the computation of Example 12, with the interval \([0, 3]\) replaced by \([0, x]\), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
F(x)
&= \int_0^x 2\,dt
&& \text{(definition of the accumulation function)}
\\
&= 2 \cdot(x - 0)
&& \text{(every Riemann sum is } 2 \text{ times the total width } x - 0 \text{)}
\\
&= 2x
&& \text{(subtract)}
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
F(0) &= 0 \\
&= 2 \cdot 0
\end{aligned}
\]
too. For example,
\[
\begin{aligned}
F(1.5) &= 2 \cdot 1.5 \\
&= 3,
\end{aligned}
\]
the area of a rectangle of height \(2\) and width \(1.5\).










RemarkRemark 2 (Why the integration variable is called \(t\))






Remark 2 (Why the integration variable is called \(t\)). The letter \(t\) inside the integral is a placeholder, renamed from \(x\) so that \(x\) can serve as the upper limit.











LemTheorem 5 (Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 1 (derivative of an integral))






Theorem 5 (Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 1 (derivative of an integral)) Let \(f\) be a continuous function on a closed interval \([a, b]\). Let \(F(x) = \int_a^x f(t)\,dt\) for \(x \in [a, b]\) be the accumulation function of \(f\) from \(a\) (Definition 16). Then \(F\) is differentiable and:
\[\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\int_a^x f(t)\,dt = f(x) \tag{1}\]






Note



Continuity on all of \([a, b]\) is a sufficient condition. More generally, Part 1 holds at any individual point \(x\) where \(f\) is integrable on \([a, b]\) (see Definition 13) and continuous at \(x\) (see Definition 4), even if \(f\) has jump discontinuities (Definition 6) elsewhere [8], Theorem 6.20, p. 133. This result is the first part of the fundamental theorem of calculus [9].


[2], Theorem 4.11, p. 288










LemTheorem 6 (Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 2 (evaluation theorem))






Theorem 6 (Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 2 (evaluation theorem)) Let \(f\) be a continuous function on a closed interval \([a, b]\). The \(F\) here may be any antiderivative of \(f\) — not just the accumulation function from Theorem 5. If \(F\) is an antiderivative of \(f\) on \([a, b]\) (i.e., \(\frac{\partial}{\partial x} F(x) = f(x)\) for all \(x \in [a, b]\)), then:
\[\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a) \tag{2}\]
Equivalently, with \(b\) replaced by a variable upper limit \(x\), integrating the derivative of \(F\) recovers the net change in \(F\):
\[\int_a^x F'(t)\,dt = F(x) - F(a) \tag{3}\]
or equivalently in Leibniz notation:
\[\int_a^x \frac{d F}{d t}\,dt = F(x) - F(a)\]
[10, Ch. 18], [2], Theorem 4.9, p. 282




The two parts of the FTC together express that differentiation and integration are inverse operations:

Part 1: differentiating the integral of \(f\) recovers \(f\) (Equation 1).
Part 2: the integral of \(f\) over \([a, b]\) equals the difference of any antiderivative’s values at the endpoints (Equation 2), which rearranges to “integrating the derivative of \(F\) recovers the net change in \(F\)” (Equation 3).

The standard form of the FTC assumes \(f\) is continuous on \([a, b]\); continuity is sufficient but not strictly necessary (see the callout note inside Theorem 5 for the more general statement). Since differentiability implies continuity (Theorem 2), the FTC applies in particular whenever \(f\) is differentiable — a common situation in applied statistics.






DefDefinition 17 (Evaluation bracket)






Definition 17 (Evaluation bracket) For a function \(F\) and numbers \(a\) and \(b\) where \(F\) is defined, the evaluation bracket is the difference
\[\mathopen{}\left[F(t)\right]\mathclose{}_{t=a}^{t=b} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}F(b) - F(a).\]
When the variable is clear from the context, it is written \(\mathopen{}\left[F(t)\right]\mathclose{}_a^b\). Computing \(F(b) - F(a)\) from the bracket is called evaluating at the limits (the limits of integration \(a\) and \(b\)).










ExmExample 21 (Evaluating \(\int_1^3 2t\,dt\) with a bracket)






Example 21 (Evaluating \(\int_1^3 2t\,dt\) with a bracket) \(F(t) = t^2\) is an antiderivative of \(f(t) = 2t\), since \(\frac{\partial}{\partial t} t^2 = 2t\), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_1^3 2t\,dt
&= \mathopen{}\left[t^2\right]\mathclose{}_{t=1}^{t=3}
&& \text{(FTC Part 2)}
\\
&= 3^2 - 1^2
&& \text{(definition of the evaluation bracket)}
\\
&= 9 - 1
&& \text{(square)}
\\
&= 8
&& \text{(subtract)}
\end{aligned}
\]










RemarkRemark 3 (The evaluation bracket and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus)






Remark 3 (The evaluation bracket and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus). With FTC Part 2 (Theorem 6), \(\int_a^b f(t)\,dt = \mathopen{}\left[F(t)\right]\mathclose{}_{t=a}^{t=b}\) for any antiderivative \(F\) of a continuous \(f\).










ExrExercise 1 (Definite integral of a polynomial)






Exercise 1 (Definite integral of a polynomial) Adapted from Miller [11], Question 1.1.31.
Evaluate the integral:
\[\int_0^1 (x^4 + x^2 + 1)\,dx\]










SolutionSolution 1






Solution 1. Integrate term by term using the power rule for integration:
\[\begin{aligned}
\int_0^1 (x^4 + x^2 + 1)\,dx &= \mathopen{}\left[\frac{x^5}{5} + \frac{x^3}{3} + x\right]\mathclose{}_0^1
\\
&= \mathopen{}\left(\frac{1}{5} + \frac{1}{3} + 1\right)\mathclose{} - 0 \\
&= \frac{3 + 5 + 15}{15} \\
&= \frac{23}{15}
\end{aligned}\]










ExrExercise 2 (Integral of a perfect square)






Exercise 2 (Integral of a perfect square) Adapted from Miller [11], Question 1.1.32.
Evaluate the integral:
\[\int_0^1 (x^2 + 2x + 1)\,dx\]










SolutionSolution 2






Solution 2. Notice that the integrand is a perfect square: \(x^2 + 2x + 1 = (x + 1)^2\).
With substitution \(u = x + 1\) (where \(du = dx\)):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^1 (x + 1)^2\,dx
&= \mathopen{}\left[\frac{(x + 1)^3}{3}\right]\mathclose{}_0^1 \\
&= \frac{2^3}{3} - \frac{1^3}{3} \\
&= \frac{8 - 1}{3} \\
&= \frac{7}{3}
\end{aligned}
\]
Alternative (term by term):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathopen{}\left[\frac{x^3}{3} + x^2 + x\right]\mathclose{}_0^1
&= \frac{1}{3} + 1 + 1 \\
&= \frac{7}{3}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExrExercise 3 (Integral of a composite power)






Exercise 3 (Integral of a composite power) Adapted from Miller [11], Question 1.1.33.
Evaluate the integral:
\[\int_0^1 (x^2 + 2x + 1)^2\,dx\]










SolutionSolution 3






Solution 3. Recognize that \(x^2 + 2x + 1 = (x + 1)^2\), so the integrand is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
(x^2 + 2x + 1)^2
&= \mathopen{}\left[(x + 1)^2\right]\mathclose{}^2 \\
&= (x + 1)^4
\end{aligned}
\]
Using the substitution \(u = x + 1\) with \(du = dx\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^1 (x + 1)^4\,dx
&= \mathopen{}\left[\frac{(x + 1)^5}{5}\right]\mathclose{}_0^1 \\
&= \frac{2^5 - 1^5}{5} \\
&= \frac{32 - 1}{5} \\
&= \frac{31}{5}
\end{aligned}
\]
Remark: Do not mistakenly write \(\int (x^2 + 2x + 1)^2\,dx = \frac{(x^2 + 2x + 1)^3}{3}\); that formula requires the derivative of the inside function (\(2x + 2\)) to be present as a factor in the integrand.










ExrExercise 4 (Integral of odd trigonometric functions)






Exercise 4 (Integral of odd trigonometric functions) Adapted from Miller [11], Question 1.1.34.
Evaluate the integral:
\[\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} (\sin^3 x \cos x + \sin x \cos x)\,dx\]










SolutionSolution 4






Solution 4. Because \(\sin(-x) = -\sin x\) and \(\cos(-x) = \cos x\):
\[\sin^3(-x)\cos(-x) + \sin(-x)\cos(-x) = -\sin^3 x \cos x - \sin x \cos x\]
The integrand is an odd function. The integral of any continuous odd function over a symmetric interval \([-a, a]\) is zero:
\[\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} (\sin^3 x \cos x + \sin x \cos x)\,dx = 0\]
Alternative (by substitution): Set \(u = \sin x\), so \(du = \cos x\,dx\). As \(x\) ranges from \(-\pi/2\) to \(\pi/2\), \(u\) ranges from \(-1\) to \(1\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{-1}^1 (u^3 + u)\,du
&= \mathopen{}\left[\frac{u^4}{4} + \frac{u^2}{2}\right]\mathclose{}_{-1}^1 \\
&= \mathopen{}\left(\frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{2}\right)\mathclose{} - \mathopen{}\left(\frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{2}\right)\mathclose{} \\
&= 0
\end{aligned}
\]










ExrExercise 5 (Separating even and odd parts of a polynomial)






Exercise 5 (Separating even and odd parts of a polynomial) Adapted from Miller [11], Question 1.1.35.
Evaluate the integral:
\[\int_{-4}^4 (x^3 + 6x^2 - 2x - 3)\,dx\]










SolutionSolution 5






Solution 5. Split the integrand into its odd part \(x^3 - 2x\) and its even part \(6x^2 - 3\):
\[\int_{-4}^4 (x^3 - 2x)\,dx = 0\]
The even part doubles over the half-interval \([0, 4]\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{-4}^4 (6x^2 - 3)\,dx
&= 2\int_0^4 (6x^2 - 3)\,dx \\
&= 2\mathopen{}\left[2x^3 - 3x\right]\mathclose{}_0^4 \\
&= 2\mathopen{}\left[2(64) - 3(4)\right]\mathclose{} \\
&= 2(128 - 12) \\
&= 232
\end{aligned}
\]










ExrExercise 6 (Substitution leading to a natural logarithm)






Exercise 6 (Substitution leading to a natural logarithm) Adapted from Miller [11], Question 1.1.36.
Evaluate the integral:
\[\int_0^1 \frac{x}{1 + x^2}\,dx\]










SolutionSolution 6






Solution 6. Let \(u = 1 + x^2\). Then \(du = 2x\,dx\), so \(x\,dx = \frac{1}{2}du\).
Transform the limits of integration:


When \(x = 0\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
u &= 1 + 0^2 \\
&= 1.
\end{aligned}
\]


When \(x = 1\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
u &= 1 + 1^2 \\
&= 2.
\end{aligned}
\]


Applying the substitution:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^1 \frac{x}{1 + x^2}\,dx
&= \frac{1}{2}\int_1^2 \frac{du}{u} \\
&= \frac{1}{2}\mathopen{}\left[\log u\right]\mathclose{}_1^2 \\
&= \frac{1}{2}(\log 2 - \log 1) \\
&= \frac{\log 2}{2}
\end{aligned}
\]
Remark: When using \(u\)-substitution with definite integrals, the transformation \(x \mapsto u(x)\) must be one-to-one on the domain of integration.










ExrExercise 7 (Substitution with a polynomial power)






Exercise 7 (Substitution with a polynomial power) Adapted from Miller [11], Question 1.1.37.
Evaluate the integral:
\[\int_0^3 (x^3 + 3x)^8 (x^2 + 1)\,dx\]










SolutionSolution 7






Solution 7. Let \(u = x^3 + 3x\). Then:
\[
\begin{aligned}
du
&= (3x^2 + 3)\,dx \\
&= 3(x^2 + 1)\,dx \\
\implies (x^2 + 1)\,dx
&= \frac{du}{3}
\end{aligned}
\]
Limits:

When \(x = 0\): \(u = 0\).

When \(x = 3\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
u &= 3^3 + 3(3) \\
&= 27 + 9 \\
&= 36.
\end{aligned}
\]


Substitute:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^3 (x^3 + 3x)^8 (x^2 + 1)\,dx
&= \frac{1}{3}\int_0^{36} u^8\,du \\
&= \frac{1}{3}\mathopen{}\left[\frac{u^9}{9}\right]\mathclose{}_0^{36} \\
&= \frac{36^9}{27}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExrExercise 8 (Substitution with a trigonometric integrand)






Exercise 8 (Substitution with a trigonometric integrand) Adapted from Miller [11], Question 1.1.38.
Evaluate the integral:
\[\int_0^2 x\cos(3x^2)\,dx\]










SolutionSolution 8






Solution 8. Let \(u = 3x^2\). Then \(du = 6x\,dx\), meaning \(x\,dx = \frac{du}{6}\).
Limits:

When \(x = 0\): \(u = 0\).

When \(x = 2\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
u &= 3(2^2) \\
&= 12.
\end{aligned}
\]


Substitute:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^2 x\cos(3x^2)\,dx
&= \frac{1}{6}\int_0^{12} \cos u\,du \\
&= \frac{1}{6}\mathopen{}\left[\sin u\right]\mathclose{}_0^{12} \\
&= \frac{\sin 12}{6}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExrExercise 9 (Integration by parts with an exponential factor)






Exercise 9 (Integration by parts with an exponential factor) Adapted from Miller [11], Question 1.1.40.
Evaluate the integral:
\[\int_a^b x^3 {\operatorname{exp}\mathopen{}\left\{-\frac{x^2}{2}\right\}\mathclose{}}\,dx\]










SolutionSolution 9






Solution 9. Factor the integrand as \(x^2 \cdot\mathopen{}\left(x {\operatorname{exp}\mathopen{}\left\{-x^2/2\right\}\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}\). Set:
\[u = x^2, \qquad dv = x{\operatorname{exp}\mathopen{}\left\{-\frac{x^2}{2}\right\}\mathclose{}}\,dx\]
Then \(du = 2x\,dx\) and \(v = -{\operatorname{exp}\mathopen{}\left\{-x^2/2\right\}\mathclose{}}\).
Using integration by parts (\(\int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du\)):
\[\begin{aligned}
\int_a^b x^3 {\operatorname{exp}\mathopen{}\left\{-\frac{x^2}{2}\right\}\mathclose{}}\,dx &= \mathopen{}\left[-x^2 {\operatorname{exp}\mathopen{}\left\{-\frac{x^2}{2}\right\}\mathclose{}}\right]\mathclose{}_a^b - \int_a^b \mathopen{}\left[-{\operatorname{exp}\mathopen{}\left\{-\frac{x^2}{2}\right\}\mathclose{}}\right]\mathclose{}(2x\,dx)
\\
&= \mathopen{}\left[-x^2 {\operatorname{exp}\mathopen{}\left\{-\frac{x^2}{2}\right\}\mathclose{}}\right]\mathclose{}_a^b + 2\int_a^b x{\operatorname{exp}\mathopen{}\left\{-\frac{x^2}{2}\right\}\mathclose{}}\,dx
\\
&= \mathopen{}\left[-x^2 {\operatorname{exp}\mathopen{}\left\{-\frac{x^2}{2}\right\}\mathclose{}}\right]\mathclose{}_a^b + 2\mathopen{}\left[-{\operatorname{exp}\mathopen{}\left\{-\frac{x^2}{2}\right\}\mathclose{}}\right]\mathclose{}_a^b
\\
&= \mathopen{}\left[-(x^2 + 2){\operatorname{exp}\mathopen{}\left\{-\frac{x^2}{2}\right\}\mathclose{}}\right]\mathclose{}_a^b
\\
&= (a^2 + 2){\operatorname{exp}\mathopen{}\left\{-\frac{a^2}{2}\right\}\mathclose{}} - (b^2 + 2){\operatorname{exp}\mathopen{}\left\{-\frac{b^2}{2}\right\}\mathclose{}}
\end{aligned}\]










ExmExample 22 (FTC Part 1 visualized: accumulation function for \(f(t) = 2t\))






Example 22 (FTC Part 1 visualized: accumulation function for \(f(t) = 2t\)) Take \(f(t) = 2t\) on \([0, 2]\). The accumulation function from \(0\) is
\[
\begin{aligned}
F(x) \;
&\stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\; \int_0^x 2t\,dt \; \\
&=\; \mathopen{}\left[t^2\right]\mathclose{}_{t=0}^{t=x} \; \\
&=\; x^2 - 0^2 \; \\
&=\; x^2,
\end{aligned}
\]
so \(F(x) = x^2\), and indeed
\[
\begin{aligned}
F'(x) &= 2x \\
&= f(x),
\end{aligned}
\]
as Theorem 5 predicts. Figure 4 shows the integrand on the left (shaded area equals \(F(x)\) at each \(x\)) and the accumulation function \(F(x) = x^2\) on the right (its slope at \(x\) equals \(f(x) = 2x\)).








Figure 4: vertical lines mark \(x \in \{1, 1.5, 2\}\). Right: \(F(x) = x^2\); for each marked \(x\), the tangent slope equals \(f(x) = 2x\).

\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^{1.5} 2t\,dt &= F(1.5) \\
&= 2.25;
\end{aligned}
\]


















ExmExample 23 (CDF and PDF of the exponential distribution)






Example 23 (CDF and PDF of the exponential distribution) In what follows, \(f\) denotes the PDF and \(F\) the CDF — the same letters as the antiderivative pair in Definition 1, because the FTC will show \(F\) is exactly an antiderivative of \(f\).
Let \(T\) be a random variable with the exponential distribution with rate \({\lambda}> 0\). Its probability density function (PDF) is [12, Sec. II], p. 295, “Survival and Hazard Functions for Selected Distributions”:
\[f(t) = {\lambda}\text{e}^{-{\lambda}t}, \quad t \ge 0\]
FTC Part 2 gives the cumulative distribution function (CDF), \(F(t) = P(T \le t)\), from the PDF. Apply the \(\text{e}^{cx}\) rule from Theorem 1 with \(c = -{\lambda}\) to antidifferentiate the integrand:
\[
\begin{aligned}
F(t)
&= \int_0^t {\lambda}\text{e}^{-{\lambda}u}\,du
&& \text{(the CDF integrates the PDF)}
\\
&= \mathopen{}\left[{\lambda}\cdot\frac{1}{-{\lambda}}\text{e}^{-{\lambda}u}\right]\mathclose{}_{u=0}^{u=t}
&& \text{(FTC Part 2, with the } \text{e}^{cx} \text{ rule)}
\\
&= \mathopen{}\left[(-1)\text{e}^{-{\lambda}u}\right]\mathclose{}_{u=0}^{u=t}
&& \text{(} {\lambda}/ (-{\lambda}) = -1 \text{)}
\\
&= \mathopen{}\left[-\text{e}^{-{\lambda}u}\right]\mathclose{}_{u=0}^{u=t}
&& \text{(multiply by } -1 \text{)}
\\
&= -\text{e}^{-{\lambda}t} - \mathopen{}\left(-\text{e}^{0}\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(evaluate at the limits)}
\\
&= -\text{e}^{-{\lambda}t} - (-1)
&& \text{(} \text{e}^{0} = 1 \text{)}
\\
&= 1 - \text{e}^{-{\lambda}t}
&& \text{(rearrange)}
\end{aligned}
\]
FTC Part 1 recovers the PDF from the CDF:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial t} F(t)
&= \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\mathopen{}\left(1 - \text{e}^{-{\lambda}t}\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(substitute } F \text{)}
\\
&= \frac{\partial}{\partial t} 1 - \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \text{e}^{-{\lambda}t}
&& \text{(derivative of a difference)}
\\
&= 0 - \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \text{e}^{-{\lambda}t}
&& \text{(constant rule)}
\\
&= 0 - \text{e}^{-{\lambda}t} \cdot\frac{\partial}{\partial t}(-{\lambda}t)
&& \text{(chain rule, with inner function } -{\lambda}t \text{)}
\\
&= 0 - \text{e}^{-{\lambda}t} \cdot(-{\lambda})
&& \text{(constant multiple rule)}
\\
&= {\lambda}\text{e}^{-{\lambda}t}
&& \text{(simplify)}
\\
&= f(t)
&& \text{(definition of } f \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
For a concrete instance: with \({\lambda}= 1\), the probability that \(T \le 2\) is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
F(2)
&= 1 - \text{e}^{-1 \cdot 2} \\
&= 1 - \text{e}^{-2} \\
&\approx 1 - 0.135 \\
&= 0.865
\end{aligned}
\]
See Figure 5.








Figure 5: Exponential distribution with \({\lambda}= 1\). Left: the PDF \(f(t) = {\lambda}\text{e}^{-{\lambda}t}\); the shaded area under the curve from \(0\) to \(2\) equals \(F(2) \approx 0.865\). Right: the CDF \(F(t) = 1 - \text{e}^{-{\lambda}t}\); the dashed lines mark the value \(F(2)\) computed via FTC Part 2.

ExrExercise 10 (Improper Gaussian-kernel integral)






Exercise 10 (Improper Gaussian-kernel integral) Adapted from Miller [11], Question 1.1.39.
Evaluate the improper integral:
\[\int_0^\infty x{\operatorname{exp}\mathopen{}\left\{-\frac{x^2}{4}\right\}\mathclose{}}\,dx\]










SolutionSolution 10






Solution 10. Let \(u = x^2/4\). Then \(du = \frac{x}{2}\,dx\), so \(x\,dx = 2\,du\).
Limits:

As \(x \to 0\): \(u \to 0\).
As \(x \to \infty\): \(u \to \infty\).

Substitute:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^\infty x{\operatorname{exp}\mathopen{}\left\{-\frac{x^2}{4}\right\}\mathclose{}}\,dx
&= 2\int_0^\infty e^{-u}\,du \\
&= 2\mathopen{}\left[-e^{-u}\right]\mathclose{}_0^\infty \\
&= 2\mathopen{}\left(0 - (-1)\right)\mathclose{} \\
&= 2
\end{aligned}
\]
Remark: Integrals of this structure arise directly in calculating moments and normalization constants for Gaussian and Rayleigh probability distributions.










ExrExercise 11 (Convolution of two uniform densities)






Exercise 11 (Convolution of two uniform densities) Adapted from Miller [11], Question 1.1.41.
Let \(f(x) = \mathbb{1}_{[0, 1]}(x)\) be the indicator of the unit interval:
\[f(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } x \in [0, 1] \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]
Evaluate the convolution:
\[(f * f)(x) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(t)f(x - t)\,dt\]
for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\).










SolutionSolution 11






Solution 11. The integrand \(f(t)f(x - t)\) equals \(1\) when both \(t \in [0, 1]\) and \(x - t \in [0, 1]\), and equals \(0\) otherwise.
The condition \(0 \le x - t \le 1\) rearranges to:
\[x - 1 \le t \le x\]
For this interval to overlap with \(t \in [0, 1]\), we must have \(x \ge 0\) and \(x - 1 \le 1\), meaning \(0 \le x \le 2\). Outside \([0, 2]\), \((f * f)(x) = 0\).
For \(x \in [0, 2]\), we distinguish two cases:


Case 1: \(0 \le x \le 1\). The overlapping bounds for \(t\) are \([0, x]\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
(f * f)(x)
&= \int_0^x 1\,dt \\
&= x
\end{aligned}
\]


Case 2: \(1 \le x \le 2\). The overlapping bounds for \(t\) are \([x - 1, 1]\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
(f * f)(x)
&= \int_{x-1}^1 1\,dt \\
&= 1 - (x - 1) \\
&= 2 - x
\end{aligned}
\]


Combining the cases:
\[(f * f)(x) = \begin{cases} x & \text{if } 0 \le x \le 1 \\ 2 - x & \text{if } 1 < x \le 2 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]
Remark: In probability theory, if \(X_1, X_2 \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)\) independently, the probability density function of their sum \(S = X_1 + X_2\) is the convolution of their individual densities, producing this symmetric triangular distribution on \([0, 2]\).










LemTheorem 7 (Convolution of two uniform densities)






Theorem 7 (Convolution of two uniform densities) Let \(f(x) = \mathbb{1}_{[0, 1]}(x)\) be the indicator of the unit interval. Then for every \(x \in \mathbb{R}\),
\[
(f * f)(x) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(t)f(x - t)\,dt
= \begin{cases}
x & \text{if } 0 \le x \le 1 \\
2 - x & \text{if } 1 < x \le 2 \\
0 & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]










ProofProof






Proof. This is the solution to Exercise 11, worked in Solution 11.
The integrand \(f(t)f(x - t)\) equals \(1\) when both \(t \in [0, 1]\) and \(x - t \in [0, 1]\), and \(0\) otherwise. The second condition is \(x - 1 \le t \le x\), so the integrand is \(1\) exactly on the overlap \([\max(0, x - 1), \min(1, x)]\), and the integral is the length of that overlap.

If \(x < 0\) or \(x > 2\), the overlap is empty, so \((f * f)(x) = 0\).
If \(0 \le x \le 1\), the overlap is \([0, x]\), so \((f * f)(x) = \int_0^x 1\,dt = x\).
If \(1 < x \le 2\), the overlap is \([x - 1, 1]\), so \((f * f)(x) = \int_{x-1}^1 1\,dt = 2 - x\).

title: Expressions and Algorithms
text:
RemarkRemark






Remark. A function can be written down as an expression and computed by an algorithm. This page defines expressions, which write down the functions in the Morrison Lab’s probability and statistics notes, the parse trees of expressions, and algorithms, which compute those functions.

title: Expressions and Algorithms
text:
1 Expressions






DefDefinition 1 (Expression)






Definition 1 (Expression) An expression [1] is a string of symbols, built from constants, variables, operations and function names according to the rules of the notation.










DefDefinition 2 (Denotes)






Definition 2 (Denotes) An expression denotes a function when evaluating the expression at each input of the function, with the expression’s variables taking that input, gives the function’s value at that input.










ExmExample 1 (Two expressions for one function)






Example 1 (Two expressions for one function) The expressions \(a x^2 + b x + c\) and \((a x + b)\,x + c\) denote the same function of \(x\) for any fixed \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\), because they give the same value at every \(x\).
Precedence parses \(a x^2 + b x + c\) as a sum of three terms: the power \(x^2\) is applied first, then \(a\) multiplies \(x^2\) and \(b\) multiplies \(x\), and the three products are added. The parentheses in \((a x + b)\,x + c\) force a different tree: \(a\) multiplies \(x\), \(b\) is added, the sum multiplies \(x\), and \(c\) is added.










DefDefinition 3 (Closed-form expression (formula))






Definition 3 (Closed-form expression (formula)) A closed-form expression (or formula) [2] is an expression built from constants and variables  using a finite number of operations from a list of accepted functions,  such as powers, roots, exponentials, logarithms, and trigonometric functions. Which functions are accepted is a convention, and a source states it when the boundary matters.










ExmExample 2 (The quadratic formula)






Example 2 (The quadratic formula) For \(a \neq 0\) with \(b^2 - 4 a c \ge 0\), the roots of \(a x^2 + b x + c = 0\) are
\[
x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4 a c}}{2 a},
\]
where the right-hand side is a closed-form expression in \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\). By contrast, no closed-form expression is known for the root of \(x - \cos x = 0\).










DefDefinition 4 (Closed-form solution)






Definition 4 (Closed-form solution) A closed-form solution of a problem, such as solving an equation or minimizing a function, is a closed-form expression for the answer.










ExmExample 3 (Least squares versus logistic regression)






Example 3 (Least squares versus logistic regression) Minimizing the squared-error cost of a linear model over \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\) gives the normal equations \({D}^{\top} D \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}= {D}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\). When \({D}^{\top} D\) is invertible, the unique minimizer is
\[
\hat{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}}= {\mathopen{}\left({D}^{\top} D\right)\mathclose{}}^{-1} {D}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}},
\]
whose right-hand side is a closed-form expression, so least squares has a closed-form solution.
For logistic regression, no closed-form expression is known for a minimizer of the negative log-likelihood over \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}\), so that problem has no known closed-form solution. When a minimizer exists, an iterative method approximates it. 










DefDefinition 5 (Parse tree)






Definition 5 (Parse tree) The parse tree [3] of an expression is the tree that shows how its symbols group into operations. Its leaves are the constants and variables of the expression, and each internal node is an operation applied to the nodes below it.










ExmExample 4 (The parse tree of a polynomial)






Example 4 (The parse tree of a polynomial) The parse tree of \((a x + b)\,x + c\), with each operation having two children, is drawn in Figure 1 (left) and written out as a list here:

the root \(+\), whose children are

the node \(\times\), whose children are

the node \(+\), whose children are

the node \(\times\), whose children are the leaves \(a\) and \(x\),
the leaf \(b\);


the leaf \(x\);


the leaf \(c\).



Read from the leaves up, the tree says to multiply \(a\) by \(x\), add \(b\), multiply by \(x\), and add \(c\). The expression \(a x^2 + b x + c\) has a different tree (Figure 1, right). Its root is the \(+\) whose children are \(a x^2 + b x\) and \(c\), and the first of these is a \(+\) whose children are \(a x^2\) and \(b x\).










Show R code# Each tree is a nested list: the first element is the node's label,
# and the remaining elements are its children.
times <- intToUtf8(215)
trees <- list(
  "(a * x + b) * x + c" = list(
    "+",
    list(times, list("+", list(times, "a", "x"), "b"), "x"),
    "c"
  ),
  "a * x^2 + b * x + c" = list(
    "+",
    list(
      "+",
      list(times, "a", list("^", "x", "2")),
      list(times, "b", "x")
    ),
    "c"
  )
)

# Leaves sit at consecutive x positions;
# each operation sits above the mean of its children.
layout_tree <- function(node, depth = 0, next_x = 0) {
  if (!is.list(node)) {
    return(list(
      nodes = data.frame(label = node, x = next_x, y = -depth, is_leaf = TRUE),
      edges = NULL,
      next_x = next_x + 1
    ))
  }
  nodes <- NULL
  edges <- NULL
  child_x <- numeric()
  for (child in node[-1]) {
    sub <- layout_tree(child, depth + 1, next_x)
    next_x <- sub$next_x
    child_x <- c(child_x, sub$nodes$x[1])
    edges <- rbind(
      edges,
      sub$edges,
      data.frame(
        x = NA_real_,
        y = -depth,
        xend = sub$nodes$x[1],
        yend = sub$nodes$y[1]
      )
    )
    nodes <- rbind(nodes, sub$nodes)
  }
  me <- data.frame(
    label = node[[1]],
    x = mean(child_x),
    y = -depth,
    is_leaf = FALSE
  )
  edges$x[is.na(edges$x)] <- me$x
  list(nodes = rbind(me, nodes), edges = edges, next_x = next_x)
}

laid_out <- lapply(trees, layout_tree)
tree_nodes <- do.call(rbind, Map(
  function(res, name) cbind(res$nodes, tree = name),
  laid_out,
  names(trees)
))
tree_edges <- do.call(rbind, Map(
  function(res, name) cbind(res$edges, tree = name),
  laid_out,
  names(trees)
))
tree_nodes$kind <- ifelse(tree_nodes$is_leaf, "leaf", "operation")
tree_nodes$tree <- factor(tree_nodes$tree, levels = names(trees))
tree_edges$tree <- factor(tree_edges$tree, levels = names(trees))

ggplot2::ggplot() +
  ggplot2::geom_segment(
    data = tree_edges,
    ggplot2::aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    colour = "grey50"
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_label(
    data = tree_nodes,
    ggplot2::aes(x = x, y = y, label = label, fill = kind),
    size = 5,
    linewidth = 0
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(operation = "#CCE5F6", leaf = "#F9DDBF")
  ) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(
    ~tree,
    scales = "free_x",
    labeller = ggplot2::label_parsed
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(fill = "node type") +
  ggplot2::theme_void() +
  ggplot2::theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(size = 12)
  )


Figure 1: The parse trees of \((a x + b)\,x + c\) and \(a x^2 + b x + c\). Each operation is a node with one child per argument, and the leaves are the symbols that are not operations. The caret is the power operation, which takes a base and an exponent.





















RemarkRemark 1 (Expressions, precedence and parse trees)






Remark 1 (Expressions, precedence and parse trees). An expression does not say how to compute the output it fixes, and many expressions denote the same function. A function is the input-output relationship itself; an expression is one way of writing it down.
The rules of operator precedence (PEMDAS: parentheses, exponents, multiplication and division, addition and subtraction) decide how the symbols group. They turn the string into its parse tree (Definition 5).

title: Expressions and Algorithms
text:
2 Algorithms






DefDefinition 6 (Algorithm)






Definition 6 (Algorithm) An algorithm [4] is a finite list of unambiguous steps that, applied to any valid input, halts and returns an output.










DefDefinition 7 (Computes)






Definition 7 (Computes) An algorithm computes a function when, for each input, it returns the function’s value at that input.










ExmExample 5 (Two algorithms for one function)






Example 5 (Two algorithms for one function) Take the function that Example 1 writes two ways. Evaluating the tree of \(a x^2 + b x + c\), with \(x^2\) computed as \(x \cdot x\), takes three multiplications and two additions. Evaluating the tree of Horner’s form \((a x + b)\,x + c\) takes two multiplications and two additions. We evaluate both forms at \(a = 2\), \(b = -3\), \(c = 5\) and \(x = 1.5\), in R and in Python, and give each intermediate quantity a name. (The code calls \(c\) c0, because c is a built-in function in R.) The two algorithms compute the same function, so the two values must agree.


R
Python




a <- 2
b <- -3
c0 <- 5
x <- 1.5
# Expanded form: 3 multiplications, 2 additions
square_term <- a * x * x
linear_term <- b * x
expanded <- square_term + linear_term + c0
# Horner's form: 2 multiplications, 2 additions
inner <- a * x + b
horner <- inner * x + c0
c(square_term, linear_term, expanded)
#> [1]  4.5 -4.5  5.0
c(inner, horner)
#> [1] 0 5




a = 2
b = -3
c0 = 5
x = 1.5
# Expanded form: 3 multiplications, 2 additions
square_term = a * x * x
linear_term = b * x
expanded = square_term + linear_term + c0
# Horner's form: 2 multiplications, 2 additions
inner = a * x + b
horner = inner * x + c0
print(square_term, linear_term, expanded)
#> 4.5 -4.5 5.0
print(inner, horner)
#> 0.0 5.0




The expanded form adds 4.5, -4.5 and 5 to reach 5. Horner’s form multiplies 0 by 1.5 and adds 5 to reach 5. Different steps give the same value.










RemarkRemark 2 (Procedures that are not algorithms here)






Remark 2 (Procedures that are not algorithms here). By the definition of an algorithm, every algorithm computes some function. That holds because an algorithm has unambiguous steps and halts on every valid input. A procedure that makes random choices can return different values for the same input. A procedure that never halts returns no value for some inputs. Neither computes a function, and neither is an algorithm in this sense, although some texts call them algorithms.










RemarkRemark 3 (How functions, expressions and algorithms relate)






Remark 3 (How functions, expressions and algorithms relate). The three ideas fit together this way:

A function is the input-output relationship.
An expression denotes a function, and many expressions denote the same one.
An algorithm computes a function, and many algorithms compute the same one.

An expression is not an algorithm, because it does not say what to do, or in what order. Given values for its variables, evaluating its parse tree from the leaves up is one algorithm for the function it denotes, and a different expression for the same function gives a different tree and a different algorithm.










RemarkRemark 4 (Values with no known algorithm)






Remark 4 (Values with no known algorithm). Some functions have no known finite algorithm for their exact values, and expressions that denote them, such as a limit, a supremum, an integral with no closed form, or an \(\arg \min\) over a set with no formula for the minimizer, cannot be evaluated by following their tree. Such a value can still be well defined and approximated by an algorithm.










ExmExample 6 (A minimizer with no known formula)






Example 6 (A minimizer with no known formula) The minimizer \(\arg \min_{x \in \mathbb{R}} \mathopen{}\left(x - \cos x\right)\mathclose{}^2\) is well defined, because \(x - \cos x\) is strictly increasing and equals zero at one point, yet that point has no known closed-form expression, so no known finite list of arithmetic steps returns it exactly. An algorithm such as bisection approximates it as closely as we like.

title: Expressions and Algorithms
text:
3 Exercises






ExrExercise 1 (Is an expression an algorithm?)






Exercise 1 (Is an expression an algorithm?) How do a function, an expression and an algorithm differ?










SolutionSolution 1






Solution 1. A function is the input-output relationship. An expression is a string of symbols that denotes a function, and many expressions denote the same one. An algorithm is a finite list of steps that computes a function, and many algorithms compute the same one.










ExrExercise 2 (Is an expression an algorithm? (part 2))






Exercise 2 (Is an expression an algorithm? (part 2)) Use the setup of Exercise 1.
Which of the three does \(a x^2 + b x + c\) name: a function, an expression or an algorithm?










SolutionSolution 2






Solution 2. It is an expression: it names a function, and it is not an algorithm.










ExrExercise 3 (Is an expression an algorithm? (part 3))






Exercise 3 (Is an expression an algorithm? (part 3)) Use the setup of Exercise 1.
Does the expression \(a x^2 + b x + c\) tell you which arithmetic steps to carry out?










SolutionSolution 3






Solution 3. Not by itself. The expression says what to compute, not how to compute it. Once \(a\), \(b\), \(c\) and \(x\) are known, evaluating its parse tree from the leaves up is an algorithm.










ExrExercise 4 (Is an expression an algorithm? (part 4))






Exercise 4 (Is an expression an algorithm? (part 4)) Use the setup of Exercise 1.
What do the rules of precedence (PEMDAS) contribute to the expression \(a x^2 + b x + c\)?










SolutionSolution 4






Solution 4. Precedence resolves how the symbols group: \(a x^2 + b x + c\) groups into three parts added together, with \(x^2\) evaluated before the multiplication by \(a\), and that grouping is a tree. Precedence is a rule for reading the expression, not a step in an algorithm that evaluates it.










ExrExercise 5 (Is an expression an algorithm? (part 5))






Exercise 5 (Is an expression an algorithm? (part 5)) Use the setup of Exercise 1.
Write a second expression that denotes the same function as \(a x^2 + b x + c\) and needs fewer multiplications.










SolutionSolution 5






Solution 5. \((a x + b)\,x + c\), Horner’s form. It uses two multiplications and two additions, where the first form, with \(x^2\) computed as \(x \cdot x\), uses three multiplications and two additions. The two expressions denote the same function and describe different algorithms.

title: Growth Rates
text:
RemarkRemark






Remark. The running time of an algorithm is a function of the size \(n\) of its input. To compare running times, we ignore fixed factors and small inputs. This page defines the notation for that comparison.

title: Growth Rates
text:
1 Upper bounds






DefDefinition 1 (Big-O)






Definition 1 (Big-O) Let \(f\) and \(g\) be functions from the natural numbers to the real numbers. Then \(f(n)\) is big-O of \(g(n)\) [1], written \(f(n) = O(g(n))\), when there exist a real number \(c > 0\) and a natural number \(N\) such that, for every natural number \(n \ge N\), \[
|f(n)| \le c \, |g(n)|.
\] In words, from some point \(N\) on, the absolute value of \(f(n)\) is at most a fixed multiple \(c\) of the absolute value of \(g(n)\). The “there exist” is an existential quantifier, and the “for every” is a universal quantifier.










ExmExample 1 (The function \(3n + 5\) is big-O of \(n\))






Example 1 (The function \(3n + 5\) is big-O of \(n\)) Let \(f(n) = 3n + 5\) and \(g(n) = n\). To show \(f(n) = O(g(n))\) by Definition 1, choose \(c = 4\) and \(N = 5\). For every natural number \(n \ge 5\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
|f(n)|
&= 3n + 5
&& \text{(} 3n + 5 > 0 \text{)}
\\
&\le 3n + n
&& \text{(} 5 \le n \text{, since } n \ge 5 \text{)}
\\
&= 4n
&& \text{(} 3n + n = 4n \text{)}
\\
&= 4 \, |g(n)|,
&& \text{(} n = |n| \text{, since } n \ge 0 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
which is the inequality in Definition 1 with \(c = 4\). Hence \(3n + 5 = O(n)\).

title: Growth Rates
text:
2 Lower bounds






DefDefinition 2 (Big-Omega)






Definition 2 (Big-Omega) Let \(f\) and \(g\) be functions from the natural numbers to the real numbers. Then \(f(n)\) is big-Omega of \(g(n)\) [1], written \(f(n) = \Omega(g(n))\), when there exist a real number \(c > 0\) and a natural number \(N\) such that, for every natural number \(n \ge N\), \[
|f(n)| \ge c \, |g(n)|.
\] In words, from some point \(N\) on, the absolute value of \(f(n)\) is at least a fixed positive multiple \(c\) of the absolute value of \(g(n)\). Dividing by \(c\) shows that \(f(n) = \Omega(g(n))\) exactly when \(g(n) = O(f(n))\) in the sense of Definition 1.










ExmExample 2 (The function \(3n + 5\) is big-Omega of \(n\))






Example 2 (The function \(3n + 5\) is big-Omega of \(n\)) Let \(f(n) = 3n + 5\) and \(g(n) = n\). To show \(f(n) = \Omega(g(n))\) by Definition 2, choose \(c = 3\) and \(N = 1\). For every natural number \(n \ge 1\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
|f(n)|
&= 3n + 5
&& \text{(} 3n + 5 > 0 \text{)}
\\
&\ge 3n
&& \text{(} 5 \ge 0 \text{)}
\\
&= 3 \, |g(n)|,
&& \text{(} n = |n| \text{, since } n \ge 0 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
which is the inequality in Definition 2 with \(c = 3\). Hence \(3n + 5 = \Omega(n)\).

title: Growth Rates
text:
3 Matching bounds






DefDefinition 3 (Big-Theta)






Definition 3 (Big-Theta) Let \(f\) and \(g\) be functions from the natural numbers to the real numbers. Then \(f(n)\) is big-Theta of \(g(n)\) [1], written \(f(n) = \Theta(g(n))\), when both \(f(n) = O(g(n))\) (big-O) and \(f(n) = \Omega(g(n))\) (big-Omega). In words, \(f(n)\) and \(g(n)\) are within fixed multiples of each other, from some point on.










ExmExample 3 (The function \(3n + 5\) is big-Theta of \(n\))






Example 3 (The function \(3n + 5\) is big-Theta of \(n\)) Let \(f(n) = 3n + 5\) and \(g(n) = n\). By Example 1, \(f(n) = O(n)\), and by Example 2, \(f(n) = \Omega(n)\). Therefore \(f(n) = \Theta(n)\) by Definition 3.

title: Indicator Functions
text:
An indicator function is a mathematical function that signals whether an element belongs to a specified set, or whether a given logical condition is satisfied. In statistics and epidemiology, indicator functions are ubiquitous. They represent:

binary variables, which take only the values \(0\) and \(1\) (Definition 3);
event and censoring indicators in survival analysis, the study of the time until an event such as death, where an observation is censored when follow-up ends before its event is seen;
membership in subpopulations;
domain restrictions in integrals and sums.

Despite their conceptual simplicity, notation for indicator functions varies substantially across textbooks, research papers, and subfields. This section summarizes the principal notational conventions.






DefDefinition 1 (Indicator function, set indicator)






Definition 1 (Indicator function, set indicator) For any subset \(A \subseteq \Omega\) of a universal set \(\Omega\), the indicator function of \(A\), [1] or set indicator, is the function \(\mathbb{1}_{A} : \Omega\to \{0, 1\}\) defined by:
\[
\mathbb{1}_{A}(x) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\begin{cases}
1, & x \in A \\
0, & x \notin A
\end{cases}
\]










DefDefinition 2 (Predicate indicator)






Definition 2 (Predicate indicator) For any logical proposition or predicate \(P\), the indicator of \(P\), or predicate indicator, takes the value \(1\) when \(P\) is true and \(0\) when \(P\) is false:
\[
{\mathbb{1}\mathopen{}\left(P\right)\mathclose{}} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if } P \text{ is true} \\
0, & \text{if } P \text{ is false}
\end{cases}
\]










ExmExample 1 (Evaluating set and predicate indicators)






Example 1 (Evaluating set and predicate indicators) Consider the real line \(\Omega= \mathbb{R}\), the set of nonnegative numbers \(A = [0, \infty)\), and a continuous random variable \(Y\) (defined in the Morrison Lab’s probability notes).

Set indicator \(\mathbb{1}_{A}(x)\):

For \(x = 3.5\): since \(3.5 \in [0, \infty)\), \(\mathbb{1}_{A}(3.5) = 1\).
For \(x = -2.1\): since \(-2.1 \notin [0, \infty)\), \(\mathbb{1}_{A}(-2.1) = 0\).

Predicate indicator \({\mathbb{1}\mathopen{}\left(Y > 5\right)\mathclose{}}\):

If an observation yields \(Y = 7.2\), the predicate \(7.2 > 5\) is true, so \({\mathbb{1}\mathopen{}\left(7.2 > 5\right)\mathclose{}} = 1\).
If an observation yields \(Y = 4.1\), the predicate \(4.1 > 5\) is false, so \({\mathbb{1}\mathopen{}\left(4.1 > 5\right)\mathclose{}} = 0\).












DefDefinition 3 (Binary variable)






Definition 3 (Binary variable) A binary variable is a variable that takes only the values \(0\) and \(1\).










ExmExample 2 (A binary variable is an indicator)






Example 2 (A binary variable is an indicator) In a study of \(n\) people, let \(s_i = 1\) if person \(i\) smokes and \(s_i = 0\) otherwise, for \(i \in \mathopen{}\left\{1, \ldots, n\right\}\mathclose{}\). Then \(s_i\) is a binary variable (Definition 3). It is also the predicate indicator (Definition 1) of the proposition “person \(i\) smokes”: \(s_i = {\mathbb{1}\mathopen{}\left(\text{person } i \text{ smokes}\right)\mathclose{}}\).
In the same way, every indicator is a binary variable, and every binary variable \(X\) is the indicator of its own value being \(1\): \(X = {\mathbb{1}\mathopen{}\left(X = 1\right)\mathclose{}}\), since both sides are \(1\) when \(X = 1\) and \(0\) when \(X = 0\).






The vast majority of indicator notations belong to one of two families: set notation or predicate notation.






DefDefinition 4 (Set notation for indicators)






Definition 4 (Set notation for indicators) An indicator (Definition 1) is written in set notation when the set \(A\) appears as a subscript, as in \(\mathbb{1}_{A}(x)\).










DefDefinition 5 (Predicate notation for indicators)






Definition 5 (Predicate notation for indicators) An indicator (Definition 1) is written in predicate notation when a proposition or predicate \(P\) (definition) appears as its argument, as in \({\mathbb{1}\mathopen{}\left(P\right)\mathclose{}}\) or \({\mathbb{1}\mathopen{}\left(x \in A\right)\mathclose{}}\).










ExmExample 3 (One indicator in both notations)






Example 3 (One indicator in both notations) Let \(A = [0, \infty)\), the nonnegative real numbers. The indicator of \(A\) is \(\mathbb{1}_{A}(x)\) in set notation, and \({\mathbb{1}\mathopen{}\left(x \in A\right)\mathclose{}}\) or \({\mathbb{1}\mathopen{}\left(x \ge 0\right)\mathclose{}}\) in predicate notation (Definition 4, Definition 5). At \(x = 3.5\), all three equal \(1\); at \(x = -2.1\), all three equal \(0\).






In set notation, the indicator is tied to a set \(A\), which appears as a subscript:

\(\mathbf{1}_A(x)\) (bold numeral one)
\(\mathbb{1}_{A}(x)\) (blackboard bold numeral one)
\(I_A(x)\) (capital letter \(I\))
\(\mathbb{I}_A(x)\) (blackboard bold letter \(I\))
\(\chi_A(x)\) (Greek letter chi, historically termed the characteristic function)

When the function is viewed as a mathematical object in its own right (for instance, as an element of an \(L^p\) function space, the set of functions \(f\) for which \(\int \mathopen{}\left|f(x)\right|\mathclose{}^p \, dx\) is finite), authors often omit the argument \(x\), writing simply \(\mathbf{1}_A\), \(\mathbb{1}_{A}\), or \(I_A\).



In predicate notation, the indicator takes a logical condition, relation, or proposition \(P\) directly as its argument or subscript:

\(\mathbb{I}(x \in A)\) or \(\mathbb{I}(P)\)
\(\mathbf{1}(x \in A)\) or \(\mathbf{1}(P)\)
\(\mathbb{1}(x \in A)\) or \(\mathbb{1}(P)\)
\(\mathbb{1}\{x \in A\}\) or \(\mathbb{1}\{P\}\)
\(I(x \in A)\) or \(I(P)\)

Predicate notation is especially common in applied statistics and survival analysis, where indicators frequently depend on inequalities (definition) involving random variables, such as \({\mathbb{1}\mathopen{}\left(T_i \le t\right)\mathclose{}}\) (an event occurring before time \(t\)) or \({\mathbb{1}\mathopen{}\left(Y_i = 1\right)\mathclose{}}\) (a binary outcome).



The two paradigms are connected by evaluating the predicate indicator at the membership statement \(x \in A\):
\[
\mathbf{1}_A(x) = \mathbb{I}(x \in A)
\]






DefDefinition 6 (Support of a distribution)






Definition 6 (Support of a distribution) The support of a discrete distribution [2] is the set of values it gives positive probability. The support of a continuous distribution is the set of values where its density is positive.










ExmExample 4 (Supports of two count distributions)






Example 4 (Supports of two count distributions)  

A fair six-sided die gives each of \(1, 2, \ldots, 6\) probability \(\tfrac{1}{6} > 0\) and every other value probability \(0\), so its support is \(\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}\).
A count that can be \(0\), \(1\), \(2\), and so on, each with positive probability, such as the number of hospital visits in a year, has support \(\mathbb{N}_0 = \mathopen{}\left\{0, 1, 2, \ldots\right\}\mathclose{}\).





Set notation is more natural when the underlying set \(A\) has a standard name (such as the support of a distribution (Definition 6), or a geometric region). Predicate notation is more natural when the condition involves compound inequalities, such as \({\mathbb{1}\mathopen{}\left(0 \le t \le u\right)\mathclose{}}\).




In 1962, Kenneth Iverson introduced a compact notation in the programming language APL, later popularized in mathematics and computer science by Donald Knuth: the Iverson bracket [3].






DefDefinition 7 (Iverson bracket)






Definition 7 (Iverson bracket) For any logical proposition \(P\), the Iverson bracket of \(P\) is [3]
\[
[P] \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if } P \text{ is true} \\
0, & \text{if } P \text{ is false}
\end{cases}
\]










ExmExample 5 (Evaluating Iverson brackets)






Example 5 (Evaluating Iverson brackets)  

\([3 > 2] = 1\), because \(3 > 2\) is true.
\([2 > 3] = 0\), because \(2 > 3\) is false.
\([4 \in \mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}] = 0\), because \(4\) is not an element of \(\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}\).











RemarkRemark 1 (The Iverson bracket is the predicate indicator)






Remark 1 (The Iverson bracket is the predicate indicator). The Iverson bracket \([P]\) is the predicate indicator \({\mathbb{1}\mathopen{}\left(P\right)\mathclose{}}\) (Definition 1) in different notation. Under this notation, set membership is written \([x \in A]\), so \([x \in A] = \mathbb{1}_{A}(x)\). For example, the values in Example 1 become
\[
\begin{aligned}
[7.2 > 5] &= {\mathbb{1}\mathopen{}\left(7.2 > 5\right)\mathclose{}} \\
&= 1
\end{aligned}
\]
and, with \(A = [0, \infty)\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
[-2.1 \in A] &= \mathbb{1}_{A}(-2.1) \\
&= 0.
\end{aligned}
\]










DefDefinition 8 (Kronecker delta)






Definition 8 (Kronecker delta) For integers \(i\) and \(j\), the Kronecker delta is [4]
\[\delta_{ij} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}[i = j]\]
that is, \(\delta_{ij} = 1\) when \(i = j\) and \(\delta_{ij} = 0\) when \(i \neq j\) (Definition 7).










ExmExample 6 (Evaluating the Kronecker delta)






Example 6 (Evaluating the Kronecker delta)  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\delta_{11} &= [1 = 1] \\
&= 1.
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
\delta_{12} &= [1 = 2] \\
&= 0.
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
\delta_{22} &= [2 = 2] \\
&= 1.
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
\delta_{23} &= [2 = 3] \\
&= 0.
\end{aligned}
\]








The primary advantage of the Iverson bracket is algebraic conciseness: it turns a sum or integral over a subset into a sum or integral over a larger, fixed set. For example, if \(U\) is a finite set that contains \(A\), then:
\[
\sum_{x \in A} f(x) = \sum_{x \in U} f(x) [x \in A]
\]
With \(A = \mathopen{}\left\{2, 4\right\}\mathclose{}\), \(f(x) = x\), and \(U = \mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\right\}\mathclose{}\), both sides equal \(2 + 4 = 6\).
However, in statistics and epidemiology, square brackets are already heavily overloaded: they denote closed intervals \([a, b]\), conditional expectations \(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X]\) (defined in the probability notes), and matrix delimiters. To prevent visual confusion with expectation brackets or intervals, statistical literature predominantly uses \(\mathbb{1}\) or \(I\) rather than the bare Iverson bracket.



Table 1 compares the major notations encountered across the literature.









Table 1: Notations for indicator functions across mathematical and statistical literature











Notation style
Typical syntax
Primary fields
Notes and potential ambiguities




Blackboard bold 1
\(\mathbb{1}_{A}(x)\), \(\mathbb{1}(P)\)
Modern probability, mathematical statistics
Unambiguous; distinct from matrices and scalars; standard in this book.


Bold numeral 1
\(\mathbf{1}_A(x)\), \(\mathbf{1}(P)\)
Probability theory, measure theory
Can be confused with a vector of ones \(\mathbf{1} = (1, \dots, 1)^{\top}\).


Blackboard bold I
\(\mathbb{I}(x \in A)\), \(\mathbb{I}(P)\)
Econometrics, machine learning, statistics
Clear predicate notation; avoids confusion with numerals.


Letter \(I\)
\(I_A(x)\), \(I(P)\)
Classical statistics, epidemiology
Can be confused with the identity matrix \(I\) or the Fisher information \(\mathcal{I}\), which measures how much a sample tells about a parameter.


Iverson bracket
\([P]\), \([x \in A]\)
Computer science, discrete mathematics
Very compact, but square brackets collide with intervals and expectation brackets.


Greek letter \(\chi\)
\(\chi_A(x)\)
Real analysis, measure theory
Often termed “characteristic function”; in probability, that name instead means \(t \mapsto \mathbb{E}[e^{itX}]\) for a random variable \(X\).












In these notes, we standardize on blackboard bold \(\mathbb{1}\) via the macros defined in latex-macros/macros.qmd:

\indic{A} produces \(\mathbb{1}_{A}\) (set subscript)
\indicp{P} produces \({\mathbb{1}\mathopen{}\left(P\right)\mathclose{}}\) (predicate in parentheses)
\indiccb{P} produces \({\mathbb{1}\mathopen{}\left\{P\right\}\mathclose{}}\) (predicate in curly braces)
\1{P} produces \(\text{1}_{P}\) (text numeral with subscript, used in legacy formulas)

Blackboard bold \(\mathbb{1}\) is preferred because it avoids all common collisions: it is visually distinct from the scalar \(1\), the identity matrix \(I\), and the observed and expected Fisher information matrices (\(I\), \(\mathcal{I}\)).



Indicator functions translate the logical connectives (definition) “and”, “or”, and “not”, applied to set membership, into ordinary arithmetic on real numbers. One of the identities below uses idempotence:






DefDefinition 9 (Idempotent)






Definition 9 (Idempotent) A number \(a\) is idempotent [5] if \(a \cdot a = a\). A function \(f\) with real values is idempotent if \(f(x) \cdot f(x) = f(x)\) for every \(x\) in its domain.










ExmExample 7 (Idempotent numbers and indicators)






Example 7 (Idempotent numbers and indicators)  

\(0\) and \(1\) are idempotent: \(0 \cdot 0 = 0\) and \(1 \cdot 1 = 1\).
\(2\) is not idempotent: \(2 \cdot 2 = 4 \neq 2\).
Every indicator function \(\mathbb{1}_{A}\) is idempotent, because each of its values is \(0\) or \(1\). For example, with \(A = [0, \infty)\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{1}_{A}(3.5) \cdot\mathbb{1}_{A}(3.5) &= 1 \cdot 1 \\
&= 1 \\
&= \mathbb{1}_{A}(3.5).
\end{aligned}
\]

The idempotent matrices of linear algebra satisfy the same equation with matrix multiplication: \(\mathbf{M}^2 = \mathbf{M}\) for a square matrix \(\mathbf{M}\).




For subsets \(A\) and \(B\) of \(\Omega\), with complement \(A^c \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\Omega\setminus A\), and for every \(x \in \Omega\):

Intersection (“and”): \(\mathbb{1}_{A \cap B}(x) = \mathbb{1}_{A}(x) \cdot \mathbb{1}_{B}(x)\)
Union (“or”): \(\mathbb{1}_{A \cup B}(x) = \mathbb{1}_{A}(x) + \mathbb{1}_{B}(x) - \mathbb{1}_{A}(x) \cdot \mathbb{1}_{B}(x)\)
Complement (“not”): \(\mathbb{1}_{A^c}(x) = 1 - \mathbb{1}_{A}(x)\)
Idempotence (Definition 9): \((\mathbb{1}_{A}(x))^2 = \mathbb{1}_{A}(x)\)
Expectation gives probability: When \(\Omega\) is a sample space and \(A\) is an event, the expectation of its indicator is the probability of the event (all four terms are defined in the Morrison Lab’s probability notes):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{1}_{A}]
&= 0 \cdot \Pr(A^c) + 1 \cdot \Pr(A) \\
&= \Pr(A)
\end{aligned}
\]

This identity turns probabilities into expectations. It is the mathematical foundation for:

empirical proportions;
estimators of survival curves, the probability of no event by each time;
regression models for binary outcomes.

The vast majority of indicator notations belong to one of two families: set notation or predicate notation.






DefDefinition 4 (Set notation for indicators)






Definition 4 (Set notation for indicators) An indicator (Definition 1) is written in set notation when the set \(A\) appears as a subscript, as in \(\mathbb{1}_{A}(x)\).










DefDefinition 5 (Predicate notation for indicators)






Definition 5 (Predicate notation for indicators) An indicator (Definition 1) is written in predicate notation when a proposition or predicate \(P\) (definition) appears as its argument, as in \({\mathbb{1}\mathopen{}\left(P\right)\mathclose{}}\) or \({\mathbb{1}\mathopen{}\left(x \in A\right)\mathclose{}}\).










ExmExample 3 (One indicator in both notations)






Example 3 (One indicator in both notations) Let \(A = [0, \infty)\), the nonnegative real numbers. The indicator of \(A\) is \(\mathbb{1}_{A}(x)\) in set notation, and \({\mathbb{1}\mathopen{}\left(x \in A\right)\mathclose{}}\) or \({\mathbb{1}\mathopen{}\left(x \ge 0\right)\mathclose{}}\) in predicate notation (Definition 4, Definition 5). At \(x = 3.5\), all three equal \(1\); at \(x = -2.1\), all three equal \(0\).






In set notation, the indicator is tied to a set \(A\), which appears as a subscript:

\(\mathbf{1}_A(x)\) (bold numeral one)
\(\mathbb{1}_{A}(x)\) (blackboard bold numeral one)
\(I_A(x)\) (capital letter \(I\))
\(\mathbb{I}_A(x)\) (blackboard bold letter \(I\))
\(\chi_A(x)\) (Greek letter chi, historically termed the characteristic function)

When the function is viewed as a mathematical object in its own right (for instance, as an element of an \(L^p\) function space, the set of functions \(f\) for which \(\int \mathopen{}\left|f(x)\right|\mathclose{}^p \, dx\) is finite), authors often omit the argument \(x\), writing simply \(\mathbf{1}_A\), \(\mathbb{1}_{A}\), or \(I_A\).



In predicate notation, the indicator takes a logical condition, relation, or proposition \(P\) directly as its argument or subscript:

\(\mathbb{I}(x \in A)\) or \(\mathbb{I}(P)\)
\(\mathbf{1}(x \in A)\) or \(\mathbf{1}(P)\)
\(\mathbb{1}(x \in A)\) or \(\mathbb{1}(P)\)
\(\mathbb{1}\{x \in A\}\) or \(\mathbb{1}\{P\}\)
\(I(x \in A)\) or \(I(P)\)

Predicate notation is especially common in applied statistics and survival analysis, where indicators frequently depend on inequalities (definition) involving random variables, such as \({\mathbb{1}\mathopen{}\left(T_i \le t\right)\mathclose{}}\) (an event occurring before time \(t\)) or \({\mathbb{1}\mathopen{}\left(Y_i = 1\right)\mathclose{}}\) (a binary outcome).



The two paradigms are connected by evaluating the predicate indicator at the membership statement \(x \in A\):
\[
\mathbf{1}_A(x) = \mathbb{I}(x \in A)
\]






DefDefinition 6 (Support of a distribution)






Definition 6 (Support of a distribution) The support of a discrete distribution [2] is the set of values it gives positive probability. The support of a continuous distribution is the set of values where its density is positive.










ExmExample 4 (Supports of two count distributions)






Example 4 (Supports of two count distributions)  

A fair six-sided die gives each of \(1, 2, \ldots, 6\) probability \(\tfrac{1}{6} > 0\) and every other value probability \(0\), so its support is \(\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}\).
A count that can be \(0\), \(1\), \(2\), and so on, each with positive probability, such as the number of hospital visits in a year, has support \(\mathbb{N}_0 = \mathopen{}\left\{0, 1, 2, \ldots\right\}\mathclose{}\).





Set notation is more natural when the underlying set \(A\) has a standard name (such as the support of a distribution (Definition 6), or a geometric region). Predicate notation is more natural when the condition involves compound inequalities, such as \({\mathbb{1}\mathopen{}\left(0 \le t \le u\right)\mathclose{}}\).




In 1962, Kenneth Iverson introduced a compact notation in the programming language APL, later popularized in mathematics and computer science by Donald Knuth: the Iverson bracket [3].






DefDefinition 7 (Iverson bracket)






Definition 7 (Iverson bracket) For any logical proposition \(P\), the Iverson bracket of \(P\) is [3]
\[
[P] \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if } P \text{ is true} \\
0, & \text{if } P \text{ is false}
\end{cases}
\]










ExmExample 5 (Evaluating Iverson brackets)






Example 5 (Evaluating Iverson brackets)  

\([3 > 2] = 1\), because \(3 > 2\) is true.
\([2 > 3] = 0\), because \(2 > 3\) is false.
\([4 \in \mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}] = 0\), because \(4\) is not an element of \(\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}\).











RemarkRemark 1 (The Iverson bracket is the predicate indicator)






Remark 1 (The Iverson bracket is the predicate indicator). The Iverson bracket \([P]\) is the predicate indicator \({\mathbb{1}\mathopen{}\left(P\right)\mathclose{}}\) (Definition 1) in different notation. Under this notation, set membership is written \([x \in A]\), so \([x \in A] = \mathbb{1}_{A}(x)\). For example, the values in Example 1 become
\[
\begin{aligned}
[7.2 > 5] &= {\mathbb{1}\mathopen{}\left(7.2 > 5\right)\mathclose{}} \\
&= 1
\end{aligned}
\]
and, with \(A = [0, \infty)\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
[-2.1 \in A] &= \mathbb{1}_{A}(-2.1) \\
&= 0.
\end{aligned}
\]










DefDefinition 8 (Kronecker delta)






Definition 8 (Kronecker delta) For integers \(i\) and \(j\), the Kronecker delta is [4]
\[\delta_{ij} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}[i = j]\]
that is, \(\delta_{ij} = 1\) when \(i = j\) and \(\delta_{ij} = 0\) when \(i \neq j\) (Definition 7).










ExmExample 6 (Evaluating the Kronecker delta)






Example 6 (Evaluating the Kronecker delta)  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\delta_{11} &= [1 = 1] \\
&= 1.
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
\delta_{12} &= [1 = 2] \\
&= 0.
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
\delta_{22} &= [2 = 2] \\
&= 1.
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
\delta_{23} &= [2 = 3] \\
&= 0.
\end{aligned}
\]








The primary advantage of the Iverson bracket is algebraic conciseness: it turns a sum or integral over a subset into a sum or integral over a larger, fixed set. For example, if \(U\) is a finite set that contains \(A\), then:
\[
\sum_{x \in A} f(x) = \sum_{x \in U} f(x) [x \in A]
\]
With \(A = \mathopen{}\left\{2, 4\right\}\mathclose{}\), \(f(x) = x\), and \(U = \mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\right\}\mathclose{}\), both sides equal \(2 + 4 = 6\).
However, in statistics and epidemiology, square brackets are already heavily overloaded: they denote closed intervals \([a, b]\), conditional expectations \(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X]\) (defined in the probability notes), and matrix delimiters. To prevent visual confusion with expectation brackets or intervals, statistical literature predominantly uses \(\mathbb{1}\) or \(I\) rather than the bare Iverson bracket.



Table 1 compares the major notations encountered across the literature.









Table 1: Notations for indicator functions across mathematical and statistical literature











Notation style
Typical syntax
Primary fields
Notes and potential ambiguities




Blackboard bold 1
\(\mathbb{1}_{A}(x)\), \(\mathbb{1}(P)\)
Modern probability, mathematical statistics
Unambiguous; distinct from matrices and scalars; standard in this book.


Bold numeral 1
\(\mathbf{1}_A(x)\), \(\mathbf{1}(P)\)
Probability theory, measure theory
Can be confused with a vector of ones \(\mathbf{1} = (1, \dots, 1)^{\top}\).


Blackboard bold I
\(\mathbb{I}(x \in A)\), \(\mathbb{I}(P)\)
Econometrics, machine learning, statistics
Clear predicate notation; avoids confusion with numerals.


Letter \(I\)
\(I_A(x)\), \(I(P)\)
Classical statistics, epidemiology
Can be confused with the identity matrix \(I\) or the Fisher information \(\mathcal{I}\), which measures how much a sample tells about a parameter.


Iverson bracket
\([P]\), \([x \in A]\)
Computer science, discrete mathematics
Very compact, but square brackets collide with intervals and expectation brackets.


Greek letter \(\chi\)
\(\chi_A(x)\)
Real analysis, measure theory
Often termed “characteristic function”; in probability, that name instead means \(t \mapsto \mathbb{E}[e^{itX}]\) for a random variable \(X\).












In these notes, we standardize on blackboard bold \(\mathbb{1}\) via the macros defined in latex-macros/macros.qmd:

\indic{A} produces \(\mathbb{1}_{A}\) (set subscript)
\indicp{P} produces \({\mathbb{1}\mathopen{}\left(P\right)\mathclose{}}\) (predicate in parentheses)
\indiccb{P} produces \({\mathbb{1}\mathopen{}\left\{P\right\}\mathclose{}}\) (predicate in curly braces)
\1{P} produces \(\text{1}_{P}\) (text numeral with subscript, used in legacy formulas)

Blackboard bold \(\mathbb{1}\) is preferred because it avoids all common collisions: it is visually distinct from the scalar \(1\), the identity matrix \(I\), and the observed and expected Fisher information matrices (\(I\), \(\mathcal{I}\)).



Indicator functions translate the logical connectives (definition) “and”, “or”, and “not”, applied to set membership, into ordinary arithmetic on real numbers. One of the identities below uses idempotence:






DefDefinition 9 (Idempotent)






Definition 9 (Idempotent) A number \(a\) is idempotent [5] if \(a \cdot a = a\). A function \(f\) with real values is idempotent if \(f(x) \cdot f(x) = f(x)\) for every \(x\) in its domain.










ExmExample 7 (Idempotent numbers and indicators)






Example 7 (Idempotent numbers and indicators)  

\(0\) and \(1\) are idempotent: \(0 \cdot 0 = 0\) and \(1 \cdot 1 = 1\).
\(2\) is not idempotent: \(2 \cdot 2 = 4 \neq 2\).
Every indicator function \(\mathbb{1}_{A}\) is idempotent, because each of its values is \(0\) or \(1\). For example, with \(A = [0, \infty)\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{1}_{A}(3.5) \cdot\mathbb{1}_{A}(3.5) &= 1 \cdot 1 \\
&= 1 \\
&= \mathbb{1}_{A}(3.5).
\end{aligned}
\]

The idempotent matrices of linear algebra satisfy the same equation with matrix multiplication: \(\mathbf{M}^2 = \mathbf{M}\) for a square matrix \(\mathbf{M}\).




For subsets \(A\) and \(B\) of \(\Omega\), with complement \(A^c \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\Omega\setminus A\), and for every \(x \in \Omega\):

Intersection (“and”): \(\mathbb{1}_{A \cap B}(x) = \mathbb{1}_{A}(x) \cdot \mathbb{1}_{B}(x)\)
Union (“or”): \(\mathbb{1}_{A \cup B}(x) = \mathbb{1}_{A}(x) + \mathbb{1}_{B}(x) - \mathbb{1}_{A}(x) \cdot \mathbb{1}_{B}(x)\)
Complement (“not”): \(\mathbb{1}_{A^c}(x) = 1 - \mathbb{1}_{A}(x)\)
Idempotence (Definition 9): \((\mathbb{1}_{A}(x))^2 = \mathbb{1}_{A}(x)\)
Expectation gives probability: When \(\Omega\) is a sample space and \(A\) is an event, the expectation of its indicator is the probability of the event (all four terms are defined in the Morrison Lab’s probability notes):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{1}_{A}]
&= 0 \cdot \Pr(A^c) + 1 \cdot \Pr(A) \\
&= \Pr(A)
\end{aligned}
\]

This identity turns probabilities into expectations. It is the mathematical foundation for:

empirical proportions;
estimators of survival curves, the probability of no event by each time;
regression models for binary outcomes.

title: Complex Vectors and Matrices
text:
DefDefinition 1 (Complex vector)






Definition 1 (Complex vector) A complex vector of length \(p\) is a column vector whose entries are complex numbers; the set of all of them is denoted \(\mathbb{C}^p\).










DefDefinition 2 (Complex matrix)






Definition 2 (Complex matrix) A complex matrix of size \(m \times n\) is a matrix with complex entries; the set of all of them is denoted \(\mathbb{C}^{m \times n}\).










ExmExample 1 (A complex vector and its conjugate)






Example 1 (A complex vector and its conjugate) \[
\underbrace{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}}_{3 \times 1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 + i \\ 2 \\ -3\,i \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{C}^3,
\qquad
\underbrace{\overline{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}}}_{3 \times 1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 - i \\ 2 \\ 3\,i \end{bmatrix}.
\]
The real entry \(2\) is its own conjugate. Every real vector is also a complex vector, since each real number \(a\) is the complex number \(a + 0\,i\), so \(\mathbb{R}^p\) is a subset of \(\mathbb{C}^p\).










DefDefinition 3 (Complex conjugate of a complex vector or matrix)






Definition 3 (Complex conjugate of a complex vector or matrix) The complex conjugate of a complex vector or matrix takes the complex conjugate of each entry: \((\overline{\mathbf{A}})_{jk} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\overline{a_{jk}}\).










DefDefinition 4 (Conjugate transpose, Hermitian adjoint, Hermitian conjugate, transjugate)






Definition 4 (Conjugate transpose, Hermitian adjoint, Hermitian conjugate, transjugate) The conjugate transpose [1] (also called the Hermitian adjoint, Hermitian conjugate, or transjugate) of an \(m \times n\) complex matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) is the \(n \times m\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}\) obtained by transposing \(\mathbf{A}\) and then taking the complex conjugate of each entry:
\[(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}})_{jk} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\overline{a_{kj}}
\quad \text{for } j \in \{1, \ldots, n\},\ k \in \{1, \ldots, m\}.\]










RemarkRemark 1 (Notation for the conjugate transpose)






Remark 1 (Notation for the conjugate transpose). The operation is denoted variously across mathematics and physics: \(\mathbf{A}^*\) in pure mathematics (Axler [2], Definition 7.7, p. 231), \(\mathbf{A}^{\dagger}\) (“\(A\)-dagger”) in physics and quantum mechanics, and \(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}\) in engineering, numerical linear algebra, and statistics. These notes write \(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}\) because \(^*\) is reserved for optimal points (as in \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^*\)) and \(^{\dagger}\) frequently denotes the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse in the broader literature.
The Hermitian adjoint matrix should not be confused with the classical adjugate matrix (the transpose of the matrix of cofactors), which older texts occasionally referred to as the “adjoint.”










ExmExample 2 (The conjugate transpose of a \(2 \times 3\) matrix)






Example 2 (The conjugate transpose of a \(2 \times 3\) matrix) For
\[
\underbrace{\mathbf{A}}_{2 \times 3} =
\begin{bmatrix}
1 + i & 2 & 0 \\
-i & 3 - 2\,i & 4
\end{bmatrix},
\]
transposing gives a \(3 \times 2\) matrix, and conjugating each of its entries gives
\[
\underbrace{\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}}_{3 \times 2} =
\begin{bmatrix}
1 - i & i \\
2 & 3 + 2\,i \\
0 & 4
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
For instance,
\[
\begin{aligned}
(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}})_{12} &= \overline{a_{21}} \\
&= \overline{-i} \\
&= i.
\end{aligned}
\]
The transpose alone would have \(-i\) in that position, so for a matrix with an entry that is not real, \(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}\) and \({\mathbf{A}}^{\top}\) differ. For a real matrix, conjugating changes nothing, so \(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}} = {\mathbf{A}}^{\top}\).










RemarkRemark 2 (Conjugate transpose of a complex vector)






Remark 2 (Conjugate transpose of a complex vector). The conjugate transpose of a column vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}} \in \mathbb{C}^p\) is the \(1 \times p\) row vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}^{\mathsf{H}} = [\overline{z_1},\; \ldots,\; \overline{z_p}]\).










LemTheorem 1 (Properties of the Hermitian adjoint)






Theorem 1 (Properties of the Hermitian adjoint) Let \(\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) be complex matrices of compatible dimensions, and let \(c \in \mathbb{C}\) be a scalar. The Hermitian adjoint (Definition 4) satisfies:

Involution: \[(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}})^{\mathsf{H}} = \mathbf{A}\]
Additivity: \[(\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B})^{\mathsf{H}} = \mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}} + \mathbf{B}^{\mathsf{H}}\]
Conjugate-homogeneity: \[(c\,\mathbf{A})^{\mathsf{H}} = \overline{c}\,\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}\]
Reversal of products: \[(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})^{\mathsf{H}} = \mathbf{B}^{\mathsf{H}}\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}\]

If \(\mathbf{A}\) is invertible, then \(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}\) is also invertible, and
\[(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}})^{-1} = (\mathbf{A}^{-1})^{\mathsf{H}}.\]










ProofProof






Proof. Properties 1-3 follow directly from entrywise conjugation and transposition:

For involution:
\[
\begin{aligned}
[(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}})^{\mathsf{H}}]_{jk} &= \overline{(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}})_{kj}} \\
&= \overline{\overline{a_{jk}}} \\
&= a_{jk}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For additivity:
\[
\begin{aligned}
[(\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B})^{\mathsf{H}}]_{jk} &= \overline{(\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B})_{kj}} \\
&= \overline{a_{kj} + b_{kj}} \\
&= \overline{a_{kj}} + \overline{b_{kj}} \\
&= (\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}})_{jk} + (\mathbf{B}^{\mathsf{H}})_{jk}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For conjugate-homogeneity:
\[
\begin{aligned}
[(c\,\mathbf{A})^{\mathsf{H}}]_{jk} &= \overline{(c\,\mathbf{A})_{kj}} \\
&= \overline{c\,a_{kj}} \\
&= \overline{c}\,\overline{a_{kj}} \\
&= \overline{c}\,(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}})_{jk}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Unlike the real transpose where \({(c\,\mathbf{A})}^{\top} = c\,{\mathbf{A}}^{\top}\), scaling conjugates the scalar.

For property 4 (reversal of products), let \(\mathbf{A}\) be an \(m \times k\) matrix and \(\mathbf{B}\) a \(k \times n\) matrix. Entry \((i, j)\) of the product’s Hermitian adjoint (for \(i \in \{1, \ldots, n\}\) and \(j \in \{1, \ldots, m\}\)) is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
[(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})^{\mathsf{H}}]_{ij}
&= \overline{(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})_{ji}}
&& \text{(}\href{#def-conjugate-transpose}{\text{Definition~4}}\text{)}
\\
&= \overline{\sum_{s=1}^{k} a_{js}\,b_{si}}
&& \text{(definition of matrix multiplication)}
\\
&= \sum_{s=1}^{k} \overline{a_{js}}\,\overline{b_{si}}
&& \text{(conjugate of sums and products)}
\\
&= \sum_{s=1}^{k} \overline{b_{si}}\,\overline{a_{js}}
&& \text{(complex multiplication is commutative)}
\\
&= \sum_{s=1}^{k} (\mathbf{B}^{\mathsf{H}})_{is}\,(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}})_{sj}
&& \text{(}\href{#def-conjugate-transpose}{\text{Definition~4}}\text{)}
\\
&= (\mathbf{B}^{\mathsf{H}}\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}})_{ij}
&& \text{(definition of matrix multiplication)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For the inverse, applying property 4 to \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^{-1} = \mathbf{I}\) gives:
\[
\begin{aligned}
(\mathbf{A}^{-1})^{\mathsf{H}}\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}
&= (\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^{-1})^{\mathsf{H}} \\
&= \mathbf{I}^{\mathsf{H}} \\
&= \mathbf{I},
\end{aligned}
\]
so \((\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}})^{-1} = (\mathbf{A}^{-1})^{\mathsf{H}}\).










LemTheorem 2 (The adjoint property for inner products)






Theorem 2 (The adjoint property for inner products) Let \(\mathbf{A}\) be an \(m \times n\) complex matrix. Under the standard inner product on complex Euclidean space, \({\mathopen{}\left\langle \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\right\rangle\mathclose{}} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}^{\mathsf{H}}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\),
\[{\mathopen{}\left\langle \mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\right\rangle\mathclose{}} = {\mathopen{}\left\langle \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}, \mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\right\rangle\mathclose{}}
\quad \text{for all } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} \in \mathbb{C}^n \text{ and } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}} \in \mathbb{C}^m.\]










ProofProof






Proof. By the definition of the standard complex inner product and the product rule for the Hermitian adjoint (Theorem 1):
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathopen{}\left\langle \mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\right\rangle\mathclose{}}
&= (\mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}})^{\mathsf{H}}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}
&& \text{(definition of standard inner product)}
\\
&= (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}^{\mathsf{H}}\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}})\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}
&& \text{(}\href{#thm-hermitian-adjoint-properties}{\text{Theorem~1}}\text{, reversal of products)}
\\
&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}^{\mathsf{H}}(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}})
&& \text{(associativity of matrix multiplication)}
\\
&= {\mathopen{}\left\langle \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}, \mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\right\rangle\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(definition of standard inner product)}.
\end{aligned}
\]










RemarkRemark 3 (Where the name “adjoint” comes from)






Remark 3 (Where the name “adjoint” comes from). This identity is the origin of the name adjoint: in functional analysis and operator theory, the adjoint of a linear map \(T: V \to W\) between inner product spaces is defined as the unique operator \(T^*: W \to V\) satisfying \({\mathopen{}\left\langle T\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\right\rangle\mathclose{}} = {\mathopen{}\left\langle \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}, T^*\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\right\rangle\mathclose{}}\) (Axler [2], Definition 7.1, p. 226). When \(V\) and \(W\) are finite-dimensional spaces equipped with their standard orthonormal bases, the matrix representing the adjoint operator \(T^*\) is precisely the Hermitian adjoint matrix \(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}\) (Axler [2], Proposition 7.9, p. 231).










LemTheorem 3 (\(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}^{\mathsf{H}}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}\) is a sum of squared absolute values)






Theorem 3 (\(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}^{\mathsf{H}}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}\) is a sum of squared absolute values) For every \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}} \in \mathbb{C}^p\),
\[\underbrace{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}^{\mathsf{H}}}_{1 \times p}\,\underbrace{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}}_{p \times 1} = \sum_{j=1}^p\mathopen{}\left|z_j\right|\mathclose{}^2,\]
which is a nonnegative real number, and is \(0\) only when \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_{p \times 1}\).










ProofProof






Proof. The last step uses the identity for a complex number times its conjugate.
\[
