\begin{aligned}
\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}^{\mathsf{H}}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}
&= \sum_{j=1}^p\overline{z_j}\,z_j
&& \text{(}\href{#def-conjugate-transpose}{\text{Definition~4}}\text{, and the row-times-column product)}
\\
&= \sum_{j=1}^pz_j\,\overline{z_j}
&& \text{(complex multiplication is commutative)}
\\
&= \sum_{j=1}^p\mathopen{}\left|z_j\right|\mathclose{}^2
&& \text{(a number times its conjugate)}
\end{aligned}
\]
By the definition of the absolute value, each \(\mathopen{}\left|z_j\right|\mathclose{}^2 = (\operatorname{Re} z_j)^2 + (\operatorname{Im} z_j)^2\) is a nonnegative real number, so their sum is too. A sum of nonnegative numbers is \(0\) only when every term is \(0\), and \(\mathopen{}\left|z_j\right|\mathclose{}^2 = 0\) only when
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Re} z_j &= \operatorname{Im} z_j \\
&= 0,
\end{aligned}
\]
that is, when \(z_j = 0\).










ExmExample 3 (Computing \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}^{\mathsf{H}}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}\))






Example 3 (Computing \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}^{\mathsf{H}}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}\)) Let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}} = {(1 + i, 2)}^{\top}\). By Theorem 3,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\underbrace{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}^{\mathsf{H}}}_{1 \times 2}\,\underbrace{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}}_{2 \times 1}
&= \mathopen{}\left|1 + i\right|\mathclose{}^2 + \mathopen{}\left|2\right|\mathclose{}^2
&& \text{(}\href{#thm-zhz-sum-squares}{\text{Theorem~3}}\text{)}
\\
&= (1^2 + 1^2) + (2^2 + 0^2)
&& \text{(definition of the absolute value, squared)}
\\
&= 2 + 4
&& \text{(add inside each group)}
\\
&= 6
&& \text{(add)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Multiplying out directly gives the same number: \(\overline{2} \cdot 2 = 4\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
\overline{(1 + i)}\,(1 + i)
&= (1 - i)(1 + i)
&& \text{(conjugate)}
\\
&= 1 + i - i - i^2
&& \text{(distribute)}
\\
&= 1 - i^2
&& \text{(cancel } i \text{)}
\\
&= 2
&& \text{(} i^2 = -1 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExmExample 4 (Why complex vectors use the conjugate transpose)






Example 4 (Why complex vectors use the conjugate transpose) For a real vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\), \({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= \sum_{j=1}^px_j^2\) is \(0\) only when \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) is the zero vector. The same formula fails for complex vectors. Let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}} = {(1, i)}^{\top}\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\underbrace{{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}}^{\top}}_{1 \times 2}\,\underbrace{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}}_{2 \times 1}
&= 1 \cdot 1 + i \cdot i
&& \text{(multiply entry by entry and add)}
\\
&= 1 + i^2
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= 0
&& \text{(} i^2 = -1 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
although \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}} \neq \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_{2 \times 1}\). Using the conjugate transpose instead,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\underbrace{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}^{\mathsf{H}}}_{1 \times 2}\,\underbrace{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}}_{2 \times 1}
&= \overline{1} \cdot 1 + \overline{i} \cdot i
&& \text{(}\href{#def-conjugate-transpose}{\text{Definition~4}}\text{)}
\\
&= 1 + (-i) \cdot i
&& \text{(conjugate each entry)}
\\
&= 1 - i^2
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= 2
&& \text{(} i^2 = -1 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
which is positive, as Theorem 3 guarantees.










DefDefinition 5 (Hermitian matrix, self-adjoint matrix)






Definition 5 (Hermitian matrix, self-adjoint matrix) A square complex matrix \(\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{C}^{n \times n}\) is Hermitian [3] (or self-adjoint) if it equals its conjugate transpose (Definition 4):
\[\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}} = \mathbf{A}.\]










RemarkRemark 4 (Why “self-adjoint”)






Remark 4 (Why “self-adjoint”). The term self-adjoint comes directly from Theorem 2: when \(\mathbf{A}\) is Hermitian, \({\mathopen{}\left\langle \mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\right\rangle\mathclose{}} = {\mathopen{}\left\langle \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}, \mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\right\rangle\mathclose{}}\) for all \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}} \in \mathbb{C}^n\). The linear operator moves across the inner product without change.










ExmExample 5 (A Hermitian matrix)






Example 5 (A Hermitian matrix) \[
\underbrace{\mathbf{A}}_{2 \times 2} =
\begin{bmatrix}
2 & 1 - i \\
1 + i & 3
\end{bmatrix}
\]
is Hermitian: transposing swaps the off-diagonal entries, and conjugating turns \(1 + i\) back into \(1 - i\) and \(1 - i\) back into \(1 + i\), so \(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}} = \mathbf{A}\). The diagonal entries of a Hermitian matrix must be real, because \(a_{jj} = \overline{a_{jj}}\), and only a real number is its own conjugate: if \(a + b\,i = a - b\,i\), then the imaginary parts give \(b = -b\), so \(b = 0\).
Every real symmetric matrix is Hermitian, because for a real matrix \(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}} = {\mathbf{A}}^{\top}\).










ExmExample 6 (A symmetric complex matrix that is not Hermitian)






Example 6 (A symmetric complex matrix that is not Hermitian) \[
\underbrace{\mathbf{B}}_{2 \times 2} =
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & i \\
i & 0
\end{bmatrix}
\]
is symmetric, \({\mathbf{B}}^{\top} = \mathbf{B}\), but it is not Hermitian:
\[
\underbrace{\mathbf{B}^{\mathsf{H}}}_{2 \times 2} =
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & -i \\
-i & 0
\end{bmatrix}
\neq \mathbf{B}.
\]










DefDefinition 6 (Skew-Hermitian matrix, anti-Hermitian matrix)






Definition 6 (Skew-Hermitian matrix, anti-Hermitian matrix) A square complex matrix \(\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{C}^{n \times n}\) is skew-Hermitian [4] (or anti-Hermitian) if it equals the negative of its conjugate transpose (Definition 4):
\[\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}} = -\mathbf{A}.\]










RemarkRemark 5 (The diagonal of a skew-Hermitian matrix)






Remark 5 (The diagonal of a skew-Hermitian matrix). Every entry of a skew-Hermitian matrix satisfies \(a_{jk} = -\overline{a_{kj}}\). In particular, its diagonal entries satisfy \(a_{jj} = -\overline{a_{jj}}\), which means
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{jj} + \overline{a_{jj}} &= 2\operatorname{Re}(a_{jj}) \\
&= 0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, every diagonal entry of a skew-Hermitian matrix must be purely imaginary (or zero). For example, \(a_{jj} = 3\,i\) works, since
\[
\begin{aligned}
-\overline{3\,i} &= -(-3\,i) \\
&= 3\,i,
\end{aligned}
\]
but \(a_{jj} = 3\) does not, since \(-\overline{3} = -3\).










ExmExample 7 (A skew-Hermitian matrix)






Example 7 (A skew-Hermitian matrix) The matrix
\[
\mathbf{A} =
\begin{bmatrix}
2\,i & 1 + i \\
-1 + i & 0
\end{bmatrix}
\]
is skew-Hermitian: transposing and conjugating gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}
&=
\begin{bmatrix}
\overline{2\,i} & \overline{-1 + i} \\
\overline{1 + i} & \overline{0}
\end{bmatrix} \\
&=
\begin{bmatrix}
-2\,i & -1 - i \\
1 - i & 0
\end{bmatrix} \\
&= -\mathbf{A}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Its diagonal entries \(2\,i\) and \(0\) are purely imaginary.










LemTheorem 4 (Hermitian and skew-Hermitian decomposition)






Theorem 4 (Hermitian and skew-Hermitian decomposition) Every square complex matrix \(\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{C}^{n \times n}\) can be uniquely expressed as the sum of a Hermitian matrix \(\mathbf{H}\) (Definition 5) and a skew-Hermitian matrix \(\mathbf{S}\) (Definition 6):
\[\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{H} + \mathbf{S},\]
where
\[\mathbf{H} = \frac{\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}}{2}
\quad \text{and} \quad
\mathbf{S} = \frac{\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}}{2}.\]










ProofProof






Proof. Existence: Define \(\mathbf{H} = \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}})\) and \(\mathbf{S} = \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}})\). Their sum is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{H} + \mathbf{S}
&= \frac{\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}}{2} + \frac{\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}}{2} \\
&= \frac{2\mathbf{A}}{2} \\
&= \mathbf{A}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Applying the properties of the Hermitian adjoint (Theorem 1):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{H}^{\mathsf{H}}
&= \mathopen{}\left(\frac{\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}}{2}\right)\mathclose{}^{\mathsf{H}} \\
&= \frac{\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}} + (\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}})^{\mathsf{H}}}{2} \\
&= \frac{\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}} + \mathbf{A}}{2} \\
&= \mathbf{H},
\\
\mathbf{S}^{\mathsf{H}}
&= \mathopen{}\left(\frac{\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}}{2}\right)\mathclose{}^{\mathsf{H}} \\
&= \frac{\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}} - (\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}})^{\mathsf{H}}}{2} \\
&= \frac{\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}} - \mathbf{A}}{2} \\
&= -\mathbf{S}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(\mathbf{H}\) is Hermitian and \(\mathbf{S}\) is skew-Hermitian.
Uniqueness: Suppose \(\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{H}' + \mathbf{S}'\) with \((\mathbf{H}')^{\mathsf{H}} = \mathbf{H}'\) and \((\mathbf{S}')^{\mathsf{H}} = -\mathbf{S}'\). Taking the Hermitian adjoint of both sides yields:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}
&= (\mathbf{H}' + \mathbf{S}')^{\mathsf{H}} \\
&= (\mathbf{H}')^{\mathsf{H}} + (\mathbf{S}')^{\mathsf{H}} \\
&= \mathbf{H}' - \mathbf{S}'.
\end{aligned}
\]
Adding \(\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{H}' + \mathbf{S}'\) and \(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}} = \mathbf{H}' - \mathbf{S}'\) gives \(\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}} = 2\mathbf{H}'\), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{H}' &= \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}) \\
&= \mathbf{H}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Subtracting the two equations gives \(\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}} = 2\mathbf{S}'\), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{S}' &= \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}) \\
&= \mathbf{S}.
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Complex Vectors and Matrices
text:
DefDefinition 1 (Complex vector)






Definition 1 (Complex vector) A complex vector of length \(p\) is a column vector whose entries are complex numbers; the set of all of them is denoted \(\mathbb{C}^p\).










DefDefinition 2 (Complex matrix)






Definition 2 (Complex matrix) A complex matrix of size \(m \times n\) is a matrix with complex entries; the set of all of them is denoted \(\mathbb{C}^{m \times n}\).










ExmExample 1 (A complex vector and its conjugate)






Example 1 (A complex vector and its conjugate) \[
\underbrace{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}}_{3 \times 1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 + i \\ 2 \\ -3\,i \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{C}^3,
\qquad
\underbrace{\overline{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}}}_{3 \times 1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 - i \\ 2 \\ 3\,i \end{bmatrix}.
\]
The real entry \(2\) is its own conjugate. Every real vector is also a complex vector, since each real number \(a\) is the complex number \(a + 0\,i\), so \(\mathbb{R}^p\) is a subset of \(\mathbb{C}^p\).










DefDefinition 3 (Complex conjugate of a complex vector or matrix)






Definition 3 (Complex conjugate of a complex vector or matrix) The complex conjugate of a complex vector or matrix takes the complex conjugate of each entry: \((\overline{\mathbf{A}})_{jk} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\overline{a_{jk}}\).










DefDefinition 4 (Conjugate transpose, Hermitian adjoint, Hermitian conjugate, transjugate)






Definition 4 (Conjugate transpose, Hermitian adjoint, Hermitian conjugate, transjugate) The conjugate transpose [1] (also called the Hermitian adjoint, Hermitian conjugate, or transjugate) of an \(m \times n\) complex matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) is the \(n \times m\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}\) obtained by transposing \(\mathbf{A}\) and then taking the complex conjugate of each entry:
\[(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}})_{jk} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\overline{a_{kj}}
\quad \text{for } j \in \{1, \ldots, n\},\ k \in \{1, \ldots, m\}.\]










RemarkRemark 1 (Notation for the conjugate transpose)






Remark 1 (Notation for the conjugate transpose). The operation is denoted variously across mathematics and physics: \(\mathbf{A}^*\) in pure mathematics (Axler [2], Definition 7.7, p. 231), \(\mathbf{A}^{\dagger}\) (“\(A\)-dagger”) in physics and quantum mechanics, and \(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}\) in engineering, numerical linear algebra, and statistics. These notes write \(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}\) because \(^*\) is reserved for optimal points (as in \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^*\)) and \(^{\dagger}\) frequently denotes the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse in the broader literature.
The Hermitian adjoint matrix should not be confused with the classical adjugate matrix (the transpose of the matrix of cofactors), which older texts occasionally referred to as the “adjoint.”










ExmExample 2 (The conjugate transpose of a \(2 \times 3\) matrix)






Example 2 (The conjugate transpose of a \(2 \times 3\) matrix) For
\[
\underbrace{\mathbf{A}}_{2 \times 3} =
\begin{bmatrix}
1 + i & 2 & 0 \\
-i & 3 - 2\,i & 4
\end{bmatrix},
\]
transposing gives a \(3 \times 2\) matrix, and conjugating each of its entries gives
\[
\underbrace{\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}}_{3 \times 2} =
\begin{bmatrix}
1 - i & i \\
2 & 3 + 2\,i \\
0 & 4
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
For instance,
\[
\begin{aligned}
(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}})_{12} &= \overline{a_{21}} \\
&= \overline{-i} \\
&= i.
\end{aligned}
\]
The transpose alone would have \(-i\) in that position, so for a matrix with an entry that is not real, \(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}\) and \({\mathbf{A}}^{\top}\) differ. For a real matrix, conjugating changes nothing, so \(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}} = {\mathbf{A}}^{\top}\).










RemarkRemark 2 (Conjugate transpose of a complex vector)






Remark 2 (Conjugate transpose of a complex vector). The conjugate transpose of a column vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}} \in \mathbb{C}^p\) is the \(1 \times p\) row vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}^{\mathsf{H}} = [\overline{z_1},\; \ldots,\; \overline{z_p}]\).










LemTheorem 1 (Properties of the Hermitian adjoint)






Theorem 1 (Properties of the Hermitian adjoint) Let \(\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) be complex matrices of compatible dimensions, and let \(c \in \mathbb{C}\) be a scalar. The Hermitian adjoint (Definition 4) satisfies:

Involution: \[(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}})^{\mathsf{H}} = \mathbf{A}\]
Additivity: \[(\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B})^{\mathsf{H}} = \mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}} + \mathbf{B}^{\mathsf{H}}\]
Conjugate-homogeneity: \[(c\,\mathbf{A})^{\mathsf{H}} = \overline{c}\,\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}\]
Reversal of products: \[(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})^{\mathsf{H}} = \mathbf{B}^{\mathsf{H}}\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}\]

If \(\mathbf{A}\) is invertible, then \(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}\) is also invertible, and
\[(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}})^{-1} = (\mathbf{A}^{-1})^{\mathsf{H}}.\]










ProofProof






Proof. Properties 1-3 follow directly from entrywise conjugation and transposition:

For involution:
\[
\begin{aligned}
[(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}})^{\mathsf{H}}]_{jk} &= \overline{(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}})_{kj}} \\
&= \overline{\overline{a_{jk}}} \\
&= a_{jk}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For additivity:
\[
\begin{aligned}
[(\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B})^{\mathsf{H}}]_{jk} &= \overline{(\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B})_{kj}} \\
&= \overline{a_{kj} + b_{kj}} \\
&= \overline{a_{kj}} + \overline{b_{kj}} \\
&= (\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}})_{jk} + (\mathbf{B}^{\mathsf{H}})_{jk}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For conjugate-homogeneity:
\[
\begin{aligned}
[(c\,\mathbf{A})^{\mathsf{H}}]_{jk} &= \overline{(c\,\mathbf{A})_{kj}} \\
&= \overline{c\,a_{kj}} \\
&= \overline{c}\,\overline{a_{kj}} \\
&= \overline{c}\,(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}})_{jk}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Unlike the real transpose where \({(c\,\mathbf{A})}^{\top} = c\,{\mathbf{A}}^{\top}\), scaling conjugates the scalar.

For property 4 (reversal of products), let \(\mathbf{A}\) be an \(m \times k\) matrix and \(\mathbf{B}\) a \(k \times n\) matrix. Entry \((i, j)\) of the product’s Hermitian adjoint (for \(i \in \{1, \ldots, n\}\) and \(j \in \{1, \ldots, m\}\)) is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
[(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})^{\mathsf{H}}]_{ij}
&= \overline{(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})_{ji}}
&& \text{(}\href{#def-conjugate-transpose}{\text{Definition~4}}\text{)}
\\
&= \overline{\sum_{s=1}^{k} a_{js}\,b_{si}}
&& \text{(definition of matrix multiplication)}
\\
&= \sum_{s=1}^{k} \overline{a_{js}}\,\overline{b_{si}}
&& \text{(conjugate of sums and products)}
\\
&= \sum_{s=1}^{k} \overline{b_{si}}\,\overline{a_{js}}
&& \text{(complex multiplication is commutative)}
\\
&= \sum_{s=1}^{k} (\mathbf{B}^{\mathsf{H}})_{is}\,(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}})_{sj}
&& \text{(}\href{#def-conjugate-transpose}{\text{Definition~4}}\text{)}
\\
&= (\mathbf{B}^{\mathsf{H}}\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}})_{ij}
&& \text{(definition of matrix multiplication)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For the inverse, applying property 4 to \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^{-1} = \mathbf{I}\) gives:
\[
\begin{aligned}
(\mathbf{A}^{-1})^{\mathsf{H}}\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}
&= (\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^{-1})^{\mathsf{H}} \\
&= \mathbf{I}^{\mathsf{H}} \\
&= \mathbf{I},
\end{aligned}
\]
so \((\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}})^{-1} = (\mathbf{A}^{-1})^{\mathsf{H}}\).










LemTheorem 2 (The adjoint property for inner products)






Theorem 2 (The adjoint property for inner products) Let \(\mathbf{A}\) be an \(m \times n\) complex matrix. Under the standard inner product on complex Euclidean space, \({\mathopen{}\left\langle \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\right\rangle\mathclose{}} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}^{\mathsf{H}}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\),
\[{\mathopen{}\left\langle \mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\right\rangle\mathclose{}} = {\mathopen{}\left\langle \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}, \mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\right\rangle\mathclose{}}
\quad \text{for all } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} \in \mathbb{C}^n \text{ and } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}} \in \mathbb{C}^m.\]










ProofProof






Proof. By the definition of the standard complex inner product and the product rule for the Hermitian adjoint (Theorem 1):
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathopen{}\left\langle \mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\right\rangle\mathclose{}}
&= (\mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}})^{\mathsf{H}}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}
&& \text{(definition of standard inner product)}
\\
&= (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}^{\mathsf{H}}\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}})\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}
&& \text{(}\href{#thm-hermitian-adjoint-properties}{\text{Theorem~1}}\text{, reversal of products)}
\\
&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}^{\mathsf{H}}(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}})
&& \text{(associativity of matrix multiplication)}
\\
&= {\mathopen{}\left\langle \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}, \mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\right\rangle\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(definition of standard inner product)}.
\end{aligned}
\]










RemarkRemark 3 (Where the name “adjoint” comes from)






Remark 3 (Where the name “adjoint” comes from). This identity is the origin of the name adjoint: in functional analysis and operator theory, the adjoint of a linear map \(T: V \to W\) between inner product spaces is defined as the unique operator \(T^*: W \to V\) satisfying \({\mathopen{}\left\langle T\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\right\rangle\mathclose{}} = {\mathopen{}\left\langle \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}, T^*\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\right\rangle\mathclose{}}\) (Axler [2], Definition 7.1, p. 226). When \(V\) and \(W\) are finite-dimensional spaces equipped with their standard orthonormal bases, the matrix representing the adjoint operator \(T^*\) is precisely the Hermitian adjoint matrix \(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}\) (Axler [2], Proposition 7.9, p. 231).










LemTheorem 3 (\(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}^{\mathsf{H}}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}\) is a sum of squared absolute values)






Theorem 3 (\(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}^{\mathsf{H}}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}\) is a sum of squared absolute values) For every \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}} \in \mathbb{C}^p\),
\[\underbrace{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}^{\mathsf{H}}}_{1 \times p}\,\underbrace{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}}_{p \times 1} = \sum_{j=1}^p\mathopen{}\left|z_j\right|\mathclose{}^2,\]
which is a nonnegative real number, and is \(0\) only when \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_{p \times 1}\).










ProofProof






Proof. The last step uses the identity for a complex number times its conjugate.
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}^{\mathsf{H}}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}
&= \sum_{j=1}^p\overline{z_j}\,z_j
&& \text{(}\href{#def-conjugate-transpose}{\text{Definition~4}}\text{, and the row-times-column product)}
\\
&= \sum_{j=1}^pz_j\,\overline{z_j}
&& \text{(complex multiplication is commutative)}
\\
&= \sum_{j=1}^p\mathopen{}\left|z_j\right|\mathclose{}^2
&& \text{(a number times its conjugate)}
\end{aligned}
\]
By the definition of the absolute value, each \(\mathopen{}\left|z_j\right|\mathclose{}^2 = (\operatorname{Re} z_j)^2 + (\operatorname{Im} z_j)^2\) is a nonnegative real number, so their sum is too. A sum of nonnegative numbers is \(0\) only when every term is \(0\), and \(\mathopen{}\left|z_j\right|\mathclose{}^2 = 0\) only when
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Re} z_j &= \operatorname{Im} z_j \\
&= 0,
\end{aligned}
\]
that is, when \(z_j = 0\).










ExmExample 3 (Computing \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}^{\mathsf{H}}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}\))






Example 3 (Computing \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}^{\mathsf{H}}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}\)) Let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}} = {(1 + i, 2)}^{\top}\). By Theorem 3,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\underbrace{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}^{\mathsf{H}}}_{1 \times 2}\,\underbrace{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}}_{2 \times 1}
&= \mathopen{}\left|1 + i\right|\mathclose{}^2 + \mathopen{}\left|2\right|\mathclose{}^2
&& \text{(}\href{#thm-zhz-sum-squares}{\text{Theorem~3}}\text{)}
\\
&= (1^2 + 1^2) + (2^2 + 0^2)
&& \text{(definition of the absolute value, squared)}
\\
&= 2 + 4
&& \text{(add inside each group)}
\\
&= 6
&& \text{(add)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Multiplying out directly gives the same number: \(\overline{2} \cdot 2 = 4\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
\overline{(1 + i)}\,(1 + i)
&= (1 - i)(1 + i)
&& \text{(conjugate)}
\\
&= 1 + i - i - i^2
&& \text{(distribute)}
\\
&= 1 - i^2
&& \text{(cancel } i \text{)}
\\
&= 2
&& \text{(} i^2 = -1 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExmExample 4 (Why complex vectors use the conjugate transpose)






Example 4 (Why complex vectors use the conjugate transpose) For a real vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\), \({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= \sum_{j=1}^px_j^2\) is \(0\) only when \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) is the zero vector. The same formula fails for complex vectors. Let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}} = {(1, i)}^{\top}\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\underbrace{{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}}^{\top}}_{1 \times 2}\,\underbrace{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}}_{2 \times 1}
&= 1 \cdot 1 + i \cdot i
&& \text{(multiply entry by entry and add)}
\\
&= 1 + i^2
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= 0
&& \text{(} i^2 = -1 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
although \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}} \neq \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_{2 \times 1}\). Using the conjugate transpose instead,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\underbrace{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}^{\mathsf{H}}}_{1 \times 2}\,\underbrace{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}}_{2 \times 1}
&= \overline{1} \cdot 1 + \overline{i} \cdot i
&& \text{(}\href{#def-conjugate-transpose}{\text{Definition~4}}\text{)}
\\
&= 1 + (-i) \cdot i
&& \text{(conjugate each entry)}
\\
&= 1 - i^2
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= 2
&& \text{(} i^2 = -1 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
which is positive, as Theorem 3 guarantees.










DefDefinition 5 (Hermitian matrix, self-adjoint matrix)






Definition 5 (Hermitian matrix, self-adjoint matrix) A square complex matrix \(\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{C}^{n \times n}\) is Hermitian [3] (or self-adjoint) if it equals its conjugate transpose (Definition 4):
\[\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}} = \mathbf{A}.\]










RemarkRemark 4 (Why “self-adjoint”)






Remark 4 (Why “self-adjoint”). The term self-adjoint comes directly from Theorem 2: when \(\mathbf{A}\) is Hermitian, \({\mathopen{}\left\langle \mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\right\rangle\mathclose{}} = {\mathopen{}\left\langle \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}, \mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\right\rangle\mathclose{}}\) for all \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}} \in \mathbb{C}^n\). The linear operator moves across the inner product without change.










ExmExample 5 (A Hermitian matrix)






Example 5 (A Hermitian matrix) \[
\underbrace{\mathbf{A}}_{2 \times 2} =
\begin{bmatrix}
2 & 1 - i \\
1 + i & 3
\end{bmatrix}
\]
is Hermitian: transposing swaps the off-diagonal entries, and conjugating turns \(1 + i\) back into \(1 - i\) and \(1 - i\) back into \(1 + i\), so \(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}} = \mathbf{A}\). The diagonal entries of a Hermitian matrix must be real, because \(a_{jj} = \overline{a_{jj}}\), and only a real number is its own conjugate: if \(a + b\,i = a - b\,i\), then the imaginary parts give \(b = -b\), so \(b = 0\).
Every real symmetric matrix is Hermitian, because for a real matrix \(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}} = {\mathbf{A}}^{\top}\).










ExmExample 6 (A symmetric complex matrix that is not Hermitian)






Example 6 (A symmetric complex matrix that is not Hermitian) \[
\underbrace{\mathbf{B}}_{2 \times 2} =
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & i \\
i & 0
\end{bmatrix}
\]
is symmetric, \({\mathbf{B}}^{\top} = \mathbf{B}\), but it is not Hermitian:
\[
\underbrace{\mathbf{B}^{\mathsf{H}}}_{2 \times 2} =
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & -i \\
-i & 0
\end{bmatrix}
\neq \mathbf{B}.
\]










DefDefinition 6 (Skew-Hermitian matrix, anti-Hermitian matrix)






Definition 6 (Skew-Hermitian matrix, anti-Hermitian matrix) A square complex matrix \(\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{C}^{n \times n}\) is skew-Hermitian [4] (or anti-Hermitian) if it equals the negative of its conjugate transpose (Definition 4):
\[\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}} = -\mathbf{A}.\]










RemarkRemark 5 (The diagonal of a skew-Hermitian matrix)






Remark 5 (The diagonal of a skew-Hermitian matrix). Every entry of a skew-Hermitian matrix satisfies \(a_{jk} = -\overline{a_{kj}}\). In particular, its diagonal entries satisfy \(a_{jj} = -\overline{a_{jj}}\), which means
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{jj} + \overline{a_{jj}} &= 2\operatorname{Re}(a_{jj}) \\
&= 0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, every diagonal entry of a skew-Hermitian matrix must be purely imaginary (or zero). For example, \(a_{jj} = 3\,i\) works, since
\[
\begin{aligned}
-\overline{3\,i} &= -(-3\,i) \\
&= 3\,i,
\end{aligned}
\]
but \(a_{jj} = 3\) does not, since \(-\overline{3} = -3\).










ExmExample 7 (A skew-Hermitian matrix)






Example 7 (A skew-Hermitian matrix) The matrix
\[
\mathbf{A} =
\begin{bmatrix}
2\,i & 1 + i \\
-1 + i & 0
\end{bmatrix}
\]
is skew-Hermitian: transposing and conjugating gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}
&=
\begin{bmatrix}
\overline{2\,i} & \overline{-1 + i} \\
\overline{1 + i} & \overline{0}
\end{bmatrix} \\
&=
\begin{bmatrix}
-2\,i & -1 - i \\
1 - i & 0
\end{bmatrix} \\
&= -\mathbf{A}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Its diagonal entries \(2\,i\) and \(0\) are purely imaginary.










LemTheorem 4 (Hermitian and skew-Hermitian decomposition)






Theorem 4 (Hermitian and skew-Hermitian decomposition) Every square complex matrix \(\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{C}^{n \times n}\) can be uniquely expressed as the sum of a Hermitian matrix \(\mathbf{H}\) (Definition 5) and a skew-Hermitian matrix \(\mathbf{S}\) (Definition 6):
\[\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{H} + \mathbf{S},\]
where
\[\mathbf{H} = \frac{\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}}{2}
\quad \text{and} \quad
\mathbf{S} = \frac{\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}}{2}.\]










ProofProof






Proof. Existence: Define \(\mathbf{H} = \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}})\) and \(\mathbf{S} = \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}})\). Their sum is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{H} + \mathbf{S}
&= \frac{\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}}{2} + \frac{\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}}{2} \\
&= \frac{2\mathbf{A}}{2} \\
&= \mathbf{A}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Applying the properties of the Hermitian adjoint (Theorem 1):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{H}^{\mathsf{H}}
&= \mathopen{}\left(\frac{\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}}{2}\right)\mathclose{}^{\mathsf{H}} \\
&= \frac{\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}} + (\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}})^{\mathsf{H}}}{2} \\
&= \frac{\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}} + \mathbf{A}}{2} \\
&= \mathbf{H},
\\
\mathbf{S}^{\mathsf{H}}
&= \mathopen{}\left(\frac{\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}}{2}\right)\mathclose{}^{\mathsf{H}} \\
&= \frac{\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}} - (\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}})^{\mathsf{H}}}{2} \\
&= \frac{\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}} - \mathbf{A}}{2} \\
&= -\mathbf{S}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(\mathbf{H}\) is Hermitian and \(\mathbf{S}\) is skew-Hermitian.
Uniqueness: Suppose \(\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{H}' + \mathbf{S}'\) with \((\mathbf{H}')^{\mathsf{H}} = \mathbf{H}'\) and \((\mathbf{S}')^{\mathsf{H}} = -\mathbf{S}'\). Taking the Hermitian adjoint of both sides yields:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}
&= (\mathbf{H}' + \mathbf{S}')^{\mathsf{H}} \\
&= (\mathbf{H}')^{\mathsf{H}} + (\mathbf{S}')^{\mathsf{H}} \\
&= \mathbf{H}' - \mathbf{S}'.
\end{aligned}
\]
Adding \(\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{H}' + \mathbf{S}'\) and \(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}} = \mathbf{H}' - \mathbf{S}'\) gives \(\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}} = 2\mathbf{H}'\), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{H}' &= \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}) \\
&= \mathbf{H}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Subtracting the two equations gives \(\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}} = 2\mathbf{S}'\), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{S}' &= \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{H}}) \\
&= \mathbf{S}.
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Direct Sums and Orthogonal Complements
text:
NoteSource





This section, Section 2 and Section 3 are adapted from Zhou [1], used under the MIT License (see the license text in Section 2 in Subspaces and Rank). The source proves that a subspace and its orthogonal complement together make up \(\mathbb{R}^p\) by extending an orthonormal basis; the proof here uses the rank-nullity theorem (Theorem 7 in Column Space, Null Space and Rank-Nullity) instead. The source defines the orthogonal complement inside an ambient vector space \(V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m\); here the ambient space is always \(\mathbb{R}^p\), which is all that the fundamental theorem and the projections need.











DefDefinition 1 (Sum of subspaces)






Definition 1 (Sum of subspaces) The sum of two subspaces \(\mathcal{S}_1\) and \(\mathcal{S}_2\) of \(\mathbb{R}^p\) (Definition 4 in Subspaces and Rank) is the set of all sums of a vector from \(\mathcal{S}_1\) and a vector from \(\mathcal{S}_2\):
\[
\mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2
\stackrel{\text{def}}{=}
\mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_1 + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_2 : \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_1 \in \mathcal{S}_1,\ \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_2 \in \mathcal{S}_2\right\}\mathclose{}.
\]










ExmExample 1 (Two lines sum to a plane)






Example 1 (Two lines sum to a plane) Let \(\mathcal{S}_1 = \operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{(1, 0, 0)\right\}\mathclose{}\) and \(\mathcal{S}_2 = \operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{(0, 1, 0)\right\}\mathclose{}\), two lines in \(\mathbb{R}^3\). A vector of \(\mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2\) has the form \(a\,(1, 0, 0) + b\,(0, 1, 0) = (a, b, 0)\), and \(a\) and \(b\) can be any numbers, so \(\mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2 = \mathopen{}\left\{(a, b, 0) : a, b \in \mathbb{R}\right\}\mathclose{}\), the plane \(z = 0\).










ExmExample 2 (The sum is not the union)






Example 2 (The sum is not the union) For the two lines in Example 1, the union \(\mathcal{S}_1 \cup \mathcal{S}_2\) contains \((1, 0, 0)\) and \((0, 1, 0)\) but not their sum \((1, 1, 0)\): every multiple of \((1, 0, 0)\) has second entry \(0\), and every multiple of \((0, 1, 0)\) has first entry \(0\). So the union is not closed under addition and is not a subspace, while the sum, the whole plane \(z = 0\), is.










LemTheorem 1 (Sums and intersections of subspaces are subspaces)






Theorem 1 (Sums and intersections of subspaces are subspaces) If \(\mathcal{S}_1\) and \(\mathcal{S}_2\) are subspaces of \(\mathbb{R}^p\) (Definition 4 in Subspaces and Rank), then \(\mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2\) (Definition 1) and \(\mathcal{S}_1 \cap \mathcal{S}_2\) are subspaces of \(\mathbb{R}^p\).










ProofProof






Proof. Both \(\mathcal{S}_1\) and \(\mathcal{S}_2\) contain \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\) (Theorem 1 in Subspaces and Rank).
The sum. It is not empty: it contains \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}+ \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\). Take two of its vectors, \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_1 + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_2\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}_1 + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}_2\), with \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_1, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}_1 \in \mathcal{S}_1\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_2, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}_2 \in \mathcal{S}_2\), and a number \(c\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}
&= (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_1 + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_2) + (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}_1 + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}_2)
&& \text{(substitute)}
\\
&= (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_1 + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}_1) + (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_2 + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}_2),
&& \text{(regroup; vector addition is entrywise)}
\end{aligned}
\]
where \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_1 + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}_1 \in \mathcal{S}_1\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_2 + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}_2 \in \mathcal{S}_2\), because each subspace is closed under addition. Likewise
\[
\begin{aligned}
c\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}
&= c\,(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_1 + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_2)
&& \text{(substitute)}
\\
&= c\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_1 + c\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_2,
&& \text{(distribute } c \text{ entrywise)}
\end{aligned}
\]
where \(c\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_1 \in \mathcal{S}_1\) and \(c\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_2 \in \mathcal{S}_2\), because each subspace is closed under scalar multiplication. So \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}\) and \(c\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}\) are in \(\mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2\).
The intersection. It is not empty: it contains \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\). If \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}\) are in both \(\mathcal{S}_1\) and \(\mathcal{S}_2\), then \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}\) and \(c\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}\) are in \(\mathcal{S}_1\), because \(\mathcal{S}_1\) is a subspace, and in \(\mathcal{S}_2\) for the same reason, so they are in \(\mathcal{S}_1 \cap \mathcal{S}_2\).










ExmExample 3 (Two planes in \(\mathbb{R}^3\))






Example 3 (Two planes in \(\mathbb{R}^3\)) Let \(\mathcal{S}_1 = \mathopen{}\left\{(a, b, 0) : a, b \in \mathbb{R}\right\}\mathclose{}\), the plane \(z = 0\), and \(\mathcal{S}_2 = \mathopen{}\left\{(0, b, c) : b, c \in \mathbb{R}\right\}\mathclose{}\), the plane \(x = 0\).

Intersection: a vector in both has third entry \(0\) and first entry \(0\), so \(\mathcal{S}_1 \cap \mathcal{S}_2 = \mathopen{}\left\{(0, b, 0) : b \in \mathbb{R}\right\}\mathclose{}\), the \(y\)-axis, which is a line through the origin.
Sum: \((a, b, 0) + (0, b', c) = (a, b + b', c)\), and any \((x, y, z)\) arises this way, with \(a = x\), \(b = y\), \(b' = 0\) and \(c = z\). So \(\mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2 = \mathbb{R}^3\).











LemTheorem 2 (The dimension of a sum of subspaces)






Theorem 2 (The dimension of a sum of subspaces) If \(\mathcal{S}_1\) and \(\mathcal{S}_2\) are subspaces of \(\mathbb{R}^p\), then
\[
\dim(\mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2)
= \dim(\mathcal{S}_1) + \dim(\mathcal{S}_2) - \dim(\mathcal{S}_1 \cap \mathcal{S}_2).
\]










ProofProof






Proof. All three sets in the formula are subspaces (Theorem 1), so each has a dimension (Definition 9 in Subspaces and Rank). Let \(k = \dim(\mathcal{S}_1 \cap \mathcal{S}_2)\), \(d_1 = \dim(\mathcal{S}_1)\) and \(d_2 = \dim(\mathcal{S}_2)\).
Build a list. Choose a basis \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}_k\) of \(\mathcal{S}_1 \cap \mathcal{S}_2\) (Theorem 9 in Subspaces and Rank). These vectors are linearly independent and lie in \(\mathcal{S}_1\), so Theorem 9 in Subspaces and Rank extends them to a basis \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}_k, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_{d_1 - k}\) of \(\mathcal{S}_1\), which has \(d_1\) vectors (Theorem 7 in Subspaces and Rank). In the same way, extend them to a basis \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}_k, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}_{d_2 - k}\) of \(\mathcal{S}_2\). We show that the \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}\)’s, \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\)’s and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\)’s together, \(k + (d_1 - k) + (d_2 - k) = d_1 + d_2 - k\) vectors, are a basis of \(\mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2\) (Definition 6 in Subspaces and Rank).
They span \(\mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2\). Any \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}} \in \mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2\) is \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1 + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_2\) with \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1 \in \mathcal{S}_1\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_2 \in \mathcal{S}_2\). \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1\) is a linear combination of the \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}\)’s and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\)’s, and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_2\) is a linear combination of the \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}\)’s and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\)’s, so their sum is a linear combination of all three groups. Conversely, each vector in the list is in \(\mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2\) (for example, \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_1 = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_1 + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\)), and \(\mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2\) is a subspace, so it contains every linear combination of them.
They are linearly independent. Suppose
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{k} a_i \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}_i
+ \sum_{j=1}^{d_1 - k} b_j \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_j
+ \sum_{l=1}^{d_2 - k} c_l \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}_l
= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}.
\]
Let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\sum_{l} c_l \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}_l\). Then \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} \in \mathcal{S}_2\), because it is a linear combination of vectors of \(\mathcal{S}_2\). Subtracting \(\sum_{i} a_i \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}_i + \sum_{j} b_j \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_j\) from both sides of the supposed equation gives
\[
\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} = \sum_{i=1}^{k} (-a_i)\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}_i + \sum_{j=1}^{d_1 - k} (-b_j)\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_j,
\]
a linear combination of vectors of \(\mathcal{S}_1\), so \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} \in \mathcal{S}_1\) too. So \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} \in \mathcal{S}_1 \cap \mathcal{S}_2\), and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} = \sum_{i} e_i \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}_i\) for some numbers \(e_i\), since the \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}\)’s span the intersection. Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}
&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} - \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}
&& \text{(a vector minus itself)}
\\
&= \sum_{i=1}^{k} e_i \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}_i - \sum_{l=1}^{d_2 - k} c_l \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}_l
&& \text{(substitute the two expressions for } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} \text{)}
\\
&= \sum_{i=1}^{k} e_i \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}_i + \sum_{l=1}^{d_2 - k} (-c_l)\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}_l,
&& \text{(write each subtraction as adding } -1 \text{ times)}
\end{aligned}
\]
and because the \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}\)’s and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\)’s are a basis of \(\mathcal{S}_2\), every \(c_l = 0\). The supposed equation then reads \(\sum_{i} a_i \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}_i + \sum_{j} b_j \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_j = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\), and because the \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}\)’s and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\)’s are a basis of \(\mathcal{S}_1\), every \(a_i\) and \(b_j\) is \(0\).
So \(\dim(\mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2) = d_1 + d_2 - k\). When some of the groups are empty (for example \(k = 0\), or \(\mathcal{S}_1 = \mathcal{S}_1 \cap \mathcal{S}_2\)), the sums over them are \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\) and the argument goes through unchanged.










ExmExample 4 (Two planes in \(\mathbb{R}^3\), by dimension)






Example 4 (Two planes in \(\mathbb{R}^3\), by dimension) For the planes \(z = 0\) and \(x = 0\) in Example 3, each has dimension \(2\): the plane \(z = 0\) has basis \((1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0)\) (Example 16 in Subspaces and Rank), and the plane \(x = 0\) has basis \((0, 1, 0), (0, 0, 1)\) by the same argument. Their intersection, the \(y\)-axis \(\operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{(0, 1, 0)\right\}\mathclose{}\), has dimension \(1\), because the single nonzero vector \((0, 1, 0)\) is linearly independent (\(c\,(0, 1, 0) = (0, c, 0)\) is \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\) only if \(c = 0\)) and so is a basis of it. Theorem 2 gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\dim(\mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2)
&= 2 + 2 - 1 \\
&= 3,
\end{aligned}
\]
which agrees with \(\mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2 = \mathbb{R}^3\) (Example 3) and \(\dim(\mathbb{R}^3) = 3\) (Example 16 in Subspaces and Rank).










CorCorollary 1 (The dimension of a sum is at most the sum of the dimensions)






Corollary 1 (The dimension of a sum is at most the sum of the dimensions) If \(\mathcal{S}_1\) and \(\mathcal{S}_2\) are subspaces of \(\mathbb{R}^p\), then
\[
\dim(\mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2) \le \dim(\mathcal{S}_1) + \dim(\mathcal{S}_2),
\]
with equality exactly when \(\mathcal{S}_1 \cap \mathcal{S}_2 = \mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\right\}\mathclose{}\).










ProofProof






Proof. By Theorem 2, the two sides differ by \(\dim(\mathcal{S}_1 \cap \mathcal{S}_2) \ge 0\). That dimension is \(0\) exactly when a basis of the intersection is the empty list, that is, when the intersection is the span of the empty list, \(\mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\right\}\mathclose{}\) (Definition 5 in Subspaces and Rank, Example 16 in Subspaces and Rank).










ExmExample 5 (Equality and strict inequality)






Example 5 (Equality and strict inequality)  

For the lines \(\mathcal{S}_1 = \operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{(1, 0, 0)\right\}\mathclose{}\) and \(\mathcal{S}_2 = \operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{(0, 1, 0)\right\}\mathclose{}\) in Example 1, a common vector satisfies \(a\,(1, 0, 0) = b\,(0, 1, 0)\), so \((a, -b, 0) = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\) and
\[
\begin{aligned}
a &= b \\
&= 0.
\end{aligned}
\]
The intersection is \(\mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\right\}\mathclose{}\), and indeed
\[
\begin{aligned}
\dim(\mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2) &= 2 \\
&= 1 + 1:
\end{aligned}
\]
the sum is the plane \(z = 0\) (Example 1), which has dimension \(2\) (Example 16 in Subspaces and Rank), and each line has dimension \(1\), with its spanning vector as a basis.
For
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{S}_1 &= \mathcal{S}_2 \\
&= \operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{(1, 0, 0)\right\}\mathclose{},
\end{aligned}
\]
the sum is the same line, because \(a\,(1, 0, 0) + b\,(1, 0, 0) = (a + b)\,(1, 0, 0)\), so \(\dim(\mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2) = 1 < 1 + 1\), a strict inequality.











LemTheorem 3 (Rank is subadditive)






Theorem 3 (Rank is subadditive) For \(m \times n\) matrices \(\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\),
\[
\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B})
\le \operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{A}) + \operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{B}).
\]










ProofProof






Proof. \(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B}) \subseteq \mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A}) + \mathcal{C}(\mathbf{B})\). Any vector of \(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B})\) is \((\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B})\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) for some \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} \in \mathbb{R}^n\) (Definition 1 in Column Space, Null Space and Rank-Nullity), and \((\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B})\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} + \mathbf{B} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) (Theorem 6 in Matrices, with \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) as an \(n \times 1\) matrix), a vector of \(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A})\) plus a vector of \(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{B})\).
Compare dimensions. All the sets involved are subspaces of \(\mathbb{R}^m\) (Theorem 1 in Column Space, Null Space and Rank-Nullity, Theorem 1), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B})
&= \dim\mathopen{}\left(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B})\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(}\href{linear-algebra-rank-nullity.qmd#thm-rank-dim}{\text{Theorem~6 in Column Space, Null Space and Rank-Nullity}}\text{)}
\\
&\le \dim\mathopen{}\left(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A}) + \mathcal{C}(\mathbf{B})\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(the containment, and part 2 of }\href{linear-algebra-subspaces.qmd#thm-dim-bound}{\text{Theorem~10 in Subspaces and Rank}}\text{)}
\\
&\le \dim\mathopen{}\left(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A})\right)\mathclose{} + \dim\mathopen{}\left(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{B})\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(}\href{#cor-dim-subadditive}{\text{Corollary~1}}\text{)}
\\
&= \operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{A}) + \operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{B}).
&& \text{(}\href{linear-algebra-rank-nullity.qmd#thm-rank-dim}{\text{Theorem~6 in Column Space, Null Space and Rank-Nullity}}\text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExmExample 6 (Subadditivity with equality and without)






Example 6 (Subadditivity with equality and without) Let \(\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf{B} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\). Each has one nonzero column and one zero column. The nonzero column on its own is linearly independent (\(c\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_2\) with \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}} \ne \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_2\) forces \(c = 0\)), and the two columns together are not, since \(1\) times the zero column is \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_2\); so each matrix has rank \(1\) (Definition 2 in Subspaces and Rank). By the same argument, \(-\mathbf{A}\) has rank \(1\).

\(\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B}\) is the \(2 \times 2\) identity matrix, which has rank \(2\) (Example 12 in Column Space, Null Space and Rank-Nullity), so the bound \(2 \le 1 + 1\) holds with equality.
\(\mathbf{A} + (-\mathbf{A})\) is the \(2 \times 2\) zero matrix, which has rank \(0\): any nonempty list of its columns contains \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_2\), and \(1 \cdot\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_2 = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_2\). So the bound \(0 \le \operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{A}) + \operatorname{rank}(-\mathbf{A}) = 1 + 1\) is strict.











DefDefinition 2 (Complementary subspaces)






Definition 2 (Complementary subspaces) Let \(\mathcal{S}_1\), \(\mathcal{S}_2\) and \(\mathcal{V}\) be subspaces of \(\mathbb{R}^p\). \(\mathcal{S}_1\) and \(\mathcal{S}_2\) are complementary in \(\mathcal{V}\) if
\[
\mathcal{V} = \mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2
\quad \text{and} \quad
\mathcal{S}_1 \cap \mathcal{S}_2 = \mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\right\}\mathclose{}
\]
(Definition 1).










DefDefinition 3 (Direct sum)






Definition 3 (Direct sum) If \(\mathcal{S}_1\) and \(\mathcal{S}_2\) are complementary in \(\mathcal{V}\) (Definition 2), then \(\mathcal{V}\) is the direct sum [2] of \(\mathcal{S}_1\) and \(\mathcal{S}_2\), written \(\mathcal{V} = \mathcal{S}_1 \oplus \mathcal{S}_2\).










ExmExample 7 (\(\mathbb{R}^3\) is a plane plus a line)






Example 7 (\(\mathbb{R}^3\) is a plane plus a line) Let \(\mathcal{S}_1 = \mathopen{}\left\{(a, b, 0) : a, b \in \mathbb{R}\right\}\mathclose{}\), the plane \(z = 0\), and \(\mathcal{S}_2 = \mathopen{}\left\{(0, 0, c) : c \in \mathbb{R}\right\}\mathclose{}\), the \(z\)-axis.

Sum: any \((x, y, z) \in \mathbb{R}^3\) is \((x, y, 0) + (0, 0, z)\), so \(\mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2 = \mathbb{R}^3\).
Intersection: a vector in both has third entry \(0\) and first and second entries \(0\), so \(\mathcal{S}_1 \cap \mathcal{S}_2 = \mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\right\}\mathclose{}\).

So \(\mathbb{R}^3 = \mathcal{S}_1 \oplus \mathcal{S}_2\).










ExmExample 8 (Two planes that sum to \(\mathbb{R}^3\) but not directly)






Example 8 (Two planes that sum to \(\mathbb{R}^3\) but not directly) The planes \(z = 0\) and \(x = 0\) sum to \(\mathbb{R}^3\) (Example 3), but they share the \(y\)-axis, so they are not complementary, and \(\mathbb{R}^3\) is not their direct sum. The shared line shows up as more than one way to split a vector:
\[
\begin{aligned}
(0, 1, 0) &= (0, 1, 0) + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\\
&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}+ (0, 1, 0),
\end{aligned}
\]
with the first term in the plane \(z = 0\) and the second in the plane \(x = 0\) both times.










LemTheorem 4 (Three ways to recognize a direct sum)






Theorem 4 (Three ways to recognize a direct sum) Let \(\mathcal{S}_1\) and \(\mathcal{S}_2\) be subspaces of \(\mathbb{R}^p\), and let \(\mathcal{V} = \mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2\). The following statements are equivalent:

\(\mathcal{V} = \mathcal{S}_1 \oplus \mathcal{S}_2\) (Definition 3).
\(\dim(\mathcal{V}) = \dim(\mathcal{S}_1) + \dim(\mathcal{S}_2)\).
Every \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} \in \mathcal{V}\) can be written as \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_1 + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_2\) with \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_1 \in \mathcal{S}_1\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_2 \in \mathcal{S}_2\) in only one way.











ProofProof






Proof. Since \(\mathcal{V} = \mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2\) is given, statement 1 says exactly that \(\mathcal{S}_1 \cap \mathcal{S}_2 = \mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\right\}\mathclose{}\).
1 and 2 are equivalent. By Corollary 1, \(\dim(\mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2) = \dim(\mathcal{S}_1) + \dim(\mathcal{S}_2)\) exactly when \(\mathcal{S}_1 \cap \mathcal{S}_2 = \mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\right\}\mathclose{}\).
1 implies 3. Every \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} \in \mathcal{V}\) has at least one such expression, because \(\mathcal{V} = \mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2\). Suppose
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} &= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_1 + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_2 \\
&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1 + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_2,
\end{aligned}
\]
with \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_1, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1 \in \mathcal{S}_1\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_2, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_2 \in \mathcal{S}_2\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_1 - \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1
&= (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_1 + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_2) - \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_2 - \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1
&& \text{(add and subtract } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_2 \text{)}
\\
&= (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1 + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_2) - \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_2 - \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1
&& \text{(substitute } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_1 + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_2 = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1 + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_2 \text{)}
\\
&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_2 - \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_2.
&& \text{(cancel } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
The left side is in \(\mathcal{S}_1\) and the right side is in \(\mathcal{S}_2\), because each subspace is closed under addition and scalar multiplication (the difference is \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_1 + (-1)\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1\)). So both sides are in \(\mathcal{S}_1 \cap \mathcal{S}_2 = \mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\right\}\mathclose{}\), which gives \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_1 = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_2 = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_2\).
3 implies 1. Take any \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} \in \mathcal{S}_1 \cap \mathcal{S}_2\). Then \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\), with \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} \in \mathcal{S}_1\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\in \mathcal{S}_2\), and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}+ \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\), with \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\in \mathcal{S}_1\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} \in \mathcal{S}_2\) (Theorem 1 in Subspaces and Rank). By statement 3 these two expressions are the same, so \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\), and \(\mathcal{S}_1 \cap \mathcal{S}_2 = \mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\right\}\mathclose{}\).










ExmExample 9 (Checking the three statements)






Example 9 (Checking the three statements) For the plane \(z = 0\) and the \(z\)-axis in Example 7:

the dimensions add up:
\[
\begin{aligned}
2 + 1 &= 3 \\
&= \dim(\mathbb{R}^3),
\end{aligned}
\]
since the plane has dimension \(2\) (Example 16 in Subspaces and Rank), the \(z\)-axis has the single nonzero vector \((0, 0, 1)\) as a basis, and \(\dim(\mathbb{R}^3) = 3\) (Example 16 in Subspaces and Rank);
the split is unique: if
\[
\begin{aligned}
(x, y, z) &= (a, b, 0) + (0, 0, c) \\
&= (a, b, c),
\end{aligned}
\]
then \(a = x\), \(b = y\) and \(c = z\).

For the planes \(z = 0\) and \(x = 0\) in Example 8, both statements fail:
\[
\begin{aligned}
2 + 2 &= 4 \\
&\ne 3 \\
&= \dim(\mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2)
\end{aligned}
\]
(Example 4), and \((0, 1, 0)\) splits in two ways.










DefDefinition 4 (Projection onto a subspace along a complement)






Definition 4 (Projection onto a subspace along a complement) Let \(\mathcal{S}\) and \(\mathcal{T}\) be subspaces of \(\mathbb{R}^p\) with \(\mathbb{R}^p = \mathcal{S} \oplus \mathcal{T}\) (Definition 3), and let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}} \in \mathbb{R}^p\). By Theorem 4, \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\) for exactly one \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} \in \mathcal{S}\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}} \in \mathcal{T}\). The vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}\) is the projection [3] of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\) onto \(\mathcal{S}\) along \(\mathcal{T}\) [4], Definition 6.3, p. 163.










ExmExample 10 (The projection depends on the complement)






Example 10 (The projection depends on the complement) Let \(\mathcal{S} = \operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{(1, 0)\right\}\mathclose{}\), the horizontal axis in \(\mathbb{R}^2\), and let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}} = (3, 2)\).

Along \(\mathcal{T}_1 = \operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{(1, -1)\right\}\mathclose{}\): \((3, 2) = (5, 0) + (-2, 2)\), with \((5, 0) \in \mathcal{S}\) and \((-2, 2) = -2 \cdot(1, -1) \in \mathcal{T}_1\), so the projection of \((3, 2)\) onto \(\mathcal{S}\) along \(\mathcal{T}_1\) is \((5, 0)\).
Along \(\mathcal{T}_2 = \operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{(0, 1)\right\}\mathclose{}\): \((3, 2) = (3, 0) + (0, 2)\), with \((3, 0) \in \mathcal{S}\) and \((0, 2) \in \mathcal{T}_2\), so the projection of \((3, 2)\) onto \(\mathcal{S}\) along \(\mathcal{T}_2\) is \((3, 0)\).

Each of \(\mathcal{T}_1\) and \(\mathcal{T}_2\) is a line that meets \(\mathcal{S}\) only at \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{R}^2 &= \mathcal{S} \oplus \mathcal{T}_1 \\
&= \mathcal{S} \oplus \mathcal{T}_2
\end{aligned}
\]
(Definition 3, Theorem 4). The same vector has a different projection onto the same subspace when the complement changes.

title: Direct Sums and Orthogonal Complements
text:
NoteSource





This section, Section 2 and Section 3 are adapted from Zhou [1], used under the MIT License (see the license text in Section 2 in Subspaces and Rank). The source proves that a subspace and its orthogonal complement together make up \(\mathbb{R}^p\) by extending an orthonormal basis; the proof here uses the rank-nullity theorem (Theorem 7 in Column Space, Null Space and Rank-Nullity) instead. The source defines the orthogonal complement inside an ambient vector space \(V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m\); here the ambient space is always \(\mathbb{R}^p\), which is all that the fundamental theorem and the projections need.











DefDefinition 1 (Sum of subspaces)






Definition 1 (Sum of subspaces) The sum of two subspaces \(\mathcal{S}_1\) and \(\mathcal{S}_2\) of \(\mathbb{R}^p\) (Definition 4 in Subspaces and Rank) is the set of all sums of a vector from \(\mathcal{S}_1\) and a vector from \(\mathcal{S}_2\):
\[
\mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2
\stackrel{\text{def}}{=}
\mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_1 + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_2 : \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_1 \in \mathcal{S}_1,\ \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_2 \in \mathcal{S}_2\right\}\mathclose{}.
\]










ExmExample 1 (Two lines sum to a plane)






Example 1 (Two lines sum to a plane) Let \(\mathcal{S}_1 = \operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{(1, 0, 0)\right\}\mathclose{}\) and \(\mathcal{S}_2 = \operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{(0, 1, 0)\right\}\mathclose{}\), two lines in \(\mathbb{R}^3\). A vector of \(\mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2\) has the form \(a\,(1, 0, 0) + b\,(0, 1, 0) = (a, b, 0)\), and \(a\) and \(b\) can be any numbers, so \(\mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2 = \mathopen{}\left\{(a, b, 0) : a, b \in \mathbb{R}\right\}\mathclose{}\), the plane \(z = 0\).










ExmExample 2 (The sum is not the union)






Example 2 (The sum is not the union) For the two lines in Example 1, the union \(\mathcal{S}_1 \cup \mathcal{S}_2\) contains \((1, 0, 0)\) and \((0, 1, 0)\) but not their sum \((1, 1, 0)\): every multiple of \((1, 0, 0)\) has second entry \(0\), and every multiple of \((0, 1, 0)\) has first entry \(0\). So the union is not closed under addition and is not a subspace, while the sum, the whole plane \(z = 0\), is.










LemTheorem 1 (Sums and intersections of subspaces are subspaces)






Theorem 1 (Sums and intersections of subspaces are subspaces) If \(\mathcal{S}_1\) and \(\mathcal{S}_2\) are subspaces of \(\mathbb{R}^p\) (Definition 4 in Subspaces and Rank), then \(\mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2\) (Definition 1) and \(\mathcal{S}_1 \cap \mathcal{S}_2\) are subspaces of \(\mathbb{R}^p\).










ProofProof






Proof. Both \(\mathcal{S}_1\) and \(\mathcal{S}_2\) contain \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\) (Theorem 1 in Subspaces and Rank).
The sum. It is not empty: it contains \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}+ \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\). Take two of its vectors, \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_1 + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_2\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}_1 + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}_2\), with \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_1, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}_1 \in \mathcal{S}_1\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_2, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}_2 \in \mathcal{S}_2\), and a number \(c\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}
&= (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_1 + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_2) + (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}_1 + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}_2)
&& \text{(substitute)}
\\
&= (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_1 + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}_1) + (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_2 + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}_2),
&& \text{(regroup; vector addition is entrywise)}
\end{aligned}
\]
where \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_1 + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}_1 \in \mathcal{S}_1\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_2 + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}_2 \in \mathcal{S}_2\), because each subspace is closed under addition. Likewise
\[
\begin{aligned}
c\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}
&= c\,(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_1 + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_2)
&& \text{(substitute)}
\\
&= c\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_1 + c\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_2,
&& \text{(distribute } c \text{ entrywise)}
\end{aligned}
\]
where \(c\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_1 \in \mathcal{S}_1\) and \(c\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_2 \in \mathcal{S}_2\), because each subspace is closed under scalar multiplication. So \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}\) and \(c\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}\) are in \(\mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2\).
The intersection. It is not empty: it contains \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\). If \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}\) are in both \(\mathcal{S}_1\) and \(\mathcal{S}_2\), then \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}\) and \(c\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}\) are in \(\mathcal{S}_1\), because \(\mathcal{S}_1\) is a subspace, and in \(\mathcal{S}_2\) for the same reason, so they are in \(\mathcal{S}_1 \cap \mathcal{S}_2\).










ExmExample 3 (Two planes in \(\mathbb{R}^3\))






Example 3 (Two planes in \(\mathbb{R}^3\)) Let \(\mathcal{S}_1 = \mathopen{}\left\{(a, b, 0) : a, b \in \mathbb{R}\right\}\mathclose{}\), the plane \(z = 0\), and \(\mathcal{S}_2 = \mathopen{}\left\{(0, b, c) : b, c \in \mathbb{R}\right\}\mathclose{}\), the plane \(x = 0\).

Intersection: a vector in both has third entry \(0\) and first entry \(0\), so \(\mathcal{S}_1 \cap \mathcal{S}_2 = \mathopen{}\left\{(0, b, 0) : b \in \mathbb{R}\right\}\mathclose{}\), the \(y\)-axis, which is a line through the origin.
Sum: \((a, b, 0) + (0, b', c) = (a, b + b', c)\), and any \((x, y, z)\) arises this way, with \(a = x\), \(b = y\), \(b' = 0\) and \(c = z\). So \(\mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2 = \mathbb{R}^3\).











LemTheorem 2 (The dimension of a sum of subspaces)
