ExmExample 10 (The \(3 \times 3\) identity)






Example 10 (The \(3 \times 3\) identity) \[
\mathbf{I}_3 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix},
\]
so, for instance, \((\mathbf{I}_3)_{22} = 1\) and \((\mathbf{I}_3)_{23} = 0\).










RemarkRemark 3 (The identity matrix and the Kronecker delta)






Remark 3 (The identity matrix and the Kronecker delta). The entries of the identity matrix are given by the Kronecker delta: \((\mathbf{I}_p)_{ij} = \delta_{ij}\).










LemTheorem 8 (Identity matrix is a multiplicative identity)






Theorem 8 (Identity matrix is a multiplicative identity) For any \(m \times p\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\):
\[\mathbf{A}\,\mathbf{I}_p = \mathbf{A}\]
\[\mathbf{I}_m\,\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{A}\]













DefDefinition 13 (Matrix-vector multiplication)






Definition 13 (Matrix-vector multiplication) The matrix-vector product of an \(m \times p\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) and a \(p \times 1\) column vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) is the \(m \times 1\) column vector \(\mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) with entries:
\[(\mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})_i = \sum_{j=1}^pa_{ij}\, x_j\]










RemarkRemark 4 (Each entry is a dot product)






Remark 4 (Each entry is a dot product). Matrix-vector multiplication extends the dot product (Definition 8 in Vectors): entry \(i\) of \(\mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) is the dot product of row \(i\) of \(\mathbf{A}\) with \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\). For example,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}
&=
\begin{bmatrix} 1 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot(-1) \\ 3 \cdot 1 + 4 \cdot(-1) \end{bmatrix} \\
&=
\begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
\]










DefDefinition 14 (Linear system, system of linear equations)






Definition 14 (Linear system, system of linear equations) A linear system [11] (or system of linear equations) with \(m\) equations in \(n\) unknowns is an equation \(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\) in which the \(m \times n\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) and the vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}} \in \mathbb{R}^m\) are given. A solution of the system is a vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\in \mathbb{R}^n\) for which \(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\) holds.










ExmExample 11 (Two equations in two unknowns)






Example 11 (Two equations in two unknowns) By Definition 13, row \(i\) of \(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\) is the equation \(a_{i1} x_1 + \cdots + a_{in} x_n = b_i\). So the two equations \(x_1 + 2 x_2 = 5\) and \(3 x_1 + 4 x_2 = 6\) form the linear system \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix}\). The vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= (-4, 4.5)\) is a solution:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} -4 \\ 4.5 \end{bmatrix}
&= \begin{bmatrix} 1 \cdot(-4) + 2 \cdot 4.5 \\ 3 \cdot(-4) + 4 \cdot 4.5 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(}\href{#def-matvec-mult}{\text{Definition~13}}\text{)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} -4 + 9 \\ -12 + 18 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(add)}
\end{aligned}
\]
The vector \((1, 2)\) is not a solution: its first equation holds, since \(1 + 2 \cdot 2 = 5\), but its second gives \(3 \cdot 1 + 4 \cdot 2 = 11 \ne 6\).













DefDefinition 15 (Linear map, linear transformation, linear function)






Definition 15 (Linear map, linear transformation, linear function) A function \(f: \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}^m\) is a linear map [12] (also called a linear transformation or linear function) if it preserves vector addition and scalar multiplication: for all \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\in \mathbb{R}^p\) and \(c \in \mathbb{R}\),

\(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}+ \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}) = f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) + f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}})\) (additivity)
\(f(c\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = c f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\) (homogeneity)











ExmExample 12 (A linear map, and two functions that are not)






Example 12 (A linear map, and two functions that are not)  

\(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = (2 x_1,\ x_1 + x_2)\) on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) is linear. For \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\in \mathbb{R}^2\) and \(c \in \mathbb{R}\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}+ \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}) &= (2 (x_1 + y_1),\ (x_1 + y_1) + (x_2 + y_2)) \\
&= f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) + f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}})
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(c \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) &= (2 c x_1,\ c x_1 + c x_2) \\
&= c f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}).
\end{aligned}
\]
\(g(x) = x + 1\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) is not linear: additivity fails, since \(g(0 + 0) = 1\) but \(g(0) + g(0) = 2\).
\(h(x) = x^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) is not linear: \(h(2 \cdot 1) = 4\) but \(2\,h(1) = 2\), so \(h(c x) \ne c\,h(x)\) for \(c = 2\), \(x = 1\).











DefDefinition 16 (Linear operator)






Definition 16 (Linear operator) A linear operator on \(\mathbb{R}^p\) is a linear map (Definition 15) from \(\mathbb{R}^p\) to itself, that is, a linear map \(f : \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}^p\) whose input and output have the same length. Some authors use “operator” more loosely, for any linear map.










ExmExample 13 (A linear operator, and a linear map that is not one)






Example 13 (A linear operator, and a linear map that is not one) The map \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = (2 x_1,\ x_1 + x_2)\) from Example 12 sends \(\mathbb{R}^2\) to \(\mathbb{R}^2\), so it is a linear operator on \(\mathbb{R}^2\). The linear map \(g(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = x_1 + x_2\) sends \(\mathbb{R}^2\) to \(\mathbb{R}\), so it is linear but not an operator: its outputs have length \(1\), not \(2\).










LemTheorem 9 (A linear map sends zero to zero)






Theorem 9 (A linear map sends zero to zero) If \(f: \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}^m\) is a linear map (Definition 15), then \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}) = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\).










ProofProof






Proof. On the left, \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\) is the zero vector of length \(p\); on the right, it is the zero vector of length \(m\).
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}})
&= f(0 \cdot\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}})
&& \text{(every entry of } 0 \cdot\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\text{ is } 0 \cdot 0 = 0 \text{; }\href{#def-scalar-mult}{\text{Definition~6}}\text{)}
\\&= 0 \cdot f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}})
&& \text{(homogeneity, with } c = 0 \text{ and } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\text{)}
\\&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}
&& \text{(every entry of } 0 \cdot f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}) \text{ is } 0 \text{; }\href{#def-scalar-mult}{\text{Definition~6}}\text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExmExample 14 (Ruling out linearity at zero)






Example 14 (Ruling out linearity at zero) In Example 12, \(g(x) = x + 1\) has \(g(0) = 1 \neq 0\), so by Theorem 9 it is not linear, without checking additivity or homogeneity.
Sending \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\) to \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\) is necessary but not sufficient: \(h(x) = x^2\) in the same example has \(h(0) = 0\) and is still not linear.










LemTheorem 10 (Multiplying by a matrix is a linear map)






Theorem 10 (Multiplying by a matrix is a linear map) For any \(m \times p\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\), the function \(f: \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}^m\) defined by \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = \mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) is a linear map (Definition 15).










ProofProof






Proof. Both conditions are checked one entry at a time. For each \(i \in \{1, \ldots, m\}\), additivity:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathopen{}\left(\mathbf{A}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}+ \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}})\right)\mathclose{}_i
&= \sum_{j=1}^pa_{ij} (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}+ \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}})_j
&& \text{(}\href{#def-matvec-mult}{\text{Definition~13}}\text{)}
\\&= \sum_{j=1}^pa_{ij} (x_j + y_j)
&& \text{(}\href{linear-algebra-vectors.qmd#def-vector-addition}{\text{Definition~7 in Vectors}}\text{)}
\\&= \sum_{j=1}^p(a_{ij} x_j + a_{ij} y_j)
&& \text{(multiplication distributes over addition)}
\\&= \sum_{j=1}^pa_{ij} x_j + \sum_{j=1}^pa_{ij} y_j
&& \text{(a sum of sums splits)}
\\&= (\mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})_i + (\mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}})_i
&& \text{(}\href{#def-matvec-mult}{\text{Definition~13}}\text{)}
\\&= (\mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}+ \mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}})_i
&& \text{(}\href{linear-algebra-vectors.qmd#def-vector-addition}{\text{Definition~7 in Vectors}}\text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
and homogeneity:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathopen{}\left(\mathbf{A}(c\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\right)\mathclose{}_i
&= \sum_{j=1}^pa_{ij} (c\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})_j
&& \text{(}\href{#def-matvec-mult}{\text{Definition~13}}\text{)}
\\&= \sum_{j=1}^pa_{ij}\, c\, x_j
&& \text{(}\href{#def-scalar-mult}{\text{Definition~6}}\text{)}
\\&= \sum_{j=1}^pc\, a_{ij} x_j
&& \text{(products are symmetric)}
\\&= c \sum_{j=1}^pa_{ij} x_j
&& \text{(a constant factor comes out of a sum)}
\\&= c\, (\mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})_i
&& \text{(}\href{#def-matvec-mult}{\text{Definition~13}}\text{)}
\\&= (c\, \mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})_i
&& \text{(}\href{#def-scalar-mult}{\text{Definition~6}}\text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
The four algebra rules cited here are on the algebra page: distributivity, a sum of sums, symmetry of products, and a constant factor.










LemTheorem 11 (A linear map preserves linear combinations)






Theorem 11 (A linear map preserves linear combinations) If \(f: \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}^m\) is a linear map (Definition 15), then for any vectors \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k \in \mathbb{R}^p\) and any coefficients \(c_1, \ldots, c_k \in \mathbb{R}\):
\[f\mathopen{}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{k} c_j \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_j\right)\mathclose{} = \sum_{j=1}^{k} c_j f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_j)\]










ProofProof






Proof. By induction on \(k\). For \(k = 1\), the claim \(f(c_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1) = c_1 f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1)\) is homogeneity.
Suppose the claim holds for \(k\) vectors. Then for \(k + 1\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
f\mathopen{}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{k+1} c_j \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_j\right)\mathclose{}
&= f\mathopen{}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{k} c_j \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_j + c_{k+1} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_{k+1}\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(split off the last term)}
\\&= f\mathopen{}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{k} c_j \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_j\right)\mathclose{} + f(c_{k+1} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_{k+1})
&& \text{(additivity)}
\\&= \sum_{j=1}^{k} c_j f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_j) + f(c_{k+1} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_{k+1})
&& \text{(induction hypothesis)}
\\&= \sum_{j=1}^{k} c_j f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_j) + c_{k+1} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_{k+1})
&& \text{(homogeneity)}
\\&= \sum_{j=1}^{k+1} c_j f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_j)
&& \text{(join the last term back on)}
\end{aligned}
\]










LemTheorem 12 (Every linear map is multiplication by a matrix)






Theorem 12 (Every linear map is multiplication by a matrix) If \(f: \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}^m\) is a linear map (Definition 15), then there is exactly one \(m \times p\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) such that
\[f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = \mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\quad \text{for all } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\in \mathbb{R}^p\]
Column \(j\) of \(\mathbf{A}\) is \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{e}}\vphantom{e}}_j)\), the value of \(f\) at the \(j\)th indicator vector (Definition 18 in Vectors); that is, \(a_{ij} = \mathopen{}\left(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{e}}\vphantom{e}}_j)\right)\mathclose{}_i\).










ProofProof






Proof. Existence. Let \(\mathbf{A}\) be the \(m \times p\) matrix with \(a_{ij} = \mathopen{}\left(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{e}}\vphantom{e}}_j)\right)\mathclose{}_i\). For any \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\in \mathbb{R}^p\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})
&= f\mathopen{}\left(\sum_{j=1}^px_j \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{e}}\vphantom{e}}_j\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(}\href{linear-algebra-vectors.qmd#thm-standard-basis-expansion}{\text{Theorem~4 in Vectors}}\text{)}
\\&= \sum_{j=1}^px_j f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{e}}\vphantom{e}}_j)
&& \text{(}\href{#thm-linear-map-lincom}{\text{Theorem~11}}\text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
and entry \(i\) of that sum is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathopen{}\left(\sum_{j=1}^px_j f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{e}}\vphantom{e}}_j)\right)\mathclose{}_i
&= \sum_{j=1}^px_j \mathopen{}\left(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{e}}\vphantom{e}}_j)\right)\mathclose{}_i
&& \text{(}\href{linear-algebra-vectors.qmd#def-linear-combination}{\text{Definition~9 in Vectors}}\text{, entry by entry)}
\\&= \sum_{j=1}^px_j a_{ij}
&& \text{(definition of } \mathbf{A} \text{)}
\\&= \sum_{j=1}^pa_{ij} x_j
&& \text{(products are symmetric)}
\\&= (\mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})_i
&& \text{(}\href{#def-matvec-mult}{\text{Definition~13}}\text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Uniqueness. Suppose \(\mathbf{B}\) is any \(m \times p\) matrix with \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = \mathbf{B}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) for all \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\). Taking \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{e}}\vphantom{e}}_j\), for each \(i\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathopen{}\left(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{e}}\vphantom{e}}_j)\right)\mathclose{}_i
&= (\mathbf{B}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{e}}\vphantom{e}}_j)_i
&& \text{(assumption on } \mathbf{B} \text{)}
\\&= \sum_{k=1}^{p} b_{ik} (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{e}}\vphantom{e}}_j)_k
&& \text{(}\href{#def-matvec-mult}{\text{Definition~13}}\text{)}
\\&= b_{ij} \cdot 1 + \sum_{k \neq j} b_{ik} \cdot 0
&& \text{(}\href{linear-algebra-vectors.qmd#def-indicator-vector}{\text{Definition~18 in Vectors}}\text{, splitting off the } k = j \text{ term)}
\\&= b_{ij} + 0
&& \text{(times } 1 \text{ changes nothing; times } 0 \text{ gives } 0 \text{)}
\\&= b_{ij}
&& \text{(adding } 0 \text{ changes nothing)}
\end{aligned}
\]
So
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_{ij} &= \mathopen{}\left(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{e}}\vphantom{e}}_j)\right)\mathclose{}_i \\
&= a_{ij}
\end{aligned}
\]
for every \(i\) and \(j\), and \(\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{A}\).










DefDefinition 17 (Matrix of a linear map)






Definition 17 (Matrix of a linear map) The matrix of a linear map \(f: \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}^m\) is the unique \(m \times p\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) with \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = \mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) for all \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) (Theorem 12). Its column \(j\) is \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{e}}\vphantom{e}}_j)\).










ExmExample 15 (Finding the matrix of a linear map)






Example 15 (Finding the matrix of a linear map) For \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = (2 x_1,\ x_1 + x_2)\) from Example 12, the values of \(f\) at the indicator vectors are
\[
f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{e}}\vphantom{e}}_1) = f\mathopen{}\left(\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\right)\mathclose{} = \begin{bmatrix}2 \cdot 1 \\ 1 + 0\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{e}}\vphantom{e}}_2) = f\mathopen{}\left(\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\right)\mathclose{} = \begin{bmatrix}2 \cdot 0 \\ 0 + 1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
\]
and these are the columns of the matrix of \(f\) (Definition 17): \(\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\).










CorCorollary 1 (Linear functions from vectors to numbers)






Corollary 1 (Linear functions from vectors to numbers) A function \(f: \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}\) is linear (Definition 15) if and only if there is a vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} \in \mathbb{R}^p\) such that
\[f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} \quad \text{for all } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\in \mathbb{R}^p\]
and then \(w_j = f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{e}}\vphantom{e}}_j)\) for each \(j\).










ProofProof






Proof. If \(f\) is linear. Theorem 12 with \(m = 1\) gives a \(1 \times p\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) with \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = \mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) and \(a_{1j} = f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{e}}\vphantom{e}}_j)\). Let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}\) be the vector with \(w_j = a_{1j}\), so that \(\mathbf{A} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}^{\top}\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})
&= \mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}
&& \text{(}\href{#thm-linear-map-matrix}{\text{Theorem~12}}\text{)}
\\&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}
&& (\mathbf{A} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}^{\top})
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
w_j &= a_{1j} \\
&= f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{e}}\vphantom{e}}_j).
\end{aligned}
\]
If \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\). Here \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}^{\top}\) is a \(1 \times p\) matrix, so \(f\) is linear by Theorem 10.










ExmExample 16 (A linear function from \(\mathbb{R}^2\) to \(\mathbb{R}\))






Example 16 (A linear function from \(\mathbb{R}^2\) to \(\mathbb{R}\)) \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = 3 x_1 + 5 x_2\) is \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) with \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} = {(3, 5)}^{\top}\), so it is linear by Corollary 1. The entries of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}\) are the values at the indicator vectors:
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{e}}\vphantom{e}}_1) &= 3 \cdot 1 + 5 \cdot 0 \\
&= 3
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{e}}\vphantom{e}}_2) &= 3 \cdot 0 + 5 \cdot 1 \\
&= 5.
\end{aligned}
\]
\(g(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = 3 x_1 + 5 x_2 + 1\) is not linear, because \(g(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}) = 1 \neq 0\) (Theorem 9).










TipVideos



Two chapters of the Essence of linear algebra series by 3Blue1Brown show the results above geometrically:

Linear transformations and matrices (Chapter 3) shows why a linear map is fixed by where it sends the indicator vectors, which become the columns of its matrix (Definition 17).
Dot products and duality (Chapter 9) shows why every linear map from \(\mathbb{R}^p\) to \(\mathbb{R}\) is a dot product with a fixed vector (Corollary 1).









DefDefinition 18 (Translation)






Definition 18 (Translation) For a fixed vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}} \in \mathbb{R}^m\), the translation [13] by \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\) is the function \(t_{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}} : \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^m\) defined by
\[t_{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}) = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}+ \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\]










ExmExample 17 (Translating two points)






Example 17 (Translating two points) The translation by \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}} = {(1, -2)}^{\top}\) sends
\[
t_{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}}\mathopen{}\left(\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\right)\mathclose{} = \begin{bmatrix}0 + 1 \\ 0 + (-2)\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
t_{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}}\mathopen{}\left(\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}\right)\mathclose{} = \begin{bmatrix}3 + 1 \\ 4 + (-2)\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}
\]
Both points move one unit right and two units down.










RemarkRemark 5 (A translation moves every point by the same vector)






Remark 5 (A translation moves every point by the same vector). A translation by \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\) moves every point by the same vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\).










DefDefinition 19 (Affine map, affine transformation, affine function)






Definition 19 (Affine map, affine transformation, affine function) A function \(f: \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}^m\) is an affine map (also called an affine transformation or affine function) if it is a matrix product followed by a translation (Definition 18) (a composition, with the matrix product as the inner function): there are an \(m \times p\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) and a vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}} \in \mathbb{R}^m\) such that
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})
&= t_{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}}(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) \\
&= \mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}+ \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}} \quad \text{for all } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\in \mathbb{R}^p
\end{aligned}
\]










DefDefinition 20 (Offset of an affine map, intercept, bias)






Definition 20 (Offset of an affine map, intercept, bias) In Definition 19, the vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\) is called the offset of \(f\) (statistics also calls it the intercept, and machine learning the bias).










RemarkRemark 6 (Real-valued affine maps)






Remark 6 (Real-valued affine maps). For a real-valued function (Definition 4 in Vectors, \(m = 1\)), \(\mathbf{A}\) is a single row, written \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}^{\top}\), and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\) is a single number \(b\), so an affine function is a linear function \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) (Corollary 1) plus an offset:
\[f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} + b, \qquad \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} \in \mathbb{R}^p, \quad b \in \mathbb{R} \tag{1}\]










DefDefinition 21 (Augmented vector)






Definition 21 (Augmented vector) The augmented vector of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\in \mathbb{R}^p\) is the vector \({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\mathrm{aug}} \in \mathbb{R}^{p+1}\) formed by placing a \(1\) above the entries of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\mathrm{aug}}
&= \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\end{bmatrix} \\
&= {(1, x_1, \ldots, x_p)}^{\top}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExmExample 18 (An affine function as a dot product with an augmented vector)






Example 18 (An affine function as a dot product with an augmented vector) For \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= {(2, 5)}^{\top}\), the augmented vector is \({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\mathrm{aug}} = {(1, 2, 5)}^{\top}\). With \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} = {(3, -1)}^{\top}\) and \(b = 4\), the affine function \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} + b\) (Equation 1) equals the dot product of \({(b, w_1, w_2)}^{\top} = {(4, 3, -1)}^{\top}\) with \({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\mathrm{aug}}\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} + b
&= 3 \cdot 2 + (-1) \cdot 5 + 4 \\
&= 5, \\
{(4, 3, -1)}^{\top} \cdot {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\mathrm{aug}}
&= 4 \cdot 1 + 3 \cdot 2 + (-1) \cdot 5 \\
&= 5
\end{aligned}
\]










LemTheorem 13 (An affine map sends zero to its offset)






Theorem 13 (An affine map sends zero to its offset) An affine map \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = \mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}+ \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\) (Definition 19) satisfies \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}) = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\).










ProofProof






Proof. First, \(\mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\): for each \(i\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
(\mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}})_i
&= \sum_{j=1}^pa_{ij} \cdot 0
&& \text{(}\href{#def-matvec-mult}{\text{Definition~13}}\text{)}
\\&= \sum_{j=1}^p0
&& \text{(any number times } 0 \text{ is } 0 \text{)}
\\&= 0
&& \text{(a sum of zeros is } 0 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}})
&= \mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}+ \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}
&& \text{(}\href{#def-affine-map}{\text{Definition~19}}\text{)}
\\&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}+ \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}
&& (\mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}})
\\&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}
&& \text{(adding } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\text{ changes no entry; }\href{linear-algebra-vectors.qmd#def-vector-addition}{\text{Definition~7 in Vectors}}\text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]










LemTheorem 14 (An affine map is linear exactly when its offset is zero)






Theorem 14 (An affine map is linear exactly when its offset is zero) An affine map \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = \mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}+ \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\) (Definition 19) is linear (Definition 15) if and only if \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\).










ProofProof






Proof. If \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\), then
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) &= \mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}+ \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\\
&= \mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}},
\end{aligned}
\]
which is linear by Theorem 10. Conversely, if \(f\) is linear, then \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}) = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\) by Theorem 9, and \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}) = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\) by Theorem 13, so \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\).










ExmExample 19 (Two affine maps with the same matrix)






Example 19 (Two affine maps with the same matrix) Let \(\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\), the matrix of the linear map in Example 12. \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = \mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) has offset \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\), so it is linear. \(g(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = \mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}+ \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\) has offset \(\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \neq \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\), so by Theorem 14 it is not linear: indeed \(g(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}) = \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\), not \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\).










CorCorollary 2 (Every linear map is affine)






Corollary 2 (Every linear map is affine) Every linear map \(f : \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}^m\) (Definition 15) is an affine map (Definition 19) with offset \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\).










ProofProof






Proof. If \(f\) is linear, Theorem 12 gives a matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) with
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) &= \mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\\
&= \mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}+ \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}},
\end{aligned}
\]
which is Definition 19 with \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\).










LemTheorem 15 (An affine map determines its matrix and offset)






Theorem 15 (An affine map determines its matrix and offset) If \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = \mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}+ \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\) and \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = \mathbf{A}'\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}+ \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}'\) for all \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\in \mathbb{R}^p\) (Definition 19), then \(\mathbf{A}' = \mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}' = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\).










ProofProof






Proof. By Theorem 13, applied to each formula,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}} &= f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}) \\
&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}'.
\end{aligned}
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}&= f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) - \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}} \\
&= \mathbf{A}'\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}
\end{aligned}
\]
for all \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\), so \(\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{A}'\) are both matrices (Definition 17) of the linear map \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\mapsto f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) - \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\) (linear by Theorem 10), and the uniqueness in Theorem 12 gives \(\mathbf{A}' = \mathbf{A}\).










RemarkRemark 7 (“Linear” in this site, and in machine learning and statistics)






Remark 7 (“Linear” in this site, and in machine learning and statistics). This site uses “linear” only in the sense of Definition 15, so by Theorem 14 a function with a nonzero offset is affine but not linear. For functions of one variable, this is the same split as affine \(a x + b\) versus linear \(a x\) on the algebra page. (The algebra page writes these as \(m x + b\) and \(m x\); here \(m\) already names the number of outputs.)
Machine learning and statistics often call any function of the form Equation 1 “linear”, as in a linear model in statistics or a linear layer in a neural network, and call the offset \(b\) the bias (machine learning) or the intercept (statistics), as Definition 19 notes. A model with an intercept is affine in \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) but linear in its coefficients \((b, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}})\), and that is the sense of “linear” in “linear model”: it stays linear in the coefficients even when the inputs are transformed: \(w_1 x + w_2 x^2 + b\) is not affine in \(x\), but it is linear in \((b, w_1, w_2)\). Separately, the affine function \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} + b\) is a linear function of the augmented vector \({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\mathrm{aug}}\) (Definition 21), with \(b\) as the coefficient on its first entry.










TipFurther reading




Zhou [14], sections 6 (“Linear functions and operators”; see Definition 16) and 7 (“Affine functions”), proves that every linear function is a matrix-vector product by the same route as Theorem 12, and that every affine function has the form \(\mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}+ \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\). It defines “affine” differently, by \(f(\alpha\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}+ \beta\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}) = \alpha f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) + \beta f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}})\) whenever \(\alpha+ \beta= 1\), and shows that this condition holds exactly for the maps \(\mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}+ \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\), so the two definitions agree.
Boyd and Vandenberghe [15], chapter 2 (“Linear functions”), covers the vector-to-number case: linear functions as inner products, affine functions, the first-order Taylor approximation as an affine function, and the regression model. Section 8.1 (“Linear and affine functions”) covers the vector-to-vector case. A free PDF is on the book’s website.









DefDefinition 22 (Hyperplane)






Definition 22 (Hyperplane) A hyperplane [16] in \(\mathbb{R}^p\) is the set of points \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\in \mathbb{R}^p\) satisfying
\[\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} + b = 0\]
for some vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} \in \mathbb{R}^p \setminus \{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\}\) and number \(b \in \mathbb{R}\). The number \(b\) is the offset of the hyperplane.










DefDefinition 23 (Normal vector of a hyperplane)






Definition 23 (Normal vector of a hyperplane) In Definition 22, the vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}\) is a normal vector [17] of the hyperplane.










ExmExample 20 (A line in \(\mathbb{R}^2\), and why the normal vector must be nonzero)






Example 20 (A line in \(\mathbb{R}^2\), and why the normal vector must be nonzero)  

With \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} = (1, 1)\) and \(b = -1\), the hyperplane in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) is the line \(x_1 + x_2 - 1 = 0\). The point \((1, 0)\) is on it, since \(1 + 0 - 1 = 0\); the point \((1, 1)\) is not, since \(1 + 1 - 1 = 1 > 0\), so it lies in the half-space where \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} + b > 0\).
With \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\), the equation reads \(b = 0\): if \(b \ne 0\) no point satisfies it, and if \(b = 0\) every point does, so the set is empty or all of \(\mathbb{R}^2\), not a line. That degenerate case is why the definition requires \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} \ne \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\).

ExrExercise 2 (Write a rule in matrix form)






Exercise 2 (Write a rule in matrix form) A clinic scores a patient’s risk from three measurements.

\(x_1\)
