// The graph z = f(x1, x2) over the square [-2, 2] x [-2, 2], drawn in 3-D:
// turn the square about the vertical axis, then look down on it from 30 degrees.
planeView = {
  const f = (x1, x2) => planeW1 * x1 + planeW2 * x2 + planeB;
  const w = 340, h = 300, s = 38, sz = 16, elev = 30 * Math.PI / 180;
  const turn = planeTurn * Math.PI / 180;
  const at = (x1, x2, z) => {
    const u = x1 * Math.cos(turn) - x2 * Math.sin(turn);
    const v = x1 * Math.sin(turn) + x2 * Math.cos(turn);
    return [w / 2 + s * u, h / 2 - s * Math.sin(elev) * v - sz * Math.cos(elev) * z];
  };
  const path = (pts) => d3.line()(pts.map(([a, b, z]) => at(a, b, z)));
  const svg = d3.create("svg").attr("width", w).attr("height", h)
    .attr("role", "img")
    .attr("aria-label", "A tilted plane drawn in three dimensions over a square of inputs, " +
      "with its two slices through the origin highlighted, " +
      "and a vertical marker at the origin showing the height b.");
  const ticks = d3.range(-2, 2.01, 0.5);
  const corners = [[-2, -2], [2, -2], [2, 2], [-2, 2], [-2, -2]];
  // the floor, z = 0, and the three axes
  svg.append("path").attr("d", path(corners.map(([a, b]) => [a, b, 0])))
    .attr("fill", "#eee").attr("stroke", "#bbb");
  const axis = (p, q, name) => {
    svg.append("path").attr("d", path([p, q])).attr("stroke", "#888");
    const [tx, ty] = at(...q);
    svg.append("text").attr("x", tx + 4).attr("y", ty).attr("font-size", 13).text(name);
  };
  axis([0, 0, 0], [2.6, 0, 0], "x1");
  axis([0, 0, 0], [0, 2.6, 0], "x2");
  axis([0, 0, -8], [0, 0, 8], "f");
  // the plane itself, as a mesh of lines along each input
  svg.append("path").attr("d", path(corners.map(([a, b]) => [a, b, f(a, b)])))
    .attr("fill", "#1f77b4").attr("fill-opacity", 0.18).attr("stroke", "#1f77b4");
  for (const t of ticks) {
    svg.append("path").attr("d", path([[t, -2, f(t, -2)], [t, 2, f(t, 2)]]))
      .attr("stroke", "#1f77b4").attr("stroke-opacity", 0.35).attr("fill", "none");
    svg.append("path").attr("d", path([[-2, t, f(-2, t)], [2, t, f(2, t)]]))
      .attr("stroke", "#1f77b4").attr("stroke-opacity", 0.35).attr("fill", "none");
  }
  // the slice along x1 (x2 = 0) has slope w1; the slice along x2 has slope w2
  svg.append("path").attr("d", path([[-2, 0, f(-2, 0)], [2, 0, f(2, 0)]]))
    .attr("stroke", "#ff7f0e").attr("stroke-width", 3);
  svg.append("path").attr("d", path([[0, -2, f(0, -2)], [0, 2, f(0, 2)]]))
    .attr("stroke", "#2ca02c").attr("stroke-width", 3);
  const [ox, oy] = at(0, 0, planeB);
  svg.append("circle").attr("cx", ox).attr("cy", oy).attr("r", 4).attr("fill", "#222");
  svg.append("text").attr("x", ox + 6).attr("y", oy - 6).attr("font-size", 13).text("b");
  return svg.node();
}

ExrExercise 2 (Write a rule in matrix form)






Exercise 2 (Write a rule in matrix form) A clinic scores a patient’s risk from three measurements.



symbol
meaning
units




\(x_1\)
age
years


\(x_2\)
systolic blood pressure
mmHg


\(x_3\)
body mass index
kg/m\(^2\)



The rule in use is
\[\text{score} = 0.4\,x_1 + 0.2\,x_2 + 1.5\,x_3 - 30\]
Write this rule in the form of Equation 1, naming \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}\), \(b\) and \(p\) explicitly.










SolutionSolution 2






Solution 2. Read the coefficients straight off the rule. There are three inputs, so \(p = 3\):
\[\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.4 \\ 0.2 \\ 1.5 \end{bmatrix},
\qquad b = -30\]
and the rule is \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}+ b\).










ExrExercise 3 (Score a patient)






Exercise 3 (Score a patient) Give the score from the rule in Exercise 2 for a patient aged \(50\) with blood pressure \(130\) and BMI \(28\).










SolutionSolution 3






Solution 3. For the patient,
\[\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= \begin{bmatrix} 50 \\ 130 \\ 28 \end{bmatrix}\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}
&= (0.4)(50) + (0.2)(130) + (1.5)(28) \\
&= 20 + 26 + 42 \\
&= 88
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})
&= 88 - 30 \\
&= 58
\end{aligned}
\]
Two things are worth noticing. The coefficients are not comparable as they stand. The weight on BMI, \(1.5\), is \(7.5\) times the weight on blood pressure, \(0.2\), but the contribution of BMI, \(42\), is less than twice the contribution of blood pressure, \(26\), because the BMI value, \(28\), is much smaller than the blood pressure value, \(130\). So the weight on a feature says nothing on its own about how much that feature contributes to the score. And \(b = -30\) changes the score: without it, the score would be \(88\) instead of \(58\).










ExrExercise 4 (Which of these are affine in \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}\)?)






Exercise 4 (Which of these are affine in \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}\)?) Each of the five expressions is a function of the weights \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} \in \mathbb{R}^p\), with the data \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) and \(y\) held fixed. Say which ones are affine (Definition 19), that is, have the form Equation 1 — an inner product plus an offset — and which of those are also linear (Definition 15).

\(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\)
\(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- y\)
\((\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- y)^2\)
\(\mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}\right\rVert\mathclose{}_2^2\)
\(w_1 x_1 + 3\)











SolutionSolution 4






Solution 4. 

Affine, and linear. It is Equation 1 with \(b = 0\), which is a linear map by Theorem 10: the matrix \({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top}\) times \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}\).
Affine. Still an inner product plus an offset; here the offset is \(b = -y\), which is a constant because \(y\) is held fixed. It is linear only when \(y = 0\): otherwise \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\) gives \(-y \ne 0\), and a linear map sends \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\) to \(0\) (Theorem 9).
Not affine. Squaring is not an inner product plus an offset. This expression is the squared error of one observation, and its curvature in \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}\) is exactly why fitting a model is an optimization problem rather than a lookup.
Not affine. By Equation 2 in Vectors this is \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}\), which has \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}\) in both slots at once. Hold either slot fixed and it is linear in the other; as a function of the single variable \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}\) it is quadratic.
Affine, not linear. It is Equation 1 with coefficient vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}= (x_1, 0, \dots, 0)^{\top}\) and \(b = 3\); at \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\) it equals \(3 \ne 0\), so it is not linear (Theorem 9). The data \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) is untouched — \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}\) is a new vector built from its first entry.

Items 1, 2 and 5 are affine and items 3 and 4 are not, which is the split that matters: a model can be affine in its weights while the quantity we minimize is not. Squared error and the norm penalty are both curved in \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}\), and that curvature is what makes fitting an optimization problem at all: there is always a downhill direction to follow. Curvature alone does not promise a single answer. The squared error of one observation is completely flat along a whole line of weight vectors, every one of which fits that observation exactly, and pinning down one of them is part of what the norm penalty is added for in week 3.














LemTheorem 16 (Transpose of a sum)






Theorem 16 (Transpose of a sum) For \(m \times n\) matrices \(\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\):
\[{(\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B})}^{\top} = {\mathbf{A}}^{\top} + {\mathbf{B}}^{\top}\]
In particular, for column vectors \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\) of the same length:
\[{(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}+ \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}})}^{\top} = {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top} + {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}}^{\top}\]










ProofProof






Proof. Entry \((i, j)\) of each side:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathopen{}\left[{(\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B})}^{\top}\right]\mathclose{}_{ij}
&= (\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B})_{ji}
&& \text{(definition of the transpose)}
\\
&= a_{ji} + b_{ji}
&& \text{(definition of matrix addition)}
\\
&= ({\mathbf{A}}^{\top})_{ij} + ({\mathbf{B}}^{\top})_{ij}
&& \text{(definition of the transpose)}
\\
&= \mathopen{}\left[{\mathbf{A}}^{\top} + {\mathbf{B}}^{\top}\right]\mathclose{}_{ij}
&& \text{(definition of matrix addition)}
\end{aligned}
\]










LemTheorem 17 (Transpose of a product)






Theorem 17 (Transpose of a product) For an \(m \times k\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) and a \(k \times n\) matrix \(\mathbf{B}\):
\[
\underbrace{{(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})}^{\top}}_{n \times m}
= \underbrace{{\mathbf{B}}^{\top}}_{n \times k}\,\underbrace{{\mathbf{A}}^{\top}}_{k \times m}
\]










ProofProof






Proof. Entry \((i, j)\) of each side:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathopen{}\left[{(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})}^{\top}\right]\mathclose{}_{ij}
&= (\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})_{ji}
&& \text{(definition of the transpose)}
\\
&= \sum_{s=1}^{k} a_{js}\, b_{si}
&& \text{(definition of matrix multiplication)}
\\
&= \sum_{s=1}^{k} ({\mathbf{B}}^{\top})_{is}\, ({\mathbf{A}}^{\top})_{sj}
&& \text{(definition of the transpose; reorder each product)}
\\
&= \mathopen{}\left[{\mathbf{B}}^{\top}\,{\mathbf{A}}^{\top}\right]\mathclose{}_{ij}
&& \text{(definition of matrix multiplication)}
\end{aligned}
\]










RemarkRemark 8 (The order of the factors reverses)






Remark 8 (The order of the factors reverses). Transposing a product reverses the order of the factors. Keeping the original order usually gives an undefined product or a different matrix. For example, with \(\mathbf{A} = [1,\; 2]\) (\(1 \times 2\)) and \(\mathbf{B} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}\) (\(2 \times 1\)),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B} &= 1 \cdot 3 + 2 \cdot 4 \\
&= 11,
\end{aligned}
\]
so \({(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})}^{\top} = 11\), and
\[
{\mathbf{B}}^{\top}\,{\mathbf{A}}^{\top}
= [3,\; 4] \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}
= 11,
\qquad
{\mathbf{A}}^{\top}\,{\mathbf{B}}^{\top}
= \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} [3,\; 4]
= \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 4 \\ 6 & 8 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
If instead \(\mathbf{A}\) is \(2 \times 3\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) is \(3 \times 1\), then \({\mathbf{B}}^{\top}\,{\mathbf{A}}^{\top}\) is a \((1 \times 3)(3 \times 2)\) product, but \({\mathbf{A}}^{\top}\,{\mathbf{B}}^{\top}\) is a \((3 \times 2)(1 \times 3)\) product, which is undefined.










LemTheorem 18 (A \(1 \times 1\) product equals its own transpose)






Theorem 18 (A \(1 \times 1\) product equals its own transpose) If \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\) are vectors of length \(p\) and \(\mathbf{M}\) is a \(p \times p\) matrix, then \({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}}^{\top}\mathbf{M}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\) is a number, and
\[
{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}}^{\top}\mathbf{M}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}
= {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}}^{\top}\,{\mathbf{M}}^{\top}\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}.
\]
In particular, \({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}}^{\top}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}} = {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}}^{\top}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}\).










ProofProof






Proof. The product \({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}}^{\top}\mathbf{M}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\) is a \((1 \times p)(p \times p)(p \times 1)\) product, so it is a \(1 \times 1\) matrix. The transpose of a \(1 \times 1\) matrix is itself, so
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}}^{\top}\mathbf{M}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}
&= {\mathopen{}\left({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}}^{\top}\mathbf{M}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\right)\mathclose{}}^{\top}
&& \text{(a } 1 \times 1 \text{ matrix equals its transpose)}
\\
&= {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}}^{\top}\,{\mathbf{M}}^{\top}\,{\mathopen{}\left({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}}^{\top}\right)\mathclose{}}^{\top}
&& \text{(transpose of a product, twice)}
\\
&= {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}}^{\top}\,{\mathbf{M}}^{\top}\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}
&& \text{(transposing twice changes nothing)}
\end{aligned}
\]
The transpose step is Theorem 17. Taking \(\mathbf{M} = \mathbf{I}\) gives the last statement.










ExmExample 21 (Two ways to write the same number)






Example 21 (Two ways to write the same number) Take \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} = (1, 2)\), \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}} = (3, -1)\) and \(\mathbf{M} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\). Then \(\mathbf{M}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}} = (1, -3)\), so
\[
{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}}^{\top}\mathbf{M}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}} = 1 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot (-3) = -5.
\]
Also \({\mathbf{M}}^{\top} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\) and \({\mathbf{M}}^{\top}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} = (1, 8)\), so
\[
{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}}^{\top}\,{\mathbf{M}}^{\top}\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} = 3 \cdot 1 + (-1) \cdot 8 = -5.
\]
The two products are equal, as the theorem says. In least squares, this is why the two cross terms of \({(\mathbf{X}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}})}^{\top}(\mathbf{X}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\beta}}\vphantom{\beta}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}})\) are equal and can be combined.

title: Column Space, Null Space and Rank-Nullity
text:
DefDefinition 1 (Column space, range, image)






Definition 1 (Column space, range, image) The column space [1] of an \(m \times n\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) is
\[
\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A})
\stackrel{\text{def}}{=}
\mathopen{}\left\{\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} : \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} \in \mathbb{R}^n\right\}\mathclose{},
\]
the set of all vectors \(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) in \(\mathbb{R}^m\). It is also called the range or image of \(\mathbf{A}\).










DefDefinition 2 (Row space)






Definition 2 (Row space) The row space of an \(m \times n\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) is \(\mathcal{C}({\mathbf{A}}^{\top})\), a set of vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^n\).










ExmExample 1 (The column space of a rank-one matrix)






Example 1 (The column space of a rank-one matrix) Let
\[
\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 & -2 \\ 3 & -6 & -6 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
For any \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} \in \mathbb{R}^3\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} &= (x_1 - 2x_2 - 2x_3,\; 3\,(x_1 - 2x_2 - 2x_3)) \\
&= (x_1 - 2x_2 - 2x_3)\,(1, 3)
\end{aligned}
\]
(Definition 13 in Matrices). The number \(x_1 - 2x_2 - 2x_3\) can be any real number (take \(x_2 = 0\) and \(x_3 = 0\)), so \(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A}) = \mathopen{}\left\{c\,(1, 3) : c \in \mathbb{R}\right\}\mathclose{}\), a line in \(\mathbb{R}^2\). The vector \((1, 0)\) is not in \(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A})\): \(c\,(1, 3)\) has second entry \(3c\), which is \(0\) only if \(c = 0\), and then the first entry is \(0\), not \(1\).










LemTheorem 1 (The column space is the span of the columns)






Theorem 1 (The column space is the span of the columns) If \(\mathbf{A}\) is an \(m \times n\) matrix with columns \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_n\), then
\[
\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A}) = \operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_n\right\}\mathclose{},
\]
so \(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A})\) is a subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^m\), and the row space \(\mathcal{C}({\mathbf{A}}^{\top})\) is a subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).










ProofProof






Proof. By Theorem 3 in Subspaces and Rank, \(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = x_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1 + \cdots + x_n \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_n\), and as \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) ranges over \(\mathbb{R}^n\), the coefficients \(x_1, \ldots, x_n\) range over all lists of \(n\) numbers. So the set of all \(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) (Definition 1) is the set of all linear combinations of the columns, which is their span (Definition 5 in Subspaces and Rank). A span is a subspace (Theorem 2 in Subspaces and Rank). Applying the same argument to \({\mathbf{A}}^{\top}\), whose columns are the rows of \(\mathbf{A}\), shows the row space is a subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).










ExmExample 2 (Reading off the column space and row space from the columns and rows)






Example 2 (Reading off the column space and row space from the columns and rows) For \(\mathbf{A}\) in Example 1, the columns are \((1, 3)\), \((-2, -6) = -2\,(1, 3)\) and \((-2, -6) = -2\,(1, 3)\), so by Theorem 1 \(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A}) = \operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{(1, 3)\right\}\mathclose{}\), the same line found in Example 1. The rows are \((1, -2, -2)\) and \((3, -6, -6) = 3\,(1, -2, -2)\), so the row space is \(\operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{(1, -2, -2)\right\}\mathclose{}\), a line in \(\mathbb{R}^3\).










DefDefinition 3 (Null space, kernel)






Definition 3 (Null space, kernel) The null space of an \(m \times n\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) is
\[
\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A})
\stackrel{\text{def}}{=}
\mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} \in \mathbb{R}^n : \mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m\right\}\mathclose{},
\]
the set of solutions of the linear system \(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m\). It is also called the kernel of \(\mathbf{A}\).










DefDefinition 4 (Left null space)






Definition 4 (Left null space) The left null space of an \(m \times n\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) is \(\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{A}}^{\top})\), a set of vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^m\).










ExmExample 3 (The null space and left null space of a rank-one matrix)






Example 3 (The null space and left null space of a rank-one matrix) For \(\mathbf{A}\) in Example 1, \(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = (x_1 - 2x_2 - 2x_3,\; 3\,(x_1 - 2x_2 - 2x_3))\), so \(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_2\) exactly when \(x_1 = 2x_2 + 2x_3\). Writing
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} &= (2x_2 + 2x_3, x_2, x_3) \\
&= x_2\,(2, 1, 0) + x_3\,(2, 0, 1)
\end{aligned}
\]
shows \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A}) = \operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{(2, 1, 0), (2, 0, 1)\right\}\mathclose{}\), a plane in \(\mathbb{R}^3\).
For the left null space, \({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}} = (y_1 + 3y_2,\; -2\,(y_1 + 3y_2),\; -2\,(y_1 + 3y_2))\), which is \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_3\) exactly when \(y_1 = -3y_2\), so \(\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{A}}^{\top}) = \operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{(-3, 1)\right\}\mathclose{}\), a line in \(\mathbb{R}^2\).










LemTheorem 2 (A null space is a subspace)






Theorem 2 (A null space is a subspace) For any \(m \times n\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\), \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A})\) (Definition 3) is a subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) (Definition 4 in Subspaces and Rank).










ProofProof






Proof. \(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_n = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m\), so \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_n \in \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A})\), and the null space is not empty. If \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} \in \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A})\) and \(c \in \mathbb{R}\), then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{A}\,(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}})
&= \mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} + \mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}
&& \text{(}\href{linear-algebra-matrices.qmd#thm-matmul-distrib}{\text{Theorem~6 in Matrices}}\text{)}
\\
&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m
&& \text{(} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} \text{ and } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} \text{ are in the null space)}
\\
&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m
&& \text{(adding } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m \text{ changes nothing)}
\end{aligned}
\]
and, for each entry \(i = 1, \ldots, m\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathopen{}\left(\mathbf{A}\,(c \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}})\right)\mathclose{}_i
&= a_{i1} (c u_1) + \cdots + a_{in} (c u_n)
&& \text{(}\href{linear-algebra-matrices.qmd#def-matvec-mult}{\text{Definition~13 in Matrices}}\text{)}
\\
&= c\,(a_{i1} u_1 + \cdots + a_{in} u_n)
&& \text{(factor } c \text{ out of each term)}
\\
&= c\,(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}})_i
&& \text{(}\href{linear-algebra-matrices.qmd#def-matvec-mult}{\text{Definition~13 in Matrices}}\text{)}
\\
&= c \cdot 0
&& \text{(} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} \text{ is in the null space)}
\\
&= 0,
&& \text{(arithmetic)}
\end{aligned}
\]
so \(\mathbf{A}\,(c \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}) = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m\). Therefore \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}\) and \(c \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}\) are in \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A})\).










ExmExample 4 (The solutions of \(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\) with \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}} \neq \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\) are not a subspace)






Example 4 (The solutions of \(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\) with \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}} \neq \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\) are not a subspace) In Example 3, \((2, 1, 0)\) and \((2, 0, 1)\) are in \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A})\), and so is their sum \((4, 1, 1)\), since \(4 - 2 \cdot 1 - 2 \cdot 1 = 0\). By contrast, the solutions of \(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = (1, 3)\) for the same \(\mathbf{A}\) are the vectors with \(x_1 - 2x_2 - 2x_3 = 1\). That set does not contain \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_3\), so by Theorem 1 in Subspaces and Rank it is not a subspace.










LemTheorem 3 (Independent columns exactly when the null space is trivial)






Theorem 3 (Independent columns exactly when the null space is trivial) For an \(m \times n\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\), the following are equivalent:

The columns of \(\mathbf{A}\) are linearly independent (Definition 1 in Subspaces and Rank).

\(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m\) only for \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_n\).

\(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A}) = \mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_n\right\}\mathclose{}\) (Definition 3).

So \(\mathbf{A}\) has full column rank (Definition 3 in Subspaces and Rank) exactly when its null space contains only the zero vector.










ProofProof






Proof. Write \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_n\) for the columns of \(\mathbf{A}\). For \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = (x_1, \ldots, x_n)\), the matrix-vector product is the combination of the columns with weights \(x_1, \ldots, x_n\):
\[
\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = x_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1 + \cdots + x_n \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_n.
\]
So \(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m\) says exactly that \(x_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1 + \cdots + x_n \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_n = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m\). By Definition 1 in Subspaces and Rank, the columns are linearly independent exactly when the only weights with this property are \(x_1 = \cdots = x_n = 0\). That is statement 2, so statements 1 and 2 are equivalent. Statement 2 says that the only vector in \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A})\) is \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_n\), which is statement 3. The last sentence is the definition of full column rank (Definition 3 in Subspaces and Rank).










ExmExample 5 (Checking independence through the null space)






Example 5 (Checking independence through the null space) For \(\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\),
\[
\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}
= \begin{bmatrix} x_1 + x_2 \\ x_1 + 2 x_2 \\ x_1 + 3 x_2 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
This is \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_3\) only if \(x_2 = 0\) (subtract the first entry from the second), and then \(x_1 = 0\). So \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A}) = \mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_2\right\}\mathclose{}\) and the two columns are linearly independent.
For \(\mathbf{B} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\), \(\mathbf{B} (2, -1) = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_3\), so \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{B})\) contains a nonzero vector and the columns of \(\mathbf{B}\) are linearly dependent.










LemTheorem 4 (The row space and null space share only the zero vector)






Theorem 4 (The row space and null space share only the zero vector) For any \(m \times n\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\),
\[
\mathcal{C}({\mathbf{A}}^{\top}) \cap \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A}) = \mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_n\right\}\mathclose{}.
\]










ProofProof






Proof. Both sets are subspaces, by Theorem 1 and Theorem 2, so both contain \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_n\) (Theorem 1 in Subspaces and Rank).
Now take any \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) in both sets. Being in the row space means \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = {\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}\) for some \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} \in \mathbb{R}^m\) (Definition 1), and being in the null space means \(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m\) (Definition 3). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}
&= {({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}})}^{\top}\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}
&& \text{(substitute } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = {\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} \text{ in the first factor)}
\\
&= \mathopen{}\left({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}}^{\top}\,{({\mathbf{A}}^{\top})}^{\top}\right)\mathclose{}\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}
&& \text{(}\href{linear-algebra-matrices.qmd#thm-transpose-product}{\text{Theorem~17 in Matrices}}\text{)}
\\
&= \mathopen{}\left({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}}^{\top} \mathbf{A}\right)\mathclose{}\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}
&& \text{(transposing twice returns the original matrix)}
\\
&= {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}}^{\top}\,(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})
&& \text{(}\href{linear-algebra-matrices.qmd#thm-matmul-assoc}{\text{Theorem~5 in Matrices}}\text{)}
\\
&= {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}}^{\top}\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m
&& \text{(substitute } \mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m \text{)}
\\
&= 0.
&& \text{(every term of the inner product is } 0 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
But \({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = x_1^2 + \cdots + x_n^2\), which is \(0\) only when every \(x_i = 0\). So \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_n\).










ExmExample 6 (The row space and null space in Example 3)






Example 6 (The row space and null space in Example 3) For \(\mathbf{A}\) in Example 1, the row space is \(\operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{(1, -2, -2)\right\}\mathclose{}\) and the null space is \(\operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{(2, 1, 0), (2, 0, 1)\right\}\mathclose{}\) (Example 3). A vector \(c\,(1, -2, -2)\) of the row space is in the null space only if
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{A}\,\mathopen{}\left(c\,(1, -2, -2)\right)\mathclose{}
&= c\,\mathopen{}\left(1 - 2 \cdot(-2) - 2 \cdot(-2),\; 3\,(1 - 2 \cdot(-2) - 2 \cdot(-2))\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(}\href{#exm-null-space}{\text{Example~3}}\text{'s formula for } \mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} \text{)}
\\
&= c\,(9, 27)
&& \text{(arithmetic)}
\end{aligned}
\]
is \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_2\), that is, only if \(c = 0\). So the two subspaces share only \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_3\).










DefDefinition 5 (Cross-product matrix)






Definition 5 (Cross-product matrix) Let \(\mathbf{A}\) be an \(m \times n\) matrix with columns \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_n\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) an \(m \times q\) matrix with columns \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}_q\). The cross-product matrix of \(\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) is the \(n \times q\) matrix \({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{B}\), whose entry \((i, j)\) is the dot product \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_i \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}_j\).





This is what R’s crossprod(A, B) computes, and crossprod(A) is \({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{A}\). In NumPy it has no name of its own: write A.T @ B.
For two column vectors it is the \(1 \times 1\) matrix holding their dot product. It is unrelated to the cross product \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} \times \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\) of two vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^3\), and differs from the Frobenius inner product \(\operatorname{tr}\mathopen{}\left({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{B}\right)\mathclose{}\), which sums the diagonal of this matrix into a single number.







ExmExample 7 (A cross-product matrix)






Example 7 (A cross-product matrix) Let \(\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf{B} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}\). Then \({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{B}\) is \(2 \times 1\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{B}
&= \begin{bmatrix} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1 \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}_1 \\ \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_2 \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}_1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(}\href{#def-cross-product-matrix}{\text{Definition~5}}\text{)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 1 + 2 + 0 \\ 0 + 2 + 3 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(multiply and add)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}.
&& \text{(add)}
\end{aligned}
\]










DefDefinition 6 (Gram matrix)






Definition 6 (Gram matrix) The Gram matrix [2] of an \(m \times n\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) is the \(n \times n\) matrix \({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{A}\), the cross-product matrix of \(\mathbf{A}\) with itself.










ExmExample 8 (A Gram matrix and its entries)






Example 8 (A Gram matrix and its entries) Let \(\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), with columns \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1 = (1, 1, 0)\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_2 = (0, 1, 1)\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{A}
&= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(}\href{linear-algebra-matrices.qmd#def-matrix-transpose}{\text{Definition~3 in Matrices}}\text{)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix}
1 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot 0 & 1 \cdot 0 + 1 \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot 1 \\
0 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 0 & 0 \cdot 0 + 1 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 1
\end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(}\href{linear-algebra-matrices.qmd#def-matrix-mult}{\text{Definition~7 in Matrices}}\text{)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}.
&& \text{(multiply and add)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Row \(i\) of \({\mathbf{A}}^{\top}\) is column \(i\) of \(\mathbf{A}\), so entry \((i, j)\) of the Gram matrix is the dot product \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_i \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_j\): for instance,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1 \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_2 &= 0 + 1 + 0 \\
&= 1
\end{aligned}
\]
is entry \((1, 2)\).










LemTheorem 5 (\({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{A}\) has the same null space as \(\mathbf{A}\))






Theorem 5 (\({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{A}\) has the same null space as \(\mathbf{A}\)) For any \(m \times n\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\),
\[
\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{A}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A}).
\]










ProofProof






Proof. \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A}) \subseteq \mathcal{N}({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{A})\). If \(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m\), then
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} &= {\mathbf{A}}^{\top}\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m \\
&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_n.
\end{aligned}
\]
\(\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{A}) \subseteq \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A})\). If \({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_n\), then
\[
\begin{aligned}
0
&= {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top}\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_n
&& \text{(every term of the inner product is } 0 \text{)}
\\
&= {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top}\,\mathopen{}\left({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(substitute } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_n = {\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} \text{)}
\\
&= \mathopen{}\left({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top} {\mathbf{A}}^{\top}\right)\mathclose{}\,(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})
&& \text{(}\href{linear-algebra-matrices.qmd#thm-matmul-assoc}{\text{Theorem~5 in Matrices}}\text{)}
\\
&= {(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})}^{\top}\,(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})
&& \text{(}\href{linear-algebra-matrices.qmd#thm-transpose-product}{\text{Theorem~17 in Matrices}}\text{)}
\\
&= (\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) \cdot (\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})
&& \text{(}\href{linear-algebra-matrices.qmd#exm-dot-product-matmul}{\text{Example~6 in Matrices}}\text{)}
\\
&= \mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\right\rVert\mathclose{}^2.
&& \text{(square both sides of }\href{linear-algebra-vectors.qmd#eq-l2-norm}{\text{Equation~2 in Vectors}}\text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
A vector whose Euclidean norm is \(0\) has every entry \(0\), so \(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m\).










ExmExample 9 (The null space of a Gram matrix)






Example 9 (The null space of a Gram matrix) For \(\mathbf{A}\) in Example 1,
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{A}
&= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ -2 & -6 \\ -2 & -6 \end{bmatrix}
  \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 & -2 \\ 3 & -6 & -6 \end{bmatrix} \\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 10 & -20 & -20 \\ -20 & 40 & 40 \\ -20 & 40 & 40 \end{bmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Every row is a multiple of \((1, -2, -2)\), so \({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_3\) exactly when \(x_1 - 2x_2 - 2x_3 = 0\), the same condition as for \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A})\) in Example 3.

title: Column Space, Null Space and Rank-Nullity
text:
DefDefinition 1 (Column space, range, image)






Definition 1 (Column space, range, image) The column space [1] of an \(m \times n\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) is
\[
\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A})
\stackrel{\text{def}}{=}
\mathopen{}\left\{\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} : \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} \in \mathbb{R}^n\right\}\mathclose{},
\]
the set of all vectors \(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) in \(\mathbb{R}^m\). It is also called the range or image of \(\mathbf{A}\).










DefDefinition 2 (Row space)






Definition 2 (Row space) The row space of an \(m \times n\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) is \(\mathcal{C}({\mathbf{A}}^{\top})\), a set of vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^n\).










ExmExample 1 (The column space of a rank-one matrix)






Example 1 (The column space of a rank-one matrix) Let
\[
\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 & -2 \\ 3 & -6 & -6 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
For any \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} \in \mathbb{R}^3\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} &= (x_1 - 2x_2 - 2x_3,\; 3\,(x_1 - 2x_2 - 2x_3)) \\
&= (x_1 - 2x_2 - 2x_3)\,(1, 3)
\end{aligned}
\]
(Definition 13 in Matrices). The number \(x_1 - 2x_2 - 2x_3\) can be any real number (take \(x_2 = 0\) and \(x_3 = 0\)), so \(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A}) = \mathopen{}\left\{c\,(1, 3) : c \in \mathbb{R}\right\}\mathclose{}\), a line in \(\mathbb{R}^2\). The vector \((1, 0)\) is not in \(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A})\): \(c\,(1, 3)\) has second entry \(3c\), which is \(0\) only if \(c = 0\), and then the first entry is \(0\), not \(1\).










LemTheorem 1 (The column space is the span of the columns)






Theorem 1 (The column space is the span of the columns) If \(\mathbf{A}\) is an \(m \times n\) matrix with columns \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_n\), then
\[
\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A}) = \operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_n\right\}\mathclose{},
\]
so \(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A})\) is a subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^m\), and the row space \(\mathcal{C}({\mathbf{A}}^{\top})\) is a subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).










ProofProof






Proof. By Theorem 3 in Subspaces and Rank, \(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = x_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1 + \cdots + x_n \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_n\), and as \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) ranges over \(\mathbb{R}^n\), the coefficients \(x_1, \ldots, x_n\) range over all lists of \(n\) numbers. So the set of all \(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) (Definition 1) is the set of all linear combinations of the columns, which is their span (Definition 5 in Subspaces and Rank). A span is a subspace (Theorem 2 in Subspaces and Rank). Applying the same argument to \({\mathbf{A}}^{\top}\), whose columns are the rows of \(\mathbf{A}\), shows the row space is a subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).










ExmExample 2 (Reading off the column space and row space from the columns and rows)






Example 2 (Reading off the column space and row space from the columns and rows) For \(\mathbf{A}\) in Example 1, the columns are \((1, 3)\), \((-2, -6) = -2\,(1, 3)\) and \((-2, -6) = -2\,(1, 3)\), so by Theorem 1 \(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A}) = \operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{(1, 3)\right\}\mathclose{}\), the same line found in Example 1. The rows are \((1, -2, -2)\) and \((3, -6, -6) = 3\,(1, -2, -2)\), so the row space is \(\operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{(1, -2, -2)\right\}\mathclose{}\), a line in \(\mathbb{R}^3\).










DefDefinition 3 (Null space, kernel)






Definition 3 (Null space, kernel) The null space of an \(m \times n\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) is
\[
\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A})
\stackrel{\text{def}}{=}
\mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} \in \mathbb{R}^n : \mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m\right\}\mathclose{},
\]
the set of solutions of the linear system \(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m\). It is also called the kernel of \(\mathbf{A}\).










DefDefinition 4 (Left null space)






Definition 4 (Left null space) The left null space of an \(m \times n\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) is \(\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{A}}^{\top})\), a set of vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^m\).










ExmExample 3 (The null space and left null space of a rank-one matrix)






Example 3 (The null space and left null space of a rank-one matrix) For \(\mathbf{A}\) in Example 1, \(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = (x_1 - 2x_2 - 2x_3,\; 3\,(x_1 - 2x_2 - 2x_3))\), so \(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_2\) exactly when \(x_1 = 2x_2 + 2x_3\). Writing
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} &= (2x_2 + 2x_3, x_2, x_3) \\
&= x_2\,(2, 1, 0) + x_3\,(2, 0, 1)
\end{aligned}
\]
shows \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A}) = \operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{(2, 1, 0), (2, 0, 1)\right\}\mathclose{}\), a plane in \(\mathbb{R}^3\).
For the left null space, \({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}} = (y_1 + 3y_2,\; -2\,(y_1 + 3y_2),\; -2\,(y_1 + 3y_2))\), which is \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_3\) exactly when \(y_1 = -3y_2\), so \(\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{A}}^{\top}) = \operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{(-3, 1)\right\}\mathclose{}\), a line in \(\mathbb{R}^2\).










LemTheorem 2 (A null space is a subspace)






Theorem 2 (A null space is a subspace) For any \(m \times n\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\), \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A})\) (Definition 3) is a subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) (Definition 4 in Subspaces and Rank).










ProofProof






Proof. \(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_n = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m\), so \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_n \in \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A})\), and the null space is not empty. If \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} \in \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A})\) and \(c \in \mathbb{R}\), then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{A}\,(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}})
&= \mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} + \mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}
&& \text{(}\href{linear-algebra-matrices.qmd#thm-matmul-distrib}{\text{Theorem~6 in Matrices}}\text{)}
\\
&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m
&& \text{(} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} \text{ and } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} \text{ are in the null space)}
\\
&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m
&& \text{(adding } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m \text{ changes nothing)}
\end{aligned}
\]
and, for each entry \(i = 1, \ldots, m\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathopen{}\left(\mathbf{A}\,(c \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}})\right)\mathclose{}_i
&= a_{i1} (c u_1) + \cdots + a_{in} (c u_n)
&& \text{(}\href{linear-algebra-matrices.qmd#def-matvec-mult}{\text{Definition~13 in Matrices}}\text{)}
\\
&= c\,(a_{i1} u_1 + \cdots + a_{in} u_n)
&& \text{(factor } c \text{ out of each term)}
\\
&= c\,(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}})_i
&& \text{(}\href{linear-algebra-matrices.qmd#def-matvec-mult}{\text{Definition~13 in Matrices}}\text{)}
\\
&= c \cdot 0
&& \text{(} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} \text{ is in the null space)}
\\
&= 0,
&& \text{(arithmetic)}
\end{aligned}
\]
so \(\mathbf{A}\,(c \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}) = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m\). Therefore \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}\) and \(c \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}\) are in \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A})\).










ExmExample 4 (The solutions of \(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\) with \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}} \neq \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\) are not a subspace)






Example 4 (The solutions of \(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\) with \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}} \neq \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\) are not a subspace) In Example 3, \((2, 1, 0)\) and \((2, 0, 1)\) are in \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A})\), and so is their sum \((4, 1, 1)\), since \(4 - 2 \cdot 1 - 2 \cdot 1 = 0\). By contrast, the solutions of \(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = (1, 3)\) for the same \(\mathbf{A}\) are the vectors with \(x_1 - 2x_2 - 2x_3 = 1\). That set does not contain \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_3\), so by Theorem 1 in Subspaces and Rank it is not a subspace.










LemTheorem 3 (Independent columns exactly when the null space is trivial)






Theorem 3 (Independent columns exactly when the null space is trivial) For an \(m \times n\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\), the following are equivalent:

The columns of \(\mathbf{A}\) are linearly independent (Definition 1 in Subspaces and Rank).

\(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m\) only for \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_n\).

\(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A}) = \mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_n\right\}\mathclose{}\) (Definition 3).

So \(\mathbf{A}\) has full column rank (Definition 3 in Subspaces and Rank) exactly when its null space contains only the zero vector.










ProofProof






Proof. Write \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_n\) for the columns of \(\mathbf{A}\). For \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = (x_1, \ldots, x_n)\), the matrix-vector product is the combination of the columns with weights \(x_1, \ldots, x_n\):
\[
\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = x_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1 + \cdots + x_n \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_n.
\]
So \(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m\) says exactly that \(x_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1 + \cdots + x_n \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_n = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m\). By Definition 1 in Subspaces and Rank, the columns are linearly independent exactly when the only weights with this property are \(x_1 = \cdots = x_n = 0\). That is statement 2, so statements 1 and 2 are equivalent. Statement 2 says that the only vector in \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A})\) is \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_n\), which is statement 3. The last sentence is the definition of full column rank (Definition 3 in Subspaces and Rank).










ExmExample 5 (Checking independence through the null space)






Example 5 (Checking independence through the null space) For \(\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\),
\[
\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}
= \begin{bmatrix} x_1 + x_2 \\ x_1 + 2 x_2 \\ x_1 + 3 x_2 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
This is \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_3\) only if \(x_2 = 0\) (subtract the first entry from the second), and then \(x_1 = 0\). So \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A}) = \mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_2\right\}\mathclose{}\) and the two columns are linearly independent.
For \(\mathbf{B} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\), \(\mathbf{B} (2, -1) = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_3\), so \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{B})\) contains a nonzero vector and the columns of \(\mathbf{B}\) are linearly dependent.










LemTheorem 4 (The row space and null space share only the zero vector)






Theorem 4 (The row space and null space share only the zero vector) For any \(m \times n\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\),
\[
\mathcal{C}({\mathbf{A}}^{\top}) \cap \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A}) = \mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_n\right\}\mathclose{}.
\]










ProofProof






Proof. Both sets are subspaces, by Theorem 1 and Theorem 2, so both contain \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_n\) (Theorem 1 in Subspaces and Rank).
Now take any \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) in both sets. Being in the row space means \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = {\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}\) for some \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} \in \mathbb{R}^m\) (Definition 1), and being in the null space means \(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m\) (Definition 3). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}
&= {({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}})}^{\top}\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}
&& \text{(substitute } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = {\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} \text{ in the first factor)}
\\
&= \mathopen{}\left({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}}^{\top}\,{({\mathbf{A}}^{\top})}^{\top}\right)\mathclose{}\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}
&& \text{(}\href{linear-algebra-matrices.qmd#thm-transpose-product}{\text{Theorem~17 in Matrices}}\text{)}
\\
&= \mathopen{}\left({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}}^{\top} \mathbf{A}\right)\mathclose{}\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}
&& \text{(transposing twice returns the original matrix)}
\\
&= {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}}^{\top}\,(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})
&& \text{(}\href{linear-algebra-matrices.qmd#thm-matmul-assoc}{\text{Theorem~5 in Matrices}}\text{)}
\\
&= {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}}^{\top}\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m
&& \text{(substitute } \mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m \text{)}
\\
&= 0.
&& \text{(every term of the inner product is } 0 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
But \({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = x_1^2 + \cdots + x_n^2\), which is \(0\) only when every \(x_i = 0\). So \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_n\).










ExmExample 6 (The row space and null space in Example 3)






Example 6 (The row space and null space in Example 3) For \(\mathbf{A}\) in Example 1, the row space is \(\operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{(1, -2, -2)\right\}\mathclose{}\) and the null space is \(\operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{(2, 1, 0), (2, 0, 1)\right\}\mathclose{}\) (Example 3). A vector \(c\,(1, -2, -2)\) of the row space is in the null space only if
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{A}\,\mathopen{}\left(c\,(1, -2, -2)\right)\mathclose{}
&= c\,\mathopen{}\left(1 - 2 \cdot(-2) - 2 \cdot(-2),\; 3\,(1 - 2 \cdot(-2) - 2 \cdot(-2))\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(}\href{#exm-null-space}{\text{Example~3}}\text{'s formula for } \mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} \text{)}
\\
&= c\,(9, 27)
&& \text{(arithmetic)}
\end{aligned}
\]
is \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_2\), that is, only if \(c = 0\). So the two subspaces share only \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_3\).










DefDefinition 5 (Cross-product matrix)






Definition 5 (Cross-product matrix) Let \(\mathbf{A}\) be an \(m \times n\) matrix with columns \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_n\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) an \(m \times q\) matrix with columns \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}_q\). The cross-product matrix of \(\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) is the \(n \times q\) matrix \({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{B}\), whose entry \((i, j)\) is the dot product \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_i \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}_j\).





This is what R’s crossprod(A, B) computes, and crossprod(A) is \({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{A}\). In NumPy it has no name of its own: write A.T @ B.
For two column vectors it is the \(1 \times 1\) matrix holding their dot product. It is unrelated to the cross product \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} \times \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}\) of two vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^3\), and differs from the Frobenius inner product \(\operatorname{tr}\mathopen{}\left({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{B}\right)\mathclose{}\), which sums the diagonal of this matrix into a single number.







ExmExample 7 (A cross-product matrix)






Example 7 (A cross-product matrix) Let \(\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf{B} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}\). Then \({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{B}\) is \(2 \times 1\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{B}
&= \begin{bmatrix} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1 \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}_1 \\ \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_2 \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}_1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(}\href{#def-cross-product-matrix}{\text{Definition~5}}\text{)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 1 + 2 + 0 \\ 0 + 2 + 3 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(multiply and add)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}.
&& \text{(add)}
\end{aligned}
\]










DefDefinition 6 (Gram matrix)






Definition 6 (Gram matrix) The Gram matrix [2] of an \(m \times n\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) is the \(n \times n\) matrix \({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{A}\), the cross-product matrix of \(\mathbf{A}\) with itself.










ExmExample 8 (A Gram matrix and its entries)






Example 8 (A Gram matrix and its entries) Let \(\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), with columns \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1 = (1, 1, 0)\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_2 = (0, 1, 1)\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{A}
&= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(}\href{linear-algebra-matrices.qmd#def-matrix-transpose}{\text{Definition~3 in Matrices}}\text{)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix}
1 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot 0 & 1 \cdot 0 + 1 \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot 1 \\
0 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 0 & 0 \cdot 0 + 1 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 1
\end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(}\href{linear-algebra-matrices.qmd#def-matrix-mult}{\text{Definition~7 in Matrices}}\text{)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}.
&& \text{(multiply and add)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Row \(i\) of \({\mathbf{A}}^{\top}\) is column \(i\) of \(\mathbf{A}\), so entry \((i, j)\) of the Gram matrix is the dot product \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_i \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_j\): for instance,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1 \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_2 &= 0 + 1 + 0 \\
&= 1
\end{aligned}
\]
is entry \((1, 2)\).










LemTheorem 5 (\({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{A}\) has the same null space as \(\mathbf{A}\))






Theorem 5 (\({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{A}\) has the same null space as \(\mathbf{A}\)) For any \(m \times n\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\),
\[
\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{A}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A}).
\]










ProofProof






Proof. \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A}) \subseteq \mathcal{N}({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{A})\). If \(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m\), then
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} &= {\mathbf{A}}^{\top}\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m \\
&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_n.
\end{aligned}
\]
\(\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{A}) \subseteq \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A})\). If \({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_n\), then
\[
\begin{aligned}
0
&= {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top}\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_n
&& \text{(every term of the inner product is } 0 \text{)}
\\
&= {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top}\,\mathopen{}\left({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(substitute } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_n = {\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} \text{)}
\\
&= \mathopen{}\left({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top} {\mathbf{A}}^{\top}\right)\mathclose{}\,(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})
&& \text{(}\href{linear-algebra-matrices.qmd#thm-matmul-assoc}{\text{Theorem~5 in Matrices}}\text{)}
\\
&= {(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})}^{\top}\,(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})
&& \text{(}\href{linear-algebra-matrices.qmd#thm-transpose-product}{\text{Theorem~17 in Matrices}}\text{)}
\\
&= (\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) \cdot (\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})
&& \text{(}\href{linear-algebra-matrices.qmd#exm-dot-product-matmul}{\text{Example~6 in Matrices}}\text{)}
\\
&= \mathopen{}\left\lVert\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\right\rVert\mathclose{}^2.
&& \text{(square both sides of }\href{linear-algebra-vectors.qmd#eq-l2-norm}{\text{Equation~2 in Vectors}}\text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
A vector whose Euclidean norm is \(0\) has every entry \(0\), so \(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_m\).










ExmExample 9 (The null space of a Gram matrix)






Example 9 (The null space of a Gram matrix) For \(\mathbf{A}\) in Example 1,
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{A}
&= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ -2 & -6 \\ -2 & -6 \end{bmatrix}
  \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 & -2 \\ 3 & -6 & -6 \end{bmatrix} \\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 10 & -20 & -20 \\ -20 & 40 & 40 \\ -20 & 40 & 40 \end{bmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Every row is a multiple of \((1, -2, -2)\), so \({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_3\) exactly when \(x_1 - 2x_2 - 2x_3 = 0\), the same condition as for \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A})\) in Example 3.
