DefDefinition 1 (Linearly independent vectors)






Definition 1 (Linearly independent vectors) Vectors \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k\) of the same length \(p\) are linearly independent [1] if the only numbers \(c_1, \ldots, c_k\) with
\[c_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1 + \cdots + c_k \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\]
are
\[
\begin{aligned}
c_1 &= \cdots \\
&= c_k \\
&= 0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Vectors that are not linearly independent are linearly dependent.










ExmExample 1 (Independent and dependent pairs of vectors)






Example 1 (Independent and dependent pairs of vectors)  

\(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1 = (1, 0)\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_2 = (1, 1)\) are linearly independent: \(c_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1 + c_2 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_2 = (c_1 + c_2, c_2)\), which is \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\) only if \(c_2 = 0\) and then \(c_1 = 0\).
\(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1 = (1, 2)\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_2 = (2, 4)\) are not: \(2 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1 - \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_2 = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\).











DefDefinition 2 (Rank)






Definition 2 (Rank) The rank [2] of a matrix \(\mathbf{A}\), written \(\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{A})\), is the largest number of columns of \(\mathbf{A}\) that are linearly independent (Definition 1).










ExmExample 2 (The rank of two \(3 \times 2\) matrices)






Example 2 (The rank of two \(3 \times 2\) matrices) The matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\) has rank \(2\): if \(c_1 (1, 1, 1) + c_2 (1, 2, 3) = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\), then subtracting the first entry from the second gives \(c_2 = 0\), and then \(c_1 = 0\).
The matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\) has rank \(1\): its second column is twice its first, so the two columns are not linearly independent, but the first column on its own is.










DefDefinition 3 (Full column rank)






Definition 3 (Full column rank) An \(n \times p\) matrix has full column rank if its rank (Definition 2) is \(p\), so that all of its columns are linearly independent.










RemarkRemark 1 (Full column rank needs at least as many rows as columns)






Remark 1 (Full column rank needs at least as many rows as columns). In Example 2, the first matrix has full column rank: its rank is \(2\), and it has \(2\) columns. The second does not, because its rank is \(1\).
An \(n \times p\) matrix can have full column rank only when \(p \le n\), because more than \(n\) vectors of length \(n\) are never linearly independent. For example, the \(2 \times 3\) matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) has \(3\) columns of length \(2\), and \(1 \cdot(1, 0) + 1 \cdot(0, 1) - 1 \cdot(1, 1) = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\), with coefficients that are not all zero. So its \(3\) columns are not linearly independent, and its rank is less than \(3\).

Remark 1 (Full column rank needs at least as many rows as columns). In Example 2, the first matrix has full column rank: its rank is \(2\), and it has \(2\) columns. The second does not, because its rank is \(1\).
An \(n \times p\) matrix can have full column rank only when \(p \le n\), because more than \(n\) vectors of length \(n\) are never linearly independent. For example, the \(2 \times 3\) matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) has \(3\) columns of length \(2\), and \(1 \cdot(1, 0) + 1 \cdot(0, 1) - 1 \cdot(1, 1) = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\), with coefficients that are not all zero. So its \(3\) columns are not linearly independent, and its rank is less than \(3\).

DefDefinition 4 (Subspace, linear subspace)






Definition 4 (Subspace, linear subspace) A set \(\mathcal{S}\) of vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^p\) is a subspace [4] of \(\mathbb{R}^p\) if it is not empty and it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication:

if \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} \in \mathcal{S}\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}} \in \mathcal{S}\), then \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}} \in \mathcal{S}\);
if \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} \in \mathcal{S}\) and \(c \in \mathbb{R}\), then \(c \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} \in \mathcal{S}\).

A subspace is also called a linear subspace.










ExmExample 3 (A line through the origin is a subspace)






Example 3 (A line through the origin is a subspace) Let \(\mathcal{S} = \mathopen{}\left\{c\,(1, 2) : c \in \mathbb{R}\right\}\mathclose{}\), the line in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) through \((0, 0)\) and \((1, 2)\).

Addition: \(a\,(1, 2) + b\,(1, 2) = (a + b)\,(1, 2)\), which is in \(\mathcal{S}\).
Scalar multiplication: \(c\,\mathopen{}\left(a\,(1, 2)\right)\mathclose{} = (ca)\,(1, 2)\), which is in \(\mathcal{S}\).

So \(\mathcal{S}\) is a subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^2\). Two other subspaces of \(\mathbb{R}^p\) are the set \(\mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\right\}\mathclose{}\) that holds only the zero vector, and \(\mathbb{R}^p\) itself.










ExmExample 4 (A line that misses the origin is not a subspace)






Example 4 (A line that misses the origin is not a subspace) Let \(\mathcal{T} = \mathopen{}\left\{(x, 1) : x \in \mathbb{R}\right\}\mathclose{}\), the horizontal line in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) at height \(1\). The vectors \((0, 1)\) and \((2, 1)\) are in \(\mathcal{T}\), but their sum \((2, 2)\) is not, because its second entry is \(2\), not \(1\). So \(\mathcal{T}\) is not closed under addition, and it is not a subspace.










LemTheorem 1 (Every subspace contains the zero vector)






Theorem 1 (Every subspace contains the zero vector) If \(\mathcal{S}\) is a subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^p\) (Definition 4), then \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\in \mathcal{S}\).










ProofProof






Proof. A subspace is not empty, so it contains some vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}\). Closure under scalar multiplication with \(c = 0\) puts \(0 \cdot\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}\) in \(\mathcal{S}\), and \(0 \cdot\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\).










ExmExample 5 (Using the zero vector to rule out a subspace)






Example 5 (Using the zero vector to rule out a subspace) The plane \(\mathopen{}\left\{(x, y, z) : x + y + z = 1\right\}\mathclose{}\) in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) does not contain \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}= (0, 0, 0)\), because \(0 + 0 + 0 = 0 \neq 1\). So, by Theorem 1, it is not a subspace. The line \(\mathcal{T}\) in Example 4 fails the same test: \((0, 0)\) is not in \(\mathcal{T}\), because its second entry is not \(1\).
Containing \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\) is necessary but not sufficient. The union of the two coordinate axes in \(\mathbb{R}^2\), \(\mathopen{}\left\{(x, 0) : x \in \mathbb{R}\right\}\mathclose{} \cup \mathopen{}\left\{(0, y) : y \in \mathbb{R}\right\}\mathclose{}\), contains \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\), but \((1, 0) + (0, 1) = (1, 1)\) lies on neither axis, so the union is not closed under addition and is not a subspace.










DefDefinition 5 (Span)






Definition 5 (Span) The span [5] of vectors \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k \in \mathbb{R}^p\) is the set of all their linear combinations:
\[
\operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k\right\}\mathclose{}
\stackrel{\text{def}}{=}
\mathopen{}\left\{c_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1 + \cdots + c_k \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k : c_1, \ldots, c_k \in \mathbb{R}\right\}\mathclose{}.
\]
The vectors \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k\) span a set \(\mathcal{S}\) if their span equals \(\mathcal{S}\).
By convention, the span of the empty list (\(k = 0\)) is \(\mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\right\}\mathclose{}\), and the empty list counts as linearly independent (Definition 1), since it has no coefficients that could fail to be zero.










ExmExample 6 (Two spans in \(\mathbb{R}^3\))






Example 6 (Two spans in \(\mathbb{R}^3\))  

\(\operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{(1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0)\right\}\mathclose{}\) is the set of vectors \((c_1, c_2, 0)\), the plane \(z = 0\) in \(\mathbb{R}^3\).
\(\operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{(1, 2, 3), (2, 4, 6)\right\}\mathclose{}\) is only the line \(\mathopen{}\left\{c\,(1, 2, 3) : c \in \mathbb{R}\right\}\mathclose{}\), because \((2, 4, 6) = 2\,(1, 2, 3)\), so \(c_1 (1, 2, 3) + c_2 (2, 4, 6) = (c_1 + 2 c_2)\,(1, 2, 3)\). Adding a vector to a list does not always enlarge its span.











LemTheorem 2 (A span is a subspace)






Theorem 2 (A span is a subspace) For any vectors \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k \in \mathbb{R}^p\), \(\operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k\right\}\mathclose{}\) (Definition 5) is a subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^p\) (Definition 4).










ProofProof






Proof. The span is not empty: it contains \(0 \cdot\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1 + \cdots + 0 \cdot\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\).
Addition. Take two vectors in the span, \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} = a_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1 + \cdots + a_k \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} = b_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1 + \cdots + b_k \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}} + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}
&= (a_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1 + \cdots + a_k \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k)
+ (b_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1 + \cdots + b_k \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k)
&& \text{(substitute the two combinations)}
\\
&= (a_1 + b_1)\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1 + \cdots + (a_k + b_k)\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k
&& \text{(regroup, and distribute each } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_i \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
which is a linear combination of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k\), so it is in the span.
Scalar multiplication. For \(c \in \mathbb{R}\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
c\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}
&= c\,(a_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1 + \cdots + a_k \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k)
&& \text{(substitute the combination)}
\\
&= (c a_1)\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1 + \cdots + (c a_k)\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k
&& \text{(distribute } c \text{ over the sum)}
\end{aligned}
\]
which is again in the span.










ExmExample 7 (The line in Example 3 is a span)






Example 7 (The line in Example 3 is a span) The line \(\mathcal{S} = \mathopen{}\left\{c\,(1, 2) : c \in \mathbb{R}\right\}\mathclose{}\) in Example 3 is \(\operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{(1, 2)\right\}\mathclose{}\), so Theorem 2 gives a second proof that it is a subspace. Likewise, the plane \(z = 0\) in Example 6 is a subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^3\), because it is \(\operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{(1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0)\right\}\mathclose{}\).










LemTheorem 3 (A matrix-vector product combines the columns)






Theorem 3 (A matrix-vector product combines the columns) If \(\mathbf{A}\) is an \(m \times n\) matrix with columns \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_n\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} \in \mathbb{R}^n\), then
\[
\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = x_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1 + \cdots + x_n \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_n.
\]










ProofProof






Proof. Compare entry \(i\) of the two sides, for each \(i = 1, \ldots, m\). Entry \(i\) of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_j\) is \(a_{ij}\), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})_i
&= a_{i1} x_1 + \cdots + a_{in} x_n
&& \text{(}\href{linear-algebra-matrices.qmd#def-matvec-mult}{\text{Definition~13 in Matrices}}\text{)}
\\
&= x_1 a_{i1} + \cdots + x_n a_{in}
&& \text{(multiplication of numbers is commutative)}
\\
&= (x_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1 + \cdots + x_n \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_n)_i
&& \text{(entry } i \text{ of each } x_j \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_j \text{ is } x_j a_{ij} \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExmExample 8 (A product as a combination of columns)






Example 8 (A product as a combination of columns) \[
\begin{aligned}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}
&= 1 \cdot\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}
+ (-1) \cdot\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(}\href{#thm-matvec-columns}{\text{Theorem~3}}\text{)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix},
&& \text{(arithmetic)}
\end{aligned}
\]
the same answer as computing each entry as a row-times-vector dot product (Remark 4 in Matrices).










LemTheorem 4 (A matrix maps a combination to the same combination of images)






Theorem 4 (A matrix maps a combination to the same combination of images) If \(\mathbf{A}\) is an \(m \times n\) matrix, \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}_k \in \mathbb{R}^n\) and \(c_1, \ldots, c_k \in \mathbb{R}\), then
\[
\mathbf{A}\,(c_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}_1 + \cdots + c_k \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}_k)
= c_1\,\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}_1 + \cdots + c_k\,\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}_k.
\]










ProofProof






Proof. The function \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\mapsto \mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) is a linear map by Theorem 10 in Matrices, and a linear map preserves linear combinations by Theorem 11 in Matrices. Applying that theorem with \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = \mathbf{A}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_i = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}_i\) gives the identity.










ExmExample 9 (Applying a matrix to a combination)






Example 9 (Applying a matrix to a combination) Let \(\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\), \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}_1 = (1, 0)\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}_2 = (0, 1)\). Then \(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}_1 = (1, 3)\) and \(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}_2 = (2, 4)\), and for the combination \(2 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}_1 - \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}_2 = (2, -1)\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{A}\,(2, -1)
&= (1 \cdot 2 + 2 \cdot(-1),\; 3 \cdot 2 + 4 \cdot(-1))
&& \text{(}\href{linear-algebra-matrices.qmd#def-matvec-mult}{\text{Definition~13 in Matrices}}\text{)}
\\
&= (0, 2)
&& \text{(arithmetic)}
\\
&= 2\,(1, 3) - (2, 4),
&& \text{(arithmetic)}
\end{aligned}
\]
which is \(2\,\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}_1 - \mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}_2\), as Theorem 4 says.










LemTheorem 5 (More than \(p\) vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^p\) are linearly dependent)






Theorem 5 (More than \(p\) vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^p\) are linearly dependent) If \(k > p\), then any \(k\) vectors \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k \in \mathbb{R}^p\) are not linearly independent (Definition 1): some numbers \(c_1, \ldots, c_k\), not all zero, satisfy \(c_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1 + \cdots + c_k \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_p\).










ProofProof






Proof. Induction on \(p\).
Base case, \(p = 1\). Each \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_i\) is a single number \(v_i\), and \(k \ge 2\). If \(v_1 = 0\), take \(c_1 = 1\) and every other \(c_i = 0\). Otherwise take \(c_1 = v_2\), \(c_2 = -v_1\) and every other \(c_i = 0\); then \(c_2 \neq 0\), and \(v_2 v_1 - v_1 v_2 = 0\).
Inductive step. Let \(p \ge 2\), assume the theorem holds for vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^{p-1}\), and take \(k > p\) vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^p\). Write \(v_{i,p}\) for the last entry of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_i\).
Case 1: every \(v_{i,p} = 0\). Deleting the last entry gives \(k > p - 1\) vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^{p-1}\), which by the inductive hypothesis have a combination with coefficients not all zero that equals \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_{p-1}\). The same coefficients combine the original vectors to \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_p\), since every last entry is \(0\).
Case 2: some \(v_{i,p} \neq 0\). Renumber the vectors so that \(v_{k,p} \neq 0\), and for \(i = 1, \ldots, k-1\) let
\[
\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}_i \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_i - \frac{v_{i,p}}{v_{k,p}}\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k.
\]
The last entry of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}_i\) is \(v_{i,p} - \frac{v_{i,p}}{v_{k,p}}\,v_{k,p} = 0\). Deleting that zero last entry gives \(k - 1 > p - 1\) vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^{p-1}\), so by the inductive hypothesis there are numbers \(c_1, \ldots, c_{k-1}\), not all zero, whose combination of the shortened vectors is \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_{p-1}\). Putting the zero last entries back gives \(c_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}_1 + \cdots + c_{k-1} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}_{k-1} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_p\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_p
&= c_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}_1 + \cdots + c_{k-1} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}_{k-1}
&& \text{(choice of } c_1, \ldots, c_{k-1} \text{)}
\\
&= \sum_{i=1}^{k-1} c_i \mathopen{}\left(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_i - \frac{v_{i,p}}{v_{k,p}}\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(definition of } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}_i \text{)}
\\
&= \sum_{i=1}^{k-1} c_i \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_i
- \sum_{i=1}^{k-1} \frac{c_i v_{i,p}}{v_{k,p}}\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k
&& \text{(distribute each } c_i \text{, and distribute the sum over the difference)}
\\
&= c_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1 + \cdots + c_{k-1} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_{k-1}
- \mathopen{}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k-1} \frac{c_i v_{i,p}}{v_{k,p}}\right)\mathclose{}\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k,
&& \text{(factor } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k \text{ out of the second sum)}
\end{aligned}
\]
a combination of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k\) equal to \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_p\) whose first \(k - 1\) coefficients are not all zero.










ExmExample 10 (Three vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^2\))






Example 10 (Three vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^2\)) Theorem 5 says the three vectors \((1, 0)\), \((0, 1)\) and \((1, 1)\) in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) are linearly dependent, and indeed \(1 \cdot(1, 0) + 1 \cdot(0, 1) - 1 \cdot(1, 1) = (0, 0)\). The theorem says nothing about \(k \le p\) vectors: \((1, 0)\) and \((0, 1)\) are linearly independent, while \((1, 2)\) and \((2, 4)\) are not (Example 1).










DefDefinition 6 (Basis)






Definition 6 (Basis) A basis [6] of a subspace \(\mathcal{S}\) (Definition 4) is a list of vectors that are linearly independent (Definition 1) and span \(\mathcal{S}\) (Definition 5).










ExmExample 11 (Two bases of \(\mathbb{R}^2\))






Example 11 (Two bases of \(\mathbb{R}^2\))  

\((1, 0)\) and \((0, 1)\) form a basis of \(\mathbb{R}^2\): they are linearly independent, and any \((x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^2\) equals \(x\,(1, 0) + y\,(0, 1)\).
\((1, 0)\) and \((1, 1)\) also form a basis of \(\mathbb{R}^2\): Example 1 shows they are linearly independent, and any \((x, y)\) equals \((x - y)\,(1, 0) + y\,(1, 1)\), because \((x - y) + y = x\) in the first entry and \(0 + y = y\) in the second.











ExmExample 12 (Lists that are not bases of \(\mathbb{R}^2\))






Example 12 (Lists that are not bases of \(\mathbb{R}^2\))  

\((1, 0)\) and \((2, 0)\) are not a basis of \(\mathbb{R}^2\). They are not linearly independent, since \(2\,(1, 0) - (2, 0) = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\), and they do not span \(\mathbb{R}^2\): every combination \(c_1 (1, 0) + c_2 (2, 0)\) has second entry \(0\), so \((0, 1)\) is not in their span.
\((1, 0)\), \((0, 1)\) and \((1, 1)\) span \(\mathbb{R}^2\), but they are not a basis: \((1, 0) + (0, 1) - (1, 1) = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\), so they are not linearly independent.











LemTheorem 6 (Coefficients in a basis are unique)






Theorem 6 (Coefficients in a basis are unique) If \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_k\) is a basis of a subspace \(\mathcal{S}\) (Definition 6), then every \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} \in \mathcal{S}\) is a linear combination \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = c_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1 + \cdots + c_k \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_k\) for exactly one list of numbers \(c_1, \ldots, c_k\).










ProofProof






Proof. At least one such list exists, because the basis spans \(\mathcal{S}\) (Definition 5).
Suppose two lists both work:
\[
\begin{aligned}
c_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1 + \cdots + c_k \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_k
&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} \\
&= d_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1 + \cdots + d_k \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_k.
\end{aligned}
\]
Subtracting the right side from the left side gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}
&= (c_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1 + \cdots + c_k \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_k)
- (d_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1 + \cdots + d_k \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_k)
&& \text{(both combinations equal } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} \text{)}
\\
&= (c_1 - d_1)\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1 + \cdots + (c_k - d_k)\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_k
&& \text{(regroup, and distribute each } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_i \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Because \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_k\) are linearly independent (Definition 1), every coefficient \(c_i - d_i\) is \(0\), so \(c_i = d_i\) for each \(i\).










ExmExample 13 (Coefficients of \((3, 5)\) in two bases)






Example 13 (Coefficients of \((3, 5)\) in two bases) In the basis \((1, 0), (0, 1)\) of Example 11, \((3, 5) = 3\,(1, 0) + 5\,(0, 1)\), and no other coefficients work. In the basis \((1, 0), (1, 1)\), the formula in Example 11 gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
(3, 5) &= (3 - 5)\,(1, 0) + 5\,(1, 1) \\
&= -2\,(1, 0) + 5\,(1, 1).
\end{aligned}
\]
The same vector has different coefficients in different bases, but within one basis its coefficients are unique.
The list \((1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1)\) in Example 12 spans \(\mathbb{R}^2\) but is not linearly independent, and the coefficients of \((3, 5)\) are not unique:
\[
\begin{aligned}
(3, 5) &= 3\,(1, 0) + 5\,(0, 1) + 0\,(1, 1) \\
&= 0\,(1, 0) + 2\,(0, 1) + 3\,(1, 1).
\end{aligned}
\]










DefDefinition 7 (Coordinates in a basis)






Definition 7 (Coordinates in a basis) Let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_k\) be a basis of a subspace \(\mathcal{S}\) (Definition 6), and let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} \in \mathcal{S}\). The coordinates [7] of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) in this basis are the numbers \(c_1, \ldots, c_k\) with \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = c_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1 + \cdots + c_k \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_k\). By Theorem 6 there is exactly one such list of numbers.










DefDefinition 8 (Coordinate vector)






Definition 8 (Coordinate vector) With \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) and its coordinates \(c_1, \ldots, c_k\) as in Definition 7, \((c_1, \ldots, c_k) \in \mathbb{R}^k\) is the coordinate vector of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\).










ExmExample 14 (Coordinates of \((4, 1)\) in two bases of \(\mathbb{R}^2\))






Example 14 (Coordinates of \((4, 1)\) in two bases of \(\mathbb{R}^2\)) In the basis \((1, 0), (1, 1)\) of Example 11, the coordinates of \((4, 1)\) are \(3\) and \(1\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
3\,(1, 0) + 1\,(1, 1)
&= (3 + 1,\; 0 + 1)
&& \text{(}\href{linear-algebra-vectors.qmd#def-linear-combination}{\text{Definition~9 in Vectors}}\text{, entry by entry)}
\\
&= (4, 1).
&& \text{(add)}
\end{aligned}
\]
In the basis \((1, 0), (0, 1)\), its coordinates are its entries, \(4\) and \(1\).










LemTheorem 7 (All bases of a subspace have the same number of vectors)






Theorem 7 (All bases of a subspace have the same number of vectors) If \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_k\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}_l\) are both bases of a subspace \(\mathcal{S}\) of \(\mathbb{R}^p\) (Definition 6), then \(k = l\).










ProofProof






Proof. Let \(\mathbf{A}\) be the \(p \times k\) matrix with columns \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_k\), and \(\mathbf{B}\) the \(p \times l\) matrix with columns \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}_l\).
Write \(\mathbf{A}\) in terms of \(\mathbf{B}\). Each \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_j\) is in \(\mathcal{S}\), and the \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\)’s span \(\mathcal{S}\) (Definition 5), so \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_j = \mathbf{B} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{c}}\vphantom{c}}_j\) for some \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{c}}\vphantom{c}}_j \in \mathbb{R}^l\) (Definition 13 in Matrices). Let \(\mathbf{C}\) be the \(l \times k\) matrix with columns \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{c}}\vphantom{c}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{c}}\vphantom{c}}_k\). Then \(\underbrace{\mathbf{A}}_{p \times k}
= \underbrace{\mathbf{B}}_{p \times l}\,\underbrace{\mathbf{C}}_{l \times k}\), because column \(j\) of \(\mathbf{B} \mathbf{C}\) is \(\mathbf{B} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{c}}\vphantom{c}}_j\).
The columns of \(\mathbf{C}\) are linearly independent. Suppose \(\mathbf{C} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\) for some \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} \in \mathbb{R}^k\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}
&= (\mathbf{B} \mathbf{C})\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}
&& \text{(substitute } \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{B} \mathbf{C} \text{)}
\\
&= \mathbf{B}\,(\mathbf{C} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})
&& \text{(}\href{linear-algebra-matrices.qmd#thm-matmul-assoc}{\text{Theorem~5 in Matrices}}\text{)}
\\
&= \mathbf{B}\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}
&& \text{(substitute } \mathbf{C} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\text{)}
\\
&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}
&& \text{(a matrix times the zero vector is } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
\(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) is the combination \(x_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1 + \cdots + x_k \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_k\) (Theorem 3), and the \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}\)’s are linearly independent (Definition 1), so \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\). So the only combination of the columns of \(\mathbf{C}\) that equals \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\) has all coefficients \(0\).
Count. \(\mathbf{C}\) has \(k\) linearly independent columns of length \(l\). More than \(l\) vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^l\) are never linearly independent (Theorem 5), so \(k \le l\). Exchanging the roles of the two bases gives \(l \le k\), so \(k = l\).










ExmExample 15 (Both bases of \(\mathbb{R}^2\) in Example 11 have two vectors)






Example 15 (Both bases of \(\mathbb{R}^2\) in Example 11 have two vectors) The bases \((1, 0), (0, 1)\) and \((1, 0), (1, 1)\) of \(\mathbb{R}^2\) in Example 11 both have \(2\) vectors, as Theorem 7 requires. So no list of \(3\) vectors is a basis of \(\mathbb{R}^2\), which agrees with Example 12: the list \((1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1)\) spans \(\mathbb{R}^2\) but is not linearly independent.










DefDefinition 9 (Dimension)






Definition 9 (Dimension) The dimension of a subspace \(\mathcal{S}\), written \(\dim(\mathcal{S})\), is the number of vectors in any basis of \(\mathcal{S}\) (Definition 6). Theorem 7 makes this number well defined. By convention, the empty list is the basis of \(\mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\right\}\mathclose{}\), so \(\dim(\mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\right\}\mathclose{}) = 0\).










ExmExample 16 (The dimensions of some subspaces)






Example 16 (The dimensions of some subspaces)  

\(\dim(\mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\right\}\mathclose{}) = 0\), by the convention in Definition 9.
\(\dim(\mathbb{R}^2) = 2\), by Example 11. More generally, \(\dim(\mathbb{R}^p) = p\): the indicator vectors \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{e}}\vphantom{e}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{e}}\vphantom{e}}_p\) (Definition 18 in Vectors) are linearly independent, since \(c_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{e}}\vphantom{e}}_1 + \cdots + c_p \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{e}}\vphantom{e}}_p = (c_1, \ldots, c_p)\), which is \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_p\) only if every \(c_i = 0\); and they span \(\mathbb{R}^p\), since any \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} = x_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{e}}\vphantom{e}}_1 + \cdots + x_p \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{e}}\vphantom{e}}_p\).
The line in Example 3 has dimension \(1\): the single vector \((1, 2)\) is linearly independent and spans the line.
The plane \(z = 0\) in Example 6 has dimension \(2\), with basis \((1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0)\).











LemTheorem 8 (Adding a vector outside the span keeps a list independent)






Theorem 8 (Adding a vector outside the span keeps a list independent) If \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k\) are linearly independent (Definition 1) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}\) is not in \(\operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k\right\}\mathclose{}\) (Definition 5), then \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}\) are linearly independent.










ProofProof






Proof. Suppose \(c_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1 + \cdots + c_k \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k + d\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\).
The coefficient \(d\) is \(0\). If \(d \neq 0\), then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}
&= \frac{1}{d}\,\mathopen{}\left(d\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(} d \neq 0 \text{)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{d}\,\mathopen{}\left(-c_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1 - \cdots - c_k \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(solve the supposed equation for } d\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} \text{)}
\\
&= \mathopen{}\left(-\frac{c_1}{d}\right)\mathclose{}\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1 + \cdots + \mathopen{}\left(-\frac{c_k}{d}\right)\mathclose{}\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k,
&& \text{(distribute } \tfrac{1}{d} \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
which puts \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}\) in \(\operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k\right\}\mathclose{}\), contrary to the assumption.
The other coefficients are \(0\). With \(d = 0\), the equation reads \(c_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1 + \cdots + c_k \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\), so every \(c_i = 0\), because \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k\) are linearly independent.










ExmExample 17 (Adding \((0, 0, 1)\) to two independent vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^3\))






Example 17 (Adding \((0, 0, 1)\) to two independent vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^3\)) The vectors \((1, 0, 0)\) and \((0, 1, 0)\) are linearly independent, and their span is the plane \(z = 0\) (Example 6). The vector \((0, 0, 1)\) has third entry \(1\), so it is not in that plane, and by Theorem 8 the three vectors \((1, 0, 0)\), \((0, 1, 0)\), \((0, 0, 1)\) are linearly independent. Adding \((1, 1, 0)\) instead would not work: \((1, 1, 0)\) is in the span, and \((1, 0, 0) + (0, 1, 0) - (1, 1, 0) = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\).










LemTheorem 9 (An independent list extends to a basis)






Theorem 9 (An independent list extends to a basis) If \(\mathcal{S}\) is a subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^p\) (Definition 4) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}}_k \in \mathcal{S}\) are linearly independent (Definition 1), then adding vectors of \(\mathcal{S}\) to the list gives a basis of \(\mathcal{S}\) (Definition 6). Starting from the empty list shows that every subspace has a basis.










ProofProof






Proof. Repeat the following step. If the current list spans \(\mathcal{S}\), stop: it is linearly independent and spans \(\mathcal{S}\), so it is a basis. Otherwise, some \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} \in \mathcal{S}\) is not in the span of the current list; add \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}\) to the list, which stays linearly independent by Theorem 8.
Every list produced is a linearly independent list of vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^p\), so it has at most \(p\) vectors (Theorem 5). Each step adds one vector, so the process stops after at most \(p - k\) steps, and when it stops the list is a basis of \(\mathcal{S}\).
For the empty list, which is linearly independent and spans \(\mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\right\}\mathclose{}\) by the conventions in Definition 5, the first step asks whether \(\mathcal{S} = \mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\right\}\mathclose{}\): if so, the empty list is already a basis; if not, the process adds vectors as described.










ExmExample 18 (Extending \((1, 1, 0)\) to a basis of \(\mathbb{R}^3\))






Example 18 (Extending \((1, 1, 0)\) to a basis of \(\mathbb{R}^3\)) Start with the single vector \((1, 1, 0)\).

\((1, 0, 0)\) is not in \(\operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{(1, 1, 0)\right\}\mathclose{}\), because every multiple \(c\,(1, 1, 0)\) has equal first and second entries. Add it.
\((0, 0, 1)\) is not in \(\operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{(1, 1, 0), (1, 0, 0)\right\}\mathclose{}\), because every combination of those two vectors has third entry \(0\). Add it.
The list \((1, 1, 0), (1, 0, 0), (0, 0, 1)\) spans \(\mathbb{R}^3\): \((x, y, z) = y\,(1, 1, 0) + (x - y)\,(1, 0, 0) + z\,(0, 0, 1)\). Stop.

The result is a basis of \(\mathbb{R}^3\) that contains the starting vector.










LemTheorem 10 (An independent list in a subspace has at most \(\dim\) vectors)






Theorem 10 (An independent list in a subspace has at most \(\dim\) vectors) Let \(\mathcal{S}\) be a subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^p\) with \(\dim(\mathcal{S}) = d\) (Definition 9).

Any linearly independent list of vectors in \(\mathcal{S}\) has at most \(d\) vectors.
If \(\mathcal{T}\) is a subspace with \(\mathcal{T} \subseteq \mathcal{S}\), then \(\dim(\mathcal{T}) \le \dim(\mathcal{S})\).











ProofProof






Proof. Part 1. If \(d = 0\), then \(\mathcal{S} = \mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\right\}\mathclose{}\), so every vector in a nonempty list from \(\mathcal{S}\) is \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\), and \(1 \cdot\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\) shows the list is not linearly independent; only the empty list, with \(0 = d\) vectors, is. Now let \(d \ge 1\), and let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_d\) be a basis of \(\mathcal{S}\), and let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_k \in \mathcal{S}\) be linearly independent. Each \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_j\) is in \(\mathcal{S}\), so \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_j = c_{1j} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_1 + \cdots + c_{dj} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_d\) for some coordinate vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{c}}\vphantom{c}}_j = (c_{1j}, \ldots, c_{dj}) \in \mathbb{R}^d\). Suppose \(k > d\). Then \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{c}}\vphantom{c}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{c}}\vphantom{c}}_k\) are \(k > d\) vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^d\), so some \(x_1, \ldots, x_k\), not all zero, satisfy \(x_1 \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{c}}\vphantom{c}}_1 + \cdots + x_k \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{c}}\vphantom{c}}_k = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_d\) (Theorem 5); entry \(i\) of that equation says \(\sum_{j=1}^{k} x_j c_{ij} = 0\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{j=1}^{k} x_j \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_j
&= \sum_{j=1}^{k} x_j \sum_{i=1}^{d} c_{ij} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_i
&& \text{(substitute each } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_j \text{)}
\\
&= \sum_{j=1}^{k} \sum_{i=1}^{d} x_j c_{ij}\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_i
&& \text{(distribute each } x_j \text{ over the inner sum)}
\\
&= \sum_{i=1}^{d} \sum_{j=1}^{k} x_j c_{ij}\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_i
&& \text{(swap the order of the finite sums)}
\\
&= \sum_{i=1}^{d} \mathopen{}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{k} x_j c_{ij}\right)\mathclose{}\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_i
&& \text{(factor } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_i \text{ out of the inner sum)}
\\
&= \sum_{i=1}^{d} 0 \cdot\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{a}}\vphantom{a}}_i
&& \text{(entry } i \text{ of } \textstyle\sum_j x_j \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{c}}\vphantom{c}}_j = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_d \text{)}
\\
&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_p,
&& \text{(a zero multiple of a vector is } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
a combination of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{u}}\vphantom{u}}_k\) with coefficients not all zero that equals \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_p\). That contradicts their linear independence, so \(k \le d\).
Part 2. \(\mathcal{T}\) has a basis (Theorem 9) with \(\dim(\mathcal{T})\) vectors. Those vectors are linearly independent and lie in \(\mathcal{S}\), so by Part 1 there are at most \(\dim(\mathcal{S})\) of them.










ExmExample 19 (Subspaces of a plane have dimension at most two)






Example 19 (Subspaces of a plane have dimension at most two) The plane \(\mathcal{S} = \mathopen{}\left\{(x, y, 0) : x, y \in \mathbb{R}\right\}\mathclose{}\) in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) has dimension \(2\) (Example 16). By Theorem 10, no three vectors with third entry \(0\) are linearly independent; for instance, \((1, 0, 0) + (0, 1, 0) - (1, 1, 0) = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\). The line \(\mathcal{T} = \operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{(1, 1, 0)\right\}\mathclose{}\) lies in \(\mathcal{S}\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
\dim(\mathcal{T}) &= 1 \\
&\le 2 \\
&= \dim(\mathcal{S}).
\end{aligned}
\]










LemTheorem 11 (A subspace inside another of the same dimension equals it)






Theorem 11 (A subspace inside another of the same dimension equals it) If \(\mathcal{T}\) and \(\mathcal{S}\) are subspaces of \(\mathbb{R}^p\) with \(\mathcal{T} \subseteq \mathcal{S}\) and \(\dim(\mathcal{T}) = \dim(\mathcal{S})\) (Definition 9), then \(\mathcal{T} = \mathcal{S}\).










ProofProof






Proof. Let \(d = \dim(\mathcal{S})\), and let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{t}}\vphantom{t}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{t}}\vphantom{t}}_d\) be a basis of \(\mathcal{T}\) (Theorem 9); it has \(d\) vectors because \(\dim(\mathcal{T}) = d\). (When \(d = 0\) it is the empty list, whose span is \(\mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\right\}\mathclose{}\) by the convention in Definition 5, and the argument is unchanged.) Suppose some \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{s}}\vphantom{s}} \in \mathcal{S}\) is not in \(\operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{t}}\vphantom{t}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{t}}\vphantom{t}}_d\right\}\mathclose{} = \mathcal{T}\). Then \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{t}}\vphantom{t}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{t}}\vphantom{t}}_d, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{s}}\vphantom{s}}\) are linearly independent (Theorem 8), and they are \(d + 1\) vectors of \(\mathcal{S}\), which contradicts part 1 of Theorem 10. So every vector of \(\mathcal{S}\) is in \(\mathcal{T}\), that is, \(\mathcal{S} \subseteq \mathcal{T}\). Together with \(\mathcal{T} \subseteq \mathcal{S}\), this inclusion gives \(\mathcal{T} = \mathcal{S}\).










ExmExample 20 (Two independent vectors in a plane span it)






Example 20 (Two independent vectors in a plane span it) Let \(\mathcal{S} = \mathopen{}\left\{(x, y, 0) : x, y \in \mathbb{R}\right\}\mathclose{}\), the plane \(z = 0\), which has dimension \(2\) (Example 16), and let \(\mathcal{T} = \operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{(1, 0, 0), (1, 1, 0)\right\}\mathclose{}\). Both vectors have third entry \(0\), so \(\mathcal{T} \subseteq \mathcal{S}\). They are linearly independent: \(c_1 (1, 0, 0) + c_2 (1, 1, 0) = (c_1 + c_2, c_2, 0)\), which is \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\) only if \(c_2 = 0\) and then \(c_1 = 0\). So \(\dim(\mathcal{T}) = 2\), and Theorem 11 gives \(\mathcal{T} = \mathcal{S}\) without solving for any coefficients. As a check, \((x, y, 0) = (x - y)\,(1, 0, 0) + y\,(1, 1, 0)\).










ExmExample 21 (Equal dimensions without containment)






Example 21 (Equal dimensions without containment) The lines \(\operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{(1, 0, 0)\right\}\mathclose{}\) and \(\operatorname{span}\mathopen{}\left\{(0, 1, 0)\right\}\mathclose{}\) in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) both have dimension \(1\), but they are not equal: \((1, 0, 0)\) is in the first and not the second. Theorem 11 does not apply, because neither line contains the other.

title: Linear Algebra
text:
1 Further reading


Strang [1] is a widely used first course in linear algebra. It covers vectors, elimination, vector spaces, orthogonality, determinants, eigenvalues, and the singular value decomposition.

Axler [2] is a proof-based treatment centered on vector spaces and linear maps. A free electronic version is available from the publisher.

Lange [3] covers computing eigenvalues and eigenvectors, including Jacobi’s method (Chapter 8), and the singular value decomposition, its properties, and its applications (Chapter 9).
Fieller [4]
Banerjee and Roy [5]
Searle and Khuri [6]

Petersen and Pedersen [7] is a free desk reference that collects matrix identities: it lists results on determinants, inverses, decompositions, and derivatives of vectors and matrices, so it is a quick place to look up a formula these pages prove.

Stanford University [8] (Stanford EE 278, taught by Tsachy Weissman) applies this page’s tools to probability and inference. Its “MMSE Geometry” lecture treats the best estimate as an orthogonal projection, and its lectures on spectral decomposition, the Karhunen-Loeve expansion and principal component analysis treat diagonalization of a covariance matrix.

Essence of Linear Algebra is a 16-video YouTube playlist by Grant Sanderson (3Blue1Brown) that develops visual and geometric intuition for vectors, linear combinations, spans, linear transformations, matrix multiplication, determinants, inverses, dot and cross products, change of basis, and eigenvectors and eigenvalues.

title: Notation
text:
Mathematical notation is not standardized. This section states the conventions these notes use, and the alternatives you may encounter in other sources.
The links for conditioning, random variables, expectation, and independence go to the Morrison Lab’s probability notes, which define those terms.

title: Notation
text:
1 Writing math in Quarto
The third column of Table 1 gives the LaTeX command for each symbol. Quarto and R Markdown documents write math in LaTeX syntax: put inline math between single dollar signs, as in $x^2$, and displayed equations between double dollar signs, as in $$x^2$$. The equations section of Quarto’s Markdown guide shows the details. These notes also use shorthand macros, such as \floor{x} for \(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor x\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\), defined in the latex-macros submodule’s macros.qmd.

title: Notation
text:
2 Subscripts and parentheses






RemarkRemark 1 (Our convention for subscripts and parentheses)






Remark 1 (Our convention for subscripts and parentheses). Subscripts and parentheses both attach extra information to a symbol, and sources divide the work between them differently. These notes follow two rules of thumb:

A subscript names which member of an indexed family we mean. It holds an index, such as the \(i\) in \(x_i\), or a parameter that picks one function or distribution out of the family, such as the \(\theta\) in \(f_\theta\).
Parentheses hold the input a function is evaluated at, as in \(f(x)\).

Under these rules, \(f_\theta(x)\) reads “the member of the family labeled \(\theta\), evaluated at \(x\)”. The notation choices page gives the reason for this split and explains how to read a source that divides the work differently.




The Notation Across Sources page of the macros site tabulates our form of each object beside the other forms you may encounter.






ExmExample 1 (Reading \(X_t(\omega)\))






Example 1 (Reading \(X_t(\omega)\)) Let \(X_t\) be the position of a particle at time \(t \ge 0\). Then \(X_3\) is the random position at time 3, and \(X_3(\omega)\) is its value when the experiment’s outcome is \(\omega\). Holding \(\omega\) fixed and letting \(t\) vary gives the particle’s whole path for that outcome. A source that writes \(X(t, \omega)\) means the same thing, with both arguments in parentheses.

title: Notation
section: 3 Why is notation in probability and statistics so inconsistent and disorganized?
text:
3 Why is notation in probability and statistics so inconsistent and disorganized?
In grad school, we are asked to learn from increasingly disorganized materials and lectures. Not coincidentally, as the amount of organization decreases, the amount of complexity increases, the amount of difficulty increases, the number of reliable references decreases, and the amount of inconsistency in notation and content increases (both between multiple references and within single references!). In other words, as you approach the cutting-edge of most fields, you start to run into content that hasn’t been fully thought through or standardized. This lack of clarity is unfortunate and undesirable, but it is understandable and inevitable.
It’s worth noting that calculus was formalized in the 1600s, elementary algebra was formalized around 820, and arithmetic even earlier. And calculus still has several competing notation systems. In contrast, the field of statistics only emerged in the late 1800s and early 1900s, so it’s not surprising that the notation and terminology is still developing. Generalized linear models were only formalized in 1972 [1], which is very recent in terms of the pace of scientific development.

title: Optimization
text:
DefDefinition 1 (Flat point (stationary point))






Definition 1 (Flat point (stationary point)) Let \(f\) be differentiable at \(c\). If \(f'(c) = 0\), then \(c\) is a flat point of \(f\) (also called a stationary point) [1].










ExmExample 1 (Flat points, and a point that is not one)






Example 1 (Flat points, and a point that is not one)  


\(f(w) = w^3\) has \(f'(w) = 3w^2\), which is \(0\) at \(w = 0\), so \(0\) is a flat point. Yet \(f(0) = 0\) is neither the minimum nor the maximum of the values \(f\) takes on any open interval around \(0\): \(f(w) < 0\) for \(w < 0\), and \(f(w) > 0\) for \(w > 0\).

\(h(w) = w^2\) has \(h'(1) = 2 \ne 0\), so \(1\) is not a flat point.











ExrExercise 1 (Differentiate a quadratic)






Exercise 1 (Differentiate a quadratic) Let \(f(w) = w^2 - 4w + 7\).
Differentiate \(f\).










SolutionSolution 1






Solution 1. Differentiating each term:
\[\frac{df}{dw} = 2w - 4\]










ExrExercise 2 (Find the flat point)






Exercise 2 (Find the flat point) In the setting of Exercise 1, find the flat point \(w\) of \(f\).










SolutionSolution 2






Solution 2. The derivative is zero where \(2w - 4 = 0\), which gives \(w = 2\).










ExrExercise 3 (Classify the flat point)






Exercise 3 (Classify the flat point) In the setting of Exercise 1, say whether \(f(w)\) at the flat point is the minimum or the maximum of the values of \(f\).










SolutionSolution 3






Solution 3. The flat point is \(w = 2\), from Solution 2. Evaluating \(f\) there gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(2) &= 4 - 8 + 7 \\
&= 3.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is the minimum of the values of \(f\). Completing the square, \(f(w) = (w - 2)^2 + 3\), since
\[
\begin{aligned}
(w - 2)^2 + 3 &= w^2 - 4w + 4 + 3 \\
&= w^2 - 4w + 7,
\end{aligned}
\]
and \((w - 2)^2 \ge 0\), so \(f(w) \ge 3 = f(2)\) for every \(w\). Equivalently, the derivative is negative below \(w = 2\) and positive above it, so the function falls into that point and rises out of it.










ExrExercise 4 (Slope at \(w = 1\))






Exercise 4 (Slope at \(w = 1\)) In the setting of Exercise 1, evaluate the derivative at \(w = 1\).










SolutionSolution 4






Solution 4. At \(w = 1\) the derivative is \(2(1) - 4 = -2\), so \(f\) is falling there.










ExrExercise 5 (Predict a nearby value)






Exercise 5 (Predict a nearby value) In the setting of Exercise 1, use the linear approximation and the derivative at \(w = 1\) from Exercise 4 to predict \(f(1.01)\).










SolutionSolution 5






Solution 5. With \(\varepsilon= 0.01\), the linear approximation predicts a change of \((0.01)(-2) = -0.02\), from
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(1) &= 1 - 4 + 7 \\
&= 4
\end{aligned}
\]
to \(3.98\).










ExrExercise 6 (Exact value)






Exercise 6 (Exact value) In the setting of Exercise 1, find the exact value of \(f(1.01)\).










SolutionSolution 6






Solution 6. The exact value is
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(1.01)
&= (1.01)^2 - 4(1.01) + 7 \\
&= 1.0201 - 4.04 + 7 \\
&= 3.9801
\end{aligned}
\]
a change of \(-0.0199\) from \(f(1) = 4\).










ExrExercise 7 (Check the prediction)






Exercise 7 (Check the prediction) Compare the prediction in Exercise 5 with the exact value of \(f(1.01)\) from Exercise 6.










SolutionSolution 7






Solution 7. The prediction \(3.98\) (Solution 5) and the exact value \(3.9801\) (Solution 6) differ by \(0.0001\), which is \(\varepsilon^2\). The linear approximation drops everything of that order and smaller, so halving the step quarters the error. That trade is the whole bargain of gradient descent, the step-by-step method of fitting models that the optimization page defines. We take a step in the direction the derivative recommends, and the recommendation is trustworthy only as far as the step is small.










DefDefinition 2 (Critical point)






Definition 2 (Critical point) Let \(f\) be a function defined on an open interval containing \(c\). The point \(c\) is a critical point of \(f\) if either \(f'(c) = 0\) or \(f\) is not differentiable at \(c\) (Definition 6 in Derivatives and Taylor Series).










ExmExample 2 (Critical points that are and are not flat points)






Example 2 (Critical points that are and are not flat points)  

\(g(w) = \mathopen{}\left|w\right|\mathclose{}\) has no derivative at \(w = 0\): its one-sided derivatives there are \(1\) and \(-1\) (worked example). So the difference quotient \(\tfrac{\mathopen{}\left|h\right|\mathclose{} - 0}{h}\) has no limit as \(h \to 0\), because the limits from the left and from the right (one-sided limits) differ. So \(0\) is a critical point of \(g\) but not a flat point.

\(f(w) = w^3\) has
\[
\begin{aligned}
f'(0) &= 3 \cdot 0^2 \\
&= 0,
\end{aligned}
\]
so \(0\) is a flat point of \(f\), and hence a critical point.

\(h(w) = w^2\) is differentiable everywhere, with \(h'(w) = 2w\), which is \(0\) only at \(w = 0\). So \(0\) is the only critical point of \(h\). For example, \(h'(1) = 2 \ne 0\), so \(1\) is not one.











LemTheorem 1 (Every flat point is a critical point)






Theorem 1 (Every flat point is a critical point) If \(c\) is a flat point of \(f\) (Definition 1), then \(c\) is a critical point of \(f\) (Definition 2).










ProofProof






Proof. A flat point \(c\) has \(f\) differentiable at \(c\) and \(f'(c) = 0\). The condition “\(f'(c) = 0\)” is the first alternative in Definition 2, so \(c\) is a critical point.










ExmExample 3 (The flat points of a cubic, and a critical point that is not flat)






Example 3 (The flat points of a cubic, and a critical point that is not flat) For \(f(w) = w^3 - 3w\), the derivative is \(f'(w) = 3w^2 - 3\). The code differentiates \(f\) with D() and evaluates \(f'\) at several points. For \(g(w) = \mathopen{}\left|w\right|\mathclose{}\), it computes the difference quotients at \(0\) from both sides.

f_prime <- D(quote(w^3 - 3 * w), "w")
points <- c(-2, -1, 0, 1, 2)
derivs <- data.frame(w = points, f_prime = eval(f_prime, list(w = points)))
derivs


  


flat <- derivs$w[derivs$f_prime == 0]

h <- c(-1e-3, 1e-3)
quotients <- abs(h) / h
quotients
#> [1] -1  1

The derivative is \(0\) at 2 of the 5 points, namely \(w = -1\) and \(w = 1\). These are flat points of \(f\), so by Theorem 1 they are critical points. The difference quotients of \(g\) at \(0\) are -1 from the left and 1 from the right, so \(g\) has no derivative at \(0\). Thus \(0\) is a critical point of \(g\) (Definition 2), but not a flat point.










ExrExercise 8 (Maximizing a gamma-family kernel)






Exercise 8 (Maximizing a gamma-family kernel) Adapted from Miller [2], Question 1.1.10.
Find the maximum value of
\[f(x) = x^4 e^{-x}\]
on the interval \([0, \infty)\).










SolutionSolution 8






Solution 8. Differentiate using the product rule:
\[
\begin{aligned}
f'(x)
&= 4x^3 e^{-x} - x^4 e^{-x} \\
&= x^3 e^{-x}(4 - x)
\end{aligned}
\]
On \([0, \infty)\), \(e^{-x} > 0\), so \(f'(x) = 0\) only at \(x = 0\) and \(x = 4\).
Evaluate \(f\) at the boundary and critical points:

At \(x = 0\): \(f(0) = 0\).

At \(x = 4\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(4) &= 4^4 e^{-4} \\
&= 256 e^{-4} \\
&\approx 4.6888.
\end{aligned}
\]

As \(x \to \infty\): exponential decay dominates polynomial growth, so \(\lim_{x \to \infty} x^4 e^{-x} = 0\).

Since \(f(x) \ge 0\) for all \(x \ge 0\) and \(f(4) > 0\), the global maximum occurs at \(x = 4\), with maximum value \(256/e^4\).










ExrExercise 9 (Classifying critical points with the second derivative test)






Exercise 9 (Classifying critical points with the second derivative test) Adapted from Miller [2], Question 1.1.11.
Find the critical points of
\[f(x) = 4x^3 - 3x^2\]
and decide whether each is a local maximum, a local minimum, or an inflection point.










SolutionSolution 9






Solution 9. Compute the first derivative:
\[
\begin{aligned}
f'(x)
&= 12x^2 - 6x \\
&= 6x(2x - 1)
\end{aligned}
\]
Setting \(f'(x) = 0\) gives critical points at \(x = 0\) and \(x = 1/2\).
Compute the second derivative:
\[f''(x) = 24x - 6\]
Apply the second derivative test at each critical point:

At \(x = 0\): \(f''(0) = -6 < 0\), so \(x = 0\) is a strict local maximum.

At \(x = 1/2\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
f''(1/2) &= 24(1/2) - 6 \\
&= 6 \\
&> 0,
\end{aligned}
\]
so \(x = 1/2\) is a strict local minimum.


Inflection points occur where the second derivative changes sign (\(f''(x) = 0\) at \(x = 1/4\)). Because \(f''\) is non-zero at both critical points, neither is an inflection point.

title: Optimization
text:
DefDefinition 1 (Flat point (stationary point))






Definition 1 (Flat point (stationary point)) Let \(f\) be differentiable at \(c\). If \(f'(c) = 0\), then \(c\) is a flat point of \(f\) (also called a stationary point) [1].










ExmExample 1 (Flat points, and a point that is not one)






Example 1 (Flat points, and a point that is not one)  


\(f(w) = w^3\) has \(f'(w) = 3w^2\), which is \(0\) at \(w = 0\), so \(0\) is a flat point. Yet \(f(0) = 0\) is neither the minimum nor the maximum of the values \(f\) takes on any open interval around \(0\): \(f(w) < 0\) for \(w < 0\), and \(f(w) > 0\) for \(w > 0\).

\(h(w) = w^2\) has \(h'(1) = 2 \ne 0\), so \(1\) is not a flat point.











ExrExercise 1 (Differentiate a quadratic)






Exercise 1 (Differentiate a quadratic) Let \(f(w) = w^2 - 4w + 7\).
Differentiate \(f\).










SolutionSolution 1






Solution 1. Differentiating each term:
\[\frac{df}{dw} = 2w - 4\]










ExrExercise 2 (Find the flat point)






Exercise 2 (Find the flat point) In the setting of Exercise 1, find the flat point \(w\) of \(f\).










SolutionSolution 2






Solution 2. The derivative is zero where \(2w - 4 = 0\), which gives \(w = 2\).










ExrExercise 3 (Classify the flat point)






Exercise 3 (Classify the flat point) In the setting of Exercise 1, say whether \(f(w)\) at the flat point is the minimum or the maximum of the values of \(f\).










SolutionSolution 3






Solution 3. The flat point is \(w = 2\), from Solution 2. Evaluating \(f\) there gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(2) &= 4 - 8 + 7 \\
&= 3.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is the minimum of the values of \(f\). Completing the square, \(f(w) = (w - 2)^2 + 3\), since
\[
\begin{aligned}
(w - 2)^2 + 3 &= w^2 - 4w + 4 + 3 \\
&= w^2 - 4w + 7,
\end{aligned}
\]
and \((w - 2)^2 \ge 0\), so \(f(w) \ge 3 = f(2)\) for every \(w\). Equivalently, the derivative is negative below \(w = 2\) and positive above it, so the function falls into that point and rises out of it.










ExrExercise 4 (Slope at \(w = 1\))






Exercise 4 (Slope at \(w = 1\)) In the setting of Exercise 1, evaluate the derivative at \(w = 1\).










SolutionSolution 4






Solution 4. At \(w = 1\) the derivative is \(2(1) - 4 = -2\), so \(f\) is falling there.










ExrExercise 5 (Predict a nearby value)






Exercise 5 (Predict a nearby value) In the setting of Exercise 1, use the linear approximation and the derivative at \(w = 1\) from Exercise 4 to predict \(f(1.01)\).










SolutionSolution 5






Solution 5. With \(\varepsilon= 0.01\), the linear approximation predicts a change of \((0.01)(-2) = -0.02\), from
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(1) &= 1 - 4 + 7 \\
&= 4
\end{aligned}
\]
to \(3.98\).










ExrExercise 6 (Exact value)






Exercise 6 (Exact value) In the setting of Exercise 1, find the exact value of \(f(1.01)\).










SolutionSolution 6






Solution 6. The exact value is
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(1.01)
&= (1.01)^2 - 4(1.01) + 7 \\
&= 1.0201 - 4.04 + 7 \\
&= 3.9801
\end{aligned}
\]
a change of \(-0.0199\) from \(f(1) = 4\).










ExrExercise 7 (Check the prediction)






Exercise 7 (Check the prediction) Compare the prediction in Exercise 5 with the exact value of \(f(1.01)\) from Exercise 6.










SolutionSolution 7






Solution 7. The prediction \(3.98\) (Solution 5) and the exact value \(3.9801\) (Solution 6) differ by \(0.0001\), which is \(\varepsilon^2\). The linear approximation drops everything of that order and smaller, so halving the step quarters the error. That trade is the whole bargain of gradient descent, the step-by-step method of fitting models that the optimization page defines. We take a step in the direction the derivative recommends, and the recommendation is trustworthy only as far as the step is small.










DefDefinition 2 (Critical point)






Definition 2 (Critical point) Let \(f\) be a function defined on an open interval containing \(c\). The point \(c\) is a critical point of \(f\) if either \(f'(c) = 0\) or \(f\) is not differentiable at \(c\) (Definition 6 in Derivatives and Taylor Series).










ExmExample 2 (Critical points that are and are not flat points)






Example 2 (Critical points that are and are not flat points)  

\(g(w) = \mathopen{}\left|w\right|\mathclose{}\) has no derivative at \(w = 0\): its one-sided derivatives there are \(1\) and \(-1\) (worked example). So the difference quotient \(\tfrac{\mathopen{}\left|h\right|\mathclose{} - 0}{h}\) has no limit as \(h \to 0\), because the limits from the left and from the right (one-sided limits) differ. So \(0\) is a critical point of \(g\) but not a flat point.

\(f(w) = w^3\) has
\[
\begin{aligned}
f'(0) &= 3 \cdot 0^2 \\
&= 0,
\end{aligned}
\]
so \(0\) is a flat point of \(f\), and hence a critical point.

\(h(w) = w^2\) is differentiable everywhere, with \(h'(w) = 2w\), which is \(0\) only at \(w = 0\). So \(0\) is the only critical point of \(h\). For example, \(h'(1) = 2 \ne 0\), so \(1\) is not one.











LemTheorem 1 (Every flat point is a critical point)






Theorem 1 (Every flat point is a critical point) If \(c\) is a flat point of \(f\) (Definition 1), then \(c\) is a critical point of \(f\) (Definition 2).










ProofProof






Proof. A flat point \(c\) has \(f\) differentiable at \(c\) and \(f'(c) = 0\). The condition “\(f'(c) = 0\)” is the first alternative in Definition 2, so \(c\) is a critical point.










ExmExample 3 (The flat points of a cubic, and a critical point that is not flat)






Example 3 (The flat points of a cubic, and a critical point that is not flat) For \(f(w) = w^3 - 3w\), the derivative is \(f'(w) = 3w^2 - 3\). The code differentiates \(f\) with D() and evaluates \(f'\) at several points. For \(g(w) = \mathopen{}\left|w\right|\mathclose{}\), it computes the difference quotients at \(0\) from both sides.

f_prime <- D(quote(w^3 - 3 * w), "w")
points <- c(-2, -1, 0, 1, 2)
derivs <- data.frame(w = points, f_prime = eval(f_prime, list(w = points)))
derivs


  


flat <- derivs$w[derivs$f_prime == 0]

h <- c(-1e-3, 1e-3)
quotients <- abs(h) / h
quotients
#> [1] -1  1

The derivative is \(0\) at 2 of the 5 points, namely \(w = -1\) and \(w = 1\). These are flat points of \(f\), so by Theorem 1 they are critical points. The difference quotients of \(g\) at \(0\) are -1 from the left and 1 from the right, so \(g\) has no derivative at \(0\). Thus \(0\) is a critical point of \(g\) (Definition 2), but not a flat point.










ExrExercise 8 (Maximizing a gamma-family kernel)






Exercise 8 (Maximizing a gamma-family kernel) Adapted from Miller [2], Question 1.1.10.
Find the maximum value of
\[f(x) = x^4 e^{-x}\]
on the interval \([0, \infty)\).










SolutionSolution 8






Solution 8. Differentiate using the product rule:
\[
\begin{aligned}
f'(x)
&= 4x^3 e^{-x} - x^4 e^{-x} \\
&= x^3 e^{-x}(4 - x)
\end{aligned}
\]
On \([0, \infty)\), \(e^{-x} > 0\), so \(f'(x) = 0\) only at \(x = 0\) and \(x = 4\).
Evaluate \(f\) at the boundary and critical points:

At \(x = 0\): \(f(0) = 0\).

At \(x = 4\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(4) &= 4^4 e^{-4} \\
&= 256 e^{-4} \\
&\approx 4.6888.
\end{aligned}
\]

As \(x \to \infty\): exponential decay dominates polynomial growth, so \(\lim_{x \to \infty} x^4 e^{-x} = 0\).

Since \(f(x) \ge 0\) for all \(x \ge 0\) and \(f(4) > 0\), the global maximum occurs at \(x = 4\), with maximum value \(256/e^4\).










ExrExercise 9 (Classifying critical points with the second derivative test)






Exercise 9 (Classifying critical points with the second derivative test) Adapted from Miller [2], Question 1.1.11.
Find the critical points of
\[f(x) = 4x^3 - 3x^2\]
and decide whether each is a local maximum, a local minimum, or an inflection point.










SolutionSolution 9






Solution 9. Compute the first derivative:
\[
\begin{aligned}
f'(x)
&= 12x^2 - 6x \\
&= 6x(2x - 1)
\end{aligned}
\]
Setting \(f'(x) = 0\) gives critical points at \(x = 0\) and \(x = 1/2\).
Compute the second derivative:
\[f''(x) = 24x - 6\]
Apply the second derivative test at each critical point:

At \(x = 0\): \(f''(0) = -6 < 0\), so \(x = 0\) is a strict local maximum.

At \(x = 1/2\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
f''(1/2) &= 24(1/2) - 6 \\
&= 6 \\
&> 0,
\end{aligned}
\]
so \(x = 1/2\) is a strict local minimum.


Inflection points occur where the second derivative changes sign (\(f''(x) = 0\) at \(x = 1/4\)). Because \(f''\) is non-zero at both critical points, neither is an inflection point.

title: Optimization
text:
2 Optimality conditions in several variables






NoteSource





This section is adapted from the multivariate calculus and optimality-condition parts of Zhou [3], used under the MIT License (see the license text in Linear Algebra). The source states the second-order Taylor approximation and the optimality conditions without proof; here they are proved from the one-variable Taylor theorem, and the approximation is made exact by evaluating the Hessian at a point between \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}} + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{h}}\vphantom{h}}\). The source calls points with zero gradient critical points; here they are stationary points, because Definition 2 gives “critical point” a wider meaning. The source states these results for differentiable functions without saying how smooth; here the first-order results assume continuous first partial derivatives, and the second-order results continuous second partial derivatives. These parts of the source are not part of this section:

its remark that maximizing \(f\) is minimizing \(-f\), and its classification of constraints
its figure of local, strict local and global minima
its one-variable Taylor example and its plots
matrix calculus
convexity
Lagrange multipliers
Newton’s method and gradient descent






A local minimizer of a differentiable function on an open interval is a flat point (Definition 1), and, at a flat point, a positive second derivative guarantees a strict local minimum.
