Let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\in \mathbb{R}^p\), \(t \in [0, 1]\), \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}t \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}+ (1 - t) \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\), and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{g}}\vphantom{g}} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}})\). Applying Equation 1 at the point \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}\), once toward \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) and once toward \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\),
\[
f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) \ge f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}) + {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{g}}\vphantom{g}}}^{\top} (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}),
\qquad
f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}) \ge f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}) + {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{g}}\vphantom{g}}}^{\top} (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}).
\]
Multiplying the first by \(t \ge 0\) and the second by \(1 - t \ge 0\) and adding,
\[
\begin{aligned}
t f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) + (1 - t) f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}})
&\ge t \mathopen{}\left(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}) + {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{g}}\vphantom{g}}}^{\top} (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}})\right)\mathclose{} + (1 - t) \mathopen{}\left(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}) + {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{g}}\vphantom{g}}}^{\top} (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}})\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(multiply by } t, 1 - t \ge 0 \text{ and add)}
\\
&= (t + (1 - t))\,f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}) + t\,{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{g}}\vphantom{g}}}^{\top} (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}) + (1 - t)\,{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{g}}\vphantom{g}}}^{\top} (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}})
&& \text{(distribute } t \text{ and } 1 - t \text{)}
\\
&= f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}) + t\,{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{g}}\vphantom{g}}}^{\top} (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}) + (1 - t)\,{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{g}}\vphantom{g}}}^{\top} (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}})
&& \text{(} t + (1 - t) = 1 \text{)}
\\
&= f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}) + {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{g}}\vphantom{g}}}^{\top} \mathopen{}\left(t (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}) + (1 - t) (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}})\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(factor out } {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{g}}\vphantom{g}}}^{\top} \text{; matrix products distribute)}
\\
&= f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}) + {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{g}}\vphantom{g}}}^{\top} \mathopen{}\left(t \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}+ (1 - t) \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(collect terms)}
\\
&= f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}).
&& \text{(definition of } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}} \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
That inequality is the defining inequality of a convex function. If Equation 1 is strict for distinct points, and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\ne \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\) and \(t \in (0, 1)\), then:


\(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}\) differs from both \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\), since \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}} = (1 - t)(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}) \ne \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}} = t (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) \ne \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\);
so both inequalities at \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}}\) are strict;
both multipliers \(t\) and \(1 - t\) are positive, so the first step of the display is strict, and \(f\) is strictly convex.











ExmExample 26 (Tangent lines under a parabola)






Example 26 (Tangent lines under a parabola) For \(f(x) = x^2\), the right side of Equation 1 is \(y^2 + 2y (x - y) = 2xy - y^2\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(x) - (2xy - y^2)
&= x^2 - 2xy + y^2 \\
&= (x - y)^2 \\
&\ge 0,
\end{aligned}
\]
with equality only at \(x = y\), confirming that \(x^2\) is strictly convex. For \(g(x) = -x^2\) the inequality fails: at \(y = 0\) the tangent line is \(s = 0\), and \(g(1) = -1 < 0\).










LemTheorem 11 (Second-derivative test for convexity)






Theorem 11 (Second-derivative test for convexity) Let \(f : \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}\) have first and second partial derivatives that are continuous on \(\mathbb{R}^p\) (continuity).

If \(\mathbf{H}_f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\) is positive semidefinite for every \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\), then \(f\) is convex.
If \(\mathbf{H}_f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\) is positive definite for every \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\), then \(f\) is strictly convex (Definition 9).











ProofProof






Proof. Let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\in \mathbb{R}^p\). By Theorem 5 with \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{z}}\vphantom{z}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{h}}\vphantom{h}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\), there is a \(\tau\in (0, 1)\) such that, with \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}+ \tau(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}})\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})
&= f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}) + {\mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}})\right)\mathclose{}}^{\top} (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}) + \frac{1}{2}\,{(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}})}^{\top}\,\mathbf{H}_f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}})\,(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}})
&& \text{(}\href{#thm-taylor-mv}{\text{Theorem~5}}\text{)}
\\
&\ge f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}) + {\mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}})\right)\mathclose{}}^{\top} (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}).
&& \text{(} \mathbf{H}_f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{w}}\vphantom{w}}) \text{ is positive semidefinite)}
\end{aligned}
\]
This inequality is Equation 1, so \(f\) is convex by Theorem 10. Under the hypothesis of part 2 and with \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\ne \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\), the quadratic-form term is positive, so the inequality is strict, and \(f\) is strictly convex by the last sentence of Theorem 10.










ExmExample 27 (Using the Hessian to show convexity)






Example 27 (Using the Hessian to show convexity)  

For a symmetric positive semidefinite \(\mathbf{A}\), \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top} \mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) has Hessian \(2 \mathbf{A}\) (Hessian of a quadratic form), which is positive semidefinite because \({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{h}}\vphantom{h}}}^{\top} (2 \mathbf{A}) \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{h}}\vphantom{h}} = 2\,{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{h}}\vphantom{h}}}^{\top} \mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{h}}\vphantom{h}} \ge 0\); so \(f\) is convex.
\(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = x_1^2 + x_2^2 - 2 x_1\) has Hessian \(2 \mathbf{I}_2\) (Example 13), which is positive definite, so \(f\) is strictly convex.

\(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = e^{2x_1 + x_2} - x_1\) has Hessian \(e^{u} \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) with \(u = 2x_1 + x_2\) (Example), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{h}}\vphantom{h}}}^{\top}\,\mathbf{H}_f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{h}}\vphantom{h}}
&= e^{u} (4 h_1^2 + 4 h_1 h_2 + h_2^2) \\
&= e^{u} (2 h_1 + h_2)^2 \\
&\ge 0,
\end{aligned}
\]
so \(f\) is convex. The Hessian is not positive definite (\(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{h}}\vphantom{h}} = {(1, -2)}^{\top}\) gives \(0\)), so part 2 does not apply, and in fact \(f\) is not strictly convex: along \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= t\,{(1, -2)}^{\top}\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
u &= 2t - 2t \\
&= 0
\end{aligned}
\]
and \(f = 1 - t\) is linear in \(t\), so the convexity inequality holds with equality there.












ExmExample 28 (Strictly convex with a singular Hessian)






Example 28 (Strictly convex with a singular Hessian) Part 2 is sufficient but not necessary. \(f(x) = x^4\) has
\[
\begin{aligned}
f''(0) &= 12 \cdot 0^2 \\
&= 0,
\end{aligned}
\]
so \(\mathbf{H}_f(0) = [0]\) is singular and not positive definite. Yet \(f\) is strictly convex, by the strict form of Equation 1: for \(x \ne y\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^4 - y^4 - 4 y^3 (x - y)
&= (x - y)(x^3 + x^2 y + x y^2 + y^3) - 4 y^3 (x - y)
&& \text{(factor } x^4 - y^4 \text{)}
\\
&= (x - y)(x^3 + x^2 y + x y^2 - 3 y^3)
&& \text{(collect the } y^3 \text{ terms)}
\\
&= (x - y)^2 (x^2 + 2 x y + 3 y^2)
&& \text{(} (x - y)(x^2 + 2 x y + 3 y^2) = x^3 + x^2 y + x y^2 - 3 y^3 \text{)}
\\
&= (x - y)^2 \mathopen{}\left((x + y)^2 + 2 y^2\right)\mathclose{},
&& \text{(complete the square)}
\end{aligned}
\]
which is positive: \((x - y)^2 > 0\), and \((x + y)^2 + 2 y^2 = 0\) would need \(y = 0\) and then
\[
\begin{aligned}
x &= 0 \\
&= y.
\end{aligned}
\]










CorCorollary 1 (Stationary points of a convex function are global minimizers)






Corollary 1 (Stationary points of a convex function are global minimizers) If \(f\) is as in Theorem 10 and convex, then every stationary point \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^*\) of \(f\) (Definition 3) is a global minimizer.










ProofProof






Proof. For every \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})
&\ge f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^*) + {\mathopen{}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^*)\right)\mathclose{}}^{\top} (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^*)
&& \text{(}\href{#eq-supporting-hyperplane}{\text{Equation~1}}\text{ with } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^* \text{)}
\\
&= f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^*) + {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}}^{\top} (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^*)
&& \text{(} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^* \text{ is stationary)}
\\
&= f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^*).
&& \text{(} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{v}}\vphantom{v}} = 0 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExmExample 29 (A convex function, and a non-convex one)






Example 29 (A convex function, and a non-convex one)  


\(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = x_1^2 + x_2^2 - 2 x_1\) is convex by Theorem 11, since its Hessian is \(2 \mathbf{I}_2\) (Example 13), so its stationary point \({(1, 0)}^{\top}\) (Example 5) is a global minimizer, as completing the square showed in Example 6.
Without convexity, a stationary point need not be a minimizer at all: \(x_1^2 - x_2^2\) has the stationary point \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\), which is not a minimizer (Example 6).
The corollary says nothing about whether a minimizer exists: \(e^{2x_1 + x_2} - x_1\) is convex (Example 27) but has no stationary point, and so no local minimizer (Example 6).

title: Optimization

text:
4 Minimizing a quadratic under linear constraints






NoteSource





This section is adapted from the Lagrange-multiplier part of Zhou [3], used under the MIT License (see the license text in Linear Algebra). The source solves the stationarity equations of the Lagrangian and reports the solution; here the solution is also proved to be the unique minimizer, directly from the positive definiteness of the matrices involved. The source assumes only that \(\mathbf{S}\) is positive definite; the added hypothesis that the columns of \(\mathbf{A}\) are linearly independent makes \({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{S}^{-1} \mathbf{A}\) invertible. The source’s example with general coefficients \(a_1, a_2, b\) is specialized here to \(3, 4, 5\). These parts of the source are not part of this section:

the Lagrange multiplier method for constraints that are not linear, or objectives that are not quadratic, including its multinomial maximum likelihood example
the eigenvalues of the block matrix of the stationarity equations, and the convexity of the Lagrangian in \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) and its concavity in the multipliers
its homework examples










DefDefinition 14 (Feasible set)






Definition 14 (Feasible set) In a problem that looks for a best point among some allowed points of \(\mathbb{R}^p\), the set \(F \subseteq \mathbb{R}^p\) of allowed points is the feasible set, [11] and its points are feasible.










DefDefinition 15 (Constraints)






Definition 15 (Constraints) When the feasible set \(F\) (Definition 14) is the set of points that satisfy some equations or inequalities, those equations or inequalities are the constraints.










ExmExample 30 (A line as a feasible set)






Example 30 (A line as a feasible set) With the single constraint \(3 x_1 + 4 x_2 = 5\), the feasible set is the line \(\mathopen{}\left\{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\in \mathbb{R}^2 : 3 x_1 + 4 x_2 = 5\right\}\mathclose{}\). \({(1, 0.5)}^{\top}\) is feasible, since
\[
\begin{aligned}
3 \cdot 1 + 4 \cdot 0.5 &= 3 + 2 \\
&= 5;
\end{aligned}
\]
\(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\) is not feasible, since \(3 \cdot 0 + 4 \cdot 0 = 0 \ne 5\).










DefDefinition 16 (Objective function, objective)






Definition 16 (Objective function, objective) Let \(f : \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}\) and let \(F \subseteq \mathbb{R}^p\) be a feasible set (Definition 14). In the problem of minimizing \(f\) over \(F\), \(f\) is the objective function (or objective).










DefDefinition 17 (Minimizer over a feasible set)






Definition 17 (Minimizer over a feasible set) With \(f\) and \(F\) as in Definition 16, a minimizer of \(f\) over \(F\) is a feasible \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^*\) with \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^*) \le f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\) for every feasible \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\): a global minimizer of \(f\) with its domain restricted to \(F\).










DefDefinition 18 (Minimization problem)






Definition 18 (Minimization problem) With \(f\) and \(F\) as in Definition 16, the minimization problem [12] is to find a minimizer of \(f\) over \(F\) (Definition 17). When \(F\) is given by constraints (Definition 15), the problem is to minimize \(f\) subject to them.










ExmExample 31 (Minimizing over a line)






Example 31 (Minimizing over a line) In the problem of minimizing \(x_1^2 + x_2^2\) subject to \(3 x_1 + 4 x_2 = 5\), the objective function is \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = x_1^2 + x_2^2\), and the feasible set is the line of Example 30. The feasible point \({(1, 0.5)}^{\top}\) has
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(1, 0.5) &= 1 + 0.25 \\
&= 1.25.
\end{aligned}
\]
\(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\) minimizes \(f\) over all of \(\mathbb{R}^2\), with \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}) = 0\), but it is not a minimizer over the feasible set, because it is not feasible.










DefDefinition 19 (Optimization algorithm)






Definition 19 (Optimization algorithm) Let:


\(f : \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}\): an objective function;

\(F \subseteq \mathbb{R}^p\): a feasible set.

An optimization algorithm [12] is a step-by-step procedure that maps the pair \((f, F)\) to a feasible point \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^\dagger\):
\[
(f, F) \mapsto \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^\dagger \in F.
\tag{2}\]
In words: given \((f, F)\), the procedure returns a feasible point \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^\dagger\) intended to make \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^\dagger)\) small.










ExmExample 32 (Exhaustive search over a finite feasible set)






Example 32 (Exhaustive search over a finite feasible set) Let \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = x_1^2 + x_2^2\), with the feasible set the three points \(\mathopen{}\left\{{(1, 0.5)}^{\top}, {(3, -1)}^{\top}, {(-1, 2)}^{\top}\right\}\mathclose{}\) of the line of Example 30. The procedure “evaluate \(f\) at every feasible point; return the point with the smallest value” is an optimization algorithm. Computing \(f\) at each point gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(1, 0.5) &= 1 + 0.25 = 1.25, \\
f(3, -1) &= 9 + 1 = 10, \\
f(-1, 2) &= 1 + 4 = 5,
\end{aligned}
\]
so it returns \({(1, 0.5)}^{\top}\), a minimizer of \(f\) over this feasible set.




Here the objective (Definition 16) is a quadratic \(\tfrac{1}{2}\,{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) with \(\mathbf{S}\) positive definite, and the constraints (Definition 15) are \(m\) linear equations \({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\), where \(\mathbf{A}\) is a \(p \times m\) matrix and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}} \in \mathbb{R}^m\). The only stationary point of the objective alone (Definition 3) is \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_{p \times 1}\) (its gradient is \(\mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\), and \(\mathbf{S}\) is invertible), which may not satisfy the constraints. A Lagrange multiplier adds one unknown per constraint, and the minimizer over the feasible set (Definition 14) is then found among the stationary points of a new function of the extended set of unknowns.






DefDefinition 20 (Lagrangian)






Definition 20 (Lagrangian) For the problem of minimizing \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\) over \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\in \mathbb{R}^p\) subject to \({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\), with \(\mathbf{A}\) a \(p \times m\) matrix and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}} \in \mathbb{R}^m\), the Lagrangian [13] is the function of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\in \mathbb{R}^p\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}}\in \mathbb{R}^m\)
\[
L(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}}) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) + {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}}}^{\top} \mathopen{}\left({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\right)\mathclose{}.
\]










DefDefinition 21 (Lagrange multipliers)






Definition 21 (Lagrange multipliers) In the Lagrangian \(L(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}})\) (Definition 20), the entries of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}}\) are the Lagrange multipliers [13], one per constraint.










ExmExample 33 (The gradients of the Lagrangian of a quadratic)






Example 33 (The gradients of the Lagrangian of a quadratic) Let \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = \tfrac{1}{2}\,{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) with \(\mathbf{S}\) symmetric and constant. By the transpose of a product, \({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}}}^{\top} {\mathbf{A}}^{\top} = {(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}})}^{\top}\), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
L(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}})
&= \tfrac{1}{2}\,{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} + {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}}}^{\top} {\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}
&& \text{(distribute)}
\\
&= \tfrac{1}{2}\,{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} + {(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}})}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}},
&& \text{(transpose of a product)}
\end{aligned}
\]
and, since \({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}}}^{\top} \mathopen{}\left({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\right)\mathclose{}\) is \(1 \times 1\) and so equals its transpose,
\[
L(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}}) = \tfrac{1}{2}\,{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} + {\mathopen{}\left({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\right)\mathclose{}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}}.
\]
The partial derivatives of a sum are the sums of the partial derivatives, entry by entry. Using the first of these forms, derivative of a quadratic form for the first term, derivative of a linear combination for the second (\(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}}\) is constant in \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\)), and constant with respect to a vector for the third,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} L(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}})
&= \tfrac{1}{2}\,\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} \mathopen{}\left({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\right)\mathclose{} + \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} \mathopen{}\left({(\mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}})}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\right)\mathclose{} - \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} \mathopen{}\left({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(sum and constant multiple)}
\\
&= \tfrac{1}{2} \mathopen{}\left(2 \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\right)\mathclose{} + \mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_{p \times 1}
&& \text{(the three derivatives)}
\\
&= \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}+ \mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}}.
&& \text{(simplify)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Using the second form, in which \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\) and \({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\) are constant in \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}}\), and derivative of a linear combination again,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}}} L(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}})
&= \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}}} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) + \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}}} \mathopen{}\left({\mathopen{}\left({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\right)\mathclose{}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}}\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(sum)}
\\
&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_{m \times 1} + \mathopen{}\left({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(the two derivatives)}
\\
&= {\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}.
&& \text{(simplify)}
\end{aligned}
\]
So \((\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}})\) makes the gradients equal \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_{p \times 1}\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_{m \times 1}\) exactly when
\[
\mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}+ \mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_{p \times 1}
\quad \text{and} \quad
{\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}},
\qquad\text{that is,}\qquad
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{S} & \mathbf{A} \\ {\mathbf{A}}^{\top} & \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_{m \times m} \end{bmatrix}}_{(p + m) \times (p + m)}
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\\ \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}}\end{bmatrix}}_{(p + m) \times 1}
= \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_{p \times 1} \\ \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}} \end{bmatrix}}_{(p + m) \times 1},
\tag{3}\]
the second equation being the constraint itself.










LemTheorem 12 (Minimizing a positive definite quadratic under linear constraints)






Theorem 12 (Minimizing a positive definite quadratic under linear constraints) Let \(\mathbf{S}\) be a \(p \times p\) positive definite matrix, \(\mathbf{A}\) a \(p \times m\) matrix with linearly independent columns, and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}} \in \mathbb{R}^m\). Then the \(m \times m\) matrix \(\mathbf{M} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{S}^{-1} \mathbf{A}\) is invertible, and \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = \tfrac{1}{2}\,{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) has exactly one minimizer over the \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\in \mathbb{R}^p\) with \({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\), namely
\[
\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^* = \mathbf{S}^{-1} \mathbf{A} \mathbf{M}^{-1} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}.
\]
With \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}}^* \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}-\mathbf{M}^{-1} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\), the pair \((\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^*, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}}^*)\) solves Equation 3, and the minimum value is \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^*) = \tfrac{1}{2}\,{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}}^{\top} \mathbf{M}^{-1} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\).










ProofProof






Proof. The steps marked “transpose of a product” use the transpose of a product, and \(\mathbf{S}\) is symmetric because it is positive definite.
\(\mathbf{M}\) is invertible. \(\mathbf{S}^{-1}\) exists and is positive definite (positive definite inverse), so \(\mathbf{M} = {\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{S}^{-1} \mathbf{A}\) is positive definite (operations that preserve definiteness, part 1), and so invertible (positive definite inverse again). \(\mathbf{S}^{-1}\) and \(\mathbf{M}^{-1}\) are symmetric (inverse of a symmetric matrix), because \(\mathbf{S}\) and \(\mathbf{M}\) are.
\(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^*\) satisfies the constraint, and the pair solves Equation 3.
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^*
&= {\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{S}^{-1} \mathbf{A} \mathbf{M}^{-1} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}
&& \text{(substitute } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^* \text{)}
\\
&= \mathbf{M} \mathbf{M}^{-1} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}
&& \text{(definition of } \mathbf{M} \text{)}
\\
&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}},
&& \text{(} \mathbf{M} \mathbf{M}^{-1} = \mathbf{I}_m \text{)}
\\
\mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^* + \mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}}^*
&= \mathbf{S} \mathbf{S}^{-1} \mathbf{A} \mathbf{M}^{-1} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}} - \mathbf{A} \mathbf{M}^{-1} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}
&& \text{(substitute } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^* \text{ and } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}}^* \text{)}
\\
&= \mathbf{A} \mathbf{M}^{-1} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}} - \mathbf{A} \mathbf{M}^{-1} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}
&& \text{(} \mathbf{S} \mathbf{S}^{-1} = \mathbf{I}_p \text{)}
\\
&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_{p \times 1}.
&& \text{(subtract)}
\end{aligned}
\]
\(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^*\) is the unique minimizer. Let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) satisfy \({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\), and let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^*\), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}} &= {\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- {\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^* \\
&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}} - \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}} \\
&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_{m \times 1}
\end{aligned}
\]
(matrix products distribute; both points satisfy the constraint). First, the cross term vanishes:
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^*
&= {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathbf{S}^{-1} \mathbf{A} \mathbf{M}^{-1} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}
&& \text{(substitute } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^* \text{)}
\\
&= {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}}}^{\top} \mathbf{A} \mathbf{M}^{-1} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}
&& \text{(} \mathbf{S} \mathbf{S}^{-1} = \mathbf{I}_p \text{)}
\\
&= {({\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}})}^{\top} \mathbf{M}^{-1} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}
&& \text{(transpose of a product; } {({\mathbf{A}}^{\top})}^{\top} = \mathbf{A} \text{)}
\\
&= {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_{m \times 1}}^{\top} \mathbf{M}^{-1} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}
&& \text{(} {\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_{m \times 1} \text{)}
\\
&= 0.
&& \text{(a product with a zero factor is zero)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})
&= \tfrac{1}{2}\,{(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^* + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}})}^{\top} \mathbf{S} (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^* + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}})
&& \text{(} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^* + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}} \text{)}
\\
&= \tfrac{1}{2} \mathopen{}\left({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^*{}}^{\top} + {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}}}^{\top}\right)\mathclose{} \mathbf{S} (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^* + \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}})
&& \text{(the transpose of a sum is the sum of the transposes)}
\\
&= \tfrac{1}{2} \mathopen{}\left({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^*{}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^* + {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^*{}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}} + {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^* + {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}}\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(distribute)}
\\
&= \tfrac{1}{2} \mathopen{}\left({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^*{}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^* + {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}}}^{\top} {\mathbf{S}}^{\top} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^* + {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^* + {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}}\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(} 1 \times 1 \text{: } {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^*{}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}} = {({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^*{}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}})}^{\top} \text{; transpose of a product)}
\\
&= \tfrac{1}{2} \mathopen{}\left({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^*{}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^* + 2\,{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^* + {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}}\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(} {\mathbf{S}}^{\top} = \mathbf{S} \text{; combine)}
\\
&= \tfrac{1}{2}\,{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^*{}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^* + {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^* + \tfrac{1}{2}\,{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}}
&& \text{(distribute } \tfrac{1}{2} \text{)}
\\
&= f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^*) + \tfrac{1}{2}\,{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}}}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}}
&& \text{(the cross term is } 0 \text{)}
\\
&\ge f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^*),
&& \text{(} \mathbf{S} \text{ is positive definite)}
\end{aligned}
\]
with equality only when \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_{p \times 1}\), that is, \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^*\).
The minimum value.
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^*)
&= \tfrac{1}{2}\,{(\mathbf{S}^{-1} \mathbf{A} \mathbf{M}^{-1} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}})}^{\top} \mathbf{S} \mathbf{S}^{-1} \mathbf{A} \mathbf{M}^{-1} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}
&& \text{(substitute } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^* \text{)}
\\
&= \tfrac{1}{2}\,{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}}^{\top}\,{(\mathbf{M}^{-1})}^{\top}\,{\mathbf{A}}^{\top}\,{(\mathbf{S}^{-1})}^{\top}\,\mathbf{S} \mathbf{S}^{-1} \mathbf{A} \mathbf{M}^{-1} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}
&& \text{(transpose of a product, applied repeatedly)}
\\
&= \tfrac{1}{2}\,{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}}^{\top} \mathbf{M}^{-1} {\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{S}^{-1} \mathbf{S} \mathbf{S}^{-1} \mathbf{A} \mathbf{M}^{-1} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}
&& \text{(} \mathbf{S}^{-1} \text{ and } \mathbf{M}^{-1} \text{ are symmetric)}
\\
&= \tfrac{1}{2}\,{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}}^{\top} \mathbf{M}^{-1} {\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{S}^{-1} \mathbf{A} \mathbf{M}^{-1} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}
&& \text{(} \mathbf{S}^{-1} \mathbf{S} = \mathbf{I}_p \text{)}
\\
&= \tfrac{1}{2}\,{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}}^{\top} \mathbf{M}^{-1} \mathbf{M} \mathbf{M}^{-1} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}
&& \text{(definition of } \mathbf{M} \text{)}
\\
&= \tfrac{1}{2}\,{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}}^{\top} \mathbf{M}^{-1} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}.
&& \text{(} \mathbf{M}^{-1} \mathbf{M} = \mathbf{I}_m \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExmExample 34 (The closest point on a line to the origin)






Example 34 (The closest point on a line to the origin) Minimize \(x_1^2 + x_2^2\) subject to \(3 x_1 + 4 x_2 = 5\). In the form of Theorem 12, \(x_1^2 + x_2^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}\,{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top} (2 \mathbf{I}_2) \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\), so \(\mathbf{S} = 2 \mathbf{I}_2\), \(\mathbf{A} = {(3, 4)}^{\top}\) (\(p = 2\), \(m = 1\)) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}} = [5]\). The hypotheses hold: \(2 \mathbf{I}_2\) is positive definite, and the single column \({(3, 4)}^{\top}\) is nonzero, so it is linearly independent. Also \(\mathbf{S}^{-1} = \tfrac{1}{2} \mathbf{I}_2\). Then, from the formulas of Theorem 12,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{M}
&= {\mathbf{A}}^{\top}\,\tfrac{1}{2} \mathbf{I}_2\,\mathbf{A} \\
&= \tfrac{1}{2}\,(3^2 + 4^2) \\
&= \tfrac{25}{2},
\\
\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^*
&= \tfrac{1}{2} \mathbf{I}_2 \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} \mathopen{}\left(\tfrac{2}{25}\right)\mathclose{} (5) \\
&= \tfrac{5}{25} \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} \\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 0.6 \\ 0.8 \end{bmatrix},
\\
\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}}^*
&= -\mathopen{}\left(\tfrac{2}{25}\right)\mathclose{} (5) \\
&= -0.4,
\\
f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^*)
&= \tfrac{1}{2} (5) \mathopen{}\left(\tfrac{2}{25}\right)\mathclose{} (5) \\
&= 1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Checks:


the constraint:
\[
\begin{aligned}
3 (0.6) + 4 (0.8) &= 1.8 + 3.2 \\
&= 5;
\end{aligned}
\]


the first block of Equation 3:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{S} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^* + \mathbf{A} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}}^* &= {(1.2, 1.6)}^{\top} + {(3, 4)}^{\top} (-0.4) \\
&= {(1.2, 1.6)}^{\top} - {(1.2, 1.6)}^{\top} \\
&= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_{2 \times 1};
\end{aligned}
\]


the value:
\[
\begin{aligned}
0.6^2 + 0.8^2 &= 0.36 + 0.64 \\
&= 1.
\end{aligned}
\]


Geometrically, \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^*\) is the point of the line nearest the origin, at distance \(1\).










ExmExample 35 (The hypotheses are needed)






Example 35 (The hypotheses are needed)  

If \(\mathbf{S}\) is not positive definite there may be no minimizer: with \(\mathbf{S} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\) and the constraint \(x_1 = 1\) (\(\mathbf{A} = {(1, 0)}^{\top}\), \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}} = [1]\)), \(f(1, x_2) = \tfrac{1}{2} (1 - x_2^2)\) decreases without bound as \(x_2\) grows.

If the columns of \(\mathbf{A}\) are dependent, \(\mathbf{M}\) is not invertible: with \(\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{I}_2\) and \(\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{M} &= {\mathbf{A}}^{\top} \mathbf{A} \\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{bmatrix},
\end{aligned}
\]
whose columns are equal. So \(\mathbf{M} {(1, -1)}^{\top} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}_{2 \times 1}\), and \(\mathbf{M}\) is not invertible (a square matrix is invertible exactly when its null space is zero). The two constraints both read \(x_1 + x_2 = b_i\), so they have no solution at all when \(b_1 \ne b_2\). When \(b_1 = b_2\) a unique minimizer still exists,
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_1 &= x_2 \\
&= b_1 / 2,
\end{aligned}
\]
but the formula of Theorem 12 cannot produce it.












DefDefinition 22 (Sensitivity)






Definition 22 (Sensitivity) Suppose a minimization problem (Definition 18) depends on a vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}} \in \mathbb{R}^m\), and let \(f^*(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}})\) be its minimum value, as a function of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\). When the gradient \(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}} f^*(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}})\) exists (gradient), it is the sensitivity of the minimum value to \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\): by partial derivative, its entry \(i\) is the limit, as a change in \(b_i\) alone shrinks to \(0\), of the resulting change in the minimum value divided by the change in \(b_i\).










ExmExample 36 (The sensitivity of a one-point problem)






Example 36 (The sensitivity of a one-point problem) Minimize \(x^2\) subject to \(x = b\), for a number \(b\). The feasible set (Definition 14) is \(\mathopen{}\left\{b\right\}\mathclose{}\), so the minimum value is \(f^*(b) = b^2\), and its sensitivity to \(b\) is \(\frac{d }{d b} f^*(b) = 2b\). At \(b = 3\) the sensitivity is \(6\): moving \(b\) from \(3\) to \(3.1\) raises the minimum value from \(9\) to \(9.61\), an increase of \(0.61\), close to \(6 \times 0.1 = 0.6\).










CorCorollary 2 (The multiplier is the sensitivity of the minimum value)






Corollary 2 (The multiplier is the sensitivity of the minimum value) In Theorem 12, write the minimum value as a function of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\), \(f^*(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}) = \tfrac{1}{2}\,{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}}^{\top} \mathbf{M}^{-1} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\). Its sensitivity to \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\) (Definition 22) is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}} f^*(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}})
&= \mathbf{M}^{-1} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}} \\
&= -\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}}^*.
\end{aligned}
\]










ProofProof






Proof. \(\mathbf{M}^{-1}\) is symmetric and does not depend on \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\), so derivative of a quadratic form applies with \(\mathbf{M}^{-1}\) in place of \(\mathbf{S}\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}} f^*(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}})
&= \tfrac{1}{2}\,\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}} \mathopen{}\left({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}}^{\top} \mathbf{M}^{-1} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(constant multiple)}
\\
&= \tfrac{1}{2} \mathopen{}\left(2 \mathbf{M}^{-1} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(derivative of a quadratic form)}
\\
&= \mathbf{M}^{-1} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}
&& \text{(simplify)}
\\
&= -\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}}^*.
&& \text{(definition of } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\lambda}}\vphantom{\lambda}}^* \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExmExample 37 (Moving the line)






Example 37 (Moving the line) In Example 34 with a general right side \(b\) in place of \(5\), \(\mathbf{M}^{-1} = \tfrac{2}{25}\) and
\[
\begin{aligned}
f^*(b) &= \tfrac{1}{2} \mathopen{}\left(\tfrac{2}{25}\right)\mathclose{}\,b^2 \\
&= \tfrac{b^2}{25},
\end{aligned}
\]
so \(\frac{d }{d b} f^*(b) = \tfrac{2b}{25}\). At \(b = 5\) this derivative is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\tfrac{10}{25} &= 0.4 \\
&= -\lambda^*:
\end{aligned}
\]
moving the line \(3 x_1 + 4 x_2 = b\) outward by a small step \(\varepsilon\) in \(b\) raises the minimum value by about \(0.4\,\varepsilon\).
