From the source, this section takes the order of ideas: the cost of Newton’s method, the secant condition, and the BFGS and limited-memory BFGS updates. The source states the updates as solutions of nearest-matrix problems without proof; here the BFGS update is written out. The Davidon-Fletcher-Powell and rank-1 updates, the nearest-matrix derivation, the history, and the Julia code are not part of this section.









DefDefinition 41 (Secant condition)






Definition 41 (Secant condition) Let \(f : \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}\) have first partial derivatives, and let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^+ \in \mathbb{R}^p\). Write \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{s}}\vphantom{s}} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^+ - \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) for the step and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^+) - \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\) for the change in the gradient. A symmetric matrix \(\mathbf{B}\) satisfies the secant condition [23, Ch. 6] for \((\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{s}}\vphantom{s}}, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}})\) when
\[
\mathbf{B} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{s}}\vphantom{s}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}.
\]










ExmExample 57 (The Hessian of a quadratic function satisfies the secant condition)






Example 57 (The Hessian of a quadratic function satisfies the secant condition) Let \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = \tfrac{1}{2} {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top} \mathbf{Q} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} - \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) with \(\mathbf{Q}\) symmetric. Then \(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = \mathbf{Q} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}\), so for any \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^+\)
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}
&= (\mathbf{Q} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^+ - \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}}) - (\mathbf{Q} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}})
&& \text{(gradient at each point)}
\\
&= \mathbf{Q} (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^+ - \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})
&& \text{(collect terms)}
\\
&= \mathbf{Q} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{s}}\vphantom{s}}.
&& \text{(definition of } \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{s}}\vphantom{s}} \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
So the Hessian \(\mathbf{Q}\) of the quadratic function satisfies the secant condition for every step. For a general \(f\), \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\approx \mathbf{H}_f \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{s}}\vphantom{s}}\) holds for a short step, with \(\mathbf{H}_f\) the Hessian of \(f\) near the step, which is why a matrix that satisfies the secant condition is a reasonable stand-in for the Hessian.










DefDefinition 42 (Quasi-Newton method)






Definition 42 (Quasi-Newton method) Let \(f : \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}\) have first partial derivatives, let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^{(0)}\) be a starting point, and let \(\mathbf{H}^{(0)}\) be a positive definite matrix. A quasi-Newton method [23, Ch. 6] produces, for \(t = 0, 1, 2, \ldots\),
\[
\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^{(t+1)} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^{(t)} - \alpha^{(t)} \mathbf{H}^{(t)} \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^{(t)}),
\]
where \(\alpha^{(t)} > 0\) is a step length chosen by a line search, and \(\mathbf{H}^{(t+1)}\) is a symmetric positive definite matrix whose inverse satisfies the secant condition, that is, \(\mathbf{H}^{(t+1)} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}^{(t)} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{s}}\vphantom{s}}^{(t)}\), with \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{s}}\vphantom{s}}^{(t)} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^{(t+1)} - \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^{(t)}\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}^{(t)} = \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^{(t+1)}) - \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^{(t)})\).










ExmExample 58 (One quasi-Newton step on a quadratic function)






Example 58 (One quasi-Newton step on a quadratic function) Take \(f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = \tfrac{1}{2} {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}}^{\top} \mathbf{Q} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}} - \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\) with \(\mathbf{Q} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{b}}\vphantom{b}} = {(1, 2)}^{\top}\) (Example 57), \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^{(0)} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\) and \(\mathbf{H}^{(0)} = \mathbf{I}_2\). For a quadratic function, the step length that minimizes \(f\) along a direction \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}}\) is \(\alpha = -\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}} / {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}}}^{\top} \mathbf{Q} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{d}}\vphantom{d}}\).

Q <- matrix(c(4, 1, 1, 3), nrow = 2)
b <- c(1, 2)
f <- function(x) 0.5 * sum(x * (Q %*% x)) - sum(b * x)
grad <- function(x) drop(Q %*% x - b)
x0 <- c(0, 0)
H0 <- diag(2)
d <- -drop(H0 %*% grad(x0))
step <- -sum(grad(x0) * d) / drop(t(d) %*% Q %*% d)
x1 <- x0 + step * d
s <- x1 - x0
y <- grad(x1) - grad(x0)

The step length is 0.25, which moves the iterate to \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^{(1)} = (0.25, 0.5)\) and lowers \(f\) from 0 to -0.625. The difference of the gradients, \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}^{(0)} = (1.5, 1.75)\), is \(\mathbf{Q} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{s}}\vphantom{s}}^{(0)}\) (the secant condition for a quadratic function).










RemarkRemark 5 (Why a quasi-Newton method is used)






Remark 5 (Why a quasi-Newton method is used). Because \(\mathbf{H}^{(t)}\) is positive definite, \(-\mathbf{H}^{(t)} \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^{(t)})\) is a descent direction, so, when the gradient is not \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\), a line search finds a step that decreases \(f\). Newton’s method needs the Hessian and the solution of a system of equations at every iteration, which costs about \(p^3\) operations for a dense \(p \times p\) Hessian, and requires the formulas for its entries. A quasi-Newton method needs only the gradient and an update of \(\mathbf{H}^{(t)}\) costing about \(p^2\) operations. Near a minimizer the method speeds up superlinearly: faster than gradient descent, slower than Newton’s method [23, Ch. 6]. Replacing \(\mathbf{H}^{(t)}\) by \(\mathbf{I}_p\) in the step formula gives gradient descent.










DefDefinition 43 (BFGS update (Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno))






Definition 43 (BFGS update (Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno)) Let \(\mathbf{H}\), an approximation of the inverse Hessian, be a \(p \times p\) positive definite matrix, and let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{s}}\vphantom{s}}, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}\in \mathbb{R}^p\) satisfy \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{s}}\vphantom{s}} > 0\). With \(\rho \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}1 / \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{s}}\vphantom{s}}\), the BFGS update [23, Ch. 6] of \(\mathbf{H}\) is
\[
\mathbf{H}^+
\stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\mathopen{}\left(\mathbf{I}_p - \rho \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{s}}\vphantom{s}} {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}}^{\top}\right)\mathclose{}
\mathbf{H}
\mathopen{}\left(\mathbf{I}_p - \rho \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}} {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{s}}\vphantom{s}}}^{\top}\right)\mathclose{}
+ \rho \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{s}}\vphantom{s}} {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{s}}\vphantom{s}}}^{\top}.
\]










ExmExample 59 (A BFGS update from the quasi-Newton step)






Example 59 (A BFGS update from the quasi-Newton step) Continue Example 58 with \(\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{I}_2\), \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{s}}\vphantom{s}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{s}}\vphantom{s}}^{(0)}\), and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}^{(0)}\).

rho <- 1 / sum(y * s)
left <- diag(2) - rho * s %*% t(y)
H1 <- left %*% H0 %*% t(left) + rho * s %*% t(s)
H1
#>         [,1]   [,2]
#> [1,]  0.6625 -0.425
#> [2,] -0.4250  0.650
drop(H1 %*% y)
#> [1] 0.25 0.50

Here \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{s}}\vphantom{s}} = 1.25 > 0\), so \(\rho = 0.8\). The updated matrix satisfies \(\mathbf{H}^+ \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}= (0.25, 0.5)\), which is \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{s}}\vphantom{s}} = (0.25, 0.5)\), and its smallest eigenvalue is 0.231204, so \(\mathbf{H}^+\) is positive definite.










RemarkRemark 6 (The curvature condition \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{s}}\vphantom{s}} > 0\))






Remark 6 (The curvature condition \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{s}}\vphantom{s}} > 0\)). If the strict inequality of Theorem 10 holds for distinct points, then \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{s}}\vphantom{s}} > 0\) for \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{s}}\vphantom{s}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^+ - \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}\ne \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}= \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^+) - \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\). Add the versions at \((\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^+, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})\) and at \((\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^+)\):
\[
f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^+) + f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})
> f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) + f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^+)
+ \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{s}}\vphantom{s}}
- \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^+) \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{s}}\vphantom{s}},
\]
so \(0 > -\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{s}}\vphantom{s}}\). For a general \(f\), a line search that enforces a curvature condition on the step length (the Wolfe conditions [23, Ch. 3]) guarantees \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}} \cdot \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{s}}\vphantom{s}} > 0\). Such a step can be found along a descent direction when \(f\) cannot keep decreasing forever.










DefDefinition 44 (Limited-memory BFGS (L-BFGS))






Definition 44 (Limited-memory BFGS (L-BFGS)) Limited-memory BFGS (L-BFGS) [23, Ch. 7] is the quasi-Newton method that never forms \(\mathbf{H}^{(t)}\). It stores only the \(m\) most recent pairs \((\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{s}}\vphantom{s}}^{(j)}, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}^{(j)})\), with \(m\) small, such as \(5\) or \(20\), and obtains \(\mathbf{H}^{(t)} \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^{(t)})\) implicitly, through a few vector operations, as if the BFGS update for those \(m\) pairs were applied to a simple starting matrix, such as a multiple of \(\mathbf{I}_p\).










ExmExample 60 (L-BFGS applies the update without forming the matrix)






Example 60 (L-BFGS applies the update without forming the matrix) Continue Example 59 with \(m = 1\) stored pair \((\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{s}}\vphantom{s}}^{(0)}, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}^{(0)})\) and starting matrix \(\mathbf{I}_2\). Below, \(\mathbf{H}^+ \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}} f(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}^{(1)})\) is formed from vectors alone, starting from H0, then compared with the matrix product.

g1 <- grad(x1)
alpha <- rho * sum(s * g1)
q <- g1 - alpha * y
r <- drop(H0 %*% q)
beta <- rho * sum(y * r)
r <- r + s * (alpha - beta)
rbind(from_vectors = r, from_matrix = drop(H1 %*% g1))
#>                [,1]   [,2]
#> from_vectors 0.4375 -0.375
#> from_matrix  0.4375 -0.375

The two rows agree to within 5.6e-17, although the first never forms the matrix. BFGS stores a dense \(p \times p\) matrix and spends about \(p^2\) operations per iteration; L-BFGS stores \(2m\) vectors with \(p\) entries and spends about \(m p\) operations per iteration, so it remains usable when \(p\) is in the millions.

title: Optimization
text:
7 Further reading


Boyd and Vandenberghe [24] is the standard reference on convex optimization, covering convex sets, convex functions, convex optimization problems, duality, unconstrained minimization, and interior-point methods.

Nocedal and Wright [23] is a comprehensive reference on continuous numerical optimization, covering line search methods, trust-region methods, conjugate gradient methods, quasi-Newton methods, and nonlinear equations.

Hua Zhou’s course page for “UCLA Biostat 257 - Statistical Computing” (2025 Spring) has lectures on optimization, from root finding to constrained problems. Its source is on GitHub under the MIT License.

Hua Zhou’s lecture notes for “UCLA Biostat 216 - Mathematical Methods for Biostatistics” (2024 Fall)


Neural Networks is a YouTube playlist by Grant Sanderson (3Blue1Brown); its chapters on gradient descent and backpropagation calculus visually illustrate how gradients of multivariate cost functions are computed and used for optimization.

title: Relations
text:
RemarkRemark






Remark. A relation says which pairs of elements of a set are related. This page defines the properties that make a relation behave like equality, and the groups of elements that such a relation puts together.

title: Relations
text:
1 Properties of relations






DefDefinition 1 (Reflexive relation)






Definition 1 (Reflexive relation) Let \(\sim\) be a relation on a set \(S\). The relation \(\sim\) is reflexive [1] if \(a \sim a\) for every \(a \in S\).










ExmExample 1 (Reflexive and non-reflexive relations on the real numbers)






Example 1 (Reflexive and non-reflexive relations on the real numbers) On \(\mathbb{R}\), the relation \(=\) is reflexive, since \(a = a\) for every real number \(a\). The relation \(\le\) is also reflexive, since \(a \le a\) for every real number \(a\). The relation \(<\) is not reflexive, since \(2 < 2\) is false.










DefDefinition 2 (Symmetric relation)






Definition 2 (Symmetric relation) Let \(\sim\) be a relation on a set \(S\). The relation \(\sim\) is symmetric [2] if, for all \(a, b \in S\), \(a \sim b\) implies \(b \sim a\).










ExmExample 2 (Symmetric and non-symmetric relations on the real numbers)






Example 2 (Symmetric and non-symmetric relations on the real numbers) On \(\mathbb{R}\), the relation \(=\) is symmetric: whenever \(a = b\), also \(b = a\). The relation \(\le\) is not symmetric, since \(2 \le 5\) is true but \(5 \le 2\) is false.

title: Relations
text:
2 Equivalence relations






DefDefinition 3 (Equivalence relation)






Definition 3 (Equivalence relation) Let \(\sim\) be a relation on a set \(S\). The relation \(\sim\) is an equivalence relation [3] if it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.










ExmExample 3 (Integers with an even difference)






Example 3 (Integers with an even difference) On the integers, define the relation \(\sim\) by \(a \sim b\) when \(a - b\) is even. For example, \(7 \sim 3\), since \(7 - 3 = 4 = 2 \cdot 2\), but \(7 \not\sim 4\), since \(7 - 4 = 3\) is odd. The relation \(\sim\) is an equivalence relation.
Reflexive. For every integer \(a\), \(a - a = 0 = 2 \cdot 0\), so \(a \sim a\).
Symmetric. Suppose \(a \sim b\), so \(a - b = 2k\) for some integer \(k\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
b - a
&= -(a - b)
&& \text{(negate the difference)}
\\
&= -2k
&& \text{(} a - b = 2k \text{)}
\\
&= 2(-k),
&& \text{(factor out } 2 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
and \(-k\) is an integer, so \(b \sim a\).
Transitive. Suppose \(a \sim b\) and \(b \sim c\), so \(a - b = 2j\) and \(b - c = 2k\) for some integers \(j\) and \(k\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
a - c
&= (a - b) + (b - c)
&& \text{(the } b \text{ terms cancel)}
\\
&= 2j + 2k
&& \text{(} a - b = 2j \text{ and } b - c = 2k \text{)}
\\
&= 2(j + k),
&& \text{(distributive law)}
\end{aligned}
\]
and \(j + k\) is an integer, so \(a \sim c\).










DefDefinition 4 (Equivalence class)






Definition 4 (Equivalence class) Let \(\sim\) be an equivalence relation on a set \(S\), and let \(a \in S\). The equivalence class [4] of \(a\) is the set of elements of \(S\) related to \(a\):
\[
[a] \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathopen{}\left\{b \in S : b \sim a\right\}\mathclose{}}.
\]










ExmExample 4 (Equivalence classes of integers with an even difference)






Example 4 (Equivalence classes of integers with an even difference) Let \(\sim\) be the equivalence relation of Example 3 on the integers. The equivalence class \([0]\) holds the integers \(b\) with \(b - 0\) even, which are the even integers: \([0] = \mathopen{}\left\{\ldots, -4, -2, 0, 2, 4, \ldots\right\}\mathclose{}\). The class \([1]\) holds the integers \(b\) with \(b - 1\) even, which are the odd integers: \([1] = \mathopen{}\left\{\ldots, -3, -1, 1, 3, 5, \ldots\right\}\mathclose{}\). The class \([2]\) is the same set as \([0]\), since \(2 \sim 0\).

title: Sets
text:
RemarkRemark






Remark. Probability and statistics describe events, outcomes, and parameters as sets. This page collects the definitions of sets that the Morrison Lab’s probability and statistics notes build on. The Functions page defines functions between sets, and the Expressions and Algorithms page defines the expressions that write functions down and the algorithms that compute them.

title: Sets
text:
1 Sets






DefDefinition 1 (Set)






Definition 1 (Set) A set [1] is a collection of distinct objects, called its elements. We write \(a \in A\) when \(a\) is an element of the set \(A\), and \(a \notin A\) when it is not. Two sets are equal when they have exactly the same elements.










RemarkRemark 1 (Naive and formal set theory)






Remark 1 (Naive and formal set theory). Definition 1 is the informal (“naive”) notion of a set, which is all these notes need. Formal set theory states axioms for sets instead [1]. For example, the last sentence of Definition 1, that two sets are equal when they have exactly the same elements, is one of those axioms, the axiom of extensionality.










ExmExample 1 (Sets of die rolls)






Example 1 (Sets of die rolls) The possible results of rolling a six-sided die form the set \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\), with \(3 \in {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and \(7 \notin {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\). The sets \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and \({\mathopen{}\left\{3, 2, 1\right\}\mathclose{}}\) are equal, because they have the same elements; the order in which the elements are listed does not matter.










DefDefinition 2 (Set-builder notation)






Definition 2 (Set-builder notation) For a set \(A\) and a statement \(P(x)\) about an element \(x\), set-builder notation [2] \({\mathopen{}\left\{x \in A : P(x)\right\}\mathclose{}}\) denotes the set of elements \(x\) of \(A\) for which \(P(x)\) is true.










ExmExample 2 (Even die rolls in set-builder notation)






Example 2 (Even die rolls in set-builder notation) \({\mathopen{}\left\{x \in {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}} : x \text{ is even}\right\}\mathclose{}} = {\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\) is the set of even rolls, and \({\mathopen{}\left\{x \in \mathbb{R}: x > 0\right\}\mathclose{}}\) is the set of positive real numbers.










DefDefinition 3 (Subset)






Definition 3 (Subset) A set \(A\) is a subset [3] of a set \(B\), written \(A \subseteq B\), if every element of \(A\) is an element of \(B\).










ExmExample 3 (Even die rolls)






Example 3 (Even die rolls) The even die rolls form a subset of the possible rolls: \({\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}} \subseteq {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\), because each of \(2\), \(4\), and \(6\) is a possible roll. The set \({\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 7\right\}\mathclose{}}\) is not a subset of \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\), because \(7\) is not a possible roll.










LemTheorem 1 (Every set is a subset of itself)






Theorem 1 (Every set is a subset of itself) For every set \(A\), \(A \subseteq A\).










ProofProof






Proof. Every element of \(A\) is an element of \(A\), which is Definition 3 with \(B = A\).










DefDefinition 4 (Strict subset, proper subset)






Definition 4 (Strict subset, proper subset) A set \(A\) is a strict subset (also called a proper subset) of a set \(B\), written \(A \subsetneq B\), if \(A\) is a subset of \(B\) and \(A \neq B\).










RemarkRemark 2 (The symbol \(\subset\))






Remark 2 (The symbol \(\subset\)). Sources disagree about the symbol \(\subset\): some use it for “subset” (\(\subseteq\)), and others for “strict subset” (\(\subsetneq\)) [3]. For example, \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}} \subset {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}}\) is true in the first reading, because \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}} \subseteq {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}}\), and false in the second, because the two sets are equal. These notes avoid \(\subset\) and write \(\subseteq\) or \(\subsetneq\).










DefDefinition 5 (Superset)






Definition 5 (Superset) A set \(B\) is a superset of a set \(A\), written \(B \supseteq A\), if every element of \(A\) is an element of \(B\).










RemarkRemark 3 (Superset and subset)






Remark 3 (Superset and subset). \(B \supseteq A\) means the same thing as \(A \subseteq B\) (subset). For example, \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3\right\}\mathclose{}} \supseteq {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 3\right\}\mathclose{}}\), and \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 3\right\}\mathclose{}} \subseteq {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3\right\}\mathclose{}}\). But \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 3\right\}\mathclose{}}\) is not a superset of \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}}\), because \(2 \in {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and \(2 \notin {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 3\right\}\mathclose{}}\).










DefDefinition 6 (Strict superset)






Definition 6 (Strict superset) A set \(B\) is a strict superset of a set \(A\), written \(B \supsetneq A\), if \(B\) is a superset of \(A\) and \(B \neq A\).










RemarkRemark 4 (Strict superset and strict subset)






Remark 4 (Strict superset and strict subset). \(B \supsetneq A\) means the same thing as \(A \subsetneq B\) (strict subset). For example, \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3\right\}\mathclose{}} \supsetneq {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 3\right\}\mathclose{}}\), because \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3\right\}\mathclose{}}\) contains \(2\) and \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 3\right\}\mathclose{}}\) does not.










ExmExample 4 (Strict subsets and supersets of die rolls)






Example 4 (Strict subsets and supersets of die rolls) For the even rolls \(A = {\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and the possible rolls \(B = {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\):

\(A \subsetneq B\), because \(A \subseteq B\) (Example 3) and \(1 \in B\) but \(1 \notin A\), so \(A \neq B\);
\(B \supseteq A\) and \(B \supsetneq A\), for the same reasons;
\(B \subseteq B\), but \(B\) is not a strict subset of itself, because \(B = B\); likewise \(B \supseteq B\), but \(B\) is not a strict superset of itself, because \(B = B\).











DefDefinition 7 (Empty set)






Definition 7 (Empty set) The empty set [4], denoted \(\emptyset\), is the set that has no elements.










RemarkRemark 5 (Other notation for the empty set)






Remark 5 (Other notation for the empty set). Other sources write \({\mathopen{}\left\{\right\}\mathclose{}}\) for \(\emptyset\) [4]. Some sources call it the null set, but in measure theory a “null set” usually means a set of measure zero, which need not be empty. For example, the interval \([0, 0] = {\mathopen{}\left\{0\right\}\mathclose{}}\) has length \(0 - 0 = 0\), so it is a null set in that sense, but it is not empty, because \(0 \in {\mathopen{}\left\{0\right\}\mathclose{}}\).










ExmExample 5 (Impossible die rolls)






Example 5 (Impossible die rolls) No roll of a six-sided die is greater than 6, so \({\mathopen{}\left\{x \in {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}} : x > 6\right\}\mathclose{}} = \emptyset\).










DefDefinition 8 (Vacuous truth)






Definition 8 (Vacuous truth) A statement of the form “every element of \(A\) has property \(P\)” is vacuously true [5] when \(A\) is the empty set: \(A\) has no elements, so no element of \(A\) fails to have property \(P\).










ExmExample 6 (Every impossible die roll is even)






Example 6 (Every impossible die roll is even) The set of die rolls greater than 6 is \(\emptyset\) (Example 5). So “every die roll greater than 6 is even” is vacuously true, and so is “every die roll greater than 6 is odd”: there is no such roll to fail either statement.










LemTheorem 2 (There is only one empty set)






Theorem 2 (There is only one empty set) If \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) are sets with no elements, then \(E_1 = E_2\).










ProofProof






Proof. Neither set has any elements, so every element of \(E_1\) is an element of \(E_2\) and vice versa, vacuously. Sets with the same elements are equal (Definition 1).










LemTheorem 3 (The empty set is a subset of every set)






Theorem 3 (The empty set is a subset of every set) For every set \(A\), \(\emptyset \subseteq A\).










ProofProof






Proof. By Definition 3, \(\emptyset \subseteq A\) fails only if some element of \(\emptyset\) is not in \(A\). The empty set has no elements, so no such element exists.










DefDefinition 9 (Lower bound and upper bound)






Definition 9 (Lower bound and upper bound) For a subset \(S \subseteq \mathbb{R}\) of the real numbers, a real number \(a\) is a lower bound of \(S\) if \(a \le x\) for every \(x \in S\), and a real number \(b\) is an upper bound of \(S\) if \(x \le b\) for every \(x \in S\); each is a bound of \(S\).










DefDefinition 10 (Interval)






Definition 10 (Interval) An interval [6] is a subset of the real numbers that consists of all real numbers between two bounds \(a \le b\) (Definition 9), possibly including one or both bounds, or of all real numbers on one side of a single bound, or all of \(\mathbb{R}\). The bounds \(a\) and \(b\) that define the interval are its endpoints.










DefDefinition 11 (Closed interval)






Definition 11 (Closed interval) For real numbers \(a \le b\), the closed interval is the interval (Definition 10) \([a, b] \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathopen{}\left\{x \in \mathbb{R}: a \le x \le b\right\}\mathclose{}}\) that includes both bounds (Definition 9).










DefDefinition 12 (Open interval)






Definition 12 (Open interval) For real numbers \(a \le b\), the open interval is the interval (Definition 10) \((a, b) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathopen{}\left\{x \in \mathbb{R}: a < x < b\right\}\mathclose{}}\) that includes neither bound (Definition 9).










DefDefinition 13 (Half-open intervals)






Definition 13 (Half-open intervals) For real numbers \(a \le b\), the half-open intervals are the intervals (Definition 10) \([a, b) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathopen{}\left\{x \in \mathbb{R}: a \le x < b\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and \((a, b] \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathopen{}\left\{x \in \mathbb{R}: a < x \le b\right\}\mathclose{}}\) that include one bound (Definition 9) and not the other.










DefDefinition 14 (Unbounded intervals)






Definition 14 (Unbounded intervals) For real numbers \(a\) and \(b\), the unbounded intervals are the intervals (Definition 10) with at most one bound (Definition 9):

\([a, \infty) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathopen{}\left\{x \in \mathbb{R}: x \ge a\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and \((a, \infty) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathopen{}\left\{x \in \mathbb{R}: x > a\right\}\mathclose{}}\);
\((-\infty, b] \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathopen{}\left\{x \in \mathbb{R}: x \le b\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and \((-\infty, b) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathopen{}\left\{x \in \mathbb{R}: x < b\right\}\mathclose{}}\);
\((-\infty, \infty) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\mathbb{R}\).











RemarkRemark 6 (Brackets and parentheses in interval notation)






Remark 6 (Brackets and parentheses in interval notation). In the notation for an interval, a bracket marks an endpoint that belongs to the interval, while a parenthesis marks an endpoint that is excluded. The symbols \(\infty\), \(-\infty\) denote no real number, so they always get a parenthesis.










ExmExample 7 (Which numbers are in an interval)






Example 7 (Which numbers are in an interval)  

\(1 \in [1, 2]\), but \(1 \notin (1, 2)\).
\(2 \in (1, 2]\), but \(2 \notin [1, 2)\).
\(1.5\) is in all four of \([1, 2]\), \((1, 2)\), \([1, 2)\), and \((1, 2]\).
\([0, \infty)\) is the set of non-negative real numbers: \(0 \in [0, \infty)\) and \(1000 \in [0, \infty)\), but \(-0.1 \notin [0, \infty)\).











DefDefinition 15 (Collection of sets, family of sets)






Definition 15 (Collection of sets, family of sets) A collection of sets (also called a family of sets) [7] is a set whose elements are themselves sets.










ExmExample 8 (The collection of all subsets of a two-element set)






Example 8 (The collection of all subsets of a two-element set) The subsets of \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}}\) are \(\emptyset\), \({\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}}\), \({\mathopen{}\left\{2\right\}\mathclose{}}\), and \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}}\) (Theorem 3 and Theorem 1 give the first and the last), so the collection of all subsets of \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}}\) is
\[{\mathopen{}\left\{\emptyset, {\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}}, {\mathopen{}\left\{2\right\}\mathclose{}}, {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}}\right\}\mathclose{}}\]
It has four elements, each of them a set. The collection \({\mathopen{}\left\{\emptyset\right\}\mathclose{}}\) has one element, the empty set, so it is not equal to \(\emptyset\), which has none.










DefDefinition 16 (Label)






Definition 16 (Label) A label is a name or symbol attached to an object, so that we can refer to the object and tell it apart from other objects.










ExmExample 9 (Labels)






Example 9 (Labels) The numbers \(1, 2, 3\) can label three students in a class list. Then “student 2” refers to one particular student. The letters \(A\) and \(B\) can label two sets.










DefDefinition 17 (Index set)






Definition 17 (Index set) An index set [8] is a set whose elements are used as labels for objects. Each element of the index set is called an index.










ExmExample 10 (Index sets)






Example 10 (Index sets) The set \(\{1, \ldots, n\}\) labels the entries of a vector with \(n\) entries. The set of nonnegative real numbers can label moments in time.










DefDefinition 18 (Indexed family)






Definition 18 (Indexed family) An indexed family [9] is a collection of objects, one for each element of a given index set. The object for the index \(i\) is written \(a_i\).










ExmExample 11 (Indexed families)






Example 11 (Indexed families) The entries \(x_1, \ldots, x_n\) of a vector are an indexed family of numbers, with index set \(\{1, \ldots, n\}\). The functions \(f_\theta\), one for each parameter value \(\theta\) in a parameter set, are an indexed family of functions.

title: Sets
text:
2 Combining sets






DefDefinition 19 (Union)






Definition 19 (Union) The union [10] of sets \(A\) and \(B\), written \(A \cup B\), is the set of elements that are in \(A\), in \(B\), or in both:
\[A \cup B \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathopen{}\left\{x : x \in A \text{ or } x \in B\right\}\mathclose{}}\]










DefDefinition 20 (Union of a family of sets)






Definition 20 (Union of a family of sets) Let \(I\) be a set of indices, such as \(\mathopen{}\left\{1, \ldots, n\right\}\mathclose{}\) or \(\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, \ldots\right\}\mathclose{}\), and let \(A_i\) be a set for each \(i \in I\). The union of the sets \(A_i\), written \(\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i\), is the set of elements that are in at least one \(A_i\). For \(I = \mathopen{}\left\{1, \ldots, n\right\}\mathclose{}\), it is also written \(\bigcup_{i=1}^{n} A_i\) or \(A_1 \cup \cdots \cup A_n\), and for \(I = \mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, \ldots\right\}\mathclose{}\), it is written \(\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i\).










DefDefinition 21 (Intersection)






Definition 21 (Intersection) The intersection [11] of sets \(A\) and \(B\), written \(A \cap B\), is the set of elements that are in both \(A\) and \(B\):
\[A \cap B \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathopen{}\left\{x : x \in A \text{ and } x \in B\right\}\mathclose{}}\]










DefDefinition 22 (Intersection of a family of sets)






Definition 22 (Intersection of a family of sets) Let \(I\) be a nonempty set of indices, such as \(\mathopen{}\left\{1, \ldots, n\right\}\mathclose{}\) or \(\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, \ldots\right\}\mathclose{}\), and let \(A_i\) be a set for each \(i \in I\). The intersection of the sets \(A_i\), written \(\bigcap_{i \in I} A_i\), is the set of elements that are in every \(A_i\). For \(I = \mathopen{}\left\{1, \ldots, n\right\}\mathclose{}\), it is also written \(\bigcap_{i=1}^{n} A_i\) or \(A_1 \cap \cdots \cap A_n\), and for \(I = \mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, \ldots\right\}\mathclose{}\), it is written \(\bigcap_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i\).










DefDefinition 23 (Set difference)






Definition 23 (Set difference) The set difference [12] of sets \(A\) and \(B\), written \(A \setminus B\), is the set of elements of \(A\) that are not in \(B\):
\[A \setminus B \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathopen{}\left\{x \in A : x \notin B\right\}\mathclose{}}\]










DefDefinition 24 (Complement)






Definition 24 (Complement) Let \(A\) be a subset of a set \(S\). The complement [12] of \(A\) in \(S\) is the set difference (Definition 23) \(S \setminus A\): the elements of \(S\) that are not in \(A\). When the set \(S\) is clear from context, the complement of \(A\) is written \(A^c\):
\[A^c \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}S \setminus A = {\mathopen{}\left\{x \in S : x \notin A\right\}\mathclose{}}\]










ExmExample 12 (Complements of sets of die rolls)






Example 12 (Complements of sets of die rolls) Let \(S = {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\) be the possible rolls of a die.

The complement of the even rolls \(A = {\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\) is \(A^c = {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 3, 5\right\}\mathclose{}}\), the odd rolls.
The complement of \(S\) itself is \(S^c = \emptyset\), and the complement of \(\emptyset\) is \(\emptyset^c = S\).

The complement depends on \(S\): in \(S = {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\), the complement of \({\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\) is \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 3, 5\right\}\mathclose{}}\), but in \(S = {\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6, 8\right\}\mathclose{}}\), it is \({\mathopen{}\left\{8\right\}\mathclose{}}\).










ExmExample 13 (Combining sets of die rolls)






Example 13 (Combining sets of die rolls) Let \(A = {\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\) (the even rolls) and \(B = {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3\right\}\mathclose{}}\) (the rolls of at most 3). Then:

\(A \cup B = {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\), the rolls that are even or at most 3;
\(A \cap B = {\mathopen{}\left\{2\right\}\mathclose{}}\), the only roll that is both;
\(A \setminus B = {\mathopen{}\left\{4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\), the even rolls greater than 3;
\({\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}} \cap {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 3, 5\right\}\mathclose{}} = \emptyset\): no roll is both even and odd.











ExmExample 14 (Unions and intersections of many sets)






Example 14 (Unions and intersections of many sets)  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\bigcup_{i=1}^{3} {\mathopen{}\left\{i, i + 1\right\}\mathclose{}} &= {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}} \cup {\mathopen{}\left\{2, 3\right\}\mathclose{}} \cup {\mathopen{}\left\{3, 4\right\}\mathclose{}} \\
&= {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4\right\}\mathclose{}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
\(\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} {\mathopen{}\left\{i\right\}\mathclose{}} = \mathbb{N}\): each natural number \(n\) is in the set \({\mathopen{}\left\{n\right\}\mathclose{}}\), and each set \({\mathopen{}\left\{i\right\}\mathclose{}}\) contains only the natural number \(i\).
\(\bigcap_{i=1}^{\infty} [0, 1/i] = {\mathopen{}\left\{0\right\}\mathclose{}}\): \(0\) is in every interval \([0, 1/i]\); a number \(x > 0\) is not in \([0, 1/i]\) once \(i > 1/x\); and a number \(x < 0\) is in none of them.











LemTheorem 4 (De Morgan’s laws)






Theorem 4 (De Morgan’s laws) Let \(S\) be a set, let \(I\) be a nonempty set of indices, and let \(A_i\) be a subset of \(S\) for each \(i \in I\). Then the complement of a union is the intersection of the complements, [13] and the complement of an intersection is the union of the complements:
\[
\begin{aligned}
S \setminus \bigcup_{i \in I} A_i &= \bigcap_{i \in I} (S \setminus A_i) \\
S \setminus \bigcap_{i \in I} A_i &= \bigcup_{i \in I} (S \setminus A_i)
\end{aligned}
\]
With the complement notation of Definition 24, these read \(\mathopen{}\left(\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i\right)\mathclose{}^c = \bigcap_{i \in I} A_i^c\) and \(\mathopen{}\left(\bigcap_{i \in I} A_i\right)\mathclose{}^c = \bigcup_{i \in I} A_i^c\).










ProofProof






Proof. Two sets are equal when they have the same elements (Definition 1), so it is enough to show that an element \(x\) is in the left-hand side if and only if (\(\iff\)) it is in the right-hand side. For the first law:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x \in S \setminus \bigcup_{i \in I} A_i
&\iff x \in S \text{ and } x \notin \bigcup_{i \in I} A_i
&& \text{(}\href{#def-set-difference}{\text{Definition~23}}\text{)} \\
&\iff x \in S \text{ and } x \notin A_i \text{ for every } i \in I
&& \text{(}\href{#def-union}{\text{Definition~19}}\text{)} \\
&\iff x \in S \setminus A_i \text{ for every } i \in I
&& \text{(}\href{#def-set-difference}{\text{Definition~23}}\text{)} \\
&\iff x \in \bigcap_{i \in I} (S \setminus A_i)
&& \text{(}\href{#def-intersection}{\text{Definition~21}}\text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
For the second law:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x \in S \setminus \bigcap_{i \in I} A_i
&\iff x \in S \text{ and } x \notin \bigcap_{i \in I} A_i
&& \text{(}\href{#def-set-difference}{\text{Definition~23}}\text{)} \\
&\iff x \in S \text{ and } x \notin A_i \text{ for some } i \in I
&& \text{(}\href{#def-intersection}{\text{Definition~21}}\text{)} \\
&\iff x \in S \setminus A_i \text{ for some } i \in I
&& \text{(}\href{#def-set-difference}{\text{Definition~23}}\text{)} \\
&\iff x \in \bigcup_{i \in I} (S \setminus A_i)
&& \text{(}\href{#def-union}{\text{Definition~19}}\text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExmExample 15 (De Morgan’s laws for die rolls)






Example 15 (De Morgan’s laws for die rolls) In \(S = {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\), let \(A = {\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and \(B = {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3\right\}\mathclose{}}\), as in Example 13, so \(A^c = {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 3, 5\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and \(B^c = {\mathopen{}\left\{4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\).

\[
\begin{aligned}
(A \cup B)^c &= {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}^c \\
&= {\mathopen{}\left\{5\right\}\mathclose{}},
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
A^c \cap B^c &= {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 3, 5\right\}\mathclose{}} \cap {\mathopen{}\left\{4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}} \\
&= {\mathopen{}\left\{5\right\}\mathclose{}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
(A \cap B)^c &= {\mathopen{}\left\{2\right\}\mathclose{}}^c \\
&= {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}},
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
A^c \cup B^c &= {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 3, 5\right\}\mathclose{}} \cup {\mathopen{}\left\{4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}} \\
&= {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}.
\end{aligned}
\]











DefDefinition 25 (Disjoint sets)






Definition 25 (Disjoint sets) Two sets \(A\) and \(B\) are disjoint if their intersection is the empty set:
\[A \cap B = \emptyset\]










ExmExample 16 (Two disjoint sets of die rolls)






Example 16 (Two disjoint sets of die rolls) For the die rolls \(D = {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\) (sets of die rolls), the sets \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and \({\mathopen{}\left\{5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\) are disjoint: no roll is in both. The sets \({\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}}\) are not, because \(2\) is in both.










DefDefinition 26 (Pairwise disjoint sets, mutually disjoint sets)






Definition 26 (Pairwise disjoint sets, mutually disjoint sets) Some sets \(A_1, A_2, \ldots\) (a list that may end or go on without end) are pairwise disjoint [14] (also called mutually disjoint) when every two of them are disjoint:
\[A_i \cap A_j = \emptyset \quad \text{for all } i \neq j\]










ExmExample 17 (Low, middle and high die rolls)






Example 17 (Low, middle and high die rolls) For the die rolls \(D = {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\) (sets of die rolls), the sets \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}}\), \({\mathopen{}\left\{3, 4\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and \({\mathopen{}\left\{5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\) are pairwise disjoint: no roll is in more than one of them. The sets \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}}\), \({\mathopen{}\left\{3, 4\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and \({\mathopen{}\left\{2, 5\right\}\mathclose{}}\) are not, because \(2\) is in both the first and the third.










DefDefinition 27 (Ordered pair)






Definition 27 (Ordered pair) An ordered pair [15] \((a, b)\) is a pair of objects listed in order, with \(a\) first and \(b\) second; two ordered pairs are equal, \((a, b) = (c, d)\), when \(a = c\) and \(b = d\).










DefDefinition 28 (Cartesian product)






Definition 28 (Cartesian product) The Cartesian product [16] of sets \(A\) and \(B\), written \(A \times B\), is the set of ordered pairs whose first entry is in \(A\) and whose second entry is in \(B\):
\[A \times B \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathopen{}\left\{(a, b) : a \in A \text{ and } b \in B\right\}\mathclose{}}\]










ExmExample 18 (Cartesian products)






Example 18 (Cartesian products)  

\({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}} \times {\mathopen{}\left\{5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}} = {\mathopen{}\left\{(1, 5), (1, 6), (2, 5), (2, 6)\right\}\mathclose{}}\). The pair \((5, 1)\) is not in it, because its first entry, \(5\), is not in \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}}\); so \((1, 5) \ne (5, 1)\).
The results of rolling a die twice form \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, \ldots, 6\right\}\mathclose{}} \times {\mathopen{}\left\{1, \ldots, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\), which has \(6 \cdot 6 = 36\) elements, such as \((3, 5)\): a 3 on the first roll and a 5 on the second.
\([0, 2] \times [0, 3]\) is the set of points \((x, y)\) in the plane with \(0 \le x \le 2\) and \(0 \le y \le 3\): a rectangle of width \(2\) and height \(3\).

3 Extended non-negative real numbers






DefDefinition 29 (Extended non-negative real numbers)






Definition 29 (Extended non-negative real numbers) The extended non-negative real numbers, written \([0, \infty]\), are the non-negative real numbers together with an extra element \(\infty\) that is greater than every real number:
\[[0, \infty] \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}[0, \infty) \cup {\mathopen{}\left\{\infty\right\}\mathclose{}}\]
Addition extends to \([0, \infty]\) by setting
\[
\begin{aligned}
x + \infty &= \infty + x \\
&= \infty
\end{aligned}
\]
for every \(x \in [0, \infty]\).










RemarkRemark 7 (Arithmetic with \(\infty\))






Remark 7 (Arithmetic with \(\infty\)). \(\infty\) is not a real number, so some real-number arithmetic does not extend to it: \(\infty - \infty\) is left undefined, and \(\infty + 1 = \infty + 2\) does not imply \(1 = 2\). Measure theory uses \([0, \infty]\) because the size of a set, such as the length of the whole real line, can be infinite [17].










ExmExample 19 (Adding with \(\infty\))






Example 19 (Adding with \(\infty\)) In \([0, \infty]\), \(2 + 3 = 5\) as usual, while \(2 + \infty = \infty\) and \(\infty + \infty = \infty\).

4 Further reading
These books and articles treat sets and the logic behind them in more depth.

Devlin [18] is an undergraduate introduction to axiomatic set theory. It covers the axioms of set theory, ordinals, and cardinals, which go well beyond the countable sets and functions in these notes.
Halmos [19] is a short, informal treatment of the same axioms, covering relations, functions, families of sets, and cardinal numbers.
Enderton [20] is a standard introduction to mathematical logic. Its first chapter collects the facts about sets, relations, and functions that the later chapters use.
Barker-Plummer et al. [21] teaches propositional and first-order logic, the language behind statements such as “for every set \(A\) there exists…”.
